parts.name: The Story of a Certain Little Family

chapters.title: Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov
chapters.intro: Background on marriage, money and family in 19th-century Russia, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Morally corrupt; behaving in a wicked or degraded way.
Lacking self-control, especially with drink, sex and money; living recklessly.
A person devoted to luxury and physical pleasures.
Someone who acts like a clown, often to amuse people or win attention.
A person who lives off other people’s hospitality or money without giving anything back.
A sudden whim; an unpredictable change of mind or mood.
Eager to please; willing to go along with what others want.
Someone who roams about raiding and plundering.
Given rights or freedom. Also used loosely to mean “freed from restrictions.”
The interval between two acts of a play. By extension, any break between episodes.
Lack of worldly experience or suspicion; innocence.
A small, bare attic room, typically lived in by poor people.
A serious infectious disease spread by lice, common in crowded, poor conditions.
French for “an accomplished fact”: something already done that others must simply accept.
Running away together to marry, usually without family approval.
Money or property a bride’s family gives at marriage.

A Russian full name has three parts: a first name, a patronymic made from the father’s first name, and a surname. Ivan Petrovich is Ivan, son of Pyotr; Anna Petrovna is Anna, daughter of Pyotr. First name plus patronymic is the polite way to address someone. Affectionate short forms are common (Aleksandr becomes Sasha, Yekaterina becomes Katya), and English spellings of the same name vary.

In 19th-century Russia the hereditary nobility owned estates worked by serfs, and many lived in provincial towns rather than the capital. Wealth was counted in land and serfs, and ready cash was often scarcer than it looked.

In 19th-century Europe a marriage was often a financial arrangement, with the bride’s family supplying a dowry. Russian law generally let a married woman keep control of her own property, so a husband could not simply take it.

Educated Russians of the 1830s and 1840s were shaped by European Romanticism, which prized strong feeling, individual freedom and rebellion, and encouraged people to model their lives on literature. The generation of the 1860s was more skeptical, scientific and politically radical. Arguments over women’s education and independence, called the “woman question,” grew in this period.
Church seminaries trained the sons of clergy. Many seminarians were poor, and some left the path to the priesthood to become teachers, writers or radicals.
The Russian currency. A few tens of thousands of roubles was a substantial fortune for a provincial landowner.
Russia’s capital from 1703 to 1918 and the center of government, publishing and fashionable ideas.
“Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace”

From Luke 2:29. It is the prayer of an old man who had been promised he would not die before seeing a long-awaited child. It is sung in evening church services and is used to mean “now I can die content.”
A young woman in Shakespeare’s Hamlet who goes mad with grief and drowns. She became one of the most painted and imitated figures of the 19th century, a symbol of doomed romantic femininity.

quiz.q: How does the narrator describe Fyodor Pavlovich’s character?
o: A devout man whose fortune was ruined by bad luck
A stern, orderly landlord who ran his estate with rigour
A depraved, muddled man who was shrewd about property
A simple-minded man who never grasped how money worked
quiz.e: Empty, depraved and muddle-headed, yet sharp about money. He started with almost nothing and left about a hundred thousand roubles.

quiz.q: What does the narrator reveal about Fyodor’s fate in the opening paragraph?
o: He would lose his whole fortune after a ruinous lawsuit with the monks
He would enter a monastery late in life as a repentant sinner
He would be exiled to Siberia after a scandal over a woman
He met a tragic, suspicious-sounding death thirteen years earlier
quiz.e: The narrator promises to report the death “in its proper context.” The ending is announced before the characters are introduced.

quiz.q: How many times did Fyodor marry, and which sons came from which marriage?
o: Once only; Dmitry, Ivan and Aleksey were all by that single wife
Twice: Dmitry by the first wife, Ivan and Aleksey by the second
Twice: Dmitry and Ivan by the first wife, Aleksey by the second
Three times, with one son born to each of the three wives
quiz.e: Adelaida Ivanovna Miusova bore Dmitry (Mitya). Ivan and Aleksey came from the second marriage, covered in the next chapters.

quiz.q: How does the narrator explain why Adelaida Ivanovna married Fyodor?
o: She had fallen deeply in love with his charm and wit
Her family pressed her to accept the first suitor who offered after a scandal
Romantic notions of independence, imagining him bolder than he was
She needed his money to pay off her father’s old debts
quiz.e: The narrator guesses at protest against family and society, the appeal of an elopement, and a brief illusion that Fyodor was daring. He says love was absent on both sides.

quiz.q: What did Fyodor do with Adelaida’s money?
o: He seized her 25,000 roubles at once and tried for her estate as well
He invested it carefully on behalf of them both in timber and land
He gave most of it to the monastery for masses for her family
He left it untouched, and she kept all of it under her own control
quiz.e: The money was gone “in one fell swoop.” Her family blocked the transfer of the estate and the town house.

quiz.q: How did the marriage end?
o: She ran off with a poor seminarian, leaving Mitya, and later died in St Petersburg
Fyodor threw her out after catching her with a lodger in the house one winter
They divorced by mutual agreement and she returned to her family
She entered a convent in Moscow, leaving three-year-old Mitya behind
quiz.e: She died suddenly in a garret. Accounts differ: typhus according to some, hunger according to others.

quiz.q: How did Fyodor behave after Adelaida left?
o: He turned the house into a den of debauchery and complained of her to all
He went into deep mourning and withdrew from all society for several years
He set off at once for St Petersburg to bring her home by force
He sold the house and moved to Moscow to start a new life
quiz.e: The mockers joked that he looked as if he had been promoted. The narrator wonders whether the naivety was real.

quiz.q: How did Fyodor react to the news of Adelaida’s death?
o: Reports differ: he either exulted or wept, perhaps both
He travelled to St Petersburg and arranged a fitting funeral
He felt nothing at all and carried on as before, uninterested
He fell silent, stopped drinking and shut himself in the house
quiz.e: He was drunk when he heard. One version has him shouting a line from Luke in joy, another has him sobbing like a child.

chapters.title: He Gets the First Son Off His Hands
chapters.intro: Background on serfdom, guardianship, Western-minded liberals and 19th-century politics, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A traditional Russian peasant log house.
A person legally appointed to look after a child, and the child’s property, when the parents cannot.
Legal responsibility for caring for someone, especially a child.
French for “a stay” in a place.
In Russia and much of Europe, a secondary school that prepares students for university.
Wanderings or travels from place to place.
Wastefully extravagant with money. A “prodigal son” squanders what he is given.
Excessive indulgence in drinking, sex and other pleasures.
A sum of money sent to someone.
In the 19th-century sense: favoring individual freedom, constitutional government and reform, and often opposed to the power of church and monarchy.
“Removed” counts generations between relatives. Your first cousin’s child is your first cousin once removed; “twice removed” means two generations apart.
A hastily built barrier, often of furniture and paving stones, used in street fighting.

Until 1861 Russian landowners owned serfs, peasants legally tied to the land and to their owner. Wealth was counted in “souls,” meaning adult male serfs, so an owner of a thousand souls was very rich. Alexander II freed the serfs in 1861, and the old order slowly unraveled.

Children who lost their parents were often placed with relatives or appointed guardians, who managed any property until the child came of age. The system depended on the guardian’s honesty and attention, and could be neglected or abused.

Young noblemen often served as army officers. Russia fought a long war to conquer the Caucasus mountains (roughly 1817 to 1864), and a posting there was a path to advancement or, for troublemakers, a kind of exile. Duelling was illegal but common, and officers who fought duels were often punished by demotion to the ranks.
Boys of the gentry typically attended a gymnasium and then university or a military academy. Many dropped out.

A label for the idealistic, Westernizing liberals of the 1840s. Many admired Europe, lived there for years, were at ease in French, and were skeptical of the Orthodox Church. Their politics was often more talk than action.

In February 1848 Parisians rose up, built barricades and overthrew King Louis-Philippe, setting up the Second Republic. Revolutions spread across Europe that year, and the events became a legendary experience for liberals and radicals.

Pierre-Joseph Proudhon (1809–65) was a French socialist and anarchist, best known for the line “property is theft.” Mikhail Bakunin (1814–76) was a Russian revolutionary and a leading anarchist. Having met them was a mark of radical credentials.

The view that churches and clergy should have less power and property. In 19th-century France, “clericals” were supporters of the Church and anticlericals their opponents. Russian liberals borrowed the terms.
Monasteries often owned land, forests and fisheries, so legal disputes with neighboring landowners were common.

quiz.q: Why did Fyodor Pavlovich abandon three-year-old Mitya?
o: Bitter resentment toward Adelaida Ivanovna for leaving him
He simply forgot him; the boy slipped out of his mind
He could not afford to raise a child on his income
He suspected the boy was not really his own son
quiz.e: Not out of ill-feeling or an injured husband’s grudge. The narrator says he altogether forgot the child existed.

quiz.q: Who first took care of Mitya, and where did the boy live?
o: Miusov himself, at his estate beside the monastery
Yefim Petrovich Polyonov, in his house in the town
Grigory the manservant, in an izba in the yard
His grandmother, in her house in Moscow
quiz.e: Grigory, the faithful servant, kept Mitya with him in an izba in the yard for almost a year. Without him no one would have changed the boy’s shirt.

quiz.q: Why did Mitya’s mother’s relatives not take him in at first?
o: Fyodor Pavlovich threatened to go to law if any of them came near
They blamed the boy for his mother’s flight and wanted nothing to do with him
No one in the family knew the boy existed until years later
The grandfather was dead, the grandmother ill in Moscow, the sisters already married
quiz.e: Old Miusov Senior had died, his widow had moved to Moscow and fallen ill, and the daughters had their own households.

quiz.q: Pyotr Aleksandrovich Miusov returned to Russia from which city, and what event did he love to recall?
o: Paris, the February Revolution of 1848, which he had witnessed
Paris, the Commune of 1871, which he had watched in person
St Petersburg, the Decembrist uprising of 1825, which he had seen
Moscow, the emancipation of the serfs in 1861, which he cheered
quiz.e: He was a ’forties-and-’fifties liberal who liked to hint that he had nearly been on the barricades in Paris in 1848.

quiz.q: What long-running dispute did Miusov have with the local monastery?
o: A will contested by his wife’s family over land
A lawsuit over fishing or wood-felling rights
A quarrel over the monastery’s serfs being conscripted
A dispute over who owned the monastery’s great bell
quiz.e: The narrator is unsure which right was at stake. Miusov saw suing the “clericals” as his enlightened civic duty.

quiz.q: When Miusov raised the subject of Mitya, how did Fyodor Pavlovich react?
o: He flew into a rage and swore he would never pay for the boy
He burst into tears and begged Miusov to bring Mitya to him that very week
He couldn’t think which child was meant and was surprised he had a son
He demanded money from Miusov for the boy’s past upkeep
quiz.e: The narrator adds that Fyodor liked suddenly playing unexpected roles, often to his own detriment.

quiz.q: After Miusov became Mitya’s guardian, where did Mitya grow up?
o: Passed from one relative to another, changing homes at least four times
In Miusov’s own household in Paris, under a French tutor and a strict governess
At a boarding school in Moscow paid for by Miusov for the sons of gentry
Back in his father’s house, living in the izba with Grigory
quiz.e: Miusov left for Paris and forgot the boy. Mitya went to an aunt in Moscow, then her married daughter, then at least one more home.

quiz.q: What set Mitya apart from his two half-brothers as they grew up?
o: He alone remained devoted to the Church and its ceremonies
He alone was left an allowance by the general’s widow in her will
He alone went on to study at a university in Moscow
He alone grew up believing he had a fortune and would be independent of him
quiz.e: That mistaken belief is what Fyodor Pavlovich later exploited.

quiz.q: Which sequence describes Mitya’s early life?
o: University, then civil service, then exile to Siberia after a duel
Gymnasium, military school, then the Caucasus, with a duel and demotion
Monastery school, then the army, then a gymnasium in Moscow
Gymnasium, then the Caucasus, then a military academy, rising steadily there
quiz.e: A disorderly youth, with plenty of extravagance and debt along the way.

quiz.q: What did Mitya discover when he returned about four years after his first visit?
o: His father had secretly sold the estate to Miusov and kept the money
A new will had left everything to the monastery and cut him out
He had already been paid his inheritance in full and might owe his father
His inheritance had doubled through careful interest and he was now quite rich
quiz.e: Fyodor had kept him quiet with small handouts and drawn up deals that left him no claim. Mitya was horror-struck and suspected fraud.

chapters.title: A Second Marriage and Second Children
chapters.intro: Background on Russian clergy, church courts, the press and provincial society, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A person who gives money or help to another, often to support a child or a cause.
A member of the clergy ranking below a priest.
A loud, domineering woman. Usually an insult.
To repay or reward someone for effort, loss or suffering.
Someone who serves a more powerful person and owes loyalty to them.
A small share of money or goods handed out, often as charity.
An old small coin. “Not a groat” means not a penny.
A teacher, often one who is strict or pedantic.
A lock of hair growing over the forehead.
A poor, ragged child, especially one left to roam.
French for “pen name”: a name a writer uses instead of their own.
A comedy full of absurd situations. Also any pointless or ridiculous event.
Quiet, gentle and unwilling to stand up for oneself.
Overwhelming, uncontrolled emotion. Historically a catch-all medical label for nervous disorders, applied mostly to women.

Russian parish priests and deacons formed a hereditary social estate. They were allowed to marry, were often poor, and sent their sons to seminaries. Monks, who took vows of celibacy, were a separate group.
An elected leader of the local nobility in a district or province. It was an honored, mostly unpaid office, and its holders were expected to be respectable and public-spirited.
A well-off widow of rank held real social power and often took poor relatives or orphan girls into her household, where they were expected to be grateful.

Peasant women in rural Russia who shrieked, barked or cried out during church services were believed to be possessed by demons. Doctors later understood many as sufferers of hysteria brought on by hardship, abuse or overwork.
After the reforms of the 1860s, newspapers and journals multiplied. Poor students earned a living by tutoring, translating, copying and writing short pieces, often under pen names.
In the 1860s natural science carried the prestige of progress. A small inheritance or savings could fund study or travel in Europe.

Since Peter the Great, the Russian Church was governed by a state-supervised Holy Synod instead of a patriarch (the patriarchate returned in 1917). The Church ran its own courts for matters such as marriage and clergy discipline. Reforms in 1864 created secular, public, jury-based courts, which raised the question of where Church authority should end.
In Orthodox culture people routinely call on God’s reward or repayment (“God will repay you”) when they cannot act against a wrong themselves.

quiz.q: Who was Sofya Ivanovna, Fyodor’s second wife?
o: The daughter of a wealthy merchant who had brought a large dowry to the match
An orphaned deacon’s daughter raised in the house of a general’s widow
A noble heiress from Fyodor’s own province, with a small estate
A governess from St Petersburg who had been left penniless
quiz.e: Sixteen at the marriage, “meek” and without family. Fyodor proposed an elopement, as in his first marriage.

quiz.q: Why did Fyodor marry her even though there was no dowry?
o: He hoped a stepmother would give little Mitya better care
He wanted to please the general’s widow and win her favour
He was captivated by her beauty and her meek, innocent look
Her relatives pressed him into the match with a threat of scandal
quiz.e: The narrator says it may have been simple lust. Fyodor himself said her innocent eyes “slashed my soul like a razor.”

quiz.q: What part did Grigory play in the second marriage?
o: He sided with Sofya, quarreled with Fyodor, and drove the women from an orgy
He left the household in protest and returned only after her death in the autumn
He reported Fyodor’s conduct to the general’s widow in Moscow
He took Fyodor’s side against Sofya and helped keep her confined
quiz.e: Sofya, intimidated since childhood, fell ill with the hysterical “wailer” disorder. She bore two sons, Ivan and Aleksey.

quiz.q: What did the general’s widow do when she arrived, three months after Sofya’s death?
o: She paid Fyodor a large sum to be allowed to raise both boys
She slapped Fyodor, tugged his forelock, and took both boys away in her carriage
She called a family council and made Fyodor sign a deed of guardianship at once
She quietly reconciled with Fyodor and left money for the boys’ keep
quiz.e: Fyodor decided afterward the arrangement suited him and drove around town telling people about the slaps.

quiz.q: Who really saw to the boys’ upbringing after the widow died?
o: Fyodor Pavlovich, who finally settled down and took the boys back into his house
Pyotr Miusov, who took an interest in them on his return from Paris
Her heir Yefim Petrovich Polyonov, who kept their 1,000 roubles each intact
Grigory the manservant, who followed the boys and raised them himself
quiz.e: Polyonov was the marshal of nobility and a decent man. The narrator asks readers to note that he grew especially fond of Aleksey, who lived in his household.

quiz.q: How did Ivan support himself in his first years at university?
o: A monthly allowance sent by Fyodor Pavlovich from his rents
A scholarship from the monastery that had taken an interest in him as a youth
Work as a copying clerk in a government office in Moscow
Lessons at twenty-five copecks an hour and items signed “Eyewitness”
quiz.e: He later wrote book reviews and became known in literary circles. He never wrote to his father.

quiz.q: What was notable about Ivan’s newspaper article?
o: It dealt with the Ecclesiastical Court and pleased both churchmen and atheists alike
It savagely attacked the monastery and the Elders, and was banned
It praised Fyodor Pavlovich’s management of his estate and household
It mocked the monks and the Elders and was condemned by the Synod as blasphemous
quiz.e: The subject was surprising because his degree was in natural science. The tone and conclusion made readers unsure where he stood.

quiz.q: What is puzzling about Ivan’s return to his father’s house?
o: He came to claim an inheritance and sued Fyodor over it at once
He lived on good terms with his neglectful father and mediated for Dmitry
He came to join the monastery where Alyosha was a novice under the Elder Zosima
He came to bring Alyosha home to Moscow at the widow’s request
quiz.e: Fyodor feared his sons might ask him for money, yet got on well with Ivan and sometimes obeyed him. Dmitry had started a legal action against his father.

chapters.title: The Third Son Alyosha
chapters.intro: Background on monastic life, icons, holy fools and ideas about hell, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A person who has entered a religious community on trial, before taking permanent vows.
A long, close-fitting robe worn by clergy and monks.
In Orthodox Christianity, a person who deliberately acts foolish or shocking, giving up comfort and convention, as a form of devotion (Russian: yurodivy).
A person who seeks direct, personal experience of the divine.
The look of a person’s face, or the supposed art of reading character from it.
Sentimental in a tearful, self-pitying way, often from drink.
Pure; abstaining from sex or from anything improper.
Trying to win favor, often insincerely.
Money, especially when seen as sordid (“filthy lucre”).
A person who is innocent or lacks worldly wisdom.
People of the same age or era.
A member of the aristocracy, especially in ancient Rome.
A state of moral or cultural decline marked by self-indulgence.
School culture could be rough. Teasing about sex and “manliness” was common, and a boy who refused to join in could be bullied or sometimes admired.

A Black Sea port city founded in 1794. It grew fast as a center of the grain trade, with a diverse population that included a large Jewish community. It lay inside the Pale of Settlement, the region where Jews were permitted to live in the Russian Empire.
Monasteries accepted gifts and donations, and new entrants sometimes brought a contribution. Wealthy people gave money so that their names would be remembered in prayer.
Convents and women’s communities existed across Russia. They were also a target of crude jokes.
Expect period prejudice, including antisemitic remarks, from some characters. These reflect the characters and the era’s attitudes.
Painted images of Christ, Mary and the saints, treated as windows to the holy. Homes kept them in a corner, often with a small lamp kept burning before them.
The Orthodox title for Mary (Greek: Theotokos, “God-bearer”). Mothers have long prayed to her for their children.
A newcomer is first a novice, in simple dress, and later may take vows and become a monk. A novice can leave. Young men normally sought a parent’s blessing.
Orthodox memorial services ask for the repose of a dead person’s soul. People donate to monasteries to have names remembered in prayer.
A tradition going back to Byzantium and well established in Russia. Holy fools were revered and feared for saying hard truths no one else dared to. Moscow’s St Basil’s Cathedral is named for one.
Medieval and folk art, including Last Judgment icons, showed devils with hooks and pitchforks dragging sinners to torment.

French Enlightenment writer (1694–1778) and sharp critic of the Church. His line “If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him” is often quoted, though in its original context it defends belief as useful to society.
A follower of the Protestant tradition begun by Martin Luther. In Russian conversation, Protestantism was often seen as the plain, rational, “Western” form of Christianity.
Writers use the late Roman Empire as a symbol of luxury, excess and decline.

quiz.q: How does the narrator describe Alyosha?
o: A fanatic and a mystic who had seen visions from childhood
An “early lover of mankind,” neither a mystic nor a fanatic
A frail, sickly dreamer who lived entirely in his own head
A cynic who joined the monastery only to find shelter
quiz.e: He was drawn to the monastery road because it impressed him as a way out of hatred toward love, and because he met Father Zosima.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha remember of his mother?
o: Her reading aloud to him at her knee in the evenings while the lamp burned low
Her funeral, with the coffin carried out past him into the churchyard
A summer evening, an icon-lamp, and his mother sobbing as she held him up
Her singing to him in a low voice beside his cradle when he was ill
quiz.e: He recalled her face as frenzied but magnificent. He seldom liked to share the memory.

quiz.q: How did Alyosha respond to being teased at school?
o: He fought back fiercely, and was beaten for it by the masters more than once
He complained to the teachers, who punished the offenders
He left the school and was taught at home by Grigory for the next two years
He put his fingers in his ears, endured in silence and held no grudge
quiz.e: He seemed not to view insults as insults at all, which disarmed the other boys. They stopped teasing him and came to feel compassion.

quiz.q: What was Miusov’s aphorism about Alyosha?
o: Left penniless in a strange city, he would be taken in and never go under in the end
He would starve if left alone in a strange city, for he knew nothing of money
He would end up a monk no matter where he was sent, as his mother had hoped
He would waste any fortune he was given on beggars and holy fools in a month
quiz.e: Miusov said he would instantly be settled and the person helping him would find it a pleasure, not a burden.

quiz.q: Why, by his own account, did Alyosha come to his father’s town?
o: To ask his father for money to finish his studies
To get to know the brothers he hardly remembered
To collect a legacy that the general’s widow had left him
To find his mother’s grave, which he had never seen
quiz.e: The narrator doubts that was the whole reason. He thinks something unknown drew Alyosha onto a new and unavoidable road.

quiz.q: Who showed Alyosha his mother’s grave, and what was unusual about it?
o: Ivan, who had paid for a marble stone and a railing on her grave
Fyodor, who kept the grave tended with fresh flowers each year out of guilt
Grigory, who paid for a cast-iron slab after Fyodor forgot the place
A monk from the monastery, who tended the cemetery plots
quiz.e: Fyodor had never revisited the grave. Alyosha listened quietly and left without a word.

quiz.q: How did Fyodor react to the episode at the grave?
o: He paid for a handsome monument and had it set over the grave in her memory
He gave Alyosha money and told him to leave town at once before his brothers heard
He avoided the subject and refused ever to speak of it again
He gave 1,000 roubles for Adelaida’s soul, then got drunk and abused monks
quiz.e: He gave it for Adelaida, the wife who beat him, not for Alyosha’s mother. The narrator says such sudden impulses are common in such men.

quiz.q: When Alyosha asked permission to become a novice, how did Fyodor respond?
o: He agreed, mused drunkenly about hell, and said Alyosha never condemned him
He refused outright and demanded that Alyosha stay at home and finish his studies
He agreed on the condition that Alyosha hand over his 2,000 roubles
He told Alyosha to ask Ivan’s permission before deciding anything
quiz.e: Alyosha’s short reply was that there are no hooks. Fyodor hoped Alyosha would return cured and bring word of what he found.

chapters.title: The Elders
chapters.intro: Background on Orthodox monasteries, spiritual elders, pilgrimage and church–state ideas, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: In Orthodox monasticism, an experienced monk recognized as a spiritual guide.
A secluded dwelling or small community set apart for a life of prayer.
A monk who has also been ordained a priest.
A monk who lives in a community, as opposed to a hermit.
A person who gives up comforts and pleasures for spiritual discipline.
Preserved remains or belongings of a saint, treated as holy.
An old Russian unit of distance, about 1.07 km (two-thirds of a mile).
Giving up or denying something, especially one’s own wants (“self-abnegation”).
To bring back to life; to revive.
Sharp insight; the ability to see through to what is really going on.
Not to be broken, violated or dishonored.
A person involved in a lawsuit.
To lie face down on the ground, in humility or worship.
A monastery or convent, or its covered walkway.
In Russia, ordinary people walked hundreds of miles to monasteries to pray, seek advice and ask for healing. Monasteries also ran hostels, charity and farms.

The tradition goes back to the early desert monks of Egypt and Sinai. An elder acts as confessor and counselor, and followers pledge obedience and open their thoughts to him. This is not the formal sacrament of confession, which only a priest can administer.

Paisy Velichkovsky (1722–94), a Ukrainian-born monk who lived on Mount Athos and later in Moldavia, helped revive the tradition and translated the Philokalia, a collection of spiritual writings, into Church Slavonic. His disciples spread it into Russia, and Optina Hermitage, south of Moscow, became its best-known center, visited by writers and thinkers including Gogol and Tolstoy.
A mountainous peninsula in northern Greece, home to a self-governing community of monasteries for over a thousand years. Women are not allowed to enter.

The Mongol-Tatar conquest of Russia in the 13th century and the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453 cut Russian monasteries off from the Greek Orthodox center and disrupted older traditions.
Church authorities sometimes distrusted elders because their influence rested on personal authority, not on office.
The main Orthodox worship service, comparable to the Catholic Mass.
Pilgrimage sites are often built around a saint’s relics or a miracle-working icon, believed to heal or help the faithful.
In John 20, the apostle Thomas says he will not believe Jesus has risen until he sees and touches him. When he does, he declares “My Lord and my God.”
In Matthew 19, a wealthy young man asks what he must do to be perfect. Jesus tells him to sell what he has, give to the poor and follow him. The young man leaves sad.
“Who made me a judge or a divider over you?”
In Luke 12, a man asks Jesus to make his brother share an inheritance with him. Jesus declines to act as judge or divider.
In Genesis 11, people build a tower to reach heaven and make a name for themselves. God confuses their language and scatters them. It stands for human pride.
In Matthew 4, the Devil tempts Jesus three times in the wilderness. The third time he offers him all the kingdoms of the world.
From Acts 6, where the apostles choose seven respected men to handle practical tasks in the early Church.

Systems differ: a state controlling the church, a church controlling the state, or the two kept apart. Ultramontanism is the Catholic view favoring strong papal authority (“beyond the mountains,” meaning Rome). Pope Gregory VII (1073–85) famously clashed with the Holy Roman Emperor over who held supreme authority.
Many 19th-century socialists and radicals were atheists who saw religion as propping up the old order. Some Christian thinkers saw socialism as a rival faith promising paradise on earth.
Some Russian thinkers, called Slavophiles, held that Orthodox Russia had a spiritual calling distinct from the West.

quiz.q: What does the narrator say about realists and miracles?
o: Faith comes first; a believing realist then willingly accepts miracles
Miracles are what produce faith in a hardened realist
Realists can never believe, whatever wonders they witness
Miracles are merely natural events that science will explain
quiz.e: In the realist, miracles come from faith, not faith from miracles. The Apostle Thomas is his example.

quiz.q: How did Alyosha reason about God and immortality?
o: He resolved to live for immortality, with no compromise
He wanted to study for several years before deciding anything
He postponed the question until after he left the monastery
He decided to try both paths to see which would suit him
quiz.e: He said he could not give two roubles instead of “all,” nor merely attend church instead of “come, follow me.”

quiz.q: According to the narrator, what is an Elder?
o: The abbot of the monastery, who governs all its monks and novices
One who takes your soul and will into his own, freeing you from yourself
A hermit who shuns visitors and lives in a remote cell far from the monastery
A professor of theology who teaches the novices doctrine in the monastery school
quiz.e: You surrender your own will in full obedience and with self-denial, in the hope of eventually mastering yourself.

quiz.q: How does the narrator say Elderhood reached the Russian monasteries?
o: Pilgrims brought it from Sinai in the Middle Ages to the Russian monasteries
The Church hierarchy established it in the 1860s to strengthen discipline
It has been universal in Russian monasteries from the beginning
Paisy Velichkovsky and his disciples revived it; it flourished at Optina
quiz.e: He says it is still rare in Russian monasteries and was even persecuted at times as a novelty.

quiz.q: What is the monastery in the story famous for?
o: Its relics of saints, which draw pilgrims every year
A wonder-working icon that brings crowds from afar
Its famous Elders and their spiritual authority
Its long record of service to the nation in wartime
quiz.e: It had no relics, no miracle-working icons, and no glorious legends. Pilgrims came for the Elders.

quiz.q: What risk does the narrator note in the practice of Elderhood?
o: It may lead to satanic pride and fetters instead of freedom
It makes the monks wealthy through the gifts of pilgrims
It cuts the monks off from the sacraments of the Church
It encourages monks to abandon the monastery for the world outside
quiz.e: He calls the tried-and-tested method a two-edged blade.

quiz.q: Why do the family members gather at Zosima’s cell?
o: Zosima summoned the family to give judgement on Alyosha’s calling at the monastery
To attend Alyosha’s ordination as a novice before the whole family that day
To settle Dmitry’s quarrel with his father; Miusov joins over a lawsuit
To hold a memorial service for Fyodor’s first wife Adelaida Ivanovna
quiz.e: Fyodor first suggested it, apparently in jest. Zosima’s reply was “Who made me a judge or a divider over you?”

quiz.q: How does Dmitry respond in his letter to Alyosha?
o: He refuses to come and tells Alyosha to say he has fallen ill
He says he will bring a lawyer and papers to settle the accounts with Fyodor
He promises to apologize to the Elder in advance for his father
He respects the Elder and Ivan but expects a trap or an unworthy farce
quiz.e: He promises to restrain himself “before baseness.” It does little to calm Alyosha.

chapters.title: They Arrive at the Monastery
chapters.intro: Background on Russian monasteries, visiting etiquette, church lands and small-town gentry, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: The main Orthodox church service, held in the morning. “Late liturgy” is the second of two morning services.
A four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a folding top, a sign of wealth.
Latin for “in the chamber”: in private, with no one else present.
French for “head to head”: a private conversation between two people.
French for a purse or small coin wallet.
A relative, often a distant one.
An odd or annoying old man.
Pretending to have skill or knowledge you do not have; fakery.
The front of a building; by extension, an outward show that hides what is really there.
Weak in body, usually from age or illness.
French for “a perfect knight”: a model of gallantry and honor.

A large monastery usually had a guesthouse or hotel for visitors, a main church, workshops and farm buildings. Some also had a separate hermitage, a more secluded and stricter enclosure a short walk away, where the most devout monks lived.
Many Russian monasteries and hermitages barred women from the inner enclosure or from the monks’ living quarters. Women were received in separate guest rooms, or at a gallery outside the walls.
A rouble is 100 copecks. A ten-copeck coin was a small gift; a thousand roubles was a major donation.
Monasteries owned forests, fisheries and fields, so disputes with neighboring landowners over timber and fishing rights were common and could drag on in the courts for years.
A grave inside a monastery or church grounds was a prized privilege, usually bought with a donation.
Tula (south of Moscow) and Kharkov (in modern Ukraine) were real provincial cities. Landowners from such places often traveled to the same monasteries.
Russians who could afford it often went to universities in Germany and Switzerland, such as Jena and Zurich, which were seen as more modern and freer than Russian ones.
A notorious 1868 murder case in St Petersburg. The victim’s body was packed into a trunk and shipped by rail to Moscow. It was widely reported and became a byword for lurid crime.
Orthodox Christians make the sign of the cross, right hand from forehead to chest and then right shoulder to left, whenever they enter a church, pass an icon, or pray.
Monasteries commonly painted saints above their gates, and visitors were expected to cross themselves before passing in.

Monks followed strict fast rules, with no meat for most of the year and often no dairy, so their meals were mostly cabbage, bread, vegetables and fish. Jokes about monks and cabbage were everyday humor.
The head of a monastery, called the abbot in the West. He ranked above the elders and ran the monastery’s daily business.

Many educated Russian noblemen in the 1860s and 70s considered themselves progressive, European and free of religious “superstition,” yet still visited monasteries out of curiosity or social obligation.

quiz.q: When is the meeting with the Elder set to take place?
o: At dawn, before the first service of the monastery day
Right after late liturgy, around half-past eleven
At sunset, after vespers, once the pilgrims had gone
At one o’clock, after dinner with the Father Superior
quiz.e: The visitors skipped the service and arrived just as it ended. The dinner with the Father Superior is set for one o’clock.

quiz.q: Who is Kalganov?
o: A novice at the monastery who serves the Elder in his cell daily
A lawyer retained by Miusov in the monastery lawsuit
A cousin of Fyodor Pavlovich who lives off his charity
A young distant kinsman of Miusov, bound for study abroad
quiz.e: He is a pensive, well-dressed young man with an independent fortune, preparing for university and on friendly terms with Alyosha.

quiz.q: How does each group of visitors arrive?
o: Fyodor and Ivan in a stylish landau; Miusov and Kalganov on foot behind them
Miusov and Kalganov in a stylish landau; Fyodor and Ivan in a rattling old cab
All four crowded into Miusov’s landau for the drive up to the gates
All four on horseback, having left the carriage at the gates
quiz.e: Fyodor’s carriage lagged far behind Miusov’s. Dmitry Fyodorovich, told the day before, had not yet arrived.

quiz.q: What is said about the visitors’ experience of monasteries?
o: All four are regular visitors who come every year for the feast
Only Fyodor had entered one; Miusov hadn’t been to church in thirty years
Only Ivan had ever visited before, and then only as a student
Miusov visits every summer for the sake of the monastery’s library and its archives
quiz.e: Miusov gazes about with curiosity and affected ease, but is unimpressed by anything except the ordinary church and farm buildings.

quiz.q: Why is it strange that no monastery official comes out to welcome them?
o: One had donated a thousand roubles; another is suing over fishing rights
They arrived at midnight, long after the gates had been shut
They had arrived uninvited and the monks had not been warned of their coming
The monastery had no officials, being governed by the Elders alone
quiz.e: Miusov’s irritation grows. His simple liberal irony is “degenerating into something that nigh approached anger.”

quiz.q: Who is Maksimov?
o: The Father Superior’s steward, sent to meet and escort the guests
A Tula landowner who offers to show the way; Fyodor likens him to von Sohn
A pilgrim who has come to the Elder in hope of being healed of a long illness
A policeman who has been following Fyodor Pavlovich since town
quiz.e: An elderly, balding man with eyes “reminiscent of a lobster.” Miusov calls him a horrible, intrusive old codger.

quiz.q: What message does the little monk deliver?
o: The Elder is too ill to see anyone and the visit must be put off
They must finish their business before noon and leave the grounds
The Father Superior invites them to dine at one o’clock, after the hermitage
Dmitry Fyodorovich has already arrived and is waiting at the cell door
quiz.e: Fyodor accepts with delight, and Miusov, after some hesitation, agrees too.

quiz.q: What does the little monk say about women and the Elder?
o: No woman has ever been allowed to see him, by his own rule
Women may enter his cell on Sundays only, after the late liturgy
He receives only men and women of high rank, never common people or pilgrims
Peasant women wait in the gallery; ladies meet him outside the enclosure
quiz.e: Mrs Khokhlakova, a landowner’s wife from Kharkov, is waiting there with her daughter. Fyodor jokes about the “loophole to the lady kind.”

chapters.title: The Old Buffoon
chapters.intro: Background on Orthodox greetings, the Enlightenment, the Great Schism and the household jester tradition, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A monk who has also been ordained a priest. The plural form used in Russian-English translations is hieromonachs.
A librarian, in a monastery the monk in charge of the library.
A gesture of respect, such as a deep bow.
Flattering and cringing in order to win favor.
Humble respect shown to someone of higher rank.
The furnishings or equipment that go with a place or an activity.
Ordinary, common, of the lower classes.
A print made from a design drawn on a flat stone or plate; a cheap way to mass-produce images.
Long-established and unlikely to change, as in an inveterate habit.
A pleasantly sharp, spicy or provocative quality.
Annoying and difficult to resolve (a vexed question).
Lack of self-control, especially with drink.
A statement recommending someone or something.

Russian noble houses often had poor relations, retired army men and professional wits who lived on hospitality, entertaining the family in return for food. They were called shuty (jesters). Acting the clown could be a survival strategy as well as a character trait.
The head of police in a Russian district, a position of real local power.
A Czech-born conductor (1839–1916) who led the Russian opera orchestra in St Petersburg for almost half a century. His name sounds like the Russian verb for “to direct.”

Denis Diderot (1713–84) was a leading French Enlightenment writer, famous as editor of the Encyclopédie and as a freethinker. He visited St Petersburg in 1773–74 as the guest of Empress Catherine II. Princess Dashkova (1743–1810), a friend of the empress and head of the Academy of Sciences, and Prince Potemkin (1739–91), her powerful favorite, were two of the best-known figures at court.

Platon Levshin (1737–1812), Archbishop of Moscow, a respected, learned churchman. A legend that he converted the atheist Diderot in debate circulated widely in Russia but is generally regarded as untrue.
A huge collection of saints’ lives and church readings, arranged by day of the year, compiled in the 16th and early 18th centuries. Educated Russians knew of it but few had read it.
A saying attributed to King Louis XVIII of France.

In Orthodox practice a layperson greets a priest or monk by asking for his blessing: hands cupped, palms up, and the cleric makes the sign of the cross over them. The person then kisses the cleric’s hand.
A deep bow in which the fingers touch the floor is a traditional gesture of humility between monks, and between a monk and an elder.
The Great Schism of Russian Orthodoxy

In the 1650s and 60s Patriarch Nikon reformed church rituals and books. Those who refused, the Old Believers, split away. Icons “painted before the Schism” are therefore considered very old and especially venerable.
A small lamp kept burning before an icon in a monk’s cell or a family’s home.

“The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God” (Psalm 14:1). “What shall I do to inherit eternal life?” (Mark 10:17). The Devil is called the “father of lies” (John 8:44). “Blessed is the womb that bare thee” (Luke 11:27) is a woman’s outcry in praise of Jesus’s mother.
Moralists have long noticed that people can become cruel, rude or showy precisely because they are ashamed of themselves and expect others to judge them.

quiz.q: Who is already in the Elder’s cell when the visitors enter?
o: Two hieromonachs and the seminarian Rakitin, standing in the corner
Only Alyosha, who was kneeling by the Elder’s bed in prayer
The Father Superior and the Father Bibliothecary, at prayer together
Mrs Khokhlakova and her daughter, waiting for a blessing
quiz.e: Rakitin is about twenty-two and lives under the patronage of the monastery. He stands through the whole interview.

quiz.q: How do the visitors greet the Elder?
o: All four kneel in turn and kiss the Elder’s hand, as is the custom
None of them greets him, and Fyodor sits down at once without a word
Miusov bows stiffly, Fyodor copies him, and Kalganov doesn’t bow at all, flustered
All four ask for his blessing and cross themselves before sitting down
quiz.e: Miusov changes his mind about asking for a blessing when he sees the hieromonachs’ elaborate bowing. Alyosha blushes with shame.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor say when the clock strikes twelve, and how does Miusov respond?
o: He says it is too early to begin; Miusov agrees and sits down again
He says punctuality is the courtesy of kings; Miusov says he is no king
He says his son Dmitry is very punctual; Miusov laughs sourly at that
He says the clock is wrong; Miusov checks it with his watch in front of everyone
quiz.e: Fyodor immediately agrees that he is no king and calls himself a buffoon.

quiz.q: In Fyodor’s police-chief anecdote, what is the punchline?
o: The chief laughed heartily and granted him the permit
The chief arrested him on the spot for insulting an officer
The chief turned out to be an old friend who forgave the debt at once
The chief’s own name was Napravnik too, ending the business plans
quiz.e: The chief insisted he was the ispravnik and “my name is Napravnik too.” Fyodor then claims such blunders are a habit.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor admit about his Diderot story?
o: Platon himself told him the story during a visit to Moscow years before
It is a true historical account recorded in the chronicles
He read it in a book of saints’ lives and reworked it
He made up Diderot’s baptism on the spot, though he’d heard the legend
quiz.e: Miusov is furious. Fyodor says he invented the baptism “to add a bit of piquancy.”

quiz.q: How does the Elder react when Miusov rises to leave?
o: He lets him go with a blessing and asks Alyosha to see him out of the cell
He takes him by both hands, sits him down again and begs him to stay
He dismisses Fyodor instead and orders Alyosha to see him out
He rises and stands in silence until Miusov sits down again
quiz.e: The Elder tells Miusov and Fyodor not to be anxious or intimidated, and to be just as they are at home.

quiz.q: What is the Elder’s main advice to Fyodor?
o: Give up his estate and money and live simply on his own labor
Stop lying to himself, for self-deceit breeds vulgar pleasures and contempt for others
Go on pilgrimage to the holy places and pray for forgiveness
Apologize to his son Dmitry before the whole assembly of monks
quiz.e: He also tells him to renounce drunkenness, voluptuousness and the worship of money, and to close his drinking houses. The deepest warning is about self-deception.

quiz.q: What does the Elder say about the story of the saint who kissed his own severed head?
o: It is in the Lives of the Saints but is only an allegory
It is a well-known tale from Kiev about a martyr there in the early centuries
It is untrue and in no saints’ lives; Fyodor says he heard it from Miusov
He has never heard of it, and asks Fyodor to explain it more fully to the monks
quiz.e: Miusov denies telling Fyodor directly and says he heard it from a Frenchman in Paris.

chapters.title: Women of Faith
chapters.intro: Background on pilgrimage, mourning, confession and the place of ordinary women in Russian religious life, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Paralysis or loss of control of the muscles, often with shaking.
A wheeled chair for an invalid, pushed or pulled by another person.
The long stole an Orthodox priest wears around his neck, used when blessing, hearing confession or praying over someone.
Relating to childbirth and the period soon after it.
A song or speech of grief.
Relief, easing of pain or distress.
Extremely thin from hunger or illness.
Suffering from tuberculosis, then called consumption.
A person who asks humbly, especially a worshipper begging for help.
Rest; in a religious setting, “repose of the soul” means peace after death.
To declare free from guilt or sin.
A military officer who rose from the ranks, such as a sergeant.
The army department that supplies food and equipment.
Russian society was divided into legally defined classes: nobles, clergy, merchants, townspeople (meshchane) and peasants. A person’s rights, taxes and manner of speech depended on class.
Ordinary Russians, women especially, walked hundreds of versts to monasteries, often for months. A verst is about two-thirds of a mile.
In 19th-century Russia, a large share of children died before age five. Families often lost several.
Rural Russia had a long tradition of ritual lamentation, chanted improvisations of grief at funerals and farewells, mostly performed by women.

Siberia was settled by Russians through exile, military posting and trade. Irkutsk, in eastern Siberia, was a major administrative city. Letters from there could take weeks and families often lost touch.
Beatings of wives were common in peasant life and were rarely punished by law.
In Orthodox villages people brought the sick, and those they thought possessed, to clergy and monks to be prayed over.
Praying for the living and the dead

Orthodox practice has separate lists for the living (“for health”) and for the dead (“for repose”). Putting a living person’s name on the list for the dead was considered an offense and associated with magic.
Orthodox and popular belief held that children who die before sinning go directly to God and become something like angels.
From the prophet Jeremiah (31:15), quoted in Matthew 2:18. Rachel, a mother of Israel, stands for inconsolable maternal grief.
Saint Alexis the Man of God
A legendary 5th-century saint who gave up wealth and family to live as a beggar. A very popular name-saint in Russia.
A title of Mary, the mother of Jesus, to whom Orthodox believers pray as an intercessor.
Orthodox Christians confess privately to a priest, who then absolves, and may be admitted to communion. A person who feels unforgiven may confess repeatedly.
“Joy in heaven over one sinner that repenteth”
Small icons on a cord (encolpions) were worn by the faithful and given as blessings.

quiz.q: Who are the Khokhlakovas?
o: A widow and her fourteen-year-old daughter, who has palsied legs
Two sisters from Kharkov who have come on pilgrimage together for the feast
A mother and her adult son, who has been blind from birth
Two nuns from the north who have walked to the monastery
quiz.e: Mrs Khokhlakova is rich, tasteful and pleasant to look at. She had already visited the Elder three days earlier.

quiz.q: What happens when the Elder places his epitrachilion on the “wailer”?
o: She faints at once and is carried out of the gallery by the nuns
She shrieks louder until the monks come to hold her
She falls to her knees and confesses her sins aloud
She stops shrieking and grows calm at once, as if soothed
quiz.e: The narrator remembers seeing such women in his childhood, brought to church and quieted before the holy gifts.

quiz.q: What does the narrator later learn about “wailers”?
o: Doctors say the illness is real, a nervous malady from toil and misery
They were always frauds who pretended in order to avoid hard work in the fields
Doctors say it is hereditary and passes down in noble families
They appeared only in monasteries, never in villages or towns
quiz.e: He explains the temporary calm as the effect of intense faith and expectation.

quiz.q: Why is the woman Nastasyushka grieving, and where has she been?
o: Her husband died, and she is on her way home to bury him in their village
Her son Aleksey, the last of her four, has died; she is on pilgrimage for months
Her cab was stolen, leaving her stranded and penniless in town
Her husband beat her and drove her from the house into the winter cold
quiz.e: Her husband Nikitushka is a cabman and they are not poor. She fears he is drinking while she is away.

quiz.q: What does the Elder tell her?
o: She should stay at the monastery and serve there as a lay sister
Grief is a sin, and she must stop weeping and trust providence in all things
Rejoice, for infants are bold advocates before God; go home today
She should have another child, and God will console her soon
quiz.e: He quotes Rachel “weeping for her children” and promises to pray for the boy’s soul, named Aleksey after Alexis the Man of God.

quiz.q: What does the old woman Prokhorovna ask, and what does the Elder say?
o: She wants to buy an icon of Saint Barbara; he sells her one
She asks to pray for her silent son’s repose; he forbids it
She asks for money for a journey; he gives her a few copecks
She asks him to heal her bad legs; he lays hands on her and she walks
quiz.e: Her son Vasenka works in the commissariat in Irkutsk. The Elder prophesies he will return or write soon.

quiz.q: How does the Elder respond to the consumptive young peasant woman who fears her sin?
o: He sends her away unforgiven until she has confessed to her priest
He orders her to make a new confession before the whole gallery
He tells her to be silent and to pray alone for forty days
God forgives any repented sin, he says, and gives her his little icon
quiz.e: He also tells her to forgive her husband from her heart. She had confessed twice and been given communion but remained afraid.

quiz.q: What does the robust woman from Vyshegorye bring him?
o: Sixty copecks for someone poorer than herself, and her baby daughter
A basket of eggs and a loaf, as a gift for the monks’ table from her village
A petition about her husband’s land, to be sent to the governor
A letter from her husband in the army, to be read aloud to him
quiz.e: She says she came to see if he was really ill, and decides he looks well and will live another twenty years.

chapters.title: A Lady of Little Faith
chapters.intro: Background on faith healing, doubt, nursing sisterhoods and the idea of loving humanity, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: To chatter on in a foolish or childish way.
To lower yourself in dignity or humble yourself.
Aimed at helping others, usually by giving money or time.
Harsh criticism of oneself. Literally, whipping oneself.
A ghost, or something thin and fleeting.
In a state of excited agitation.
Prone to tender emotion, sometimes excessively.
A square dance popular in 19th-century ballrooms.
Living forever; in religion, the continued existence of the soul after death.

In the 19th century many educated people thought doctors and science would replace religion, while others still went to holy men for healing. Church authorities were cautious about declaring a miracle.
Nursing sisterhoods, begun in Russia during the Crimean War (1853–56), whose members cared for the sick and wounded. For a lady of society, volunteering as a Sister of Mercy was an admired ideal.
A remote settlement on the Arctic edge of western Siberia (now Salekhard). A monastery there would be poor and tiny, and its monks would be far from the usual pilgrim routes.
Many educated Russians spoke warmly of “the people” (narod), meaning the peasantry, as simple, pure and deeply religious, while having little contact with actual peasants.
Landowners’ wives and daughters moved between estates, towns and monasteries. A trip to a famous holy man was a social event as well as a religious one.
A gesture of blessing or healing found in the Gospels, used by priests and elders.
Orthodox teaching holds that only God heals; a holy man may pray, but must not claim the power himself.
The New Testament repeatedly stresses love of neighbor shown in deeds. “Let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:18).
In Orthodox thought saints are often described as joyful. Sadness and despair are counted as spiritual dangers.
By the 1860s and 70s, scientific materialism had made many Russians doubt the soul’s survival of death. Some felt anguish about it, and others dismissed the question.

A label for the radical young skeptics of the 1860s who rejected authority, tradition and religion. Turgenev’s novel Fathers and Sons (1862), whose hero is a scientific “nihilist,” made the word famous.
A long-standing moral question: can someone devote themselves to “humanity” in general while being unable to bear actual neighbors? Writers from Rousseau on have noticed the gap.

quiz.q: What does Mrs Khokhlakova say about her daughter Lise?
o: She has died of her illness in the weeks since his last visit
Lise is cured by his prayer, with no night fevers for two days
She has grown worse since his last blessing and cannot stand
She is cured thanks to a German doctor her mother brought from Moscow
quiz.e: Dr Herzenstube shrugged and said he was puzzled. Lise has bet her mother she will dance the quadrille in two weeks.

quiz.q: How does the Elder respond to the claim of a cure?
o: He accepts the credit and tells her to publish the news at once to the town
He declares it a miracle and orders a thanksgiving service
He says it is too early to tell; if anything happened, it is God’s will
He ignores the claim and turns to speak with the next visitor in line
quiz.e: A visiting monk from Obdorsk had asked how he dared to perform such deeds.

quiz.q: What does Lise give Alyosha, and from whom?
o: A book of poems from her mother, to be returned unread by Sunday
A ribbon from her own hair, tied around a folded note and a sprig of lilac
A small letter from Katerina Ivanovna, asking him to visit her soon
A letter from his father, begging him to come home
quiz.e: Mrs Khokhlakova says it concerns Dmitry Fyodorovich and “recent happenings.” Alyosha agrees to go.

quiz.q: What is the lady’s spiritual torment?
o: She has lost faith in the life to come and fears nothing follows death
She doubts that God himself exists and can no longer pray
She hates the Church and its priests, and cannot enter one without trembling
She fears her daughter will die and be damned for her sins
quiz.e: She says she believed as a child, but now fears “burdock growing on a grave.”

quiz.q: What does the Elder say is the way to become convinced?
o: Argument and proof, studied patiently with learned churchmen
Reading the Gospels aloud each day for forty years
Active love for one’s neighbor, pursued untiringly
Strict fasting and long vigils in a monastery cell
quiz.e: He says that as far as one succeeds in love, one will be convinced of God and the soul’s immortality.

quiz.q: What does the lady admit would cool her dream of nursing the sick?
o: Fear of infection from the sick she would be nursing
Ingratitude: she would want thanks and a reward right away
Disgust at the sight of sores and the smell of the wards
Lack of money to pay for medicine, linen and bandages
quiz.e: She says she is “the kind of woman who works for a reward.” The Elder notes she may be hoping for praise for her candor.

quiz.q: What does the doctor in the Elder’s story confess?
o: The more he loves mankind in general, the less he loves individual people
He lost his faith in God after years of watching the sick die in agony
He never loved a single person in his life, nor wished to
He gave all his money to the poor, and was ruined by his own generosity
quiz.e: The Elder contrasts “fanciful love,” which wants quick, public deeds, with “active love,” which is work and self-mastery.

quiz.q: How does Lise explain her behavior toward Alyosha?
o: She dislikes him and wants nothing more to do with him after his behavior today
She says she is bored with the whole company and wants to leave
She is angry he has avoided her, though he once taught her to read
She is jealous of Katerina Ivanovna and says so openly to him
quiz.e: The Elder says he will send Alyosha to her without fail.

chapters.title: May It Come to Pass, May It Come to Pass!
chapters.intro: Background on church and state, church courts, punishment and social theory in the 19th century, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: The area or range of matters over which an authority has legal power.
Relating to the Church or its clergy.
Naturally accompanying or going along with something.
To formally exclude someone from membership and sacraments of a church.
The platform on which an execution is carried out.
French for “cold blood”: calm composure under pressure.
A person who dabbles in a subject for pleasure without real commitment.
From the very beginning; original and fundamental.
A short account of the main points.
Describing an ideal, perfect society that may not be achievable.

Peter the Great abolished the Moscow patriarchate in 1721 and replaced it with the Holy Synod, a body supervised by a government official. For two centuries the Russian Church was effectively a department of the state.
Church courts handled marriage, divorce and clergy discipline. In 1864 Russia introduced modern, secular, jury-based courts and the role of the Church in law was a live debate.

Serious criminals were sentenced to penal servitude (katorga) in Siberia, sometimes with flogging. Many corporal punishments were curtailed in 1863 but not abolished. Executions were rare for ordinary crimes.
European thinkers, including socialists, argued that crime was largely produced by poverty and bad social conditions, not simply by individual wickedness.

On 2 December 1851 Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte seized power in France, later becoming Emperor Napoleon III. Socialists and republicans were hunted by his police, and spies and informers were widely feared.
Early socialists included devout Christians who saw their program as the true fulfillment of the Gospel, and also atheists who regarded religion as a prop of the old order. Governments feared both.
Russian thinkers who believed Orthodox Russia had a unique spiritual mission and could heal a divided, materialist West. “Ex Oriente lux,” light from the East.

From Latin “beyond the mountains,” meaning beyond the Alps, i.e., in Rome. It names the Catholic view that the pope should have supreme authority, in politics as well as faith. Orthodox and liberal critics used it as an insult.
Pope from 1073 to 1085, who asserted papal authority over emperors and bishops. In a famous clash he forced Emperor Henry IV to wait barefoot in the snow at Canossa (1077).
“My kingdom is not of this world”
Jesus’s words to Pontius Pilate (John 18:36). Theologians have argued for centuries about what they imply for the Church’s relation to worldly power.
In Matthew 4, the Devil offers Jesus all the kingdoms of the world. Orthodox writers often cite it as a warning against the Church seeking political power.
Formal exclusion from the Church’s sacraments. Orthodox Christians regarded it as a grave penalty.
Orthodox Christians recognize seven ecumenical councils (AD 325–787) as authoritative. The seven men of honest report (Acts 6:3) are the first helpers chosen by the apostles.
The Christian belief that Christ will return at the end of time.

quiz.q: What is being discussed when the Elder returns?
o: Ivan’s article on Church and courts, replying to a churchman’s book on the subject
Dmitry’s debt to Fyodor, which he promised to settle at once
The monastery’s lawsuit with Miusov over fishing and felling rights
A new icon for the church, offered by a wealthy merchant
quiz.e: Father Iosif introduces the article, which had been published in a journal. The Elder says he has not read it but has heard of it.

quiz.q: What is Ivan’s central thesis?
o: The Church should take only a small corner of the State’s life
The Church should be entirely separated from the State
The State should absorb the Church, which becomes a department of it
The Church must absorb the whole State, not merely sit inside it
quiz.e: He argues that when pagan Rome became Christian it absorbed the Church but remained pagan in many ways.

quiz.q: How does Miusov react?
o: He calls it Ultramontanism and a utopian dream akin to socialism
He fully agrees and congratulates Ivan on his article in front of the monks
He leaves the room in disgust at such clerical nonsense
He asks for the article to be read aloud to the whole room
quiz.e: He says not even Pope Gregory VII dreamed of it. Father Iosif quips that Russia has no mountains.

quiz.q: What does Father Paisy say about the phrase “the Church is a kingdom not of this world”?
o: It is the heart of Orthodox teaching and must be upheld without question
It should be set aside as a misreading of the Gospel
A play on words; the Church must rule over the whole earth
Ivan said it first in his article and Paisy repeats it
quiz.e: He calls such “worldly puns” impermissible and unworthy.

quiz.q: According to Ivan, what would happen to crime if society became the Church?
o: Nothing would change, because criminals fear no Church
Crime would double as men grew free of the State’s punishments
Every criminal would be executed publicly before the people of the town
Hardened criminals would be excommunicated and feel their guilt in full
quiz.e: Miusov suspects Ivan of joking. Ivan says the Church’s present view of crime is mechanical, like amputating an infected limb.

quiz.q: What does the Elder say is genuine punishment?
o: Awareness of one’s own conscience; flogging and exile reform no one
Penal servitude in Siberia, which reforms the criminal over time
Public shaming before the town, which teaches him repentance
Heavy fines that strip the offender of his wealth and standing in the community
quiz.e: He says only the Church’s law of Christ working through conscience can truly deter and reform. He ends: “May it come to pass.”

quiz.q: How does Father Paisy correct Miusov’s reading?
o: The Church is to become a State, as the Roman Church once did
The State must rise into a Church over the earth, the reverse of Rome
Church and State should stand as equals, each ruling its own sphere of life
The State should rule the Church, as in the old Byzantine order
quiz.e: The chapter’s title repeats the Elder’s and Paisy’s prayer, “May it come to pass.”

quiz.q: What anecdote does Miusov tell?
o: A story of a miracle he once saw at a monastery in Paris
A Paris police official feared Christian socialists most of all
A tale about Napoleon and the burning of Moscow, told to him by a veteran
How he lost a lawsuit to a rival landowner in Tula
quiz.e: Father Paisy asks bluntly whether Miusov applies this to them. Before he can answer, Dmitry Fyodorovich walks in.

chapters.title: Why Is a Man Like That Alive?
chapters.intro: Background on Schiller’s The Robbers, duels, military honor, debt, and the debate over morality without religion, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A person who enjoys stating paradoxes, claims that seem to contradict common sense.
Acting in one’s own interest as a guiding principle.
The art of arguing by reasoning back and forth; sophisticated debate.
French for a joker; someone who plays tricks or fakes.
A woman engaged to be married.
A written promise to repay a sum of money.
A person chosen to settle a dispute.
A feeling that something bad is about to happen.
An old word for “fellow,” used scornfully.
Wasted on pleasure and indulgence; living wildly.
A 19th-century officer lived by a code of honor. Insults were answered by duels. Debts to fellow officers were matters of honor, and seducing or abandoning a respectable girl was a disgrace.
A deadly form of duel in which the two opponents hold opposite corners of a handkerchief and fire at point-blank range, almost certain to kill one or both.
A mid-ranking officer, often poor after dismissal from service. Pulling a man’s beard in public was a grave insult.
A Russian decoration. A colonel wearing it “with crossed swords” had distinguished himself in war.
Cohabitation without a church wedding, often used for relationships that society did not formally recognize.
In Orthodox Russia a parent’s blessing was needed for a marriage, and a parent’s curse was feared as having real spiritual force.
A local judge introduced in 1864 to handle minor cases quickly.
Property from a dead parent was often held for children by a guardian or the surviving parent. Quarrels over accounts were frequent.

A famous German play. Old Count von Moor has two sons: Karl, a generous idealist who falls in with a band of outlaws, and Franz, a calculating schemer who plots against his father and brother. The play was a staple of the Russian stage and of educated reading.

A major 19th-century debate: if there is no God and no life after death, what keeps people moral? Kant argued that belief in immortality was a necessary assumption of morality. Others thought ethics could rest on reason, sympathy or enlightened self-interest.
The idea, made popular in Russia by Chernyshevsky’s novel What Is to Be Done? (1863), that people naturally pursue their own interests and that a rational society can be built on this basis.
In Orthodox life, a full prostration with the forehead touching the floor expresses repentance, reverence or request for forgiveness. It is normally directed to God, icons or holy persons.

quiz.q: How is Dmitry Fyodorovich described when he enters?
o: A weak, sickly man in his fifties, leaning on a stick and a servant’s arm
A muscular man of twenty-eight, looking older, with a morbid yellowish face
A monk in a patched cassock, sent down from the hermitage with a message
A clerk in a shabby coat, hat in hand, with a petition
quiz.e: He strides in officer-fashion, bows to the Elder, asks for a blessing and also bows deeply to his father.

quiz.q: Why does Dmitry say he was late?
o: His horse fell lame on the road and he had to walk the rest of the way
He overslept after a night of carousing at the inn in town
He had been ill and kept to his bed at the inn all morning
Smerdyakov told him twice that the audience was set for one o’clock
quiz.e: The Elder tells him not to worry.

quiz.q: What idea of Ivan’s does Miusov relate?
o: That the Church should be abolished and replaced by the State
That God is a myth invented by priests to keep the people docile and obedient
That without immortality nothing compels love, and all is lawful
That crime is a form of illness and criminals ought to be cured
quiz.e: Dmitry demands to confirm what he heard and says, “I shall remember.”

quiz.q: What does the Elder say about Ivan’s article and his beliefs?
o: That he is a hypocrite who writes what he does not believe for effect
His heart hasn’t settled the question, and he toys with despair
That he should give up writing and enter the monastery
That he is already a saint and needs no further counsel
quiz.e: He says that if the question cannot be resolved positively it will never be resolved negatively either. Ivan, unusually, receives his blessing.

quiz.q: What literary comparison does Fyodor make?
o: Ivan is Franz Moor and Dmitry is Karl Moor, with himself as the old Count
Alyosha is Karl Moor, Ivan is Franz, and Dmitry is the old Count
The family is straight out of Shakespeare’s King Lear and his three daughters
Ivan is Karl Moor, Dmitry is Franz Moor, and he is Count von Moor
quiz.e: He asks the Elder to be arbiter between his sons.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor accuse Dmitry of?
o: Squandering thousands, seducing decent girls, shaming a colonel’s daughter
Beating the monks of the hermitage and breaking the sacred lamps in their cells
Burning down the outbuildings of the estate to cheat the insurers
Stealing from the church collection box and then lying about it
quiz.e: Dmitry roars at him not to speak of Katerina Ivanovna, whose name he will not allow to be soiled.

quiz.q: What does Dmitry accuse his father of?
o: Planning to enter the monastery and leave his money to it after his death
Jealousy over the same woman; sending a captain to call in his notes
Giving money to the poor in order to spite his own sons
Informing on him to the police over a duel in the Caucasus
quiz.e: Dmitry admits that he beat the captain by his beard and is full of remorse, but says his father’s agent provoked him.

quiz.q: How does the scene end?
o: Dmitry apologizes to the Elder and kneels for his blessing in front of everyone
Fyodor storms out in tears, accusing the monks of plotting against him
The Father Superior expels them all and bars the cell door
The Elder bows to the ground before Dmitry, who cries out and rushes off
quiz.e: Alyosha is too stunned to support him. The Elder says “Forgive me! All of you, forgive me!”

chapters.title: A Seminarian–Careerist
chapters.intro: Background on monastic vows, seminarians, the St Petersburg press, heredity and the ideas of the 1860s, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Someone whose main aim is to get ahead in their profession.
A person who lives without moral restraint, especially in sexual matters.
Empty boasting, or a boastful person.
The shaving of part of the head as a sign of entering a monastic order. To be tonsured is to become a monk.
Making a show of being morally superior.
A woman who lives with a man, usually of higher status, without being his wife.
A Russian peasant man; sometimes used scornfully.
A person whose abilities or plans are not known to others.
Run with the hare and hunt with the hounds
To support both sides in a conflict at once.
Priests’ sons and the radical press
Many 1860s radical writers and critics were popovichi, sons of village clergy, educated at church seminaries but bitter about their poverty and prospects. Some turned to journalism.
Thick monthly magazines of fiction, criticism, politics and science that dominated Russian intellectual life. Their critics and editors were influential, and ownership could be profitable.

Owning an apartment house was a typical way for a successful man to turn savings into regular rent. Liteyny Prospect and the Vyborg Side are real districts of the city on either side of the Neva River.
A bride’s dowry might be a substantial sum, and a poor young man might aim at a wealthy fiancée.
A theme of the 1860s: older gentry who had come of age in the 1840s found the new generation scornful and impatient.
Monastic obedience and leaving the monastery
A novice normally stays under his elder’s direction. An elder can bless a novice to leave the cloister to serve in the world.
Monks regard death as a departure to be prayed over with hope, not simply mourned.
Orthodox tradition honors people who foretell events through symbolic acts. Skeptics regarded such acts as fraud.
Novices commonly waited on guests at the abbot’s table as part of their obedience.
After Darwin’s Origin of Species (1859) became known in Russia, educated people were eager to apply ideas of inheritance, species and selection to human families and society.
The motto of the French Revolution, often invoked by 19th-century liberals and socialists as a substitute for religious values.
In Eugene Onegin (1823–31), Pushkin included a famous digression praising women’s small feet.
An idiom for failing because you cannot decide between two options.

quiz.q: What does the Elder tell Alyosha to do after the scene in the cell?
o: Stay with him all night and read the Gospel at his bedside until dawn
Go to the Father Superior’s dinner, serve at table, and be useful
Return to his father’s house and keep watch over his brothers
Visit Katerina Ivanovna immediately and deliver the letter
quiz.e: Alyosha begs to stay but the Elder says he is needed more where there is discord.

quiz.q: What does the Elder say about Alyosha’s future?
o: He will become abbot of the monastery after the Elder dies and the novices
He will inherit the Elder’s cell and his place as counsellor
He should go into seclusion and never meet his brothers again
After the Elder’s death he must leave, travel, marry, and endure much
quiz.e: He also tells Alyosha to stay close to both his brothers, not just one.

quiz.q: How does Rakitin interpret the Elder’s bow to Dmitry?
o: As a miracle, proof that the Elder had foreseen Dmitry’s fate long before
A trick: sensing foul play, he bowed so people would later say he foretold it
As a sincere apology for Fyodor’s rudeness to Dmitry
As a sign of old age, since the Elder is failing and confused
quiz.e: Rakitin says holy fools “make the sign of the cross at the tavern and cast stones at the church.”

quiz.q: What does Alyosha admit when Rakitin pushes him?
o: That the thought of a crime in the family has crossed his mind
That he agrees with Rakitin about the Elder’s trickery and showmanship
That he wants to leave the monastery at once and go to his brothers
That he is secretly in love with Katerina Ivanovna and has been for years
quiz.e: He first says “I have,” then backs off, saying he only felt it when Rakitin began speaking.

quiz.q: How does Rakitin sum up the Karamazovs?
o: They are all monks at heart, though they hide it well
They are all scholars who waste their talents in drink and idle talk
They are all voluptuaries, money-grubbers or holy fools
They are all misers who hoard every copeck they get
quiz.e: He says the voluptuary streak “has increased until it’s become a raging inflammation” and calls Alyosha a dark horse.

quiz.q: What does Rakitin say about Ivan and Katerina Ivanovna?
o: Ivan despises her and avoids her house on principle
Ivan would like to marry Grushenka and rescue her from Fyodor
Ivan has long since given up on her and left for Moscow
Ivan is waiting to win Mitya’s fiancée with her sixty-thousand-rouble dowry
quiz.e: Alyosha insists that Ivan is not after money and is tormented by an unresolved idea.

quiz.q: What career does Ivan predict for Rakitin?
o: Abbot of the monastery, after taking monastic vows in his middle age
A professor of history in Moscow, loved by students and their parents
Moving to St Petersburg to edit a “fat” journal and buy a tenement
A government clerk, living on a small salary in a provincial town
