quiz.e: Rakitin repeats it in resentment. Alyosha laughs, saying it will probably come true.

quiz.q: How does Rakitin react when Alyosha mentions Grushenka as his relation?
o: He agrees warmly and offers to take Alyosha to her house soon
He laughs it off and teases Alyosha about his ties
He changes the subject and asks about the Elder’s health
He is furious and denies any tie to a “public prostitute”
quiz.e: Alyosha apologizes. They then reach the monastery and see Fyodor and Ivan rushing out.

chapters.title: A Scandal
chapters.intro: Background on monastic meals, church councils, confession, fasts, and the luxury goods of 19th-century Russia, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Eager to argue or fight; aggressive.
Not suitable or appropriate for the occasion.
Excessive pride in one’s own achievements.
A formal curse or condemnation by the Church.
A creature that sucks blood; a person who lives off others.
Plus de noblesse que de sincérité
A mildly fermented drink made from rye bread.
An alcoholic drink made from fermented honey.
A small, prized species of sturgeon.
A fruit jelly dessert, often served with milk.
A porridge made of grain, commonly buckwheat.
Vegetable oil used on fast days, when butter and animal fats are forbidden.
A red wine from the Bordeaux region of France.
A famous firm of grocers and wine merchants in St Petersburg and Moscow, known for luxury goods.
A sweet northern berry used for liqueurs.
An abbot might hold a formal dinner for important visitors and donors. Monastic fast rules still applied, but the table could be quite lavish by the standards of the day.
The governing body of the Russian Church after 1721. A complaint to the Synod was a serious step.
Monasteries lived by gifts, and a donor who felt overlooked could withdraw support and talk against the monastery.
Peasants paid for church upkeep in cash, labor and goods, while educated people sometimes accused monks of living off them.
In the 1860s and 70s steamships and railroads symbolized progress, and people proudly called their era “enlightened.”
In Orthodoxy, confession is made to a priest in private, before an icon, and is treated as a sacred secret. Public or group confession is regarded with suspicion.
In Western Christianity, groups who whipped themselves in penance. In Russia the term was applied to the Khlysty (“whips”), a secret sect known for ecstatic rites.
Orthodox Christians recognize seven ecumenical councils. Condemnation by “all seven councils” is rhetorical exaggeration.
The Orthodox Church observes fast days on roughly half the days of the year. Fish is allowed on some of them.
Humility in the face of insult
Monastic writings counsel monks to accept insults as healing and to thank their abusers.
Aesop was the legendary ancient Greek fable-teller, said to have been a deformed slave. Pierrot is the sad clown of French pantomime. Both are common figures for a jester who hides pain.
The German play (1781) about the two sons of Count von Moor.

quiz.q: What does Miusov resolve before entering the Father Superior’s chambers?
o: To denounce the monastery’s abuses to the Father Superior’s face at dinner
To leave at once and take a carriage back to town
To be polite to the monks, avoid Fyodor, and yield in the lawsuit
To demand an apology for how the monks had treated him
quiz.e: He is ashamed of his earlier anger and decides to show he is a man of good manners.

quiz.q: What is notable about the Father Superior’s table?
o: Only bread and water, as monastic rule requires on fast days
No meal at all; the guests are sent away fasting
Plenty of vodka is served, though the monks themselves drink none
A good meal with three breads, wine, mead and kvas, but no vodka
quiz.e: Rakitin spied on the kitchen. He is described as restless, envious and unaware of his own dishonor.

quiz.q: How does the Father Superior answer Miusov’s apology for Fyodor?
o: He regrets Fyodor’s absence and welcomes the guests to the meal
He accuses Fyodor of heresy and demands his expulsion from the monastery
He cancels the dinner and asks the guests to leave
He demands payment for the damage done in the cell
quiz.e: He prays before the icon and the others bow their heads.

quiz.q: Why does Fyodor Pavlovich return?
o: He wanted to apologize to the Elder for the scandal in the cell
He forgot his hat and came back for it, then stayed on a whim
He changed his mind about dinner and wanted the food after all
He decides to see his buffoon’s role through and spit on them
quiz.e: He bursts in laughing: “They all thought I’d left, but here I am!”

quiz.q: Why does Fyodor call Maksimov “von Sohn”?
o: He mocks him, recalling the von Sohn murder and the packing case
He misheard his name and nobody has corrected him
Maksimov is a German whose real name is von Sohn
Von Sohn is the Father Superior’s nephew, known to all
quiz.e: The hieromonachs are shocked. Maksimov stammers that his name is Maksimov.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor say about confession?
o: It should be public, with the whole parish as witness to every sin
It should be abolished, as a relic of monkish tyranny
The monks should hear his own confession that very evening
Confession should be secret, not aloud; he will write to the Synod about it
quiz.e: The narrator notes that no one confessed aloud in the cell. Fyodor is repeating old rumours.

quiz.q: How does the Father Superior answer Fyodor’s insults?
o: He orders the novices to remove him from the table
He cites sayings on accepting dishonor, thanks Fyodor, and bows low
He sues him before the district court for insulting the monks
He ignores him and speaks only to Miusov for the rest of dinner in public
quiz.e: Fyodor scoffs at “old phrases and old gestures,” then mocks the fasts, the gudgeon and the wines.

quiz.q: How does the chapter end?
o: Dmitry arrives at the monastery and fights his father at the gate
The monks forgive everyone and the guests part on good terms
Fyodor orders Alyosha home with his bedding; the ride is silent
Ivan quarrels with Fyodor and goes off alone on foot to town
quiz.e: Fyodor asks Ivan why he is angry, since it was Ivan’s idea to go. Ivan tells him he has spouted enough nonsense.

chapters.title: In the Lackeys’ Hall
chapters.intro: Background on household servants, serfdom and its end, folk religion and devotional reading in provincial Russia, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A male servant in a household, especially one who waits on others; also, a person who behaves servilely.
A smaller building on a property, separate from the main house, used for servants, storage or animals.
A very small, snug room or storage space.
A clown or fool; someone who plays the fool to amuse others.
A way of life given to unrestrained pleasure, especially sexual indulgence.
Devoted to or arising from sensual pleasure; also, physically alluring.
A mocking remark meant to hurt or tease.
A man who has many casual affairs with women.
Quick, unsympathetic treatment, as in “to give someone short shrift.”
Having to do with marriage or the relationship of husband and wife.
With steady, careful and persistent effort.
The features of a person’s face, especially as an index of character.
A common infection of the mouth, causing white patches; dangerous to very young infants in the era before modern medicine.
So astonished that one cannot speak.

Tsar Alexander II freed Russia’s serfs, peasants legally bound to the land and to their owners. Freed peasants, including household servants, could in principle leave, but many stayed on, bound by habit, loyalty or lack of money.
Besides field workers, landowners kept house serfs as cooks, maids, coachmen, valets and so on. Some of the wealthiest owners trained them as actors, singers and dancers.
In the 18th and early 19th centuries some rich landowners maintained private theatres staffed by serfs, with imported dancing-masters and singing teachers.
In Russian country and town houses, servants often slept in a separate building in the yard, reachable only by crossing open ground.
“In the Meadows” is a traditional Russian folk song. The “Russkaya” (“The Russian”) is a lively folk dance, performed to a tune of the same name.
After emancipation a former serf could work for a wage. A small “nest-egg” of savings was usually the most a servant could hope for.
“Readings for each month”: a huge collection of saints’ lives and edifying writings, arranged by the day of the year. It was standard devout reading for Orthodox believers.
A book of the Old Testament in which a righteous man loses everything and questions God about why the innocent suffer.
A 7th-century Syrian bishop and monk whose spiritual sermons were widely read in Russian monasteries. “Godbearing” (Greek theophoros) is an honorific for saints and church fathers.

A name loosely applied in Russia to dissenting sects that broke from the official Orthodox Church and practised ecstatic worship and bodily discipline. Such sects were persecuted but existed in many provinces.
In Orthodox practice an infant is baptized by full immersion, usually within weeks of birth, with a godfather who vouches for the child’s upbringing.
The long fast before Easter, when devout Orthodox believers read scripture and prayers more often and attended extra services.
A religious outlook that seeks direct, personal experience of the divine or of hidden spiritual truths, rather than only doctrine.

quiz.q: What is Fyodor Pavlovich’s nightly custom regarding his servants?
o: He keeps all of them in the house at night, posted in the passage to guard against Dmitry
He sends them into town on errands each night and leaves the gate unlocked until dawn
He sends them off to the outbuilding and locks himself in the house until morning
He lets them go for the night and walks out himself to sleep at a friend’s house
quiz.e: He sends the servants to the yard outbuilding for the night, and his meals are brought across the yard from the kitchen he had built there.

quiz.q: Who lives in the servants’ outbuilding at the time of the story?
o: Grigory, his wife Marfa and the young servant Smerdyakov, who works as cook
Grigory, Marfa and Ivan Fyodorovich, who has taken a room above the kitchen
Grigory alone, since Marfa and Smerdyakov are lodged with the widow Kondratyeva
Marfa, Smerdyakov and Alyosha, who has moved out of the monastery guesthouse
quiz.e: Only Fyodor Pavlovich and Ivan are in the house; the staff in the outbuilding are the old couple and Smerdyakov.

quiz.q: Why did Grigory insist on staying with Fyodor Pavlovich after the emancipation of the serfs?
o: He feared the new freedom and had nowhere else to go after the emancipation
He ruled that duty bound them to stay with a master of long standing
Fyodor Pavlovich threatened to withhold the wages and pension owed to him if he left
Marfa wanted to remain near the church and the priest who had married them
quiz.e: Marfa wanted to go to Moscow and start a small business, but Grigory ruled that duty bound them to their old master.

quiz.q: Why does Fyodor Pavlovich value having a faithful man like Grigory nearby?
o: Grigory is his only drinking companion and joins him over cognac in the kitchen
Grigory handles all the household accounts and keeps the books on the money
Grigory reports to him on his sons’ doings and on whom they meet in town
In drunken terror he wants a devoted, undepraved man near who won’t reproach him
quiz.e: He needs someone steady in the outbuilding, someone to look at and speak a word to, who would not threaten him or reproach him.

quiz.q: What happened when Marfa Ignatyevna danced the ‘Russkaya’ before the village women?
o: Grigory lectured her and pulled her hair, the only beating of their marriage
She was applauded by the village women and promoted by the master to cook
Fyodor Pavlovich dismissed her from service for a week and Grigory pleaded for her
The village women jeered, and she was ashamed to appear at church for a year
quiz.e: She danced in the style she had learned on the Miusovs’ domestic stage. Grigory pulled her locks and she never danced again.

quiz.q: How did Grigory react to his newborn six-fingered son?
o: He was delighted and held a feast for the village, calling the child a sign of blessing
He sent for a doctor at once and rode to town for the priest, fearing for the child
He called it a ‘dragon’ and said it should not be baptized; it was, and died in two weeks
He asked Fyodor Pavlovich to stand godfather and take the child into the household
quiz.e: He muttered about an ‘adulteration of nature’, hardly looked at the child, and the infant died of thrush after two weeks.

quiz.q: How does the narrator describe Grigory’s reading after the child’s death?
o: He read only novels and magazines, in secret from Marfa, in the hayloft by candlelight
He read the Chet’i-Minei, Job and St Isaac of Nineveh, and heard the flagellants’ teachings
He read the newspapers aloud to Marfa every evening and followed the news of the emancipation
He gave up reading entirely, took to drink, and spent evenings at the tavern with coachmen
quiz.e: He read devotional works in large silver spectacles, understood little of Isaac but loved him, and took an interest in the flagellants without joining them.

quiz.q: What did Grigory find in the garden bathhouse on the night the child was buried?
o: A stray dog with a litter of newborn puppies, whose whimpering Marfa had mistaken for a baby
Fyodor Pavlovich asleep and drunk on the floor, mumbling to himself about his sons
A runaway convict hiding from the police, with a bundle of stolen linen
The holy fool Lizaveta Smerdyashchaya, who had just given birth and was dying
quiz.e: Marfa heard what she thought was a baby crying; Grigory followed the groans to the bathhouse and found the town’s holy fool with her newborn.

chapters.title: Lizaveta Smerdyashchaya
chapters.intro: Background on holy fools, Russian naming, the civil-service ranks and provincial small-town life, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter. This chapter touches on distressing subject matter.

items: An old-fashioned word for a girl or young woman, often of the lower classes.
A person’s face or facial expression.
Made of hemp, a coarse plant fibre used for rough cloth and rope.
A simple, loose, sleeveless undergarment or dress.
A person who does odd jobs of many kinds, with no single trade.
Living off others without giving anything back.
A pleasantly sharp or provocative quality that adds interest.
A false statement made to damage someone’s reputation.
A guess based on incomplete evidence.
To urge or encourage someone, especially to do something foolish.
A thin, crinkled black fabric traditionally worn as a sign of mourning.
A baby or child found abandoned, whose parents are unknown.

A distinctive figure in Russian Orthodox tradition: a person, sometimes truly disabled and sometimes feigning folly, who lived as a wanderer in rags, owned nothing and was believed to be close to God. Holy fools were often permitted to speak truths to the powerful. St Basil the Blessed, after whom Moscow’s famous cathedral is named, was one.
Giving money or bread to the poor, to the church and to prisoners was a central pious duty in Orthodox Russia. Collection boxes stood at churches and prisons.
The covered entrance of a church. Beggars and pilgrims gathered there for alms.
A child was christened with a saint’s name, usually the saint of the day or one chosen by the godparents.
An old Russian measure of length, about 28 inches (71 cm). “Two arshins” is a little over four and a half feet.
Traditional Russian ring-shaped wheat breads, sold at markets. The kalatch is a larger, rounder roll with a handle-like twist.
The governor was the tsar’s chief representative in a province. He made periodic inspection tours of the district towns.
In many Russian towns, garden and yard enclosures were made of woven twigs rather than timber, and were easy to climb over.
Provincial towns often had a club where the local gentry and officials met to drink, play cards and dine.

A Russian middle name formed from the father’s first name: Fyodorovich means “son of Fyodor.” Using it in addressing a person is normal and respectful. Giving it to a foundling implies a recognised parentage.

A civil-service rank. The Russian Table of Ranks, set up by Peter the Great, assigned every civil servant and officer a numbered class. State councillor was fifth from the top and carried personal respectability.
Escapes from provincial prisons were not rare, and a notorious escaped convict could become the explanation for any crime in a district.
A bereaved man would show it by wearing a band of black cloth on his hat or sleeve.

quiz.q: How is Lizaveta Smerdyashchaya described?
o: Tall and thin, with a sharp tongue, always wrapped in a black shawl and shod in felt boots
A tiny young woman with a broad, idiotic face and thick curly hair, barefoot in a shift
A middle-aged woman, tidily dressed and quiet, who sat in the church porch and begged
A large, pale girl with fair braids who spoke in riddles and wore a nun’s headscarf
quiz.e: She is ‘nobbut two arshins’ tall, about twenty, with an idiot’s face, and goes barefoot summer and winter in a shift.

quiz.q: What does she do with money and food she is given, and with clothes people give her?
o: She sells them at the market and buys candles and sweets for the town’s children
She hides them in a cowshed behind a merchant’s house until the winter comes
She keeps the clothes and sells the food, putting the money by for her family
She puts coins in collection boxes, gives food away, and leaves donated clothes behind
quiz.e: She will not keep money or clothes: coins go into collection boxes, bread to a child or a rich lady, and coats are left at the church porch.

quiz.q: What does Lizaveta live on?
o: Black bread and water alone, taking no money for herself
Soup from the monastery kitchen, given daily at the gate
Meals cooked for her by the merchants’ wives on feast days
Food bought at the market with the alms she collected
quiz.e: She lived solely on black bread and water, and no shopkeeper feared that she would take a copeck.

quiz.q: What did Fyodor Pavlovich say when the tipsy gentlemen found Lizaveta asleep by a fence?
o: That she should be taken to the police station and the widow Kondratyeva informed
That she should be left to sleep where she lay, since a holy fool cannot come to harm
That she was a woman, even very much so, with a special piquancy
That she was a witch, and ought to be driven out of town before the next fair
quiz.e: While the others decided with ‘proud repugnance’ that she could hardly count as a woman, he leapt up and insisted she was.

quiz.q: When the town’s rumour pointed to Fyodor Pavlovich, how did Grigory respond?
o: He gave notice and quit his service, taking Marfa to live with a sister in the town
He defended his master and blamed the escaped convict Karp the Screwbore
He demanded that Fyodor Pavlovich leave town until the rumour had died down
He said nothing and stayed away from town, going to church only at dawn
quiz.e: Grigory argued with people on his master’s behalf and persuaded many that Karp was to blame, since Karp had been at large and burgling.

quiz.q: How did Lizaveta end up in Fyodor Pavlovich’s garden?
o: Grigory invited her in from the lane and gave her supper in the outbuilding
Marfa found her at the gate that evening and led her to the bathhouse to sleep
A midwife from the almshouse brought her over in a cart after the town had gone to bed
She slipped away from Kondratyeva’s house and somehow got over the tall fence
quiz.e: Kondratyeva had taken her in to watch over her until the birth, but she left in stealth; how she climbed the fence remained an enigma.

quiz.q: What name was given to the infant?
o: Pavel, with the patronymic Fyodorovich and the surname Smerdyakov
Ivan Grigoryevich Kutuzov, taking Grigory’s surname as the old man’s adopted son
Aleksey Fyodorovich, named after the saint on whose day he was born
Pavel Lizavetin, since he was known by his mother’s name among the townsfolk
quiz.e: He was christened Pavel; people began to call him Fyodorovich, and Fyodor Pavlovich invented the surname from his mother’s nickname.

quiz.q: What role does Smerdyakov fill in the household by the time of the story?
o: Coachman, driving the master to town in the droshky
Secretary to Ivan, copying his papers and letters
Fyodor Pavlovich’s second manservant, also used as cook
Gardener, tending the apple trees and the bathhouse
quiz.e: He lives in the outbuilding with Grigory and Marfa and works as a cook; the narrator says further details will emerge as the story goes on.

chapters.title: The Confession of an Ardent Heart. In Verse
chapters.intro: Background on Schiller’s ‘Ode to Joy’, classical myth, biblical references, Russian measures and garden life, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A formal order or strong instruction.
Done for show, to attract attention.
A statement accepted as obviously true, needing no proof.
French for “head to head”: a private conversation between two people.
A long close-fitting robe worn by clergy and monks.
Skill and quickness in using the hands or mind.
French for “up to date” with something; well informed.
Requiring or showing great strength, like the hero Hercules.
To ask urgently and earnestly; to beg.
Carried off by force (old sense); also, filled with delight.
To roll about in mud or, figuratively, to indulge oneself in something unpleasant.
To understand something deeply, after careful thought.
A shrub with clusters of white flowers and red berries (viburnum).

A poem written in 1785 by the German poet Friedrich Schiller, celebrating joy as a divine, unifying force that makes all people brothers. Beethoven set parts of it in his Ninth Symphony (1824). Schiller was greatly admired by Russian readers, and Dostoevsky loved him from youth.

Ceres (Greek: Demeter) was the Roman goddess of grain and harvest. Her daughter Persephone was carried off to the underworld by Hades, and Ceres wandered the earth searching for her, while the earth went barren. The myth explains the seasons.
In Greek myth, the old, drunken companion and tutor of the wine-god Dionysus, usually shown riding unsteadily on a donkey.
Early thinkers imagined human history as a march from cave-dwelling and wandering hunters toward settled farming, cities and law. Ceres, the goddess of agriculture, symbolised that step.
Fairy tale of the golden fish
A Russian folk tale, retold in verse by Alexander Pushkin (1833): a poor old fisherman catches a golden fish that grants wishes. It is a story of luck dropping into one’s lap.
A line from the angels’ song in the Gospel of Luke (2:14), sung in church services; “Glory to the highest” alludes to it.
A city in the Book of Genesis destroyed by God for its wickedness. “The ideal of Sodom” stands in speech for vice and lust.
Italian for “my lady”: the Virgin Mary. “The ideal of the Madonna” stands for purity and holy beauty.
From the 18th century on, thinkers such as Kant and Schiller debated whether beauty and the good were the same thing. The Romantics held that beauty could be awe-inspiring and even frightening.
In 1860s–70s Russia, “progressive” people were those who followed Western science and radical social ideas, and were often critical of religion.
Orthodox Christians make the sign of the cross, right hand from forehead to chest and then right shoulder to left, at moments of prayer, decision or fear.
A Russian land measure, about 2.7 acres (1.09 hectares).
A Russian unit of weight, about 36 pounds (16.4 kg).
A small, often trellised garden structure used for shade and refreshment in warm weather. Many provincial gardens had one.
Owners with little income often let gardens or hayfields to tenants for a few roubles in summer.

quiz.q: Why is Alyosha not frightened by his father’s shouted order that he come home with his pillow and mattress?
o: He had already decided to leave the monastery and live in town with his brother Ivan
He knew it was staged for effect, like a drunken artisan smashing his own crockery
He trusted that Ivan would protect him and not let their father lay a hand on him
He believed Father Zosima would forbid it, since the elder wanted him to stay put
quiz.e: Alyosha compares his father to an artisan who smashed everything ‘for the sake of aesthetic effect’, and is sure no one wants to insult him.

quiz.q: What is the other fear that torments Alyosha as he walks to town?
o: Meeting Rakitin on the road and being drawn into another of his cynical conversations
Being refused re-entry to the monastery by Father Paissy after leaving without leave
Visiting Katerina Ivanovna, who had sent him a note asking him to come
Finding his brother Dmitry drunk at a tavern and unable to be led home
quiz.e: He fears this particular woman, whom he remembers as beautiful, proud and imperious, in a way he cannot name.

quiz.q: Where does Alyosha meet Dmitry?
o: Over the wicker fence of the neighbouring garden, on a short cut ‘by the rears’
In the monastery guesthouse, where Dmitry had come to look for him after the meeting
At the market-square, where Dmitry was waiting beside a hired troika
On the front steps of Katerina Ivanovna’s house, where Dmitry waited for him
quiz.e: Mitya is beckoning from behind the fence next to the garden near their father’s house, and helps Alyosha jump over.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha see in the old summerhouse?
o: A letter in Dmitry’s hand lying beside an unlit candle on the table
Two glasses and a steaming samovar laid out on the table
A pistol lying on the bench beside Dmitry’s folded coat
A half-bottle of cognac and a liqueur glass on the table
quiz.e: Mitya laughs, saying Alyosha must think he is drinking again, but claims he is merely ‘tasting the nectar’.

quiz.q: Why has Dmitry longed to see Alyosha?
o: To ask him to teach him to pray before he faced their father
To send him as an ‘angel’ to their father and to Katerina Ivanovna
To warn him that Ivan had turned against them both and sided with their father
To borrow money from him for a trip to Chermashnya to sell the grove
quiz.e: He is delighted that Alyosha is already on his way to both, and says he wanted to send them an angel.

quiz.q: Which poem does Dmitry recite as he begins his ‘confession’?
o: Pushkin’s ‘The Prophet’, with its vision of the six-winged seraph
Lermontov’s ‘The Demon’, with its lines on the fallen angel and Tamara
Schiller’s ‘Ode to Joy’ (An die Freude), with its lines on Ceres
Goethe’s ‘Faust’, with the pact between Mephistopheles and the doctor
quiz.e: He says he knows no German but An die Freude, and recites the verses on Ceres seeking Persephone and the joy of nature.

quiz.q: What does Dmitry say about the line ‘Gives the insects – lust voluptuous’?
o: That it was about him, and that all the Karamazovs, even Alyosha, share the insect’s lust
That it was mistranslated into Russian and lost the sense Schiller gave the line
That it was written by Schiller to mock the nobility and had nothing to do with him
That it described only their father, who alone among the Karamazovs was a sensualist
quiz.e: He calls himself one of those insects, and says it is crawling in Alyosha too, ‘engendering storms within your blood’.

quiz.q: What does Dmitry say about beauty?
o: That it is a gift reserved for the pure of heart, who alone can look on it without desire
That it fades with age, and a wise man must learn to value kindness above it
That it is only a matter of taste, and the ideal of the Madonna differs from one age to the next
That it is terrible and mysterious, for God and the Devil fight there, and the field is man’s heart
quiz.e: He says that men can hold the ideal of the Madonna and the ideal of Sodom at once, and that beauty resides even in Sodom.

chapters.title: The Confession of an Ardent Heart. In Anecdotes
chapters.intro: Background on the Russian army in provincial garrisons, institutes for noble girls, gypsy entertainers, merchants and bonds, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A rude, ill-mannered person; originally a peasant.
French for “living pictures”: a group of costumed people who hold a pose, silent and still, to represent a scene or painting.
Plump, healthy and full-figured (of a woman).
Close observation of a person, especially by authority.
Polite respect shown to a person of higher status.
To confuse or upset someone's composure.
To proclaim or display something widely.
On even terms, with no debt owed either way.
A unit of regular infantry stationed in a garrison, usually in a remote provincial town, as opposed to the elite guards regiments. Officers there led a dull life.
Officer ranks included lieutenant, major and lieutenant-colonel. A lieutenant-colonel might command a battalion, and he was often one of the most prominent men in a small garrison town.
An artillery officer in charge of a battery of guns.
Units kept cash for pay, supplies and fodder in a regimental chest, which was periodically inspected by superiors. Misuse of such public funds was a serious offence.
Officers could be ordered to hand in their papers, i.e. resign, as a way of removing them without a formal trial.
Provincial towns were full of low-ranking clerks and officials, and their widows often let rooms to officers.

Boarding schools in St Petersburg, Moscow and other cities, set up by the state for daughters of the nobility and officers. Graduates were known as “institute girls” and had a reputation for polish, sentimentality and refinement.

Gypsy (Roma) choirs and dancers were a fashionable part of Russian nightlife, especially in Moscow and St Petersburg and at wealthy parties and spending sprees. Their singing was celebrated for its passion.
A sleigh or carriage drawn by three horses abreast. Parties of sleighs went out together on winter evenings.

A French novelist (1793–1871) who wrote light, popular and mildly risqué comic novels about Parisian middle-class life. Calling something “à la Paul de Kock” meant it was frivolous and slightly improper.
In small towns women often sewed for friends and neighbours; skill with the needle was a respectable accomplishment even for officers’ daughters.
Russian merchants (kuptsy) traded at great seasonal fairs. They were often thought of as shrewd, coarse and rich. A “merchant’s sort of trick” meant a vulgar, stingy one.
Without banks, private moneylending was common, with merchants or officials lending out funds for a share of the profit.
A bond payable to whoever holds it (bearer security). Five per cent meant it paid five per cent interest a year. Selling one cost a commission.
A rouble is 100 copecks. Several thousand roubles was a very large sum for a junior officer.

quiz.q: What does Dmitry say happened to the civil servant’s daughter he kissed on the troika picnic?
o: She entered a convent, and he never forgave himself for what had passed in the sleigh that night
She married his friend, a cavalry captain, and Dmitry was asked to be best man
He said nothing more; she later married a civil servant and he never blackened her name
She followed him to St Petersburg, where he abandoned her after a month
quiz.e: He pressed her hand in the dark sleigh, said nothing afterwards, and she later married a civil servant; he never blackened her name.

quiz.q: Why does Alyosha say he blushed at Dmitry’s stories?
o: Because he is the same as Dmitry: on one ladder, he on the lowest rung and Dmitry near the top
Because he was shocked by his brother’s boasting and ashamed to have listened at all, as a novice
Because he had never heard such language, least of all from a brother of his, in a summerhouse
Because he felt faint from the heat of the summerhouse and the cognac Dmitry pressed on him
quiz.e: He says it is ‘one and the same story’ and that whoever can had better not get on the ladder at all, though he is not sure he is able.

quiz.q: Who is Agafya Ivanovna?
o: The lieutenant-colonel’s second wife, a merchant’s widow who kept house for the garrison
A cook in Dmitry’s lodgings, who also took in sewing for the officers
Katerina Ivanovna’s governess, who accompanied her to the garrison soirées
The lieutenant-colonel’s elder daughter, a dressmaker in her twenties and Dmitry’s friend
quiz.e: She is a buxom, ordinary, kind woman by his first wife, who sews for the town and is on friendly terms with Dmitry.

quiz.q: How did Katerina Ivanovna treat Dmitry when she visited the garrison town?
o: She was warm and open with him, laughing at his jokes and encouraging him to call
She barely glanced at him and met his attempts to talk with a contemptuous smile
She spoke politely with him about her father’s health and asked after his regiment
She treated him as an equal, discussing army affairs with him at length
quiz.e: At soirées she measured him with her gaze and then snubbed him, and Dmitry resolved to take his revenge.

quiz.q: What did Dmitry tell Agafya Ivanovna?
o: That her father was short about four and a half thousand roubles, and Katerina should come to him in secret
That he wanted to marry Katerina and asked Agafya to arrange a betrothal with her father’s blessing
That he was leaving the army for good and wished to say farewell to her family before spring
That her father was to retire soon and he himself had been named to take over the regiment’s chest
quiz.e: He hinted he would lend the sum to Katerina in exchange for her coming in person, and Agafya called him a scoundrel.

quiz.q: What was the secret about the lieutenant-colonel’s public money?
o: He kept it in the town bank, which failed the very week the new commander arrived
He spent it on his daughters’ education, expecting to replace it from his pay and his daughters’ dowries
He hid it in a cellar under the barracks to keep it from the commander’s inspection
He lent it yearly to the merchant Trifonov, who repaid it, and this time denied receiving it
quiz.e: Trifonov’s son told Dmitry that this time his father came back from the fair without the money and claimed to have received nothing.

quiz.q: What did the lieutenant-colonel do when ordered to surrender the public sum within two hours?
o: He ran off to Moscow in the night, leaving his daughters to face the new commander and the debts
He tried to shoot himself, and Agafya’s grabbing at him sent the shot into the ceiling
He fell ill with a fit that evening and died before the commander’s men arrived
He went to Trifonov again to beg for the money, and was thrown out of the house
quiz.e: She had remembered what Dmitry said, crept after him and spoiled his aim; nobody was hurt.

quiz.q: How did the scene between Dmitry and Katerina Ivanovna in his lodgings end?
o: He sent her away with a mocking refusal, and she left in tears and swore revenge
He proposed marriage on the spot, and she slapped his face and fled the room
He gave her the bond and bowed deeply; she bowed to the floor and ran out
He had his landladies escort her home, after sending her father a note of apology
quiz.e: After a struggle with a base impulse, he handed her the bond and made a reverential bow; she then touched her forehead to the floor and fled.

chapters.title: The Confession of an Ardent Heart. ‘Heels Last’
chapters.intro: Background on betrothal and dowry customs, Russian roads and distances, moneylending, folk sayings and faith in providence, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Money or property a bride brings to her marriage.
An item of movable personal property; used figuratively of a person treated as a possession.
Speaking in a dramatic, rhetorical way, as if giving a speech.
A lover, especially one outside marriage.
A person of immoral habits (also used as an adjective).
Waterproof overshoes worn over ordinary shoes in wet weather.
A written promise to pay a certain sum to a named person on demand or at a fixed date.
Legal steps to force someone to pay what they owe.
God’s care and guidance of the world; also, fate seen as a guiding force.
A servant who looks after the yard of a household, sweeping and guarding it.

In Orthodox Russian society a betrothal was often marked at home by a family blessing with an icon, usually given by the parents or an elder relative. A formal betrothal was a serious public commitment, not easily broken.
A bride’s dowry was the usual means of setting up a household. An elderly relative without heirs could change her will freely and give gifts in her lifetime.
A large metal urn with a spigot and an internal charcoal fire, used to heat water for tea. The centrepiece of a Russian household.
A Russian unit of distance, about two-thirds of a mile (1.07 km). Twenty-five versts is about seventeen miles.
A deadly infectious disease that killed many people before vaccination became widespread.
Wealthy widows, merchants and clerks often lent small sums to neighbours at high rates. “Wicked rates of interest” described what was called usury.
A creditor holding someone’s note could sue for payment, so notes were sometimes bought up to put pressure on a debtor.
Large sums sent through the post were registered, and the sender received a postal receipt as proof.
The main town of a province held the government offices, the bank and the main post office.
The Christian belief that God directs events for the good of his creation, and that human beings may rely on him in desperate need.
In Russian popular belief, appeals to a miracle were common at moments of crisis, expressed through prayer and vows.
In Russian folk speech a “falcon” (sokol) is a proud, bold, free man. “Poor as a bald falcon” suggests a reckless fellow stripped of everything.
Wealthy carousers hired gypsy choirs, champagne and troikas for days-long binges in distant villages.
The lump at the front of a man’s throat.

quiz.q: What did Katerina Ivanovna’s chambermaid bring Dmitry the day after Katerina’s visit?
o: A note of thanks and a request that he call on her aunts in Moscow
The change from the bond, about two hundred and sixty roubles, with no note
A bunch of flowers from her aunts’ garden, with a card in her sister’s hand
Her father’s dress sword, wrapped in tissue paper and sent back with the maid
quiz.e: The package contained only the money left over after the sale of the bond, with no pencil mark or explanation.

quiz.q: What happened to Katerina Ivanovna and her sister in Moscow?
o: They entered a convent in Moscow after their father’s death and gave away their property
They went to live abroad with an aunt after the scandal, taking little money
They were taken in by Ivan Fyodorovich, who found them lodgings and a tutor
A general’s widow, her nieces dead of smallpox, made Katya heiress with an eighty-thousand dowry
quiz.e: The old lady received Katya ‘like a saving star’, rewrote her will in her favour, and made an immediate gift of eighty thousand.

quiz.q: What did Katerina Ivanovna’s letter to Dmitry contain, and what did Dmitry do next?
o: An offer of her hand; he replied in tears and wrote to Ivan in Moscow, asking him to visit her
A demand for the return of her money at once; he refused and went off to Grushenka’s house
A farewell announcing her engagement to another man; he never replied, out of pride
An invitation to her aunt’s name-day party in Moscow; he accepted and prepared to go
quiz.e: She offered herself as his wife, the carpet he walked on; he wrote back, regretting a remark about her dowry, and also sent Ivan a six-page letter.

quiz.q: What does Dmitry want Alyosha to do today?
o: Report to the Father Superior that he had been seen at the tavern, and ask forgiveness
Take a letter to Grushenka and wait for her answer, whatever the hour
Ask their father for three thousand roubles, then bow to Katerina Ivanovna for him
Find Ivan and bring him to the garden before their father sat down to dinner
quiz.e: He wants Alyosha to deliver his farewell to Katerina Ivanovna today, with the money or without it, and to try their father first.

quiz.q: Why did Dmitry first go to see Grushenka?
o: To buy a horse from her merchant Samsonov, who had promised him a fair price
To whip her, believing she had been handed a note of his to sue him with
To deliver a message from Katerina Ivanovna, who wanted her to leave town
To borrow money from her on the strength of his father’s promise of the three thousand
quiz.e: He believed Grushenka had been given a promissory note of his, intending to sue and frighten him off; he went to whip her and stayed.

quiz.q: What happened to the three thousand roubles Katerina Ivanovna had entrusted to Dmitry?
o: He sent them to Moscow by registered post as promised, and Agafya Ivanovna received them
He lost them at cards in a single night to the garrison officers and ran into debt
He gave them to his father to settle the dispute over his inheritance
He spent them at Mokroye with Grushenka, on gypsies and champagne, and never mailed them
quiz.e: She had asked him to mail the money to Agafya Ivanovna; instead he took it to Grushenka’s and spent it, so he calls himself a pilferer.

quiz.q: What does Dmitry say about the envelope in his father’s possession?
o: It holds three thousand roubles, marked ‘For my angel Grushenka’, and only Smerdyakov knows of it
It holds Dmitry’s mother’s will, which leaves her estate to her sons, and only Grigory has read it
It holds a letter to Katerina Ivanovna proposing marriage, and the old man means to post it tomorrow
It holds the title deed to the birch grove at Chermashnya, kept under the old man’s pillow
quiz.e: Smerdyakov, whose honesty the old man trusts completely, told Dmitry about it and promises to signal if Grushenka or the old man appears.

quiz.q: Why is Ivan going to Chermashnya, and what does Dmitry say he might do if Grushenka comes to his father?
o: Ivan is going to visit Katerina in town; Dmitry says he will forgive his father if Grushenka comes to him
Ivan will sell the birch grove at the old man’s request; Dmitry says he might kill his father
Ivan is leaving the district for good; Dmitry says he will leave town himself if she comes
Ivan is going to hunt grouse; Dmitry says he will fight Ivan for the right to see her
quiz.e: A buyer will pay eight thousand for the grove, and the father wants Ivan away; Dmitry says he may kill the old man if she comes, since he hates his face.

chapters.title: Smerdyakov
chapters.intro: Background on Russian household servants, epilepsy in the nineteenth century, a few literary and artistic references, and Russian foods, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A male servant in uniform or livery; also, a servile person who obeys without question.
A small entrance hall or lobby just inside the outer door of a building.
A loose white garment with wide sleeves worn by clergy and choir members.
Swinging a vessel of burning incense (a censer) as an act of worship or honor.
A bundle of birch twigs, or a rod made of them, once widely used for beating as punishment.
Lack of interest or concern; neither liking nor disliking.
Excessive fussiness about small details, especially food and cleanliness.
Of a sickly yellowish or pale-brown complexion.
Out of proportion; not matching in size or degree.
A scented, greasy ointment used to style and shine the hair.
Calm, composed and unhurried in manner.
Someone who claims to judge a person’s character from their facial features.
Long, quiet, thoughtful looking or thinking, without any particular goal.
A Russian peasant (a man of the lower, farming class).
An anchorite is a religious hermit; a pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place.

Even modest landowners and townsmen kept several servants. Long-serving couples such as a manservant and housekeeper often raised orphans or the children of the household and had real authority over them. Servants slept in halls and entry rooms so as to be on call.

Epilepsy was called the “falling sickness” because sufferers collapse in a seizure. In the nineteenth century there was no effective treatment, it was poorly understood, and it carried a strong social stigma. Dostoevsky himself suffered from epilepsy.
Russian gentry households often sent promising servants to Moscow or St Petersburg to learn a skilled trade such as cooking, barbering or tailoring. A trained cook could earn a salary and was valued.
The 100-rouble note of the period was multicolored and was nicknamed the “rainbow” note. It was a very large sum, several months’ wages for a laborer.

A secretive Russian religious sect of the 18th and 19th centuries, whose male members practiced castration. They were persecuted by the state. Observers described them as pale, wrinkled and beardless.
Peasants in the north and center of Russia wore shoes woven from strips of linden bark (bast) and long coarse coats called caftans. Both were symbols of rural poverty.

Ivan Kramskoy (1837–87), a leading Russian realist painter, a founder of the Wanderers (Peredvizhniki), who painted in a realistic style the ordinary people and great figures of his day. His painting The Contemplator (1876) shows a peasant standing alone in a winter forest.
A group of Russian realist painters who broke from the official Academy in 1870 and sent traveling exhibitions around the country, showing everyday Russian life.
Gogol: Evenings on a Farmstead near Dikanka
A collection of comic and fantastical tales (1831–32) by Nikolai Gogol, set in Ukrainian villages and full of witches, devils, folk customs and humor. It made Gogol famous.
A school textbook of world history by the Russian author Smaragdov, used in the early nineteenth century. It was the sort of dry, factual book given to schoolchildren.
A mildly fermented, slightly sour drink made from rye bread. It is cheap, common and nonalcoholic or nearly so.
A large Russian pie of dough filled with fish, meat or cabbage, often layered with rice and eggs.
A clear Russian fish soup, traditionally made with river fish.

quiz.q: Where is Fyodor Pavlovich’s table laid, and what state is he in when Alyosha arrives?
o: In the proper dining room; he is drunk and sleeping at the head of the table
In the garden under the apple trees; he is angry and refuses to speak to Alyosha
In the old-fashioned reception room; he is in good humour, far from drunk
In the kitchen beside the stove; he is ill and complaining of his heart
quiz.e: The table is laid in the reception room though the house has a dining room, and Alyosha deduces from his father’s laughter that he is “far from drunk, but … wallowing in good humour.”

quiz.q: What strange pastime did Smerdyakov have as a child?
o: Hanging cats and then burying them with a ceremony, as if censing them
Setting fire to hay in the yard and watching from the loft as neighbours came running
Collecting broken icons and lining them along the bathhouse wall to pray to
Drawing caricatures of Grigory on the fence and on the cowshed door
quiz.e: He draped a sheet like a surplice, chanted and waved something over the dead cat as if censing it. Grigory caught him once and beat him with the birch.

quiz.q: What question did the boy ask Grigory that provoked a blow?
o: Why the devil was cast out of heaven, if God had made all things good
Why God allowed the Flood to destroy the innocent along with the wicked
Who Cain’s wife was, if there were as yet no other people on earth
Where the light came from on the first day, since the sun was made on the fourth
quiz.e: Grigory could not answer, shouted “This is where it came from!” and slapped him. A week later the boy’s epilepsy appeared for the first time.

quiz.q: How does Fyodor Pavlovich’s treatment of the boy change after the illness appears?
o: He sends him away to a monastery, hoping the monks might cure the illness
He grows concerned, summons a doctor, forbids Grigory to punish him and lets him upstairs
He ignores him as before, and leaves the cure to Grigory and Marfa
He adopts him formally, giving him his name and a place at the family table
quiz.e: Previously indifferent (though giving him a copeck or two), Fyodor became concerned, summoned a doctor and forbade physical punishment and further instruction.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov say after being given Gogol’s Evenings on a Farmstead near Dikanka to read?
o: He says it made him laugh till he cried, and asks for the second volume
He says it is nonsense, ‘about things that aren’t true’, and puts it down
He says it is too frightening, and keeps it hidden under his bed at night
He says it is written in a language he cannot follow, and hands it back
quiz.e: He read it with a frown and never smiled. Fyodor then handed him Smaragdov’s General History, but he gave up after ten pages.

quiz.q: Why does Fyodor decide Smerdyakov should become a cook, and what is the result?
o: He meant to open an inn and set Smerdyakov to run its kitchen; the plan failed for want of money
He won a cooking contest in town and was sent to Moscow as the prize, returning a year later
Marfa Ignatyevna asked for help in the kitchen, and he returned a year later, unchanged
He grew finicky about food, was sent to study in Moscow, and came back wrinkled, a splendid cook
quiz.e: He studied for several years, came back looking old and resembling a Skopets, yet remained as unsociable as before, and spent his salary on clothes, pomade and scent.

quiz.q: What incident convinces Fyodor of Smerdyakov’s honesty?
o: He found three ‘rainbow’ notes Fyodor dropped in the muddy yard and returned them
He refused a large bribe offered by Dmitry to unlock the garden gate at night
He returned a purse lost by a neighbour’s wife, and accepted no reward for his trouble
He reported another servant for stealing silver spoons from the sideboard
quiz.e: Fyodor had been drunk and noticed the loss only the next day; the notes appeared on the table, and he gave Smerdyakov ten roubles.

quiz.q: Which painting does the narrator compare Smerdyakov to, and what does it show?
o: A soldier asleep on a snowy battlefield, with a rifle across his knees
A monk at prayer in a bare cell, with a single candle before an icon
A ragged peasant standing alone in a winter forest, ‘contemplating’
A man waiting at a crossroads, with a staff in hand and a pack at his feet
quiz.e: Kramskoy’s The Contemplator shows a ragged peasant in a winter forest. The narrator says such people store up impressions, and might one day go on pilgrimage to Jerusalem or burn down their village.

chapters.title: A Disputation
chapters.intro: Background on Christian martyrdom, apostasy and excommunication, casuistry and the Jesuits, and the Gospel saying about faith moving mountains, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Apostasy is the formal abandonment of one’s religion. To renounce is to give something up or declare that one rejects it.
Suffering or being put to death because one refuses to give up one’s religious faith.
To strip the skin from a person or animal.
A formal curse by the church, cutting someone off from the faithful; also, a person or thing strongly detested.
To officially exclude someone from membership and the sacraments of a church.
Someone who uses clever, hair-splitting arguments, especially about moral or religious questions, to justify an action.
Generous and forgiving, especially to a rival or someone weaker.
To make amends for a wrong or sin.
A religious hermit who lives alone, apart from society.
The highest point or peak of something; literally, raising a person to the status of a god.
In the 1800s Russians used “Asiatics” for the peoples of Central Asia and the Caucasus, where the empire’s southern and eastern frontiers lay.
Not a standard word; a clumsy coinage meaning credibility, being believable.

Accounts of Christians tortured for refusing to convert to Islam were a standing theme in Orthodox literature, especially from the Ottoman period. Russian newspapers of the 1860s–70s reported such stories from the empire’s borders and from the Balkans.
In Orthodox belief baptism makes a person a member of the church. Excommunication, a formal cutting-off from the church’s sacraments, was a recognized penalty.
In Orthodox practice an anathema is a solemn denunciation pronounced by the church against heretics and notorious unbelievers, such as the one read out each year on the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

In the Gospels (Matthew 17:20; Luke 17:6) Jesus says that faith as small as a mustard seed could tell a mountain, or a mulberry tree, to move and it would obey. It became a proverb for the power of true faith.
Early Christian hermits who lived in the deserts of Egypt from about the third century, seeking God through solitude and austerity. They became models of Christian holiness.
A person who follows a religion other than Christianity (or Judaism and Islam); here a loose word for an unbaptized person.

Casuistry means reasoning about particular moral cases rather than from fixed rules. The Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, a Catholic order, became known (and was attacked, notably by Pascal in his Provincial Letters) for subtle moral reasoning, and “jesuitical” became an insult in Orthodox Russia for crafty, evasive argument.

A long-standing question in ethics and theology: whether a person is guilty for an inner intention alone or only for what they actually do. The Sermon on the Mount, for example, treats inner anger and lust as serious.
Orthodox Russians regarded Catholics and Protestants as heterodox, and the stereotype of the sly Jesuit was common in nineteenth-century Russian writing.
Provincial Russians learned national news from the press and by word of mouth from shopkeepers. Merchants, a distinct social estate, were typically conservative and pious.
In Russian households it was common for a manservant to stand by the door during meals, ready to fetch things, and to overhear everything.

quiz.q: How did Grigory come to raise the topic at table?
o: He had read about it in a church pamphlet that Marfa brought home
A priest had told him about it during confession last week
He heard it from the merchant Lukyanov and read it in the paper
Ivan had mentioned it over breakfast, laughing at the soldier
quiz.e: The story was of a Russian soldier captured on the frontier who refused to convert to Islam and died under flaying, praising Christ.

quiz.q: What is Fyodor Pavlovich’s mocking comment on the soldier?
o: That the soldier should be made a saint and his skin sent to a monastery
That the soldier was a fool who should have run to the nearest Russian fort
That the soldier deserved a military medal and a pension from the Tsar
That such tales about captives of the Muslims are never true at all
quiz.e: Grigory frowned, recognizing that Fyodor was not moved but was indulging his usual blasphemy.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov claim, with a grin, about the soldier?
o: That the soldier should have been given a monument in the square for his courage
That his captors were not truly Muslims at all, so the test was meaningless
That he must have been a deserter, since no true soldier is ever taken captive
That it would have been no sin to renounce Christ’s name once and save his life
quiz.e: Smerdyakov says the soldier could later atone for the cowardice by good deeds. Fyodor replies that it is balderdash and the soldier would be roasted in hell.

quiz.q: What is the heart of Smerdyakov’s argument that no sin would be committed?
o: God would pardon anything said under torture, since He judges the heart and not the lips
He would be excommunicated the moment he intended to renounce, so no Christian remained to renounce
Only ordained priests can commit that sin, and a simple soldier in the field is no priest
The Bible expressly permits denying the faith whenever a man’s life is in real danger
quiz.e: He claims God would cancel his Christianity at once, so he would not be lying to his tormentors and could not be called to account as a Christian.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor call Smerdyakov after hearing the argument?
o: A saint in the making, fit to be sent to a monastery
A casuist and a Jesuit, nicknamed smerdyashchiy (stinking) Jesuit
A heretic and an atheist who deserves a flogging in the stable
A good lad and a scholar whom he promises to send to Moscow
quiz.e: Fyodor laughs and asks who taught him; he says he must have been with the Jesuits, though he insists it is all rot.

quiz.q: How does Smerdyakov turn Grigory’s anger against him?
o: By daring him to command the mountain to move to the river, and it would not
By accusing him of stealing from Fyodor Pavlovich and then hiding the money
By quoting the Psalms back at him until the old man fell silent in shame at table
By threatening to tell Marfa Ignatyevna what Grigory had said about her
quiz.e: He says Grigory’s faith is no better than his own, since no one in the world can move mountains except perhaps two hermits hidden in the Egyptian desert.

quiz.q: How do Ivan and Alyosha respond to the detail about the “two anchorites”?
o: Both say it is a foreign idea, imported from the Jesuits and unknown to Russian peasants
Both are shocked by it, and Ivan demands that Fyodor send Smerdyakov out of the room
Ivan scolds Smerdyakov for blasphemy; Alyosha stays silent, looking at the floor throughout the scene
Ivan calls it typically Russian; Alyosha says Smerdyakov’s faith isn’t Russian but the trait is
quiz.e: Fyodor is delighted, promises Smerdyakov a gold sovereign for the remark, and calls it “the whole of the Russian character.”

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov say would happen if he truly had the faith that moves mountains?
o: He would never fear torture at all and would welcome martyrdom gladly, like the saints
He would be taken up to heaven alive, like Elijah, before his captors could lay a hand on him
He would command the mountain to squash his tormentor and go off praising God, so no martyrdom
He would convert his captors on the spot and baptize them all in the nearest river
quiz.e: But if the mountain did not move at his word, doubt would assail him in his terror, and he trusts in the Lord’s mercy to forgive his saving his own skin.

chapters.title: Over Some Cognac
chapters.intro: Background on corporal punishment in Russia, French and Russian literary references, Christian ideas about God and immortality, and folk beliefs about possession, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter. Note: this chapter contains drunken, crude talk about women.

items: A person devoted to luxury, sensual pleasure and the satisfaction of bodily appetites.
A clown; someone who plays the fool to make others laugh.
Speech or action that insults God or sacred things.
Devilish, sly and cynical, like Mephistopheles, the devil in the Faust legend.
People treated as expendable, used up in large numbers for someone else’s purpose.
Tout cela c’est de la cochonnerie
French for “all of that is filth (or rubbish).”
Il y a du Piron là-dedans
French for “there is something of Piron in it.” Alexis Piron (1689–1773) was a French playwright and wit famous for his sharp epigrams.
French for “bad”; here used as a noun for a plain or unattractive woman.
Russian for “master” or “gentleman”: a landowner or noble, as addressed by a peasant.
The state institution that makes coins.
An old-fashioned word for a girl or young woman, especially a peasant or servant.
Courage and spirit; the quality of a person’s character when tested.

Beating with rods or lashes was a standard punishment in the army, in schools and for serfs. Serfdom was abolished in 1861 and the courts’ use of the lash was cut back in 1863, but peasant courts could still order floggings for decades afterwards. Landowners often declared that peasants understood nothing but the stick.

Tsar Alexander II freed Russia’s serfs, roughly a third of the population, in 1861. It was followed by a decade of “Great Reforms” in the courts, the army and local government. This is the period in which the novel is set, though it is told from a later vantage.
A mountainous peninsula in northern Greece, home to a federation of Orthodox monasteries, regarded as the holiest center of Orthodox monastic life. Russian monks had long gone there.
The chief official of a Russian province, appointed by the tsar. A governor visiting a monastery was a notable event.
Russia had a distinct merchant estate (kupechestvo). Some merchants grew very rich and gave to the church; stories about deposits and frauds involving them were common.
A gentleman insulted, especially by a slap in the face, was expected to demand a duel. The practice was fading in Russia by the 1860s but still shaped notions of honor.
Feasts of the Mother of God

The Orthodox Church keeps a number of feasts honoring the Virgin Mary (the Mother of God) through the year, such as the Dormition and the Nativity of the Virgin. Devout women marked them with prayer and sometimes fasting.
Orthodox believers hold certain icons to be miraculous. Desecrating an icon was a grave sacrilege.

In Russian villages, women who shrieked, convulsed or barked in church, especially when holy objects or prayers were present, were called klikushi and were thought to be possessed by a demon. Modern observers would describe a hysterical or nervous disorder.
Sprinkling water on a fainting person
A common domestic remedy was to spray or splash water, sometimes from the mouth, on the face of someone who had fainted or had a fit.
Latin for “I believe,” the first word of the Creed, the Christian statement of faith.
“With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again”: a Gospel saying that people will be judged as they judge others.
A French aristocrat (1740–1814) whose novels dwell on sexual cruelty. His name gave us “sadism.”
Lermontov: A Hero of Our Time

A novel (1840) by Mikhail Lermontov, with a bored, cynical, seductive officer as its central character, a type known as the “superfluous man.” Arbenin is the hero of a different Lermontov work, the verse play Masquerade (1835), a jealous and brooding man.
The devil figure in the Faust legend and in Goethe’s play Faust, a witty, mocking spirit who denies and sneers at everything.
Many educated Russians of the 1860s believed that religion held society back and that progress required science and reason. Others replied that social order depended on faith.
Christians hold that the soul survives bodily death; materialists denied it. The question of whether there is a God and an afterlife was a central intellectual debate of the century.

quiz.q: How does Ivan describe Smerdyakov to his father?
o: A secret friend of Dmitry who carries tales to him from the house
A future priest, thanks to Grigory’s Bible lessons and Marfa’s care
The cleverest servant in the district, though sly and ungrateful
A lackey and boor, “progressive cannon fodder” for the time to come
quiz.e: Ivan says Smerdyakov has decided that he is worthy of respect, and adds that there will be others better than him but to start with they will all be like him.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor Pavlovich say Russian peasants need?
o: Free schooling in every village, paid out of the landowners’ pockets
The birch (flogging), since the Russian land is mighty in the birch
More land from their masters, as the emancipation had promised them
To be sent to monasteries, where the monks would teach them humility
quiz.e: He says the muzhik is a knave and not to be spared, and that Russians have stopped flogging out of cleverness while peasants go on flogging themselves.

quiz.q: What is Fyodor’s wish about the monastery, and how does Ivan reply?
o: He wants to bequeath it his estate; Ivan says the monks would only squander it
He wants monasteries abolished; Ivan says he would then be the first robbed
He wants to be buried there beside the saints; Ivan refuses to promise to see it done
He wants to rebuild its walls and cells; Ivan offers to pay for a new bell tower
quiz.e: Fyodor laughs, admits Ivan may be right, and says the clever people should stay in the warm with their cognac.

quiz.q: How do Ivan and Alyosha answer Fyodor’s questions about God and immortality?
o: Both say yes, although Ivan adds that no one can prove it and Alyosha agrees with him
Both say no, though Alyosha adds quietly that he has lost his faith since yesterday
Ivan denies both God and immortality; Alyosha affirms both, immortality being in God
Ivan says God exists but not the Devil; Alyosha stays silent and looks at the floor
quiz.e: Asked who is laughing at man then, Ivan says “The Devil, probably,” then adds that the Devil does not exist either.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor claim about the Elder?
o: That he does not really believe in God; he once told Governor Shults so
That he is a fraud who steals from the pilgrims’ offerings at the hermitage
That he is the holiest man in Russia and a prophet to the whole people
That he was once a famous gambler who lost an estate at cards in Petersburg
quiz.e: Fyodor says there is something of Piron in him and compares him to Mephistopheles. He tells a story of the merchant Demidov but admits he has mixed up two people.

quiz.q: What is Fyodor’s “principle” about women?
o: That they should be educated just like men and allowed to hold property
That he cannot bear any woman near him, and has not for twenty years
That a man should marry only once, and never a woman with money
That there has never been an ugly woman, since each has something interesting
quiz.e: He lectures his sons on this, saying they still have milk, not blood, in their veins, and boasts of a girl at Chermashnya he has picked out.

quiz.q: What happens to Alyosha when Fyodor tells the story about Alyosha’s mother and the icon?
o: He rises and leaves the room in silence, and goes to pray in the hermitage cell
He bursts into hysterical laughter and then faints dead away on the floor beside Ivan
He suffers a fit identical to his mother’s, with shattering tears and trembling hands
He leaps up, strikes his father across the face, and runs out into the garden
quiz.e: The resemblance to his mother startles the old man, who calls for water and tells Ivan to spray it from his mouth as he used to do for her.

quiz.q: What does Ivan say that makes Fyodor forget himself, and how does the chapter end?
o: Ivan announces he is leaving for Moscow at dawn; Fyodor weeps and falls asleep at the table
Ivan says Alyosha’s mother was his mother too; Dmitry bursts in and Fyodor clings to Ivan
Ivan insults the Elder to Fyodor’s delight; Alyosha leaves, and Smerdyakov clears the table
Ivan accuses Fyodor of stealing Dmitry’s inheritance; Grigory arrives with a lantern
quiz.e: For one second Fyodor seems actually to have forgotten that Alyosha’s mother was also Ivan’s. Then Dmitry storms in amid a terrible clamour.

chapters.title: Voluptuaries
chapters.intro: Background on Aesop, old Russian houses and manners, and a few words and customs, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter. Note: this chapter contains scenes of violence between family members.

items: A person devoted to luxury and the pleasures of the senses.
To travel all the way around something.
A rough, short scuffle or struggle.
The state of being unconscious or unaware; also, being forgotten.
A cold-blooded creature such as a snake or lizard; used of a person it means someone contemptible and repulsive.
Freedom of action or choice; also, distance from the equator.
Latin for “father”; a formal or humorous way of addressing one’s father.
Woven from thin flexible twigs, as in a basket or fence.
A bold or immoral woman (insulting and old-fashioned).
A piece of bedroom furniture with several drawers.
The wish to do harm to another person.
A small hinged mirror, often kept in a bedroom or purse.

A semi-legendary Greek storyteller (about 6th century BC) credited with many fables, traditionally said to have been a slave and deformed. His name is used here as a nickname for a person who is a comic, ugly or crafty fool.

Russians use many affectionate short forms of names: Mitya, Mitka and Dmitry are all forms of Dmitri; Vanya, Vanechka and Ivan are forms of Ivan; Lyosha, Lyoshechka and Alyosha of Aleksey. The same person may be addressed warmly or crudely depending on the form.
A prosperous Russian house had a large reception room (zala) with double doors leading to private inner chambers; doors and keys were jealously guarded.
In a country house the master often kept the keys to back doors and cupboards on his own person, and a servant bringing them could be an event.
Standing with arms out can look like a crucifix, which is a powerful gesture of defense or sacrifice in a Christian culture.
In Orthodox practice a priest or elder blesses with a raised hand. A father also gives his parental blessing to a child, especially at a big moment such as a journey or marriage.
Icon of the Mother of God
A painted image of the Virgin Mary with the Christ child. Orthodox families kept such icons in the “beautiful corner” of a room, often with a lamp burning before them.
Curse and renunciation of a child
A father could solemnly curse a son. In traditional belief a parent’s curse had real spiritual weight.

quiz.q: How do Grigory and Smerdyakov try to stop Dmitry as he bursts in, and what happens to Grigory?
o: They bolt the front door against him; Dmitry smashes a window and climbs in over Grigory’s back
Grigory bars the door with arms spread like a cross; Dmitry knocks him down and leaps over
They plead with him in turn, and he gives way and leaves the house quietly, ashamed
Smerdyakov seizes him from behind while Grigory faints at the sight of his own blood
quiz.e: Grigory collapses “as though the legs had been cut from under him,” and Dmitry bursts through the door into the inner rooms.

quiz.q: Why does Dmitry rush through the house?
o: To find a hidden pistol that his father keeps under the pillow
To rescue Alyosha from his father, who he fears is beating him
To look for Grushenka, whom he thinks has slipped into the house
To take back his mother’s portrait, which his father had kept
quiz.e: He found the back door locked (Fyodor has the key) and all windows shut, so there was nowhere she could have entered or left.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor Pavlovich shout, and what does Dmitry do to him?
o: Fyodor shouts for a priest to bless him; Dmitry kneels and begs his forgiveness
Fyodor accuses him of theft; Dmitry drags him by the hair and strikes him in the face with his heel
Fyodor shouts for the police and Grigory; Dmitry hurls a chair and flees at once
Fyodor calls Dmitry his son and begs for mercy; Dmitry weeps and embraces him on the floor
quiz.e: Ivan and Alyosha pull Dmitry away. Dmitry says he deserves it and that he will come back and do it again.

quiz.q: What message does Dmitry give Alyosha as he leaves?
o: To ask Ivan to lend him the three thousand and bring it to the inn by nightfall
To tell Father Zosima he is sorry for the scandal and ask for the Elder’s blessing
To keep their father locked inside until Dmitry returns from town with the money
To go to Katerina Ivanovna, “bow to her” in farewell, and say nothing of the money
quiz.e: He then places a curse on his father and renounces him, warning him to “look out for your dream, because I too have a dream.”

quiz.q: What does Grigory repeat after the fight?
o: “Where is Marfa? I must see her this instant!”
“I will go to the police and tell them everything!”
“Let Smerdyakov go first, then fetch the master!”
“He dursed me! I used to wash him in the trough!”
quiz.e: He means Dmitry has insulted and struck the man who raised him as a child; Ivan replies that Dmitry has “dursed” his father too.

quiz.q: What remark of Ivan’s startles Alyosha?
o: That he wants to leave town at once and never see either brother again
That one vile reptile may consume the other, and good riddance to them both
That the Elder is a fraud and that the monastery is a nest of idle, hypocritical monks
That Dmitry should be handed to the police and locked up before dark
quiz.e: Ivan then says he won’t allow murder, any more than he did just now, and goes out into the yard with a headache.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor Pavlovich ask of Alyosha when he wakes up in bed?
o: To bring a priest to bless his bruises, and come back with Father Paisy
To learn which man Grushenka means to marry, and return in the morning without telling Ivan
To fetch Smerdyakov and ask him to bring cognac, then wait for Ivan to return
To burn a letter hidden under the icon in the bedroom, and never tell Ivan or Smerdyakov a word
quiz.e: He is overjoyed when told Grushenka won’t take Mitya, gives Alyosha the icon, says he was joking and lets him return to the monastery. He admits he fears Ivan more than Dmitry.

quiz.q: What does Ivan say to Alyosha at the end of the chapter?
o: That he regrets not stopping Dmitry, and will beg their father’s forgiveness at dawn
That he will leave for Moscow tomorrow, and wants Alyosha to come along to look after him in the city
That a man may wish another dead; he will protect Dmitry but keeps “ample latitude” for his wishes
That Alyosha must leave the monastery and become a lawyer, as it is no place for him
quiz.e: They shake hands firmly “as never before,” and Alyosha senses that Ivan has taken the first step toward him for some reason.

chapters.title: The Twain Together
chapters.intro: Background on institutes for noble girls, provincial society, etiquette and dress, and a few references to art and manners, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A coming together or restoring of friendly relations.
Deprived of something; left without it.
A long, low sofa-like chair on which one can recline with legs outstretched.
A lace or silk scarf or short cape worn over the head and shoulders by women.
Plump, full-figured and healthy-looking (of a woman).
French for “bad tone”: bad manners or vulgar style.
A famous ancient Greek marble statue of Aphrodite, with missing arms, in the Louvre; a symbol of ideal female beauty.
To look down on with scorn.
Open to bribery; motivated by money, willing to sell one’s favors or principles for pay.
A female fox; also, a quarrelsome, spiteful woman.
A descriptive word or phrase attached to a person, often insulting.
A raised platform on which punishments, including executions, were carried out in public.

From the time of Catherine the Great, Russia had boarding schools for daughters of the nobility, called institutes (Smolny Institute in St Petersburg was the most famous). Girls entered as children, lived as boarders and were taught languages, music, manners and religion. Graduates were known as “institute girls” and were often regarded as sheltered and romantic.
Wealthy widows, often generals’ widows, frequently took up an orphaned or poor girl of good birth, paid for her education and expected obedience and regular reports in return.

Even small towns had a few well-furnished houses on the main street where gentlewomen held receptions, received visitors for tea or chocolate, and gossiped. Visitors were announced and taken to a reception room.
A household of a young woman of fortune often included poor older female relatives who served as chaperones and kept up the appearance of propriety.
A young unmarried woman of good family was expected to be chaperoned and not to seek out men or rivals in person. Receiving someone of doubtful reputation at home would break social convention.
The telegraph had reached Russian towns and was used for urgent inquiries, such as checking whether a money transfer had been made.
Merchants and the “old man” with money
Rich elderly merchants sometimes acted as protector or financial backer to a young woman in a provincial town, an arrangement that invited gossip.
Chocolate, sponge cakes, raisins and sweets were typical refreshments served to women guests in a prosperous drawing room.
Large dark raisins, probably from grapes grown in Central Asia or imported from the south, served as a delicacy.
Sable is a fine dark fur; “sable eyebrows” means dark, glossy brows. Silk dresses were a mark of wealth.
In nineteenth-century Russia (as in Britain) accent, pitch and manner of speaking were taken as marks of upbringing and class. A drawling, affected voice was thought to show a vulgar upbringing.
Observers of the day often described the ideal as fair, full-figured and rosy, and often remarked that such beauty faded fast.

quiz.q: What is Alyosha’s state of mind as he leaves his father’s house?
o: Calm and ready for sleep, having left his father’s quarrel behind him
Cheerful, since he believes the day’s quarrels will be settled by morning
Angry and resolved to confront Dmitry about the blow he struck Grigory in the hall
Gloomy and close to despair, uneasy about Ivan’s sudden friendliness toward him
quiz.e: He feels dread about how his father and Dmitry will settle their differences over Grushenka, and he also dreads Ivan’s step toward him.

quiz.q: Who lives in Katerina Ivanovna’s house, and to whom does she report?
o: Her widowed father and younger brother; she reports weekly to a priest in Moscow
Her two aunts, who defer to her; she writes twice a week to a general’s widow in Moscow
A married sister and her husband, the colonel; she writes monthly to her lawyer in Petersburg
Only a governess and a cook; she consults Ivan Fyodorovich on every decision of the day
quiz.e: One aunt is a stately but impoverished Moscow lady; the other was the unmurmuring aunt of her sister who had looked after the girls.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha find in the reception room that shows she has guests?
o: A man’s coat and umbrella left in the hall, and a pair of wet galoshes
A printed invitation to a ball on the tea table, and two unlit candles
Two unfinished cups of chocolate, a cast-off silk mantilla, and sweets
Two crystal glasses of wine, a half-eaten orange, and a man’s cigar case
quiz.e: Alyosha realizes he has arrived in the middle of a social visit, and frowns.

quiz.q: What does Katerina Ivanovna want from Alyosha first?
o: Money for Dmitry, which she hopes Alyosha will carry to him that very night
A promise to leave the monastery and take up a post as Ivan’s secretary
A letter for Ivan, which she begs Alyosha to deliver before he goes to bed
His honest, unvarnished opinion of Dmitry and of his position after today’s events
quiz.e: She asks him to be as crude as he likes. When he reports the “bow,” she reads it as a sign of bravado and despair rather than final ruin.

quiz.q: How did she learn that the three thousand roubles had been spent?
o: Fyodor Pavlovich told her himself, taking malicious delight in the scandal
Dmitry confessed it to her himself, weeping and begging her forgiveness for everything
She made inquiries by telegram in Moscow and learned the money had never arrived
Her aunt found a pawnbroker’s receipt in a coat Dmitry had left behind
quiz.e: She says she has long known he did not send the money, but kept silent so he would know who his faithful friend is.

quiz.q: Who is waiting behind the curtain, and what is notable about the way she moves and speaks?
o: Mrs Khokhlakova; she bursts out shouting and flings the curtain wide at once
Grushenka; she steps almost soundlessly and speaks in a sugary, drawling voice
Lise; she giggles behind her hand and speaks in a high, breathless whisper
Agafya; she whispers without moving and keeps her eyes on the floor throughout
quiz.e: She is twenty-two, buxom, with chestnut hair and blue-grey eyes. Alyosha reflects that her beauty is the transient kind often found in Russian women.

quiz.q: What does Katerina Ivanovna say Grushenka has agreed to, and how does Grushenka answer?
