o: That Grushenka agreed to repay the three thousand Dmitry owed; Grushenka refuses and calls it a bribe from a rival
That Grushenka promised to leave town for good; Grushenka agrees but demands money for the journey to Moscow
That Grushenka agreed to marry old Fyodor; Grushenka laughs and says she would sooner marry his servant
That Grushenka would tell Dmitry she loves another; Grushenka replies she promised nothing and may yet take Mitya
quiz.e: Katerina presents her as an angel, abandoned five years ago by an officer and saved by an old merchant. Grushenka then calls herself a capricious creature.

quiz.q: What does Grushenka do with Katerina’s hand?
o: She kisses it passionately, kneeling, and begs forgiveness for all the trouble she has caused
She raises it to her lips, then declines to kiss it so Katerina will recall who kissed whose hand
She pushes it away at once, saying she would sooner kiss a serving girl’s hand than hers
She slaps it lightly, laughing, then runs from the room without a word to anyone
quiz.e: She says she will tell Mitya, who will laugh. Katerina cries “Brazen hussy!” and the quarrel erupts.

quiz.q: What insult does Grushenka throw at Katerina before leaving, and what does Alyosha receive on his way out?
o: That she once stole money from her own aunts; Alyosha is handed a heavy iron key by a servant girl
That she never attended the institute at all; Alyosha is given a silver ring by one of the aunts
That she once sold her charms for money; Alyosha receives a small pink letter from Mrs Khokhlakova
That she is a coward who trembles before Dmitry; Alyosha is shown out empty-handed by the maid
quiz.e: Katerina, in a fit, shrieks that Dmitry has betrayed the secret of that fatal day. The housemaid catches Alyosha in the street with the forgotten letter.

chapters.title: Yet One More Ruined Reputation
chapters.intro: Background on Russian monastic confession and the role of elders, church terms, French phrases and some everyday customs, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A Russian measure of distance, a little over a kilometer (about two-thirds of a mile).
French for “your purse or your life!”: the cry of a highwayman holding up a traveler.
A shrub with long green stems and yellow flowers; a “broom willow” is a willow-like bush.
Extreme shame or a wicked, disgraceful act.
A legal phrase for a deliberate intention to do harm, formed in advance.
Stealing money or property entrusted to one’s care, especially by an official.
Help and support in time of need.
Beneficial; good for one even if unpleasant.
Whether one likes it or not.
To warn or reprimand gently but firmly.
A meeting at an agreed time and place (French).
In Orthodoxy the sacraments are called “mysteries.” Private confession to a priest is one of them, and the priest is bound to secrecy. A communal confession to an elder was a different practice.

Elders were experienced monks, regarded as spiritually gifted, to whom both monks and lay visitors came for guidance. The tradition revived in the monasteries of Russia in the early nineteenth century (notably at Optina Pustyn, which Dostoevsky visited). Each monk gave an elder complete obedience and made frequent confession of thoughts.

Church traditionalists and some bishops distrusted the elders, regarding them as an unofficial authority, and objected to the practices of open confession, obedience to a single man and bowing before him.
An eparchy is an Orthodox diocese, the territory governed by a bishop. The “see” is the bishop’s seat of authority.
A small secluded monastic settlement set apart from the main monastery, where the monks lived in the strictest manner.
A novice is a person on probation, not yet a monk. A hieromonach is a monk who has also been ordained a priest.
The Orthodox Eucharist, bread and wine received as the body and blood of Christ. The dying often wish to receive it again before death.
Lying face down or bowing to the ground as an act of worship or humility; Orthodox monks make them often during prayer.
In monastic life obedience to one’s elder was a central vow; an elder’s instruction to a novice carried the weight of a command.
A long black garment worn by clergy and monks, which could double as a blanket for a monk sleeping on a hard sofa.
Sign of the cross before sleeping
Orthodox believers cross themselves and say evening prayers before going to bed, often kneeling before icons.
In some monasteries a superior inspected incoming letters; critics saw it as a violation of privacy, supporters as part of full openness and obedience.
Country crossroads were the traditional place for robbers. Superstition also associated crossroads with suicides and devils.
For a young unmarried woman of the gentry, a love letter or an unchaperoned meeting could be called a ruin of her reputation; many novels turn on such an event.
Gypsy singers and dancers were a popular entertainment at inns and country taverns, sometimes accompanying all-night drinking parties.

quiz.q: How does Dmitry greet Alyosha at the crossroads, and what does he admit thinking beforehand?
o: With a whispered prayer; he admits he had been thinking of entering the monastery himself
With “La bourse ou la vie!”; he admits he had considered hanging himself before Alyosha came
With a sealed letter for Ivan; he admits he had been thinking of fleeing the country tonight
With a drawn pistol; he admits he had been thinking of shooting his father in the garden
quiz.e: He says the thought of his brother, whom he loves above all others, saved him, and then the foolish urge to frighten him took over.

quiz.q: How does Dmitry react when Alyosha tells him about the scene with Grushenka and Katerina Ivanovna?
o: He weeps silently into his hands, then rises and says Grushenka has ruined him for good and all
He draws a knife in a rage and swears to cut Katerina’s throat before the week is out
He stays furious to the end, cursing both women and striking a tree with his bare fist
He turns menacing, then breaks into laughter at the detail that Grushenka did not kiss her hand
quiz.e: He calls Grushenka the “Empress of Brazenry” and agrees she ought to be taken to the scaffold, but says first he must get over her.

quiz.q: What does Dmitry say about Katerina Ivanovna and her aunt?
o: That Katya fell in love with her own dream of Grushenka; the aunt, whose husband embezzled, has been humbled
That Katya is a calculating schemer who kissed Grushenka’s hand to win her over; the aunt is delighted
That Katya invented the whole scene to ruin him; her aunt is a rich widow who will leave her a fortune
That the aunt arranged the meeting to trap Grushenka; Katya was merely obeying her orders and regrets it
quiz.e: He says Katerina really did fall in love with Grushenka, or rather with her own dream and delirium.

quiz.q: How does Dmitry realize he is responsible for Grushenka’s taunt?
o: Katerina sent him a note that evening accusing him of betraying her secret to Grushenka at the inn
Alyosha confesses that he himself let the story slip to Grushenka earlier today
He remembers telling Grushenka himself about that “fatal day” at Mokroye, in tears
Ivan tells him he once repeated the story to Grushenka at Fyodor’s house
quiz.e: He remembers gypsy girls singing and that Grushenka wept too. He then calls himself an uncontestable scoundrel and tells Alyosha to say he accepts the title.

quiz.q: What “confession” does Dmitry make to Alyosha before leaving for good?
o: That he will flee abroad that night with Grushenka, and Alyosha must tell no one, not even Ivan or Katerina
That he means to marry Katerina after all to save his honor, and Alyosha must stand beside him
That he has killed Smerdyakov in a rage, and Alyosha must help him hide the body
That he will commit a deliberate infamy he could still prevent, and Alyosha must not pray for him
quiz.e: He strikes his own chest as if the infamy were hidden there, and says Alyosha will learn the rest soon enough.

quiz.q: What practice in the Elder’s cell have opponents of the elders objected to?
o: The monks’ open confession of their sins to the Elder, which critics said profaned the sacrament
Fasting twice a week on bread and water, which critics said ruined the monks’ health and tempers
Wearing rough hair shirts under the cassock, which critics called a Catholic custom
Keeping a separate treasury for the Elder’s offerings, which critics called simony
quiz.e: Some brethren allegedly invented sins beforehand. Letters from relatives were also opened by the Elder first, which angered some. Senior monks answered that those who find the discipline a burden belong in the world.

quiz.q: What does Father Paisy tell Alyosha, and what does Alyosha decide?
o: That Zosima is dying and orders him to leave the monastery forever; Alyosha reluctantly agrees to go
That Zosima is failing and wants him in the world; Alyosha resolves to stay by the Elder tomorrow
That Zosima has recovered and asks for him; Alyosha rejoices and resolves to keep his promised visits
That Zosima has cursed him for the scandal; Alyosha runs away to Dmitry in despair
quiz.e: Paisy cautions that returning to the world is a vow of obedience, not a chance for frivolity. Alyosha reproaches himself for forgetting the Elder even for a moment.

quiz.q: What does the pink envelope contain, and how does Alyosha react?
o: A bill from the Khokhlakovas for the doctor’s visit; he is angry and tears it up before bed
A summons from Ivan to meet him at the tavern; he is anxious and lies awake until dawn
A love letter from Lise asking him to leave the monastery; he laughs, prays, and falls asleep
An appeal from Katerina Ivanovna for help; he weeps and hurries out into the night to find Dmitry
quiz.e: Lise asks him not to look into her eyes tomorrow lest she burst out laughing at his long dress. His inner confusion passes and he sleeps “a stormless slumber.”

chapters.title: Father Ferapont
chapters.intro: Background on Orthodox rites, fasting, holy fools, monastic ranks and Siberia, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A monk who has also been ordained a priest, and so can celebrate the liturgy and hear confessions.
A rite of anointing with consecrated oil, in Orthodox practice performed for the sick or the dying.
A monk who lives in a community under a common rule, as opposed to a hermit living alone.
A Russian type of ascetic who behaves in a deliberately odd or shocking way, or seems mad. Holy fools were often believed to see hidden things and were allowed to say harsh truths to anyone.
Russian for a person who pursues a “podvig”: a heroic spiritual feat of self-denial, such as extreme fasting or prayer.
A traditional Russian peasant log hut.
A long, loose coat made of coarse wool, worn by peasants.
An old Russian measure of length, about 28 inches (71 cm).
Lending money at an excessive rate of interest.
Russian noodles, often served in soup.
Porridge boiled from grains such as buckwheat, millet or oats; a staple of Russian cooking.
A type of mushroom (genus Lactarius) that Russians salt and pickle; a traditional food during fasts.
Restraint in eating and drinking; sparing consumption.
Ignorant or unenlightened; lacking education or knowledge.
To leave something to a person at one’s death, or to hand it down to them.
Not serious; silly or lacking proper weight.
Two of the sacraments of the Orthodox Church. A person confesses sins to a priest, called the confessor, and receives bread and wine as the body and blood of Christ.
In Russian the rite is called “soborovanie”, from a word meaning “gathering”, because tradition called for several priests to take part.

A starets is an experienced monk regarded as a spiritual guide, to whom monks and laypeople brought their troubles. The tradition was revived in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably at the Optina Hermitage, and some churchmen distrusted it as a novelty.
Some monks took on long periods of silence as an ascetic discipline.
A hermitage or skete is a smaller, more secluded enclosure attached to a monastery. Monks lived in individual “cells”, which were simple rooms or small huts.

Great Lent lasts seven weeks before Easter. Holy Week is the final week, and the strictest. Maundy Thursday marks the Last Supper, and Good Friday the crucifixion. Pentecost falls fifty days after Easter, when the Holy Spirit is said to have descended on the apostles.
In Orthodox practice, names of the living and of the dead are written on separate lists and prayed for separately. Prayers “for the repose” of a soul are only for the dead.
A church council held in Asia Minor in the 4th century. Its rulings, called canons, were later accepted into the Orthodox body of church law.
An Old Testament prophet who, according to the Second Book of Kings, was carried up to heaven in a whirlwind. The phrase “in the spirit and power of Elias” comes from the Gospel of Luke.
The Holy Spirit as a dove
In the Gospels the Spirit descends “like a dove” at the baptism of Jesus, which is why the dove became its symbol.
“The gates of hell shall not prevail”
A saying of Jesus to Peter in the Gospel of Matthew about the Church.
Monasteries often kept bees for the wax used in church candles, and the beekeeper was a recognised monastery job.

Siberia is the vast territory east of the Urals. Yekaterinburg stands at the Urals on the road eastward, and Irkutsk is a major city near Lake Baikal. Soldiers, officials and exiles were sent there, and mail took weeks.
A remote settlement in the far north of Siberia, near the Arctic Circle, reached only with great difficulty.
A non-commissioned officer, such as a sergeant. Military widows were a common class of poor townswomen.
In the 19th century German scholars such as D. F. Strauss, and the Frenchman Ernest Renan, applied historical criticism to the Gospels. Their work was widely discussed and fiercely opposed in Russia.

quiz.q: How does the day begin for Father Zosima?
o: He asks at once for confession, Communion and holy unction
He asks to be carried outside to see the sunrise over the hermitage
He sends for the Father Superior so that he can dictate his will
He stays silent all morning and refuses to speak to the brethren
quiz.e: Waking enfeebled but cheerful, he says he may not survive the day and asks for confession and Communion, after which the unction service begins.

quiz.q: What does Mrs Khokhlakova’s letter report as a “miracle of prophecy”?
o: A blind peasant at the gate regained his sight when the Elder blessed him
A silver icon in the hermitage chapel began to weep on the eve of his death
A soldier’s widow, told her Siberian son was alive, received his letter
The Elder foretold the day the monastery’s new bell would be hung, and it was
quiz.e: Prokhorovna, an NCO’s widow, had been told her son Vasya was alive and would return or write; on returning home she found his letter from Yekaterinburg.

quiz.q: How does Father Paisy react to the news?
o: He is moved, but asks for silence since it may have natural causes
He announces it aloud in the church to strengthen the brethren’s faith
He scolds Alyosha for bringing a worldly lady’s gossip into the cell
He dismisses the whole story as peasant superstition unworthy of notice
quiz.e: Even the stern Paisy is moved, but he cautions against frivolity and adds that the event may have come about by natural means.

quiz.q: Where had the visiting monk from Obdorsk gone the evening before?
o: To the Father Superior’s private dinner for the guests
To the guesthouse, to question the arriving pilgrims
To the Elder’s cell, to ask for a last blessing
To Father Ferapont’s cell, out beyond the monastery beehives
quiz.e: He visited Ferapont and came away with an extreme and terrible impression, which inclined him towards Ferapont rather than Zosima.

quiz.q: What is said of Father Ferapont’s way of life?
o: A hearty meal each Sunday at the Father Superior’s table, and little else
Almost nothing: two pounds of bread every three days, plus water
Mostly honey from the hermitage hives, which the beekeeper sets out for him
Meals at the monastery refectory with the brethren, but only after dark
quiz.e: The beekeeper brings him bread every three days, and the Father Superior sends the communion loaf; his water is changed daily.

quiz.q: What does Ferapont claim about the devils he has seen?
o: That none has entered the monastery walls in his lifetime, thanks to the Elder
That devils dread only the Elder Zosima and flee wherever he walks
He jammed a devil’s tail in the door at the Father Superior’s
That he has driven them all out of the beehives with holy water
quiz.e: At the Father Superior’s he saw many devils on the monks, and one with a thick brown tail whose tail he jammed in the door.

quiz.q: How does Ferapont speak of the great elm tree beside his cell?
o: He says it was planted by Father Iona and will one day shelter his grave
He says its roots hold the cell up, so it must never be cut down
He says it is a devil in disguise that he blesses each night with the cross
He says two of its boughs are Christ’s hands at night, and he trembles
quiz.e: He says it is terrifying, because Christ may seize him and carry him up alive, like Elias.

quiz.q: What does Father Paisy tell Alyosha as he leaves?
o: That the Elder’s teaching has already been refuted by scholars in the capital
That worldly scholars study holy things in pieces and miss the whole
That Alyosha must stay at the monastery until the Elder is buried
That he should shun his family and keep to his cell until the funeral
quiz.e: Paisy warns that the world’s scholars have missed the whole, and calls Alyosha “orphan”; Alyosha realises he has gained a new friend.

chapters.title: At His Father’s
chapters.intro: Background on Russian names and forms of address, household life, generational conflict in the 1860s and atheist ideas, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Latin for “father”, used as a jocular or formal way to refer to one’s father.
A light overcoat worn over other clothing.
In a pompous, moralising way, as if delivering a wise saying.
Hiding one’s true feelings or intentions behind a false appearance.
A person given to heavy drinking, lust and other excess.
An old informal word for the head.
The face, and the expression on it.
To manage to do something by scheming or ingenuity.
Showing ill will; hateful or harmful.
An old idiom meaning to deal with someone decisively and put a stop to him.
An idiom meaning nothing at all (“he won’t get a bean out of me”).
To give up or let go of something.
Old-fashioned word for the person one is engaged to marry.

A Russian has a first name, a patronymic from the father’s name (Fyodor’s son is “Fyodorovich”) and a surname. Using the first name and patronymic is polite. Diminutives, such as Mitya for Dmitry or Grushenka for Agrafena, show affection, while shortened forms such as Mitka or Vanka can sound rough or contemptuous.
A rouble is 100 copecks. A three-copeck roll was a very cheap purchase, while a thousand roubles was a large sum.
Fish soup (ukha) was a traditional dish, especially on fast days, and plain versions were everyday food.
Cockroaches were a common nuisance in the wooden houses of provincial Russia.
After the legal reforms of 1864, assault could be brought before newly created courts, so a person who had been beaten might file a complaint rather than settle privately.
Home remedies such as handkerchiefs and compresses tied round the head were everyday ways of treating injuries.

Turgenev’s novel “Fathers and Sons” (1862) made the conflict between generations a major theme. Young radicals of the 1860s, the so-called nihilists, questioned inherited authority, including that of parents.
Many educated Russians held that death is the end, that the soul does not survive and that there is no paradise. Others on the contrary defended Christianity against such views.
The view that pleasure is the aim of life. In popular speech it means living for physical enjoyment without self-denial.
In Russia, kissing someone’s hand or shoulder, or being kissed by them, was a gesture of respect or tenderness, especially from a younger person to an elder.
A Russian landowner could leave his property by will, and relatives often quarrelled over whether and how much they would receive.

quiz.q: Who tells Alyosha that Ivan has gone out?
o: Smerdyakov, from the kitchen
Grigory, from the outbuilding
Marfa Ignatyevna, at the gate
Fyodor Pavlovich, from his window
quiz.e: Marfa Ignatyevna opens the gate and says it is two hours since Ivan Fyodorovich left; Grigory is ill in the outbuilding.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor Pavlovich claim is the reason for Ivan’s staying in town?
o: He is angling to draw his share of the inheritance out of his father early
He is devoting himself to winning Katerina Ivanovna away from Mitya
He is quietly paying Smerdyakov to keep watch on the house and on Mitya
He is waiting for a post in Moscow that a university friend has promised
quiz.e: The old man says Ivan is devoting all his energy to capturing Katerina Ivanovna from Mitya, and that Ivan told him so three weeks ago.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of Fyodor Pavlovich’s stated “philosophy”?
o: He wants to live out his mucky life to the end, with no paradise and no waking
He plans to save his soul with almsgiving and a monastery gift in old age
He holds that every father should divide his property among his children
He maintains that suffering is the only road to true knowledge of God
quiz.e: He says the mucky way is sweeter, that he has no wish for “that paradise of yours”, and that he expects nothing after death.

quiz.q: Why does Fyodor Pavlovich say he will not file a complaint against Dmitry?
o: He is afraid that the court would examine his accounts for Mitya’s inheritance
Alyosha has begged him not to, and he promises it for the Elder’s sake
He has forgiven Dmitry in his heart after the Elder’s example of forgiveness
Ivan advised against it, and jailing Mitya would send Grushenka to him
quiz.e: He would rather she heard that Dmitry beat his frail old father half to death, so that she will have nothing more to do with him.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha take away with him from his father’s table?
o: A half-glass of cognac, poured for him from the cupboard
A piece of cheese wrapped in paper from the table
A three-copeck roll, put in the pocket of his cassock
A loaf of white bread that his father pressed on him
quiz.e: He picks up the roll, saying he will take it with him, and later eats it as he walks.

quiz.q: What was the “stupid notion” that Fyodor Pavlovich says he had yesterday, and what does he say about it now?
o: To give Alyosha a sum of money outright, which he has decided to do
To pay Mitya a thousand or two to go away and drop Grushenka; now withdrawn
To make a will in Ivan’s favour, which he says he has already done
To bring Grushenka to the house for dinner, which he has since carried out
quiz.e: He had thought of buying Mitya off, but says he has thought better of it and will squash him like a cockroach instead.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha say when his father asks whether Katerina Ivanovna will marry Dmitry?
o: That she will marry Ivan instead, as the household has long hoped
That she has gone back to Moscow and broken with both brothers
That Dmitry himself asked her to release him from the engagement
That she will not give Dmitry up on any account, whatever he does
quiz.e: Alyosha, who visited her the day before, replies that she will not give Dmitry up under any circumstances.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor Pavlovich do after Alyosha leaves?
o: He follows Alyosha to the gate to press money on him, then locks up
He sits down and writes out his complaint against Dmitry for the court
He gulps another half-glass, locks the cupboard, and is soon asleep
He locks himself in with the lamp and burns his old accounts and letters
quiz.e: He says he will have no more, but gulps another half-glass, locks the cupboard, lies down in exhaustion and falls asleep in an instant.

chapters.title: He Gets Mixed Up with Schoolboys
chapters.intro: Background on Russian schools, bathhouse customs, children’s quarrels and monastic dress, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A rapid, continuous discharge of firearms or missiles.
To walk or act with a bragging, self-important air.
A small folding pocket knife; originally used for sharpening quill pens.
A rough fibrous scrubbing sponge used for washing in a bath.
Prevented from growing to the normal size.
A rounded stone formerly used to pave streets.
Intended to stir up anger or a reaction.
Gathered to confer and decide together.

Boys from families of some means attended classical secondary schools called gymnasia, with preparatory classes for younger pupils. Pupils were generally aged about ten and up, and carried books in a satchel.
Clothes showed a family’s wealth. A spoiled son of a rich father wore smart high boots, while poor children wore patched, cast-off garments.
In the 19th century left-handedness was widely regarded as a defect and children were often pressed to use the right hand.
Among schoolboys, “sneaking” on a classmate to the teachers was despised, while teasing and physical fights were common.
Stone-throwing and mass fights between groups of boys were a familiar sight in Russian towns.
A steam bath central to Russian life. Bathers scrub with a bundle of fibre, often linden bast, called a mochalka, which is often translated as “loofah”. When worn out it frays into a ragged tangle.
The long black robe worn by monks and novices. It has deep pockets and looks very distinctive on the street.
Russian towns of the period had a main square, cathedral and shops on a principal street, and side lanes with timber houses. Streets were often unpaved and cut by ditches crossed by small bridges.
Streets named for saints and nobles
Street names such as Mikhailovsky (after St Michael) were common in Russian towns.

quiz.q: How does Alyosha open his conversation with the schoolboys?
o: By asking why they are loitering in the street when they should be in class
By pointing out that a satchel is easier to reach if worn on the left
By offering them a few copecks if they will stop throwing stones
By announcing he is a monk and calling for silence in the name of the Elder
quiz.e: He begins in a serious, down-to-earth way about the satchel on a boy’s right side, as an adult must if he wants to win children’s confidence.

quiz.q: Who is Smurov?
o: The left-handed boy, whose satchel hangs on his right side
The sickly boy across the ditch whom the others are pelting
The boy who ran to fetch a teacher when the stones began
The ringleader of a rival gang of boys from the town school
quiz.e: The sprightly boy explains that the satchel is on his right because he is left-handed; Smurov then returns the first stone.

quiz.q: What do the six boys accuse the lone boy of?
o: Stealing sweet buns from a baker’s shop on the market square
Insulting the schoolmaster to his face in front of the class
Jabbing Krasotkin with a penknife in class that morning, drawing blood
Betraying their gang to the headmaster for a small reward
quiz.e: A boy in a red shirt says the lone boy drew blood from Krasotkin with his penknife, and that Krasotkin refused to sneak on him.

quiz.q: What taunt do the boys want Alyosha to shout at the lone boy?
o: Whether he is hungry, since his coat is so thin and worn
Whether he likes monks, since the monk is so keen to help
Whether he is afraid of the dark, and sleeps with a lamp
Whether he likes bathhouse loofahs, the broken, hairy kind
quiz.e: They roar with laughter and tell Alyosha to ask him about loofahs, which Alyosha refuses to do because he suspects they are teasing.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha do when the boys start throwing stones at the boy across the ditch?
o: He steps into the line of fire to shield the lone boy
He runs to fetch a teacher from the school on the corner street
He picks up a stone and hurls it back at the nearest boy
He walks away in silence, since it is none of a monk’s business
quiz.e: He leaps in front of the stones to protect the boy with his own body, shouting that six against one will kill him.

quiz.q: How is Alyosha hurt by the boy?
o: Struck full in the face by a stone, splitting his eyebrow
Shoved into the ditch, where he badly twists his ankle
Bitten hard on the middle finger of his left hand
Slashed across the forearm with the boy’s penknife
quiz.e: After a stone strikes his back and another his elbow, the boy rushes at him and clamps his teeth on the finger for about ten seconds.

quiz.q: How does the boy react when Alyosha calmly asks what he has done to him?
o: He mumbles an apology and offers Alyosha his hand
He hurls another volley of stones as Alyosha turns away
He begs Alyosha to walk him home to his father
He bursts into loud tears and runs off up the street
quiz.e: Alyosha follows him up to Mikhailovsky Street and watches him run without once looking back; he resolves to solve the mystery when he has time.

quiz.q: How is the lone boy described?
o: About fourteen, big and well fed, in a good coat with a bandaged head
About nine, puny and stunted, in a threadbare coat too small for him
Tall for his age and ruddy, with a new satchel and fine leather boots
Fair and curly-haired, in a red shirt with a penknife in his belt
quiz.e: He is pale and sickly with large dark eyes, a patched trouser knee and pockets stuffed with stones.

chapters.title: At the Khokhlakovas’
chapters.intro: Background on provincial gentry households, nineteenth-century ideas of hysteria and “nerves”, rabies, medicine and courtship customs, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: French for “it is tragic”. Educated Russians scattered French phrases through their speech.
French for “mother”. Upper-class Russian children often addressed their mothers in the French way.
A wheeled chair for invalids, named for the English spa city of Bath.
Soft fabric, originally scraped linen, used as a dressing for wounds.
A substance that tightens tissue and reduces bleeding or swelling, used on cuts and bruises.
A cloudy, mildly astringent solution of lead acetate once used on bruises and sprains (also called Goulard’s water). It was a common home remedy.
To bathe a body part with warm or medicated liquid; also, a lotion or poultice of this kind.
A basin for waste water or rinsing.
A deadly viral disease passed on by the bite of an infected animal, often a dog. It was dreaded in the 19th century, before Pasteur’s vaccine of 1885.
A sudden, unreasoned wish or fancy.
In the 19th century, a word for a state of uncontrolled emotion such as fits of crying or laughing. It was thought to affect women especially.
A made-up word of the speaker’s, meaning “not clever or amusing”.
To make up for a wrong or fault.
A landowner such as Mrs Khokhlakova might own several estates in different provinces, a house in Moscow and another in the district town, spending the year moving between them.
Many physicians in Russian towns were Germans or of German descent, with names like Herzenstube. A doctor was often a figure of mild comedy, famous for his catchphrases.
In the 19th century a cut or bite was washed and kept in cold water, then dressed with lint and a lotion.
Nineteenth-century doctors and novelists spoke of “nervous” women. The word “hysteria” comes from the Greek word for the womb, because it was once thought to originate there.
In Russian polite speech people use first name and patronymic, so Alyosha is “Aleksey Fyodorovich”. Girls such as Lise (Elizaveta) were often called by pet names.
In imperial Russia the minimum legal age to marry was generally 18 for men and 16 for women.
In a wealthy household a maid might carry messages or keep watch at windows.
Young people of the gentry often exchanged letters, sometimes secretly, because direct speech between unmarried young men and women was supervised by relatives.

The Russian word “nadryv” means a strain, tear or rupture. It is used for an emotional breakdown in which feelings are strained to a painful pitch, often by acting against one’s own true feelings. Translators render it as “crack-up” or “laceration”.

quiz.q: Who is with Katerina Ivanovna in the drawing room when Alyosha arrives?
o: Dmitry Fyodorovich, her fiancé
Father Paisy, come from the monastery
Dr Herzenstube, the German physician
Ivan Fyodorovich, Dmitry’s brother
quiz.e: Mrs Khokhlakova says it is “the other one, Ivan Fyodorovich” whom Katerina is talking to so solemnly.

quiz.q: What does Mrs Khokhlakova complain that Dr Herzenstube always says?
o: That “nothing can he understand” and that they must simply wait
That the patient must be bled and kept in a darkened room
That Lise must be taken abroad to a clinic in Germany
That it is only nerves and will pass with the spring
quiz.e: She says he always comes and says that “nothing can he understand” and that they must wait.

quiz.q: What makes Lise suddenly fling the door open?
o: Hearing her mother laugh with Katerina Ivanovna in the drawing room
The sight of the blood-soaked handkerchief on Alyosha’s finger
Hearing Ivan’s raised voice from the drawing room next door
A hurried message from Dr Herzenstube, brought by the maid
quiz.e: She takes charge, ordering water, ice, lint and lead lotion, and is plainly in a panic over the wound.

quiz.q: What does Lise urgently demand of Alyosha when her mother is out of the room?
o: That he swear never to speak of her visit to the Elder or to Ivan
That he take her at once to see the doctor her mother distrusts
That he return the letter she sent him yesterday, a silly joke
That he tell her exactly what happened at his father’s house
quiz.e: She repented of the letter all night; Alyosha says it is back where he came from and that he did not laugh, because he believed it all.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha say about the letter and its contents?
o: That he took it for a girl’s joke and laughed at it in his cell
That he believed every word and thinks he could find no better wife
That he burned it unread, as the Elder would have wished
That he showed it to the Elder, who advised him to wait
quiz.e: He says that when the time prescribed by law arrives they shall marry, and he offers to wheel her around himself.

quiz.q: Why does Mrs Khokhlakova worry about the bite?
o: That the schoolboy must have had a fever when he bit
That Alyosha will be too lame to return to the monastery
That the schoolboy’s parents will punish him severely
That the schoolboy might have rabies, like a mad dog
quiz.e: Lise mocks the idea of “rabid boys” and asks Alyosha if he is afraid of water.

quiz.q: How does Lise treat Alyosha when he says he will go and see Katerina Ivanovna?
o: She calls him a monster and sends him out, saying she wants to sleep
She agrees warmly and gives him a message to carry to Katerina Ivanovna
She begs to come with him and makes her mother fetch her shawl
She orders the maid to wrap his finger again before he may go
quiz.e: Her sharp, whimsical moods swing from fussing over him to dismissing him, and Alyosha’s offer to stay a few more minutes only makes her call him a monster.

quiz.q: What does Mrs Khokhlakova whisper to him as they approach the drawing room?
o: That Katerina Ivanovna has resolved to enter a convent after the wedding
That Ivan wishes to marry Lise and has asked her for her hand
That Katerina loves Ivan but is forcing herself to believe it is Dmitry
That the Elder has already died, but the monks are keeping it quiet
quiz.e: She calls it an outrage and a fantastic comedy, and says she will come in and await the ending.

chapters.title: Crack-up in the Drawing Room
chapters.intro: Background on Russian military ranks, the Table of Ranks, honour and duty, Schiller, banknotes and women’s lives in the gentry, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A feeling that something is going to happen.
Generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival or someone less powerful.
French for a heavy curtain hung across a doorway.
A sum of money given to help someone, without any obligation to repay it.
A clerk who copies out documents.
Deliberately contrary or unreasonable; doing the opposite of what is wanted.
Conformity to accepted standards of behaviour.
Arrogantly proud; looking down on others.
To restore friendship, or to bring oneself to accept something.
To take for granted, or to take liberties.
The Russian army rank “shtabs-kapitan”, usually rendered staff-captain or second-grade captain, ranked just below a captain. It was a junior officer’s grade.
Peter the Great’s 1722 system that gave every military and civil post a grade. Officials and officers moved up by rank, which determined titles of address, such as “Your Excellency” for a general.
A man dismissed from state employment for an offence lost both his salary and much of his standing, and often had to take any work he could find.
A common nickname for the Russian hundred-rouble note, which was printed in many colours. Two of them make 200 roubles, a very large sum for a poor family.
Young unmarried women of good family often lived under the care of aunts and kept in close contact with distant female relatives, who played a part in their marriages.
Moscow was an old merchant and noble city, where wealthy families kept town houses and visited from provincial towns by railway.
A woman’s honour after a public scene
In gentry circles, a public humiliation was felt to damage a person’s standing and could not simply be ignored.

Schiller (1759–1805) was a German poet and dramatist, author of plays like “The Robbers” and “Don Carlos” and many ballads and poems. Educated Russians knew German literature well and often quoted it from memory.
Educated Russians of the period often quoted poetry in German or French in conversation, as a mark of education.
Nineteenth-century literature often idealised a woman who sacrifices herself out of fidelity or duty, such as Tatyana in Pushkin’s “Eugene Onegin”, who keeps faith with a husband she does not love.
Moralists long debated whether pity is a form of love or a substitute for it, and whether love can be entangled with pride, gratitude or the wish to feel oneself virtuous.
To call someone a “holy fool” in conversation could mean an innocent who blurts out truths, or be used as a taunt against naive or tactless behaviour.
A sudden insight or flash of understanding, sometimes spoken of in religious language.

quiz.q: What is Katerina Ivanovna’s “decision” about Dmitry?
o: She will break off the engagement and go abroad with her aunts
She will return to Moscow and enter a convent after the wedding
She will never give him up, even if he marries Grushenka
She will hand him over to the authorities for the missing money
quiz.e: She declares she will become the “instrument, the mechanism of his happiness” and says Ivan gives her his unqualified approval.

quiz.q: What does Ivan announce that dramatically changes Katerina Ivanovna’s mood?
o: That he is leaving for Moscow again tomorrow
That he has decided to marry Lise Khokhlakova
That Dmitry has just been arrested at the inn
That Father Zosima has died in his cell tonight
quiz.e: Her tears vanish instantly and she exclaims “what a stroke of good luck!”, then hastily corrects herself, saying he can explain everything to her aunt and Agasha.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha say in his sudden “illumination”?
o: That Ivan should return to Moscow at once, before the Elder dies
That she should confess everything to Father Zosima at the monastery
That Dmitry has secretly married Grushenka and told no one in town
That she has never loved Dmitry, and torments Ivan with a false love
quiz.e: He begs that Dmitry be summoned to unite her hand with Ivan’s, since she loves Ivan.

quiz.q: How does Katerina Ivanovna react to Alyosha’s words?
o: She thanks him tearfully and begs him to say it all again
Her face goes pale and she snaps that he is “a little holy fool”
She orders him from the house and tells the maid to bar the door
She faints into Mrs Khokhlakova’s arms and must be carried out
quiz.e: Her face goes pale and her lips twist with malice as she snaps that he is “a little holy fool”.

quiz.q: What does Ivan say about his own place in Katerina Ivanovna’s life?
o: That he has loved her openly all along and has never hidden it
That he has been her closest friend and confidant since Moscow
That she keeps him close only for revenge, and loves Dmitry from pride
That he is leaving because of a bitter quarrel with Dmitry over Grushenka
quiz.e: He says he has never been even for one day her friend, and that her love for Dmitry rests on his insulting her, and then declares he does not want to sit next to a crack-up.

quiz.q: How does Ivan leave the room?
o: He quotes Schiller in German, refuses her hand, and stalks out
He embraces Alyosha, weeping, and begs him to forgive his brother
He slams the door in silence, leaving Alyosha to face the room
He asks Alyosha to follow him out and walk him back to the inn
quiz.e: He recites “Den Dank, Dame, begehr ich nicht”, surprising Alyosha with his Schiller, and stalks out.

quiz.q: What favour does Katerina Ivanovna ask of Alyosha?
o: To bring Dmitry to her at once, wherever he may be hiding
To carry a letter to Lise Khokhlakova and bring back an answer
To take 200 roubles to the beaten captain Snegiryov as Dmitry’s bride
To find Grushenka’s address and report it to her at once
quiz.e: She gives him two rainbow banknotes and says Snegiryov lives on Ozyornaya Street in the house of the artisan’s widow Kalmykova.

quiz.q: What does Mrs Khokhlakova reveal in the hallway?
o: That Lise has been secretly writing to Ivan for a month
That the household has conspired to turn Katerina toward Ivan
That she means to sell her house and move to Petersburg
That Dmitry called on her the night before to beg for money
quiz.e: She says all of them, even Lise, have wished and prayed for it, and that this conspiracy is possibly the only thing keeping her in town.

chapters.title: Crack-up in the Izba
chapters.intro: Background on the Russian peasant hut, old-fashioned servile speech, poverty among minor officials, and the “little man” in Russian literature, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A traditional Russian peasant log house, usually with one main room built around a large stove.
A durable cotton cloth, usually pale yellow, once used for clothing.
Looking down on others with disdain.
Weighed down or cluttered by burdens.
An old Russian measure of liquid, about 1.2 litres. A half-shtof was a common bottle size for vodka.
British slang for lame or crippled.
A clown; a person who plays the fool.
Very hard to please; excessively particular.
Subject to sudden changes of mood.
A feeling that something is going to happen, especially something bad.
The owner of a house who rents rooms to tenants.
A craftsman who makes wooden furniture and fittings.
A metal fitting; here, an iron door handle fixed to a wall or door.
A huge brick-and-clay stove stood in the middle of an izba. It cooked food, heated the room, dried clothes, and its top was a warm place to sleep.
Peasant houses often had a “clean” room kept for visitors or the better part of the house, distinct from the passage and the working areas.
A shelf of holy icons stood in the corner opposite the stove, often with a small lamp. It was the most honoured place in the house.
In a crowded room, cords strung across a corner with sheets could be hung to make a bedroom or hide laundry.
Poor families slept on benches, built-in beds, the stove or makeshift cots made of chairs.
Spirits were commonly sold in bottles of defined size, and drunkenness among the poor was a major social problem.

In old Russia, lower-ranking people added the syllable “s” to the end of their words, a shortened form of “sudar” (sir), as a servile sign of politeness. The mannerism is called “slovoyers”, and in translations is often rendered by “sir”.
Clerks and low-ranking officers on small salaries lived close to poverty, and losing a post could bring a family to ruin.
Retired officers kept their rank in name and often liked to be addressed by it, even in poverty.
A member of the clergy ranking below a priest. A deacon’s wife was a familiar figure of provincial society.
A theme of Russian literature, from Pushkin’s “The Station Master” to Gogol’s “The Overcoat”, about poor and humiliated minor officials. Dostoevsky’s first novel, “Poor Folk” (1846), belongs to it.
Russian writers often showed a character who clowns and talks wildly out of shame or bitterness, so that humour and tragedy are mixed.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha suspect on his way to the second-grade captain’s lodgings?
o: That Dmitry himself is hiding at the captain’s lodgings
That the captain has already left town with his family
That the captain’s schoolboy son is the boy who bit him
That Katerina Ivanovna has sent someone to follow him there
quiz.e: When Katerina mentioned the captain’s boy running and crying beside his father, Alyosha felt almost sure he was the biter.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha learn at Dmitry’s lodgings?
o: That Dmitry left him a short note, which the old joiner hands over at once
That Dmitry has been missing three nights, and his landlords shield him
That Dmitry is asleep upstairs after a night of drinking, and cannot be woken
That Dmitry has gone to the monastery to see the Elder before he dies
quiz.e: The old joiner says they haven’t seen him for three nights; Alyosha concludes “they like him, so they’re giving him their support”.

quiz.q: How does Snegiryov strike Alyosha at first sight?
o: Heavy and ruddy, with a bald head and a loud commanding voice like a sergeant’s
Tall and well fed, with a neat grey beard and a military bearing
Calm and dignified, with the quiet manner of a retired officer of rank
Short and lean, with a sparse reddish beard like a bedraggled loofah
quiz.e: He speaks with an agitated, cracked humour and adds “sir” to his speech, which he says he acquired in degradation.

quiz.q: What does Snegiryov say when he learns that Ilyusha bit Alyosha?
o: He swears to flog the boy and offers to chop off four of his own fingers
He laughs it off as a schoolboy prank and offers Alyosha a glass of tea
He apologises humbly and begs Alyosha to take pity on a poor family
He ignores it entirely and changes the subject to his wife’s illness
quiz.e: Alyosha says he does not want the boy flogged; Snegiryov nonetheless works himself into a frenzy.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha say Dmitry would do to make amends?
o: Pay Snegiryov a handsome sum in compensation for the insult
Beg forgiveness before everyone, even kneeling in the inn or square
Meet him in a duel, on whatever terms Snegiryov cares to name
Leave town for good and never trouble Snegiryov’s family again
quiz.e: He says Dmitry repents and would kneel if asked. Snegiryov is “too, too touched”.

quiz.q: What upsets Arina Petrovna, Snegiryov’s wife?
o: That her air is thought foul, and she weeps and begs forgiveness
That Alyosha was not properly introduced to her by her husband
That the stove has gone out and there is no wood to relight it
That Ilyusha has not come home from school and she fears for him
quiz.e: She says even a general told her to open a window because her air was not fresh, and weeps; Snegiryov dashes to her, kissing her hands.

quiz.q: Which member of the family is a lame hunchback of about twenty?
o: Arina Petrovna, the captain’s wife and mother
Varvara Nikolayevna, who stands by the window
The landlady’s daughter, who keeps the house
Nina Nikolayevna, a daughter of the captain
quiz.e: Nina is described with withered legs and crutches beside her, and with kind, beautiful eyes; Varvara is the disdainful girl by the window.

quiz.q: How does Snegiryov end the visit?
o: He sends Alyosha off rudely, shouting that he wants no charity here
He seizes Alyosha’s arm for a serious word outside and hurries him out
He invites Alyosha to stay for dinner and meet Ilyusha behind the curtain
He asks Alyosha to wait for Dmitry, who he says will come at noon
quiz.e: After Varvara scolds him for his clowning, he seizes Alyosha’s arm and hurries him out.

chapters.title: And Out in the Fresh Air
chapters.intro: Background on duels and honour, the law courts, women’s higher education, medical treatment and travel in Russia, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A leisurely walk, especially one taken for pleasure or show.
An old-fashioned way of saying to go somewhere.
Was proper or necessary for (“it behoved him to speak”).
French-derived word for a woman student attending the women’s higher courses of the period.
A covered wagon or sledge used in Russian travel; a light carriage with a hood.
An old word for a clown or buffoon.
Reluctant to speak about one’s feelings; reserved.
To soothe or lessen pain, hunger or grief.
A person who does another’s bidding, especially one who is used.
Not belonging to the matter in hand; irrelevant.
Too great to be expressed in words.
To come alive; to become active.
A stone beside a road marking distance; in Russia, usually in versts.

A duel was a formal fight with swords or pistols between two men to settle a point of honour. In Russia it was largely a custom of officers and gentlemen, and forbidden by law yet tolerated. Each man chose a “second” to arrange the terms and act as his representative.
In the code of honour, to “give satisfaction” meant to accept a challenge to a duel after an insult.
The judicial reforms of 1864 introduced public trials, juries and justices of the peace. Yet going to law was still expensive, and a poor litigant often feared a powerful opponent.
A creditor who held a person’s signed receipts or notes could use them to take him to court for debt.
Every official had a “service list”, an official record of postings, rewards and offences. Being struck off, or having a good entry, mattered for pensions and careers.
People of modest means lent small sums and often struggled to recover them.

From the late 1860s Russian women pressed for higher education. Courses for women opened in St Petersburg, Moscow and other cities, and many young women moved there to study and to take part in the movement for women’s rights.
The capital stood on the Neva River and was the centre of government, the universities and radical student circles.
Physicians prescribed mineral waters, baths and footbaths for rheumatism, and the pharmacy sold bottled mineral water.
A poor clerk or retired officer might earn only a small number of roubles a month, so 200 roubles was a major sum.
A province in central Russia, south of Moscow, known for its black earth, farming and its fair.
Kite flying was a popular boys’ pastime, and in autumn the sky over Russian towns was often full of them.
Without railways, families moved by cart, with the family riding and the man walking beside the horse. Horses held a special place in rural Russian life.
Heavy drinking was common among poor men in the period, and was spoken of with both sympathy and shame.
To pull a man by the beard in public was a grave insult, since the beard was a sign of dignity.

quiz.q: What did Ilyusha do when his father was dragged by the beard into the square?
o: He begged the attacker “forgive him” and kissed his hand
He ran to fetch the police from the station house by the market
He ran home to his mother and sisters, crying out for help
He flew at Dmitry and pelted him with stones from the road
quiz.e: Snegiryov recounts that the boy cried “Papa!”, threw himself on him, embraced the insulter and kissed his hand, asking forgiveness for his father.

quiz.q: Why does Snegiryov say he could not challenge Dmitry to a duel?
o: Because his faith forbids a man to take up arms against his neighbour
Because Dmitry had already apologised to him through Alyosha
Because he has no pistol and cannot afford to buy or hire one
Because if he were killed or maimed, nobody would feed his family
quiz.e: He lists the dependent “lower depths” in his household and concludes that a duel would be a stupid idea.

quiz.q: Why does he say he did not take Dmitry to court?
o: He could not afford a lawyer, and no advocate would take his case
Grushenka threatened to expose his crooked dealings and have him fired
The case was thrown out by the justice of the peace before it began
The Elder Zosima counselled him to forgive and forget the insult
quiz.e: He says Grushenka threatened to have him dismissed and exposed for crooked dealings carried out at her and Fyodor Pavlovich’s bidding.

quiz.q: What does Ilyusha say he will do when he grows up?
o: To become a monk like Alyosha and spend his life praying for his father’s enemies
To run away to another town and never again speak to a single schoolmate
To become an officer and, sword in hand, challenge Dmitry and forgive him
To become a lawyer and sue every schoolboy who ever threw a stone at him
quiz.e: The boy had also asked whether rich people are the strongest in the world and said the Tsar would give him a medal.

quiz.q: What dream do father and son share on their walk?
o: To buy a horse and cart and move to a town where no one knows them
To build a house of their own out on the common beyond the town
To save up for a small shop on the market square of the town
To take the train to Petersburg and find the boy a better school
quiz.e: They imagine setting off with the women covered up in the back, and Ilyusha begs for a raven-black horse.

quiz.q: What does Snegiryov say he will do with the 200 roubles?
o: Pay off his debts to Fyodor Pavlovich and settle with the landlady
Buy Ilyusha a sword and a uniform so he can enlist as an officer
Give half back to Alyosha as thanks and keep the other half
Better feed his family, send Varvara to Petersburg, and move away
quiz.e: He also mentions a lawyer friend in Kursk province who might give him a clerk’s post.

quiz.q: What “conjuring trick” does Snegiryov perform?
o: He folds them into his sleeve with a conjurer’s flourish and bows
He crushes both notes and stamps on them in the sand
He tears them in half and presses one half back into Alyosha’s hand
He holds a match to them to show how little he thinks of money
quiz.e: Having seemed overjoyed, he suddenly grinds the notes underfoot with savage malice.

quiz.q: What happens at the end of the chapter?
o: Snegiryov comes back ashamed, picks up the notes and thanks Alyosha
Alyosha runs after him and presses the notes into his coat pocket
Snegiryov runs off in tears, and Alyosha takes the notes to Katerina
Alyosha leaves the notes lying in the sand and walks off, defeated
quiz.e: He blows a kiss, turns back in tears and wails his last words, and Alyosha, knowing the man had not planned it, smooths out the unharmed notes.

chapters.title: A Betrothal
chapters.intro: Background on provincial Russian households, nineteenth-century medicine and manners, and a famous Russian comedy, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A medical term for general weakness and lack of energy.
An old-fashioned term for any serious illness with high fever and delirium, thought to be an inflammation of the brain.
A state of confused, feverish raving in which a person does not know what is real.
A memory of the past, or the act of recalling it.
French for “on the subject of”; concerning.
French for “between two”: done by two people together.
French for “Thank you, Mamma.” Educated Russian families often spoke French at home.
A person who gives help or money to someone.
Someone who makes a show of minor rules and fine points of learning.
A stiff cotton fabric with a raised ribbed pattern, used for waistcoats and summer clothes.
Felt made from goat hair, used for hats.
A sleeveless, buttoned garment worn under a jacket; a vest.
The care of God over the world; also, a person who watches over and guides your life.
Not honorable; mean or low in character.
A wheeled chair for an invalid, pushed by an attendant.

Russians are addressed by first name plus a name from the father’s first name: Aleksey Fyodorovich is “Aleksey, son of Fyodor.” A woman’s form ends in -ovna, as in Katerina Osipovna. This polite form is used between people who are not close.
Russian names have pet forms: Aleksey becomes Alyosha, Elizaveta becomes Lise. The affectionate form shows intimacy.
In the mid-1800s a widowed lady of property might run a large house with servants, daughters and visiting relatives. Aunts and other relatives often stepped in when a young woman fell ill.

Doctors had few effective treatments. “Nerves,” “hysterics” and “fevers” were common diagnoses, and rest, sedatives and bedside watching were the usual care. A family physician often attended a household for years.
Young unmarried women were expected to be chaperoned, and letters between a young man and woman were improper unless they were engaged. Parents often read or screened their daughters’ mail.

A comedy in verse by Aleksandr Griboyedov (written 1823, published after his death in 1829), one of the best-known plays in Russian. Chatsky, a clever young man, returns to Moscow society and falls out with its conservative establishment. Famusov is the pompous, status-conscious head of a household, and his daughter Sofya is the girl Chatsky loves. Educated Russian readers knew its lines and characters so well that they became everyday shorthand.
In Orthodox custom it is common to make the sign of the cross over someone who is leaving, as a wish for God’s protection.
Orthodox Christians pray for the dying and the departed and ask others to do so. Monasteries keep long lists of names to pray for.
A spiritual guide in Russian monasticism, an experienced monk whom others consult for advice and healing of the soul. People sometimes called him “father.”
“Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters”
A line from the Book of Genesis describing God’s Spirit at the creation of the world; people used it when speaking of God’s presence in some matter.
A way of describing raw, physical, passionate energy; “earth” in Russian thought also meant native soil and the common people.

quiz.q: What does Mrs Khokhlakova first tell Alyosha when he arrives?
o: Lise has fallen ill overnight and the doctor has been sent for
Katerina Ivanovna swooned after hysterics and now lies in fever
Herzenstube has examined Katerina Ivanovna and pronounced her quite well
Katerina Ivanovna has quietly left town with Ivan for Moscow
quiz.e: She reports that Katerina Ivanovna collapsed, is feverish and raving, and that Herzenstube and her aunts have been sent for. She fears it may be brain fever.

quiz.q: Alyosha tells Lise he did not deliver the two hundred roubles. How does he explain why this is for the best?
o: The captain would only have drunk the money away with his cronies
Alyosha dropped the envelope on the road and never found it again
Lise had begged him to keep the money until the following morning
Having proved his honour, the captain will likely take it tomorrow
quiz.e: He argues that had the captain taken the money he would have wept over his degradation, whereas now, proud and in need, he will likely take it the next day.

quiz.q: Lise asks whether their analysis of the captain’s soul contains an element of what?
o: Contempt toward the captain
Envy of the captain’s freedom
Fear of the captain’s violence
Pity for the captain’s daughters
quiz.e: Alyosha replies firmly that there is no contempt in it, since everyone is the same as the captain and he himself has a petty soul.

quiz.q: What does Lise confess to Alyosha with her hand over her eyes?
o: That she would never agree to see him again after today
That she had already told her mother everything he said
That yesterday’s letter was meant in earnest, not as a joke
That she secretly meant to enter a convent after all
quiz.e: She confesses that the letter was in earnest and kisses his hand three times. Alyosha says he was certain it was serious.

quiz.q: What clothes does Lise tell Alyosha she wants him to wear when he leaves the monastery?
o: A dark-blue velvet coat, white piqué waistcoat and grey felt hat
A black frock coat, grey silk waistcoat and a glossy top hat
A grey military greatcoat, tall boots and a peaked officer’s cap
A white linen suit, a pale cravat and a broad-brimmed straw hat
quiz.e: She says it is very important to her, and Alyosha answers that he will wear whatever she likes.

quiz.q: What agreement do Alyosha and Lise reach about eavesdropping and submission?
o: Lise will read all his letters openly, and he must answer each at once
Lise vows never to spy on him, and they agree to submit to each other’s judgement
Alyosha promises to report every conversation to Mrs Khokhlakova, who will arbitrate
Alyosha refuses to discuss the matter, and Lise agrees to ask no more questions
quiz.e: Lise first says she will spy on him, then swears she never will because he finds it ignoble. Alyosha reserves the right to act on duty in important matters.

quiz.q: What troubling statement does Alyosha make about himself and his faith?
o: That he is sure he must remain a monk for the rest of his life
That he has decided to burn Lise’s letter unread before he sees her again
That he wants to follow Ivan abroad as soon as the Elder is buried
That he is a Karamazov and perhaps does not even believe in God
quiz.e: He says his brothers and father are ruining themselves with the “earthen force of the Karamazovs” and that he is a Karamazov too. He adds that it is possible he does not believe in God, and that his dying friend’s departure leaves him alone.

quiz.q: What does Mrs Khokhlakova demand of Alyosha on the staircase, and what is his answer?
o: She demands the two hundred roubles for Katerina Ivanovna; he gives them to her at once
She asks him to carry a message to Ivan about the engagement; he agrees and runs off
She demands Lise’s letter, which he refuses to give, promising to call tomorrow
She demands he marry Lise at once to save her reputation; he agrees and kisses her hand
quiz.e: She calls it folly, threatens to forbid him the house, compares the scene to Woe from Wit, and begs for the letter. Alyosha refuses, says he will come tomorrow, and runs off.

chapters.title: Smerdyakov with a Guitar
chapters.intro: Background on servants and the lower middle class in provincial Russia, Napoleon’s invasion, duels and Moscow, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A male servant in livery; also an insulting word for a servile person.
A high, light male singing voice above the normal range.
A high adult male singing voice.
With the hair dressed with scented grease to make it smooth and glossy.
Leather with a hard, shiny, varnished surface, worn on dressy shoes.
A Russian unit of length equal to about 71 centimeters (28 inches). “Two arshins” is a little over four and a half feet.
A soldier in the light cavalry, famous for showy uniforms and daring.
A young trainee at a military school.
A man who is very concerned with fashionable clothes and appearance.
To ask for something persistently and annoyingly.
In a calm manner that cannot be upset.
To smile in a silly, affected way.
Flattering someone in a servile, over-eager way.
Dreamy, slow and lazy, often in a romantic way.
To grant or give, as a favor.
Large households employed cooks, footmen and housekeepers. A trained cook could rise to a respectable trade, and Moscow and St Petersburg had many restaurants and cafés.
A class of small townspeople: shopkeepers, craftsmen, clerks and their families. They ranked below the gentry and were often the daughters and sons of local landladies and small proprietors.
A young woman who had spent time in Moscow often came home with city fashions, such as long-trained dresses, and with airs and romantic notions picked up from novels.

In 1812 Napoleon I (Emperor of the French) led a huge army into Russia and reached Moscow, which was set on fire. The army was destroyed during its winter retreat. In Russia it is remembered as the “Patriotic War.” The Emperor who ruled France in the 1870s was Napoleon III, Napoleon I’s nephew.
Among nobles and officers, a duel with pistols or swords was the traditional way to settle a point of honor, though Russian law forbade it. Writers such as Pushkin and Lermontov both died in duels.
A well-known, busy street in central Moscow with shops, restaurants and trading houses.
On a town plot, a main house often had a smaller cottage in the yard let to tenants, with a garden, a wicker or board fence and a gate padlocked at night.
Until 1861 millions of Russian peasants were serfs bound to their landlord’s estate. After emancipation their families moved into service and the towns, and some resented their low origin.
The town police and local officials. Reporting a threat to them meant going to the police.

A long argument among educated Russians: Westernizers held that Russia should follow Europe in law, learning and manners, while Slavophiles held that Russia’s own faith and customs were superior. Both sides existed in the 1870s, along with people who simply admired anything foreign.
An enthusiasm for French culture, fashion and language, common among the Russian upper and aspiring classes since the 1700s.
Servants and townspeople sang sentimental songs about love, sickness and parting, often accompanied by a guitar, which was a very popular household instrument.

quiz.q: Why does Alyosha go back to the garden and the summerhouse?
o: To meet Grushenka secretly before she goes to Fyodor Pavlovich
To question Foma and the cottage mistress about Dmitry’s debts
To lie in wait for Dmitry, certain that a catastrophe is coming
To retrieve a letter he left behind in the summerhouse that morning
quiz.e: He sneaks over the wicker fence again to ambush Dmitry, convinced that a terrible catastrophe is coming and that he must see him before returning to the dying Elder.

quiz.q: Who is singing to a guitar, and who is he with?
o: Smerdyakov, in his Sunday best, with Marya Kondratyevna
Grigory, humming old hymns, with Marfa on the back steps
Dmitry, drunk and alone, under the window of the cottage
Ivan, in a mocking mood, with Grushenka by the fence
quiz.e: Alyosha recognises the voice and then sees Smerdyakov, pomaded and in patent-leather shoes, beside Marya Kondratyevna, a freckled, round-faced young woman in a blue dress with a long train.

quiz.q: What is Smerdyakov’s view of verse?
o: That verses are beautiful but far too difficult for him to learn
That verses are rubbish, since no one in the world talks in rhyme
That he writes verses himself and reads them to the landlady’s daughter
That only the clergy should be allowed to sing them in public
quiz.e: He tells Marya Kondratyevna that “the essential of verses is that they’re rubbish,” and asks who talks in rhyme.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov say about the French invasion of 1812?
o: That he is proud of how the Russian peasants rose up and drove Napoleon out
That Russian soldiers should have been better paid and better fed after the war
That he himself would gladly have become a soldier in the campaign against France
That a clever nation would have done well to conquer a stupid one like Russia
quiz.e: He also says he hates all Russia and wishes the destruction of all soldiers. He claims the Russian people need the whip.

quiz.q: What future does Smerdyakov imagine for himself?
o: To take monastic vows at the monastery after the Elder dies
To go to Moscow and open a café-restaurant on the Petrovka
To inherit a large share of Fyodor Pavlovich’s money and leave
To study at a university in Petersburg on a merchant’s grant
quiz.e: He calls himself a professional cook and a mere “bouillon-boy,” but says that with a bit of luck, and some money, he could open a café-restaurant in Moscow.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov say Dmitry has threatened him with?
o: Dismissal from service, should he carry tales to Fyodor Pavlovich
Death, should he let Grushenka into the house to spend the night
A thrashing, should he be caught talking with Ivan in the yard
A lawsuit, should he ever claim a share of the old man’s money
quiz.e: He says Dmitry has pressed him for news of the master and twice threatened him with death. Marya Kondratyevna adds that Dmitry said he would crush him in a mortar.

quiz.q: What news does Smerdyakov give Alyosha about Ivan, and what does he ask in return?
o: Ivan has left for Moscow already; he asks Alyosha to follow him there
Ivan has fallen ill with fever at home; he asks Alyosha to fetch the doctor
Ivan has been waiting all day at Katerina Ivanovna’s; he asks Alyosha to fetch him
Ivan sent him to fetch Dmitry to the inn; he begs Alyosha not to tell
quiz.e: Smerdyakov says Ivan sent him that morning to call Dmitry to the inn on the market square. He begs Alyosha to say nothing, because Dmitry would kill him.

quiz.q: How does Alyosha end up sitting with Ivan?
o: Ivan shouts down from an inn window and invites him upstairs
Ivan is waiting for him at the monastery gate with a carriage
Smerdyakov guides him by the arm to the table where Ivan sits
He finds Ivan and Dmitry already quarrelling over their father’s money
quiz.e: Alyosha is hesitant to go into the inn dressed as he is, but Ivan shouts down from a window and invites him up to sit with him.

chapters.title: The Brothers Become Acquainted
chapters.intro: Background on Russian inns and young intellectuals, Euclid and non-Euclidean geometry, Voltaire, and the ideas of belief and doubt, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A mechanical or hand-cranked musical instrument, a kind of street organ.
A puzzling, mysterious person or thing.
Fresh and clean, in its original untouched state.
Like a young bird with a yellow beak: young and green, inexperienced. In Russian the idiom is “yellow-mouthed.”
The loss of illusions; disappointment about how life really is.
Suffering from tuberculosis (“consumption”); also, thin and weak.
A timid, weak man who lacks spirit.
The force that pulls a moving object toward the center of its path; here, a force of attraction that holds things together.
French for “professions of faith”: declarations of one’s beliefs.
A person devoted to physical pleasure and luxury.
A clown or fool who jokes to amuse others.
A French-style word for something typically and peculiarly Russian.
To speak in a vague way in order to avoid committing yourself.
Living forever, or the continued existence of the soul after death.
A political belief that rules and government should be abolished.
A hypothesis is a proposed explanation not yet proven; an axiom is a statement accepted as self-evidently true.

A provincial inn had a main hall, side rooms behind screens or doors, a counter, waiters in white and often billiards and a mechanical organ. Merchants, clerks and students met there to eat, drink tea and talk.

Girls from the upper classes were often educated in boarding schools called institutes, where they lived, studied and were trained for polite society. “An institute girl” suggested a well-bred, educated young lady.
Fruit preserves (varenye) served alongside tea is a Russian custom. Fish soup (ukha) is a traditional dish.
Wealthy and educated Russians commonly traveled to Western Europe for study, health cures and sightseeing.

Russian thinkers of the 1800s spoke of the “eternal” or “accursed” questions: whether God exists, whether the soul is immortal, what makes life meaningful, how to build a just society. Debates on these were a feature of student and intellectual life.
Young educated Russians were drawn to various socialist and radical movements, many inspired by writers in Europe. Some believed society had to be rebuilt on a new basis.
The geometry described by the Greek mathematician Euclid (about 300 BC). It works on a flat surface, and a key rule is that parallel lines never meet however far they extend.

In the 1800s mathematicians such as Lobachevsky (a Russian) and Riemann developed geometries in which parallel lines can meet or diverge, showing that Euclid’s was one possible description of space. Popular science writers discussed the idea of curved space and extra dimensions.

The French writer Voltaire (1694-1778), a leading figure of the Enlightenment and often critical of the Church, wrote that “if God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him.” The remark is often quoted in debates about religion.
An eighteenth-century European movement stressing reason, science and individual freedom over tradition and religious authority.
Agnostics hold that God’s existence cannot be known; atheists hold that there is no God. Discussions of both were fashionable among Russian students in the 1860s-70s.
The Gospel of John begins: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” “Logos” is Greek for word, reason or principle.
In Genesis, Cain kills his brother Abel. When God asks where Abel is, Cain answers, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” The phrase is used when someone denies responsibility for another.
A novice is a person on probation in a monastery who has not yet taken permanent vows.

quiz.q: Where are Ivan and Alyosha sitting, and what does Ivan order for Alyosha?
o: A private room upstairs; roast meat, pickles and a bottle of wine
The inn garden under the lindens; kvass, black bread and cheese
A screened-off corner; fish soup, tea and cherry preserves
The billiard room at the back; tea, sugar-cake and plum jam
quiz.e: It is not really a private room but a window place divided off by a folding screen. Ivan orders fish soup, tea and cherry preserves, which Alyosha loved as a boy.

quiz.q: Why does Ivan say he never approached Alyosha during the three months he has been in town?
o: He could not stand Alyosha’s expectant look, but now respects him
He was occupied with Katerina Ivanovna and had no time for family
He thought Alyosha disliked him and had sided with their brother Dmitry
He wanted to avoid their father and so kept clear of the whole family
quiz.e: Ivan says that look repelled him, but that he has learned to respect Alyosha, who knows how to stand his ground.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha say he has worked out about Ivan since this morning?
o: That he is secretly in love with Katerina Ivanovna, whatever he says
That he is plotting to do some harm to their father before leaving
That he is a thorough unbeliever who has long ago lost his faith
That he is just a yellow-beaked boy of twenty-three like any other
quiz.e: Ivan is delighted, because the same thought about his own “yellow-beakedness” had been occupying him.

quiz.q: What does Ivan say about his “thirst for life”?
o: It will fade away as soon as he has seen the cities of Europe
It will carry him to thirty, whatever disenchantment he feels
It is a base trait of the Karamazov blood he is ashamed of
It is a gift from God, for which he gives humble thanks
quiz.e: He says even if he lost faith in the order of things he would still drink the cup of life until he is about thirty. He loves life “with one’s insides, one’s belly,” not logic.

quiz.q: According to Alyosha, what is the “second half” of Ivan’s task, now that he loves life?
o: To forgive their father for everything he has done to them
To enter the monastery and take up the Elder’s place
To raise up his dead, who may perhaps never have died
To marry Katerina Ivanovna and settle down in Moscow
quiz.e: Alyosha says that Ivan, having already won the love of life, must now apply himself to raising up his dead, “which may never perhaps have died.”

quiz.q: How does Ivan describe his feelings about Katerina Ivanovna, and how does Alyosha react to the idea of champagne?
o: Ivan feels free and loves her not at all; Alyosha declines, feeling sad
Ivan says he still adores her; Alyosha eagerly orders the champagne for them
Ivan is sorrowful about her; Alyosha leaves the inn at once in tears
Ivan says he will marry her soon; Alyosha raises a toast to them both
quiz.e: Ivan is jovial, relieved to be free of nearly half a year of torment, and wants champagne to celebrate. Alyosha says they had better not drink, as he feels sad.

quiz.q: What does Ivan say when Alyosha asks what will become of Dmitry and their father?
o: He promises to stay on in town and keep watch over them both
He says he will leave Smerdyakov to look after the old man and Dmitry
He asks Alyosha to take Dmitry abroad and away from Grushenka
He snaps that he is not Dmitry’s keeper, like Cain, and is leaving
quiz.e: Ivan bitterly alludes to Cain’s reply to God. He adds that he has finished his tasks and cannot remain their keeper.

quiz.q: What does Ivan say Russian boys do when they meet in a place like this inn?
o: Play billiards, drink and wager money on each game until midnight
Discuss the eternal questions: God, immortality, socialism, anarchism
Argue over land, money and property, and who will inherit what
Sing folk songs and recite verses by Pushkin to one another
quiz.e: He says they huddle in corners and discuss the questions of the universe, and those who don’t believe in God speak of socialism and anarchism, which is the same question “from the other end.”

quiz.q: What is Ivan’s position on God, as he states it?
o: He accepts God, but rejects the whole world that God created
He denies that God exists and mocks all who say He does
He thinks God a human invention and gives the matter no thought
He believes in eternal harmony but cannot accept any personal God
quiz.e: He says, “It isn’t God I don’t accept, it’s the world created by Him,” even if the final harmony is revealed.

quiz.q: Why does Ivan bring up Euclid and parallel lines?
o: To show off the mathematical education he received at Moscow University
To prove that God designed the world with perfect geometrical order
To say his Euclidean mind cannot grasp God, whatever geometry shows
To mock Alyosha’s piety by comparing his faith to a geometry lesson
quiz.e: Ivan says his mind is Euclidean and made for three dimensions, so he leaves such questions aside. He adds that even if the parallel lines converge and he sees it, he will not accept it.

chapters.title: Mutiny
chapters.intro: Background on Orthodox saints, the Bulgarian crisis of the 1870s, serfdom, Russian courts and juries, the poet Nekrasov and the Book of Genesis, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes upsetting accounts of cruelty to children and other violence, presented within a serious philosophical argument. Read it when you are ready for that.
A person who travels from place to place, such as a wandering beggar.
A person who gives money or goods to the poor.
Greek for desire or longing; in Christian writing, a strong craving or passion, sometimes taken on deliberately as a discipline.
Repayment, reward or punishment given in return for an act.
A young descendant or member of a family.
Excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures such as drink and sex.
A worn-out, ill-tempered or broken-down horse.
A heavy Russian whip of leather thongs, used in beating punishment.
A fixed regular payment, such as a scholarship or allowance.
A tall, thin Russian hunting dog used to chase wolves and hares.
A monk who has taken the highest and strictest degree of monastic vows (the “great schema”).
A large, imposing building; also, a large structure of ideas or society.
To speak with disrespect of God or sacred things.
Held in custody; kept under guard or supervision.
The Russian word poema means a long narrative poem, as distinct from a short lyric.
