Until Tsar Alexander II’s emancipation in 1861, Russian landowners owned peasants (serfs) attached to their estates. A landlord could buy, sell, punish and in practice dispose of his serfs. The ruler who freed them is called the “Liberator.” The size of an estate was counted in “souls”, meaning male serfs.
Flogging with birch rods, the lash and the knout was a normal punishment in Russia for peasants, soldiers and convicts. It was abolished for most of the population in the 1860s.

Alexander II’s legal reforms created public trials, trial by jury and a professional bar of defence lawyers. Juries sometimes acquitted defendants, and public opinion and the press debated the verdicts.
Under the new system lawyers (advokaty) argued cases in open court. Some were admired, and some were mocked, as the popular saying implies, as speaking for pay.

Bulgaria was part of the Ottoman (Turkish) Empire. In 1876 an uprising there was crushed with great brutality by irregular Turkish troops, and the news shocked Europe. Russian public opinion strongly supported the Slavic Christians and Russia declared war on Turkey in 1877. The Circassians were Muslim peoples from the Caucasus who had been resettled in Ottoman lands.
Geneva was the center of Calvinist Protestantism and had a reputation for strict morality and charity.
Russian Archive (Russkii arkhiv) and Russian Antiquity (Russkaya starina) were real monthly journals publishing old memoirs, letters and documents from the 1700s and 1800s.
In the 1870s some members of the Russian upper class, influenced by foreign evangelical preachers (including Lutherans), took an interest in revivalist and charitable religion.
A seventh-century Patriarch of Alexandria in Egypt, remembered for giving away the Church’s wealth to the poor. Lives of saints (hagiography) told many stories of his charity.

In the Book of Genesis, Adam and Eve ate the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, against God’s command. The serpent promised that they would be “as gods, knowing good and evil.” Christians traditionally call this the Fall, and say its effects were passed on to later generations as original sin.

The Old Testament says God visits the guilt of the fathers upon later generations (Exodus 20). Other passages, such as Ezekiel 18, say each person is responsible only for their own sin. Theologians debate how the two fit together.

In a parable in the Gospel of Luke (chapter 15), a young man who wastes his inheritance ends up so hungry that he longs to eat the husks fed to the pigs, then returns home repentant and is welcomed by his father.
A vision in the Book of Isaiah (chapter 11) of a peaceful future in which predators and prey live together.
A line from the Book of Revelation (15:3): “Just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.” The Orthodox liturgy uses similar language of praise.
A Christian title for Jesus Christ, who in doctrine is without sin and whose suffering is believed to redeem humanity.
The branch of theology and philosophy that tries to explain how a good, all-powerful God can allow evil and suffering.
A major Russian poet and journal editor whose poems depict the suffering of the peasants and the poor. Dostoevsky and Nekrasov knew each other from the 1840s.
In Shakespeare’s Hamlet, Polonius is the talkative old counselor to the king of Denmark, fond of clever turns of phrase and of repeating proverbs.

quiz.q: What is Ivan’s opening confession about love?
o: He loves every human being equally, whether near or far away
He cannot love his neighbour up close, only people far away
He has never loved anyone at all, not even his own brothers
He loves only the poor and the humble, and none of the rich
quiz.e: Ivan says he has never understood how one can love one’s neighbour. In his view, once a person shows his face, love disappears. He cites the story of Ioann the Almsgiver as a case of dutiful, hysterical love.

quiz.q: Why does Ivan choose to talk about the suffering of children?
o: Because he saw such cruelty with his own eyes in Geneva as a boy
Because children are stronger than adults and endure suffering better
Because adults are too corrupt to be moved by any suffering at all
Because they have not eaten the apple and are guilty of nothing
quiz.e: Ivan says adults have eaten of the apple and have requital, whereas small children are as yet guilty of nothing and are a different species. He says it narrows his topic about tenfold.

quiz.q: What hobby does Ivan say he has?
o: Collecting anecdotes of cruelty from newspapers and reports
Writing satirical verse about the monks and landowners he knows
Collecting old books on theology and the lives of the saints
Keeping hunting dogs and training them on his father’s estate
quiz.e: He says he cuts out and notes down small facts from newspapers and reports, foreign and “home-bred,” and calls it a fine collection.

quiz.q: How does the story of Richard from Geneva end?
o: He escapes from prison and goes back to the mountains and shepherds
He is pardoned by the pious citizens of Geneva after his conversion
He goes to the guillotine, hailed by Geneva as a repentant brother
He becomes a pastor and preaches to the other prisoners in Geneva
quiz.e: Richard, brought up almost like an animal by shepherds, committed murder and was condemned. In prison he was taught the faith, and he went to the scaffold repeating that he was going to the Lord. Ivan calls it characteristic.

quiz.q: What scene from Nekrasov does Ivan describe?
o: A muzhik lashing a horse across its meek eyes to haul his cart
A peasant wedding in which the bride is dragged to church in tears
A landowner selling his serfs one by one at the provincial fair
A soldier taking his farewell of mother and village at dawn
quiz.e: Ivan calls the flogging of a horse a Russian specialty, a russisme, and says the poet’s scene is terrible.

quiz.q: In Ivan’s story of the cultured father who beat his daughter, how did the trial end?
o: The father was sentenced to hard labour in Siberia for years
The jury acquitted him, the advocate calling it a family matter
The mother was found guilty of neglect and sent to a convent
The case was dropped before it reached the court, by arrangement
quiz.e: Ivan quotes the Russian saying “the advocate is a hired conscience” and says the jury returned a verdict of not guilty, to the roar of the crowd.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha say when Ivan asks what should be done with the general who set his dogs on the serf boy?
o: “Forgive him,” he says gently, with a calm and tender smile
“Send him to Siberia,” he says firmly, staring at the floor
“Make him beg the mother’s pardon,” he says, voice trembling
“Shoot him!” he says quietly, with a pale, distorted smile
quiz.e: Alyosha says it quietly, with a pale, distorted smile. Ivan cries “Bravo!” and calls him a fine schemonach with a little devil in his heart.

quiz.q: What does Ivan say he is doing with “eternal harmony,” and what does Alyosha call it?
o: He gladly accepts it in the end as his reward; Alyosha calls it faith
He postpones it to the next life, content to wait; Alyosha calls it patience
He returns his ticket to God respectfully; Alyosha calls it mutiny
He demands his full share of it from God; Alyosha calls it greed
quiz.e: Ivan says no harmony is worth one tortured child’s tears. He adds that it is not God but His ticket he returns. Alyosha says quietly, “That is mutiny.”

quiz.q: What does Ivan ask Alyosha about building an edifice of human happiness, and how does Alyosha reply?
o: Would he be the architect at the price of one tortured child; Alyosha says no
Would he help Ivan to flee abroad after quarrelling with Dmitry; Alyosha says yes
Would he renounce his faith for the happiness of mankind; Alyosha says he would
Would he forgive their father if he repented before the Elder; Alyosha says he would
quiz.e: Alyosha says no, and that he cannot believe the people would agree to be happy on those terms.

quiz.q: How does Alyosha answer Ivan’s question about whether any being has the right to forgive?
o: That no being whatever has that right, so the tears must stay unforgiven
That one Being has that right, who shed His innocent blood for all
That only the mother of the tortured child can forgive, and no one else
That the Church holds that right and may exercise it in God’s name
quiz.e: Ivan replies that he has not forgotten “the only sinless one” and that he once composed a poema, which he calls “The Grand Inquisitor.”

chapters.title: The Grand Inquisitor
chapters.intro: Background on the Spanish Inquisition, the Gospel temptation accounts, the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant divide and medieval religious drama, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: The Russian word for a long narrative poem. It can also be used loosely for any ambitious imaginative work.
The front part of a theatre stage, in front of the curtain; by extension, the stage itself.
An open space or enclosed court in front of a church, often with a porch or steps.
A long, close-fitting garment worn by clergy and monks.
A member of a monastic community who lives in common with others, as opposed to a hermit.
A person who asks humbly and earnestly for something, especially in prayer.
A person who rebels against authority, originally against a ship’s officers.
Latin and French for “one thing for another”: a mistake in which one person or thing is taken for another.
Cannibalism; the eating of human flesh.
German for “world-pain”: a deep, sad feeling about the imperfection of the world.
Gloomy and funereal, like a tomb.
A bishop, and in particular the Pope.
Latin for “to the greater glory of God.” It is the motto of the Jesuit order.
Latin for “I have spoken.” It is used to close a speech or argument.
Speaking or writing about someone in an abusively critical way.
A lover, especially one outside marriage.

A church-and-state court set up in 1478 by King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella to enforce Catholic orthodoxy in Spain. It investigated converts from Judaism and Islam and, later, suspected Protestants, and it lasted until 1834. Tomás de Torquemada was its first Inquisitor General.
A belief that contradicts the official teaching of a church. In the Middle Ages and early modern period it was treated as a crime against both church and state.

Portuguese for “act of faith.” It was a public ceremony in which the Inquisition announced its verdicts, with processions, sermons and sentences. Those condemned to death were handed over to the civil authorities for burning.
A major city in southern Spain, in Andalusia. It was a wealthy port and the seat of the first Inquisition tribunal, set up in 1480. Its Gothic cathedral is one of the largest in Europe.
A senior Catholic official appointed by the Pope, ranking just below him. Cardinals wear red and elect each new Pope.

The Society of Jesus, a Catholic order founded in 1540 by Ignatius of Loyola. It was known for education, missions and loyalty to the Pope, and in Protestant and Orthodox countries it had a reputation for cunning and intrigue.

Members of a secretive fraternal society with its own rituals, widespread in Europe from the eighteenth century. The Catholic Church condemned it, and Russian conservatives often suspected it of subversion.
The period of roughly two and a half centuries, from about 1240 to 1480, when the Russian principalities paid tribute to the Mongol-Tatar Golden Horde.
Russia before Peter the Great (ruled 1682-1725), who pushed westernization. Moscow before him was more insular and Byzantine in its customs and culture.

The Gospels of Matthew and Luke tell how, after forty days of fasting in the wilderness, Jesus was approached by the Devil three times. The Devil asked him to turn stones into bread, to throw himself from the pinnacle of the Temple, and to accept all the kingdoms of the world. Jesus answered each with a line from Scripture, including “man shall not live by bread alone.”

Christianity split into Eastern (Orthodox) and Western (Catholic) churches in 1054, largely over the Pope’s authority. In 1517 the Reformation, begun by Martin Luther in Germany, broke Protestant churches away from Rome in turn. Orthodox Russians traditionally viewed the Pope’s claims with suspicion.
The Pope, as Bishop of Rome, claims authority over the whole Catholic Church. Through the Middle Ages the papacy also held lands and political power in Italy.
The Christian belief that Christ will return at the end of time. The New Testament, notably the Book of Revelation, describes it in dramatic imagery.

The last book of the New Testament, a visionary and symbolic text attributed to John. Its images, such as a woman riding a beast, stars falling and numbered multitudes, have been interpreted in many ways.
A story in Genesis 11 about people who tried to build a tower to heaven. God confused their languages and scattered them.
The Catholic Church’s response in the sixteenth century to the Protestant Reformation. It stressed doctrine, discipline, new orders such as the Jesuits, and the Inquisition.

Religious dramas performed in the Middle Ages by guilds, clergy or townspeople. They staged stories from the Bible and saints’ lives, and characters such as Christ, the Virgin and angels often appeared on stage.
The Italian poet Dante Alighieri (1265-1321), author of the Divine Comedy, an epic journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise.
A French novel from 1831, known in English as The Hunchback of Notre-Dame. It is set in Paris in 1482, under Louis XI, and includes a scene of a public play staged in the city’s hall.
Louis XI ruled France from 1461 to 1483. The Dauphin was the title of the heir to the French throne.
In medieval Russia and Byzantium, monks translated and copied saints’ lives and popular religious tales, including some that were not part of the official Scriptures.
Fyodor Tyutchev (1803-1873) was a Russian lyric poet and diplomat, known for brief, philosophical poems on nature, history and Russia’s destiny, and for his deeply Orthodox patriotism.
Two famous conquerors of Asia: Timur, known in the West as Tamburlaine or Tamerlane (1336-1405), and Genghis Khan (c. 1162-1227), founder of the Mongol Empire.

quiz.q: In his preface, what literary custom does Ivan cite to introduce the idea of putting Christ into a poem?
o: That Russian folk epics always ended with a saint appearing to the hero
That poets and monks once brought Christ and the saints down to earth
That Dante had forbidden any poet from portraying Christ in verse
That medieval French law required religious plays to feature only angels
quiz.e: Ivan mentions Dante, French mystery plays, pre-Petrine Moscow and a monastic poem of the Mother of God visiting hell, all as examples of such custom.

quiz.q: Where and when is Ivan’s poem set?
o: Rome, in the reign of Pope Alexander, the day after a great procession
Moscow, in the time of the Tartar yoke, the day after a great battle
Paris, in the age of Louis XI, the day after a famous public hanging
Seville, at the height of the Inquisition, the day after a mass burning
quiz.e: Christ comes down to the hot streets of Seville the day after a magnificent auto-da-fé at which the Cardinal Grand Inquisitor burned nearly a hundred heretics.

quiz.q: Whom does He raise from the dead outside Seville Cathedral?
o: A seven-year-old girl, a citizen’s only daughter, in an open coffin
An old man who had been blind since childhood, at the cathedral steps
A young soldier killed during the auto-da-fé, laid before the church
The infant son of a poor widow, brought in on a funeral bier
quiz.e: The blind man is healed, but the child in the white coffin is raised after her mother begs Him, and she sits up with the white roses still in her arms.

quiz.q: How does the Grand Inquisitor react, and what does he say when he visits the prisoner that night?
o: He kneels and asks for His blessing, then offers Him shelter in his palace
He denounces the crowd and has the guards flogged for stirring them up
He has Him arrested and says he will burn Him tomorrow as the worst heretic
He questions Him gently about the miracle and promises to let Him leave
quiz.e: The Inquisitor points a finger, the guards arrest Him, and the awed crowd bows to the old man. At night he declares that the people who kissed His feet will rake up the embers of His bonfire.

quiz.q: According to the Inquisitor, what will people eventually say once they realize that freedom and earthly bread cannot go together?
o: “Take back your freedom and give us back our old gods.”
“Make slaves of us if you will, but only feed us at last.”
“We shall feed ourselves, and need neither Church nor Christ.”
“Let the strong rule over the weak, as it has always been.”
quiz.e: He says no science will give bread while people are free, so they will place their freedom at the Church’s feet and ask to be enslaved in return for food.

quiz.q: Which three powers does the Inquisitor say can conquer the consciences of the weak for their own happiness?
o: Wealth, written law and the sword
Fear, hunger and plain ignorance
Love, sacrifice and meek humility
Miracle, mystery and authority
quiz.e: He argues that Christ rejected all three, and that the Church has corrected His work by founding it on miracle, mystery and authority.

quiz.q: What does the Inquisitor reveal about whose side he and his kind are on?
o: They have sided with the clever Spirit for eight centuries, taking Rome and the sword
They secretly serve the king of Spain, using the Inquisition as his political weapon
They remain loyal to Christ at heart but dare not say so before the Pope and cardinals
They are the true heirs of the Tartar khans and Tamburlaine, ruling by terror
quiz.e: He says they took from the clever Spirit the final gift that Christ rejected, the kingdoms of the world, and so aim to be Caesars, though the task is not yet complete.

quiz.q: How does Alyosha react to the poem?
o: He declares it proves every Catholic is a secret atheist and should be banned
He laughs it off as a clever joke and asks Ivan to write it all down for him
He protests that it praises Jesus, and the Inquisitor simply has no faith in God
He asks whether it is quoted from Father Paisy’s sermons or the Elder’s teaching
quiz.e: Alyosha blames Rome, the Jesuits and the worst of Catholicism, and says the Inquisitor’s only secret is atheism. Ivan replies that it may well be so, and that such a man’s suffering would still be a tragedy.

quiz.q: How does Ivan say the poem ends?
o: The Prisoner curses the Inquisitor and is led off to the stake at dawn
The Prisoner kisses him; the Inquisitor frees Him but keeps to his idea
The Inquisitor kneels before Him, is converted and gives up his office
The crowd rises, frees the Prisoner by force and storms the cathedral
quiz.e: The kiss burns in the Inquisitor’s heart, he opens the door and releases the Captive into the dark streets, but he remains with his former idea.

quiz.q: How do Ivan and Alyosha part?
o: Ivan strikes Alyosha in anger for his reproach and walks off without a word
Alyosha promises to follow Ivan to Moscow, and they leave the inn together
Both agree to go to Dmitry together at once and ask his forgiveness
Alyosha silently kisses Ivan; Ivan begs silence on the subject and Dmitry
quiz.e: Alyosha kisses him (Ivan calls it “literary thieving”). Ivan then asks for silence on the subjects and on Dmitry, and promises that at thirty he will come specially, even from America, to talk with him.

chapters.title: One as Yet Very Indistinct
chapters.intro: Background on household servants, epilepsy in the nineteenth century, folk remedies and a few religious and social terms, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A male servant, such as a footman, often one who is servile.
A small gate set into, or beside, a larger gate or door.
A person’s facial features and expression, or the study of judging character from them.
Russian for a member of the Skoptsy, an outlawed religious sect whose men practised castration. The word suggested a smooth, beardless, ageless face.
Polite respect shown to someone of higher rank.
Overly concerned with minor details or formal correctness.
Brevity; the quality of saying much in few words.
Clear broth made by simmering meat or bones.
In law, a person who helps another to commit a crime, without necessarily carrying it out.
A small room just under the roof of a house, an attic.
A separate building on a property, such as a shed, lodge or servants’ quarters.
Pain in the lower back, caused by strain or stiffness.
Old word for paralysis, often with tremors.
A long, confused and meaningless set of statements.
To fit together neatly, like a joint in woodworking.
Calmness and composure, especially under pressure.

Landowners’ households relied on cooks, footmen, coachmen and nurses, many of them former serfs. Serfdom ended in 1861, but the relationship of master and servant stayed formal and unequal for decades.
Russian words for “master” and “mistress” of a house or estate, used by servants and peasants. Servants used them in place of a name.

Russians are addressed by first name plus a patronymic taken from the father’s name, such as Ivan Fyodorovich (“Ivan, son of Fyodor”). Using both shows respect, and a servant would use both in speaking to a master.
Servile speakers often ended their sentences with a deferential “sir,” which in the Russian is a tiny suffix. A heavy use of it can sound either humble or mocking, depending on the tone.
A rouble was worth 100 copecks. A servant earned only a few roubles a month, so a sum in the thousands was a large fortune to such a person.
A sect that grew out of the underground Christian movements of the eighteenth century, believing that castration brought salvation. Authorities persecuted them and exiled many to Siberia.

An old name for epilepsy, a brain disorder that causes seizures. In nineteenth-century Russia there was little effective treatment, and sufferers were often feared or pitied, and sometimes thought to be touched by divine or evil forces.

A person with epilepsy may collapse suddenly, cry out, convulse and foam at the mouth, and fail to remember the episode afterwards. Doctors of the time believed fits could sometimes be brought on by shock, injury or fear.
Ice or cold water on the head was a common nineteenth-century remedy for fever, headache and fits.
Peasant and servant households made their own tinctures, herbs soaked in vodka or spirit, used as rubbing alcohol for back pain, and sometimes drunk along with a prayer.
A small Russian town usually had one or two physicians. Many were of German or Baltic origin, and they were highly respected for their thoroughness.

In Genesis 1, God creates light on the first day, but makes the sun, moon and stars only on the fourth. Readers have long asked how light could exist before the sun, and Bible commentators have offered symbolic and literal answers.

quiz.q: What is Ivan’s state of mind as he walks home, and what does he realize when he nears the house?
o: He is overjoyed at the thought of leaving and can’t wait to pack his things
He feels growing, unaccountable anguish, and sees Smerdyakov is its cause
He feels guilty about the poem and resolves to go back and apologise to Alyosha
He worries over Katerina Ivanovna and decides to go and see her at once
quiz.e: The anguish grows with each step, and he identifies its source in a flash when he sees Smerdyakov sitting by the entrance.

quiz.q: Why had Ivan’s feelings toward Smerdyakov changed over time?
o: He first found him original, then resented his vain, secretive familiarity
He had always despised him, ever since the servant’s boyhood in the yard
Smerdyakov had once insulted the memory of Ivan’s mother before the servants
Smerdyakov had borrowed money from Ivan and never repaid a single rouble
quiz.e: They once discussed such topics as light on the first day of creation before the sun, but Ivan grew disgusted by Smerdyakov’s oblique questions and his air of a shared secret.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov first ask Ivan on the bench?
o: Whether the old master has woken from his afternoon sleep
Whether Grushenka has come to the house yet this evening
Whether Ivan could lend him a little money to start a business
Why Ivan hasn’t yet gone off to Chermashnya, as his father begged
quiz.e: He asks it with a sly smile and a narrowed left eye, adding that Fyodor Pavlovich himself kept begging Ivan to go.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov say about his own position, and what does he predict for tomorrow?
o: He says he will resign, and predicts he will leave for Moscow tomorrow
Both Fyodor Pavlovich and Dmitry hound him; he expects a long fit tomorrow
He says he has grown rich and predicts he will soon quit the Karamazovs
He says Ivan ought to serve in his place, and predicts a quiet night’s rest
quiz.e: Both father and son hound him about whether Grushenka has come, Dmitry threatens to kill him, and he says he can feel a fit coming on out of fear.

quiz.q: What secret does Smerdyakov reveal about the old man’s house, and who else knows it?
o: A hidden cellar where the old man keeps his money, known only to Grigory
A gap in the garden fence that Grushenka will use, known only to Marfa
Knocking signals announcing Grushenka’s arrival, which Dmitry also knows
A password for the garden gate, which Ivan himself once devised for him
quiz.e: Five knocks mean that Grushenka has come and three mean something urgent, and Smerdyakov says he gave Dmitry the signals out of fear.

quiz.q: Why does Smerdyakov say Grigory and Marfa will not hear anyone enter the house tomorrow?
o: Marfa’s strong tincture will put them both into a deep sleep
Both have been given leave to visit relatives in the town
Both are by now too deaf to hear anyone moving in the house
Fyodor Pavlovich has sent them away for the night to the cottage
quiz.e: Marfa treats Grigory’s lumbago with this strong tincture, and since neither is a drinker, they both fall soundly asleep afterwards.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov say about the envelope and about inheritance?
o: Fyodor Pavlovich’s will leaves everything to Ivan; if the old man dies, Dmitry gets nothing
The envelope holds a letter forgiving Dmitry’s debts; if the old man dies, Ivan inherits it all
The envelope holds three thousand for Grushenka; if she marries him, the sons lose all
Grushenka has taken the money and left town; if the old man dies, Dmitry inherits alone
quiz.e: He lays out the stakes calmly, adding that Dmitry badly needs money and regards the three thousand as his own.

quiz.q: How does the conversation end?
o: Ivan strikes Smerdyakov in a rage and goes in without a further word
Ivan announces he is going to Moscow, then laughs strangely and goes in
Ivan promises to guard the house himself, and sits down on the bench
Smerdyakov falls into a fit in front of Ivan, who carries him inside
quiz.e: Ivan nearly attacks him, then blurts out his plan, and after a tense exchange about Chermashnya he laughs unnaturally and enters the gate.

chapters.title: ‘It’s Always Interesting to Talk to a Clever Man’
chapters.intro: Background on Russian country travel, post stations, the timber trade, peasant dress and drink, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: To drink, especially alcohol; also, to absorb ideas.
A biblical-sounding phrase for one’s own child.
A large Russian metal urn with a spigot and an inner chamber for hot coals, used to boil water for tea.
Russian appetizers or snacks, such as pickles, smoked fish, cold meats and bread, served with vodka or cognac.
A long, fitted, waisted peasant coat, often of dark cloth.
A Russian measure of distance, about two-thirds of a mile or about 1.07 kilometers.
An unexpected gain, usually of money.
Friendly, talkative and generous in manner.
Deserving respect because of age and dignity.
Not producing the desired effect. The usual spelling is “inefficacious.”
Servants who do low or humble work.
French for “to the purpose”; here, “as it happens to be relevant.”
Gradually spread through or over, as with color or feeling.
A small group of trees, or a small wood.
Russia’s road network was served by relay stations (posting-houses), where travelers could change horses, rest, and eat. A stationmaster ran each one, and the traveler paid per horse and per verst.
Many ordinary country vehicles had no springs, which made rural roads very rough. A traveler might hire a driver and changing teams at each station.

The first main line, from St Petersburg to Moscow, opened in 1851. By the 1870s lines were spreading but still far apart, and a country gentleman might drive for many hours to reach the nearest station.
A landowner’s woods were a main source of cash. Standing timber was sold to merchants who cut it themselves, and prices depended on which buyers were in the area.

The merchant class (kuptsy) ran trade and small industry in provincial Russia. Some were shrewd millionaires who dressed like peasants, and local merchants often formed a close circle that outsiders had trouble entering.

The Orthodox parish priest was usually married and lived on modest means, partly from his parishioners. In provincial life he was often the only educated person in a village, and could also act as a local agent or correspondent.
Giving money to the servants as one left a house was a normal courtesy, and a coachman or messenger expected a small gift (“tea money”).
Educated Russians of the era often traveled to Italy, Germany and France, and Venice was a famous city for tourists, artists and writers.
Russians often had two forms of the same name, and a familiar or diminutive form, like Mitya for Dmitry, could sound affectionate or contemptuous depending on the speaker.
Tea was the standard daily drink in Russian homes, served strong and diluted from the samovar, often with sugar, jam or lemon.
A type of brandy from western France, popular among well-off Russians in the nineteenth century.
Zakuski traditionally accompany alcohol. A host who offered them with cognac was marking an occasion.

quiz.q: How does Ivan treat his father when he comes into the house that evening?
o: He sits and drinks tea with him, chatting about Moscow and the grove
He argues furiously over money until Fyodor Pavlovich threatens a lawsuit
He says he’s going up to his room and walks past without looking at him
He asks him to lend the carriage and horses for an early start tomorrow
quiz.e: Ivan shouts that he is going upstairs and says goodbye, openly avoiding his father, which surprises even Fyodor Pavlovich.

quiz.q: What action on the staircase that night does Ivan later call the basest of his whole life?
o: Going downstairs in the dark to give Smerdyakov a thrashing
Listening for a long time to his father pacing downstairs
Burning a letter from Katerina Ivanovna without opening it
Going out to the garden and watching his father’s lit windows
quiz.e: He did not even hate his father then, but listened with a strange curiosity, imagining him waiting for a knock. He felt the urge to beat Smerdyakov too, but did not act on it.

quiz.q: What happens when Ivan wakes up in the morning?
o: He packs at once and says he is leaving for Moscow for good
He is undecided and asks Marfa whether he ought to go at all
He goes out at once to find Dmitry and have it out with him
He sends a note to Alyosha at the monastery before breakfast
quiz.e: He wakes at seven, packs his suitcase at once, and tells his father he will travel to Moscow for good and needs horses.

quiz.q: What does Fyodor Pavlovich ask Ivan to do on the way?
o: To deliver a sealed letter to the lawyer in Moscow about the estate
To stop at the monastery on the way and fetch Alyosha back home
To visit Chermashnya and test whether Gorstkin will pay eleven thousand
To collect an old debt of three thousand roubles from the Maslovs
quiz.e: The Maslovs offer only eight thousand, while Gorstkin, not afraid of them since he is from elsewhere, is said to offer eleven and will be there only a week.

quiz.q: How is Ivan told to tell whether Gorstkin is honest?
o: By his handshake: a firm, dry grip means he is honest, a limp one a cheat
By his beard: angry shaking means earnest, smooth chuckling means cheating
By asking him to swear on an icon before witnesses and watching his face
By his coat: a worn, faded caftan means a poor but honest man indeed
quiz.e: Fyodor Pavlovich adds that he should never look him in the eye, and that Gorstkin’s real name is Lyagavy, which must not be used.

quiz.q: How do Ivan and his father part?
o: Fyodor Pavlovich weeps and kisses him on both cheeks, and Ivan lets him
Ivan refuses the carriage and sets off on foot along the high road
Ivan silently hands the old man a letter for Alyosha and drives away
The old man tries to kiss him; Ivan wards it off with a handshake
quiz.e: Smerdyakov replies that it is always interesting to talk to a clever man, a remark that troubles Ivan on the road.

quiz.q: What does Ivan do at Volovya Station?
o: He gives up Chermashnya, sends word to his father and takes the Moscow train
He turns the carriage around and drives back to the house to confront his father
He goes on to Chermashnya after all and quickly settles the grove with Gorstkin
He telegraphs Katerina Ivanovna and waits at the station for her reply all evening
quiz.e: He tips Mitry to carry the message, boards the seven o’clock train, feels sudden gloom instead of joy, and at dawn in Moscow calls himself a scoundrel.

quiz.q: What happens in the household after Ivan has gone?
o: Dmitry arrives and breaks down the garden gate while the house sleeps
Grushenka sends Fyodor Pavlovich a note promising to come by midnight
Fyodor Pavlovich dismisses Marfa for burning the soup and sends her off
Smerdyakov has a fit in the cellar and Grigory is laid up with lumbago
quiz.e: Dr Herzenstube is called and says the fit may prove dangerous. Smerdyakov is put to bed in the outbuilding, and Fyodor Pavlovich waits in a state of sweet hope.

chapters.title: The Elder Zosima and His Guests
chapters.intro: Background on Russian monastic elders, church ranks, devotional customs, saints’ lives and the literary device of the found manuscript, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A long, serious talk on a subject, often with a teaching purpose.
Physical weakness, especially from illness or age.
A monk who has also been ordained as a priest.
The monk in charge of a monastery or smaller religious community.
A small, secluded religious community, often attached to a larger monastery.
Someone training to become a monk or nun who has not yet taken final vows.
The small private room in which a monk lives.
Money or food given to the poor or to a religious house as charity.
A penance: an act of spiritual discipline set by a confessor or taken on voluntarily.
A woman who gives money or other help.
A person’s face or facial expression.
Lying or bowing right down to the ground as a sign of reverence.
The idea that something has been decided in advance by God or fate.
A poetic, devotional name for the Russian land.
An old word meaning soon or shortly.

A monk of long experience who guides others in their spiritual lives, whatever his official rank. The tradition revived in Russia from the late eighteenth century, and followers placed themselves under an elder’s direction in strict obedience.
A monastery south-west of Moscow that became the most famous centre of the elder tradition in the nineteenth century. Writers and thinkers visited it; Dostoevsky went there in 1878.
A community might include novices, ordinary monks and monks ordained as priests. An abbot (igumen) led a monastery, and an archimandrite was a senior head of an important one.
Small oil lamps kept burning before holy images, in homes as well as churches. Lighting one was an everyday act of prayer.
In Orthodox worship a full bow touches the forehead to the floor. It expresses repentance or deep reverence, and it is a striking thing to do before another person.
Poor monasteries sometimes sent monks on long journeys on foot to gather donations from ordinary people.
John’s Gospel, chapter 12, says a grain of wheat stays alone unless it falls to the ground and dies, but bears much fruit if it does. Dostoevsky chose this verse as the novel’s epigraph.
A very old and popular form of Russian reading. A saint’s life followed a familiar pattern: a devout childhood, a turning point, years of spiritual struggle and an edifying end.

Novelists have long presented part of a story as a document that someone else wrote, with the narrator acting as editor. It lets an author change voice and raises questions about how reliable the record is.
The ancient language of Russian Orthodox worship. Echoes of it make Russian prose sound solemn and old-fashioned, rather as the King James Bible does in English.

quiz.q: How does Alyosha find the Elder when he enters the cell?
o: Lying unconscious while the monks keep a silent vigil
Sitting up exhausted but cheerful, talking with his guests
Asleep in the outer room as Porfiry reads the psalms
Kneeling alone at the icons and refusing all visitors
quiz.e: Alyosha feared finding him unconscious. Instead the Elder has just risen and sits in his armchair, merry and holding a quiet discourse.

quiz.q: Who is Father Anfim, and what is his history with the Elder?
o: A learned abbot who taught him theology in Kostroma
A wealthy donor who paid to rebuild the small hermitage
A young priest who has served as his personal confessor
A near-illiterate old monk who once wandered with him
quiz.e: Forty years earlier the two walked across Russia gathering alms for their poor Kostroman monastery, and the Elder has always honoured him.

quiz.q: What became of the six ten-copeck pieces the Elder was given?
o: They went to a widow burned out of her home, from an unknown giver
They were placed in the monastery’s fund for repairing the chapel
They were returned to the woman who had brought them from afar
They were spent on wax candles to burn before the icons that night
quiz.e: Porfiry delivered them to an artisan’s widow who had lost everything in a fire, saying they came from ‘an unknown benefactress’.

quiz.q: Whom does the Elder urge Alyosha to hurry and find?
o: Ivan, whose article they had discussed at the meeting
Rakitin, whose ambitions the Elder had long mistrusted
Dmitry, the older one, to whom he had bowed down
Smerdyakov, whose sickness the Elder had foreseen
quiz.e: He means ‘the older one, to whom I bowed down to the ground’, and says Alyosha may still prevent something dreadful.

quiz.q: Why does the Elder say he bowed to the ground the day before?
o: To shame a quarrelling family into making peace
To honour the man’s future suffering, which he foresaw
To ask forgiveness for a wrong done long ago
To give thanks for a gift made to the hermitage
quiz.e: He says he bowed to the man’s great future suffering, having seen the man’s whole destiny expressed in his gaze.

quiz.q: What does the Elder foretell for Alyosha himself?
o: He will live in the world as a monk and bless life despite misfortune
He will succeed Father Paisy and lead the hermitage for many years
He will take the great vow and withdraw into silence in the far north
He will leave the Church entirely, and return to it only in old age
quiz.e: Alyosha will go beyond the walls but abide in the world as a monk, happy even in misfortune, and will make others bless life too.

quiz.q: Why has Alyosha’s face been so dear to the Elder?
o: It recalls the mother who raised him in the far north
It resembles that of his teacher at the Kostroman monastery
It reminds him of himself as a young officer long ago
It seems spiritually akin to his brother who died young
quiz.e: Alyosha reminds him, more in spirit than in features, of the brother who died at seventeen and shaped his whole path.

quiz.q: What does the narrator say about the record of this last discourse?
o: It was taken down word for word by Father Paisy that night
It is Alyosha’s partial account, written later from memory
It was dictated by the Elder in the weeks before that evening
It survives only as hearsay gathered among the townspeople
quiz.e: Alyosha wrote it from memory after the Elder’s death, and it likely blends in earlier talks; the real conversation was less continuous.

chapters.title: From the Life of the Elder Zosima
chapters.intro: Background on Russian military schools, serfdom and army recruitment, the Decembrists, duelling, Lent and Bible stories, saints’ legends and the rural clergy, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes illness and death, violence and references to a murder.
A monk-priest who has taken the strictest and highest level of monastic vows.
In Russia, a secondary school that prepared pupils for university.
A fast-moving form of tuberculosis, a lung disease.
French, literally ‘cold blood’: calmness under pressure.
A person legally bound to serve a master; a serf.
A woman who has been released from slavery or serfdom.
A metal container on chains in which incense is burned and swung during worship.
A small dome on a roof.
A soldier assigned as an army officer’s personal servant.
Russian for a landowner or gentleman; how a servant addressed a master.
A four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a folding top.
A friend who assists a person fighting a duel and helps arrange it.
Ornamental shoulder pieces on a military uniform.
An elegant evening party, often at a private home.
A charitable home for poor or elderly people.
To do with a meal, especially dinner.
French for a share or lot in something.
Russian military boarding schools that trained sons of the nobility to become officers.
The tsar’s elite regiments, based mainly around St Petersburg. A place in one was prestigious and very expensive to keep up.
Before serfdom ended in 1861, serfs could in practice be sold by their owners, sometimes apart from the land they lived on.
Landowners and communities had to supply men for the army. Service lasted up to twenty-five years for much of the period, so being sent was often a final parting.
In December 1825 a group of army officers staged a failed uprising as Nicholas I came to the throne. Five leaders were hanged and many others were sent to Siberia.
The tsarist government could banish people suspected of dangerous ideas to provincial towns, where they lived under police watch.
Paper notes issued from 1769 and worth less than the same sum in silver; they were replaced in the 1840s.
Great Lent is the long Orthodox fast before Easter, without meat or dairy foods. Holy Week is its solemn final stage.
Russians often took communion only about once a year, after several days of fasting, attending services and confession.
A righteous and prosperous man loses his children, wealth and health when God allows Satan to test him. Passages from it are read in Orthodox services during Holy Week.
In Genesis, jealous brothers sell young Joseph into slavery. He rises to power in Egypt and meets them again years later, when they come to buy grain.
A penitent saint of the early Church who, by tradition, gave up a sinful life and spent decades alone in the desert.
A saint who, by legend, left a wealthy Roman family to live as a beggar, then returned home unrecognised. His story was much loved in Russia.
Russian collections of saints’ lives arranged by the days of the church year, for reading aloud or at home.
A fourteenth-century hermit and monastery founder, one of Russia’s most revered saints. Legends tell of his gentleness with a wild bear.
Church services used Church Slavonic. A New Testament in modern Russian appeared in the 1820s, but a complete Russian Bible was not finished until 1876.
Rural clergy were poorly paid, formed almost a hereditary caste and often farmed to get by. Their low status was openly discussed in the press.

quiz.q: How does Markel change as his illness advances?
o: He grows bitter and refuses to see his family
He clings to atheism, mocking every visitor
He becomes joyful, and begs everyone’s forgiveness
He leaves home to follow the exile to Petersburg
quiz.e: The young atheist who ridiculed fasting undergoes a complete spiritual change, full of joy and love and calling himself guilty before all.

quiz.q: What does Markel do when he watches the birds from his window?
o: He asks the birds of God to forgive him
He asks the servants to chase them away
He asks to be carried out into the garden
He asks his brother to go and feed them
quiz.e: He tells the birds he has sinned against them too, having lived in disgrace amid all that glory, and weeps for joy.

quiz.q: What does Markel tell his little brother when they are last alone?
o: To study hard and enter the Cadet Corps
To look after their mother when he is gone
To forgive the exile who led him astray
To go off and play, and to live for him
quiz.e: He takes the boy by the shoulders and sends him to play and ‘live for me’, words Zosima remembers with tears throughout his life.

quiz.q: Which reading in church first moves the eight-year-old boy?
o: The story of Abraham and Isaac
The story of Job and his losses
The story of Jonah and the whale
The story of Joseph in the pit
quiz.e: On the Monday of Holy Week he understands for the first time what is read in church: the tale of Job, which ever after moves him to tears.

quiz.q: What does Zosima say a poorly paid village priest could still do?
o: Sell his small field and live on the offerings of pilgrims
Write to the bishop each season to ask for a higher stipend
Read Scripture to his people at home for one hour a week
Learn to argue with the Lutherans who are arriving nearby
quiz.e: Just one hour a week in his own izba, reading simply and tenderly, would reach the people, who would repay his kindness.

quiz.q: What does Zosima do the evening before the duel?
o: He writes farewell letters to his mother and the bride
He strikes his batman Afanasy twice in the face
He prays through the night before his old Bible
He drinks with his second and mocks his rival
quiz.e: Enraged, he beats Afanasy until he draws blood. His shame about this, at dawn, overturns everything.

quiz.q: What does he do at the duel itself?
o: He fires into the ground before his rival can take aim
He refuses to appear and resigns his commission by letter
He wounds his rival slightly, then apologises to the lady
He takes the shot, throws away his pistol, and apologises
quiz.e: The first shot grazes his cheek. He hurls his loaded pistol into the forest and asks forgiveness, to his second’s fury.

quiz.q: What secret does the mysterious visitor finally reveal?
o: That he killed a woman fourteen years ago and let a servant be blamed
That he had once betrayed a friend in the uprising of the Decembrists
That he was the hidden father of the young woman Zosima had loved
That he had made his fortune by defrauding the town’s charity funds
quiz.e: He stabbed the widow who rejected him and staged the scene as a servant’s theft. The servant Pyotr was arrested and died of fever.

quiz.q: How does the town respond when he publicly confesses?
o: The police arrest him and send him to penal exile
His friends arrange for him to flee the country
Nobody believes it, and he is judged deranged
The whole town turns away from him in disgust
quiz.e: Despite his evidence, people hear him as a sick man, and the verdict in every household is that he has lost his mind.

quiz.q: Why, he admits at the end, did he come back that night at midnight?
o: To beg Zosima to keep his secret from the police
To return the handkerchief he had borrowed earlier
To say he had resolved to enter a monastery himself
To kill Zosima, whose knowledge had become unbearable
quiz.e: He came back hating the one person who knew. ‘Never in your life were you more close to death,’ he tells Zosima.

chapters.title: From the Discourses and Teachings of the Elder Zosima
chapters.intro: Background on the end of serfdom, the 1870s radical movements, Russian ideas about the people and the West, monastic vows and Orthodox beliefs about the dead, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter briefly mentions suicide, child labour and cruelty within families.
A person with no settled home who wanders from place to place.
Someone who lives off other people without giving anything back.
The condition of being a slave or being completely under another’s control.
Russian for ‘fist’: a well-off peasant, often one who lent money at harsh terms.
Someone who takes money by threats or unfair pressure.
Someone who sells goods in the street or from place to place.
A large, imposing building; also a large system of ideas.
The state of touching or lying directly next to something.
Someone who must answer for something, especially in a court.
Balanced and harmonious in form, whether in outward appearance or in character.
To become infected or rotten; to go on getting worse.
To soothe or ease a pain or strong feeling.
Payment or reward given in return for something.
Serfdom was fixed in Russian law in 1649. Alexander II’s decree of 1861 freed about twenty-three million privately owned serfs, but former serfs had to pay for their land for decades.
Young children worked long hours in Russian industry until a law of 1882 banned factory employment under the age of twelve.
Both spread rapidly across Russia after the 1850s. Many people saw them as proof that progress would draw humanity together.
Taxes on vodka provided a large share of government income, while heavy drinking was widely condemned as a curse on peasant life.
Uprisings swept the continent in 1848, and the Paris Commune of 1871 ended in mass bloodshed. Russian conservatives took these events as warnings.
In 1874 thousands of young radicals went to the countryside to win peasants over to socialism. Most met suspicion, and many were arrested and put on trial.
A view popularised by Chernyshevsky’s novel What Is to Be Done? (1863): that reason and enlightened self-interest could build a just society.
The nineteenth-century belief, associated with Auguste Comte, that real knowledge comes only from observation and science.
Thinkers who held that Russia’s Orthodox faith and communal life offered something better than Western individualism.
A phrase expressing the belief, held by Dostoevsky among others, that Russia’s ordinary people carry a special Christian truth for the world.
An 1816 poem imagining the sun’s extinction and the slow end of humankind, down to a last pair of survivors.
Orthodox monks promise obedience, chastity and a life without personal possessions, and they keep frequent and strict fasts.
In Luke’s Gospel a rich man in torment begs for a drop of water from Lazarus, a beggar now at Abraham’s side, but a great gulf divides them. ‘Dives’ is Latin for ‘rich’.
A seventh-century Christian monk and spiritual writer, widely read in Orthodox monasteries, who described the suffering of hell in terms of love.
Orthodox Christians pray regularly for those who have died and hold memorial services for them.
The Russian Church traditionally refused funeral rites and burial in consecrated ground to people who had taken their own lives.
In Russian folk belief the earth is a living, holy mother. Peasant customs included bowing to it and even swearing oaths by it.

quiz.q: What does Zosima say the world now means by freedom?
o: The right of each nation to choose its own laws
The right to have more needs and to satisfy them
The right to speak openly against the authorities
The right of every peasant to leave his village
quiz.e: The world teaches people to satisfy and multiply their needs, bringing solitariness to the rich and envy and murder to the poor.

quiz.q: What nearly made a ‘fighter for the cause’ betray it in prison?
o: The fear that he would never again see his family
A promise from his jailers of a very early release
The news that his comrades had already informed
Being deprived of tobacco, which tormented him
quiz.e: Zosima uses him to ask whether such a slave to habit is free, or could long endure in any fight for mankind.

quiz.q: What sight in factories leads Zosima to cry out to the monks?
o: Stunted, depraved children of about ten at work
Owners forcing their workers to labour on feast days
Machinery that had taken the place of whole villages
Priests accepting gifts from cruel factory masters
quiz.e: He has seen ten-year-olds, unhealthy and bent, in airless halls. A child needs sun, games and a little love: ‘This shall not be, O monks.’

quiz.q: What does Afanasy do when they meet again after eight years?
o: He turns away, still resentful about the old beating
He asks the monk to find his son a place at school
He brings him home for tea and presses coins on him
He denounces him at market for abandoning his duty
quiz.e: Overjoyed, he takes Zosima home, heats the samovar and gives him fifty-copeck pieces. Zosima sees in it a great act of human unity.

quiz.q: How did Zosima reply when asked if servants should sit on the sofa and be brought tea?
o: It would embarrass the servants most of all
Well, why not, if only on occasion
Masters should first give up their sofas
Only after the servants had been freed
quiz.e: Everyone laughed. He admits the question was frivolous and his reply unclear, yet he thinks it held some truth.

quiz.q: What daily prayer does Zosima urge on the young?
o: For mercy on all who have appeared before God this day
For the strength to go on fasting until the next feast
For the conversion of all the unbelievers in the land
For the health of the tsar and his household in peril
quiz.e: Thousands die alone each hour, and such a prayer, even from a stranger far away, lets a soul feel that someone on earth loves it.

quiz.q: Why, for Zosima, is asking forgiveness of the birds not simply foolish?
o: Birds are sent from heaven to report human sins
Scripture directly commands it of penitent sinners
Any kindness to animals earns merit before God
All is like an ocean; a touch reverberates everywhere
quiz.e: All flows and connects, so if you were better within, birds, children and animals would feel easier, even if only by a single drop.

quiz.q: On what condition can someone judge a criminal, according to Zosima?
o: Only if a court has lawfully appointed him to the task
Only if he sees he is as much a criminal as the accused
Only if the accused has freely confessed before witnesses
Only if he has himself suffered from the crime committed
quiz.e: No one can be a judge until he perceives that he may be more guilty of the man’s crime than anyone. ‘However insane this sounds, it is true.’

quiz.q: How does Zosima define hell?
o: Being eternally parted from one’s family
Being burned forever in material flames
The suffering of no longer being able to love
The remorse of being known by all as a sinner
quiz.e: He leaves the question of material fire aside: the torment is inward, a thirst for active love when the earthly life that allows it is over.

quiz.q: How does the Elder die, according to the narrator?
o: In bed while asleep, as Father Paisy reads the Gospel
In his chair, in the middle of a sentence to Alyosha
At the altar, as the brothers are gathering for prayer
On his knees, kissing the earth, with a joyful prayer
quiz.e: After sudden chest pain he lowers himself to the floor, bows his face to the earth, spreads his arms and dies joyfully, as he had taught.

chapters.title: A Putrid Smell
chapters.intro: Background on Orthodox funeral customs and hymns, holy fools, ascetic practices, Mount Athos and the Russian elder tradition, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: People who live in ordinary society rather than in a monastery.
A monk who has taken the strictest and highest level of vows.
A cowl or hood worn by a monk.
In Orthodox worship, the cloth that covers the chalice and plate used at communion.
An Orthodox memorial service for the dead.
The Book of Psalms, especially as used in prayer and worship.
A person of low social rank; a commoner.
A vague feeling that something is about to happen.
To scold or criticise someone sharply.
Russian for someone who lives a life of heroic religious self-denial.
A tomb, especially a grand one.
An old word for a librarian.
Objection or hesitation, as in ‘without demur’.
A broom made from a bundle of twigs.
In a commanding way that allows no refusal.
A deliberately antique form of ‘come’, in imitation of very old English.
Orthodox Christians often speak of someone who has died as having ‘fallen asleep’ in the Lord, and may call the dead person ‘the sleeper’.
Orthodox monks have their own burial rite. The body is dressed in the monastic habit and wrapped in the mantle, and the face is covered.
In Orthodox custom the Psalms are read aloud beside the coffin until the funeral. Over a priest, the Gospel is read instead.
An English name for the Trebnik, the Orthodox service book that holds the rites for baptisms, marriages, funerals and similar occasions.
Two forms of Orthodox hymn. A canon is a long, structured sequence of odes, and a stikhira is a shorter verse sung between lines of a psalm.
The Orthodox rite for making a bishop includes solemn formal questions to the candidate, asking why he has come and what he believes.
Christians who lived as outcasts and behaved like madmen for the sake of Christ. Russians often revered them and allowed them to say shocking things, even to the powerful.
Some ascetics wore heavy iron chains or fetters beneath their clothes as a lifelong act of penance.
Orthodox Christians honour the bodily remains of saints. Pilgrims travelled great distances to pray at them, often bringing the sick.
On fast days the devout give up meat and dairy foods, and on the strictest days fish, oil and wine as well. Zealous ascetics went far beyond the rules.

A mountainous peninsula in northern Greece with about twenty great Orthodox monasteries. Deeply revered, it lay under Ottoman rule until 1912, and its monks were traditionally summoned to prayer by striking a wooden board.
The elder tradition was not universally welcomed. Some Russian clergy and monks regarded it as a dangerous novelty that weakened church authority.
A remote settlement near the Arctic Circle at the mouth of the river Ob; today it is the city of Salekhard.
A leading conservative statesman and friend of Dostoevsky, later the official who oversaw the Russian Church for the state. He gave the novelist information about monastic burial customs.
Russians commonly drank tea from a glass with a spoonful of fruit preserves on the side, or sometimes stirred in.

quiz.q: What is Father Paisy’s attitude to the crowd’s impatient expectation?
o: He takes it as proof of the people’s sincere devotion
He barely notices it, being absorbed in his Gospel reading
He rebukes it as frivolous but secretly expects the same
He stirs it up in order to silence the Elder’s old enemies
quiz.e: He reprimands the agitated brethren and calls such instant expectation a frivolity, while owning to himself that he has been awaiting almost the same thing.

quiz.q: Why has Rakitin come to the hermitage so early?
o: Mrs Khokhlakova wants everything reported to her by letter
The Father Superior summoned him to help control the crowds
Father Paisy asked him to keep a watchful eye on Alyosha
He hopes to write an article on the Elder for the journals
quiz.e: Unable to enter the hermitage herself, she sends him to observe and write to her about every half-hour. She takes him for a most devout young man.

quiz.q: How does Father Paisy find Alyosha that morning?
o: Kneeling silently in prayer beside the Elder’s coffin
Asleep on the floor of the cell beside the novice Porfiry
Walking alone through the pines on the road into town
Weeping bitterly on a tombstone in a remote corner
quiz.e: He sits on the Elder Iov’s tomb with his back to the hermitage, sobbing. Paisy first urges him to rejoice, then decides these tears may be sent by Christ.

quiz.q: Why do the monks take the smell to be a sign from God?
o: It began at the very hour the Elder had once foretold
It came so quickly that it had ‘got ahead of nature’
No monk’s body had ever done this in the monastery before
It was noticed first by the Elder’s most devoted followers
quiz.e: They argue that a natural smell would have come more slowly, so God’s ‘deliberate finger’ must be at work. The narrator notes that other righteous monks had smelled without scandal.

quiz.q: To what does the narrator chiefly attribute the ugly excitement?
o: Drunkenness among the pilgrims who had come from the town
A plot by the Father Superior to end the rule of the Elders
Old hostility to Elderhood and envy of the Elder’s holiness
Long hunger and exhaustion after the strict fast of that week
quiz.e: He names a confluence of causes: ingrained hostility to the Elderhood as a harmful innovation and, principally, envy of a holiness so firmly established in the Elder’s lifetime.

quiz.q: What is Father Iosif’s reply to the scandal-mongers?
o: That this is no dogma, and that Athos looks to the colour of bones
That the Bishop had already confirmed the Elder’s holiness in writing
That any speculation on the matter was forbidden by monastic statute
That the smell came from the flowers and candles around the coffin
quiz.e: He says non-putrefaction is only an opinion; on Mount Athos yellow bones are the sign of glory. The monks dismiss this as novelty, and he goes away in sorrow.

quiz.q: Which complaints do the Elder’s critics now make about him?
o: He hid money from the brethren and took gifts from the rich
He read French philosophers at night and doubted the Creed
He forbade the old monks from keeping the vow of silence
He taught that life is joy and had a weakness for sweets
quiz.e: They say he taught that life is a great joy rather than a tearful humbling, mixed cherry preserves with his tea, denied material fire in hell and abused confession.

quiz.q: What does Father Ferapont do on the threshold of the cell?
o: He bows to the coffin and begs the dead Elder’s forgiveness
He makes the sign of the Cross to drive out the unclean force
He declares himself the new Elder before all of the brethren
He demands that Father Paisy hand over the Gospel to him
quiz.e: Arms raised, he howls ‘Exorcizing shall I exorcize!’ and crosses all four corners, as he does wherever he enters. He then blames the Elder’s purgatives for letting devils multiply.

quiz.q: What does Father Ferapont lament, tearfully, before he leaves?
o: That no one had come to him for counsel in all of these years
That the Elder had died without ever asking for his pardon
That the Elder gets a glorious canon and he a little hymn
That the younger monks no longer know how to keep the great fast
quiz.e: Gazing at the coffin, he complains that ‘The Helper and Protector’ will be sung over the Elder but only ‘What Earthly Sweetness’ over himself, a difference set by rank.

quiz.q: How does Alyosha answer when Father Paisy asks if he has also succumbed?
o: With a crooked smile and a wave of his arm, leaving without a word
With tears, and a request for a blessing before he goes to pray
With a firm declaration that he still believes in the Elder’s holiness
With a bitter speech against the monks who are jeering at the coffin
quiz.e: He gives no reply at all, smiles strangely, waves his arm and strides out of the hermitage without taking a blessing. ‘You will be back again!’ Paisy whispers.

chapters.title: The Right Moment
chapters.intro: Background on Orthodox devotion, the problem of evil, nineteenth-century materialism and radicalism, Russian liberals and the Table of Ranks, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Necessary as a duty, as in ‘it is incumbent upon me’.
Good judgement and caution in what one says or does.
In a way that must not be broken or harmed.
Formed in advance, before knowing the facts.
Overwhelming feelings, especially of joy or love.
Someone with the power to judge or settle a matter.
God’s care and guidance of the world.
To tolerate or allow, as in ‘would not brook delay’.
In an excessively flattering, eager-to-please way.
Bread that has been blessed but not consecrated, handed out to worshippers at the end of the Orthodox liturgy.
Orthodox teaching honours saints and holy people but reserves worship for God alone.
Orthodox monks and novices seek a superior’s blessing before doing anything outside the daily routine, including going beyond the monastery walls.
The attempt to explain how a good and all-powerful God can allow evil and injustice. The term comes from the philosopher Leibniz, in a work of 1710.
In ‘Of Miracles’ (1748) David Hume argued that reports of a miracle could never outweigh the evidence for nature’s regular workings. Nineteenth-century science seemed to many to strengthen the case.
The view that only matter exists and that thought and feeling arise from physical processes. Ludwig Büchner’s Force and Matter (1855) was eagerly read by Russian students.

A loose name for the outlook of young Russian radicals of the 1860s, who rejected traditional authority, including religion, in the name of science. Turgenev’s Fathers and Sons (1862) made the word famous.
Seminaries gave the sons of clergy a rare chance of education, and a number of leading radicals began there, among them Chernyshevsky and Dobrolyubov.
In 1870s Russia a liberal favoured gradual reform, legal rights and freer speech. Conservatives and radicals alike often used the word as a sneer.
Introduced by Peter the Great in 1722, it placed state officials and officers on a ladder of fourteen grades. Promotions and medals became a national preoccupation and a standing joke.
Street obstructions thrown up by insurgents, and the best-known image of European revolution, especially in Paris in 1830, 1848 and 1871.

quiz.q: According to the narrator, what did Alyosha truly want?
o: Proof that would silence the sceptics among the educated
A miracle that would lead the whole town back to the Church
Revenge on the monks who had mocked his beloved teacher
Higher justice for the person he revered, not miracles
quiz.e: Not miracles nor the triumph of any idea, says the narrator: before him stood one beloved person, and he thirsted for the ‘higher justice’ that had been infringed.

quiz.q: How does the narrator regard Alyosha’s failure to be reasonable at this moment?
o: He is glad of it: a youth who is always reasonable is cheap
He regrets it, as a sign of Alyosha’s poor progress in his studies
He excuses it, on the grounds that Alyosha was ill and very tired
He condemns it, as the kind of frivolity the Elder often warned against
quiz.e: He refuses to apologise for his hero. Giving oneself up to an enthusiasm born of great love is more worthy of respect, he says, and reason will have its day.

quiz.q: In his grief, what does Alyosha completely forget to do?
o: Write to Mrs Khokhlakova about the Elder’s final teachings
Attend the midday requiem as Father Paisy had ordered
Find Dmitry and deliver the money to Ilyushechka’s father
Collect his things and ask a blessing of the Father Superior
quiz.e: He forgets his anguished concern for Dmitry from the day before, and also the two hundred roubles he had been so determined to take to Ilyushechka’s father.

quiz.q: What besides the Elder’s disgrace stirs troublingly in Alyosha’s mind?
o: A memory of his mother’s prayers before the icon
A dim, malicious image of his talk with Ivan
A fear that he has wasted a year at the monastery
A suspicion that Rakitin has been spreading the news
quiz.e: A clouded, tormenting image from yesterday’s conversation with Ivan keeps rising in him, though the narrator insists his basic faith in God is not shaken.

quiz.q: When Rakitin accuses him of mutiny against God, what does Alyosha say?
o: That he simply does ‘not accept his world’, with a crooked smile
That he has never believed in the Elder’s power to work miracles
That God has no need of defenders such as Rakitin and his friends
That he intends to leave the monastery at once and go to Moscow
quiz.e: Echoing Ivan and smiling ironically, he says he is not mutinying against his God but simply does not accept his world. He declines to explain further.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha accept from Rakitin that astonishes him?
o: Five roubles and a lift into town in Rakitin’s cart
A place to sleep and a suit of ordinary clothing
Sausage and vodka, which Rakitin had not expected
An offer of work writing for a provincial journal
quiz.e: Rakitin assumes a monastery novice will refuse, but Alyosha says ‘Let me have some sausage’ and then ‘Let me have vodka, too.’ Rakitin calls it a real mutiny.

quiz.q: What happens when the image of Dmitry crosses Alyosha’s mind on the road?
o: He stops short and insists on going to find him at once
He tells Rakitin of the danger that he fears for his brother
He starts to weep and says that he has failed the Elder
It hints at an urgent duty, but does not reach his heart
quiz.e: When Rakitin mentions Ivan’s leaving for Moscow, Dmitry’s image flits by, recalling some fearsome obligation, but it does not touch him. He remembers this long after.

quiz.q: Why, in truth, does Rakitin take Alyosha to see Grushenka?
o: To have her persuade him to return to the monastery
To see a righteous man fall, and for a material gain
To win Grushenka’s favour away from the Karamazovs
To show him that Mrs Khokhlakova has been deceived
quiz.e: His purpose is twofold: to savour the disgrace and ‘fall’ of a righteous man, and a certain advantageous material aim, which the narrator holds back for now.

chapters.title: The Onion
chapters.intro: Background on Russian merchants, women and property, the buying and selling of debts, forms of address and religious folklore, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes references to sexual exploitation, threats of violence and self-harm, and one antisemitic expression typical of the period.
A woman guided and supported by an older, influential person.
Extra; additional to the regular number needed.
A Yiddish word for a business deal.
A signed written promise to pay a sum of money.
A light, decorative headdress worn by women.
A long, low, four-wheeled Russian travelling carriage without springs.
A team of three horses harnessed side by side.
To pester someone with repeated demands.
A servant, or someone who behaves like one.
Literally meat-eating; by extension, predatory and greedy.
A state of intense joy or spiritual excitement.
An old, condemning word for a woman who has sex outside marriage.
Suffering from tuberculosis, a wasting disease of the lungs.
In older usage, full of strong emotion or high drama, rather than pitifully weak.

Russian merchants formed a legally recognised class, enrolled in guilds according to wealth. They had a reputation for piety, tight-fistedness and autocratic rule over their families, which Ostrovsky’s plays made famous.
Unusually for Europe at the time, Russian law allowed married women to own and manage property in their own right.
Promissory notes could be passed on to others. A speculator might buy a desperate debtor’s note for a small fraction of its value and then press for payment in full.
Russian, like French, has an intimate and a formal word for ‘you’. Which one a person uses signals closeness or rank, and a change can be highly charged.
First names have many affectionate or slighting variants. Ivan may be Vanya, Vanechka or Vanka, and each carries its own shade of tenderness, familiarity or contempt.
A bead frame, the schyoty, was the standard tool of Russian traders and clerks, and stayed common in shops well into the twentieth century.
Imported French champagne was costly and, in Russia, a byword for extravagant celebration.
A deacon assists the priest at services but ranks below him. The Russian clergy formed a near-hereditary class, and most of its minor members lived poorly.
Orthodox Christians traditionally believe that each person has a guardian angel who watches over them for life.
The Book of Revelation describes a ‘lake of fire’ as the final place of punishment, an image that entered the Christian popular imagination.
Peasant Russia had a rich oral tradition of legends about saints, angels, devils and the next life, passed on by word of mouth at home.

quiz.q: How does the old merchant Samsonov provide for Grushenka?
o: He names her as chief heir in a carefully guarded will
He signs over his house and the whole of his business
He offers to marry her, if she gives up all other men
He gives her modest capital and advice, but no legacy
quiz.e: He allots her some eight thousand roubles and teaches her business, but warns she will get nothing more, and in the end he leaves everything to his sons.

quiz.q: Why is Grushenka dressed up and so frightened when the visitors arrive?
o: She has come back from a ball and fears a scene at home
She awaits a message from her officer and fears Mitya’s arrival
She is expecting Fyodor Pavlovich and dreads the old man’s temper
She plans to leave that night for Moscow with Samsonov’s money
quiz.e: She has tricked Mitya into thinking she is at Samsonov’s, and has dressed ready to fly the moment a message comes from her officer in Mokroye.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha feel when Grushenka jumps on to his knee?
o: A pure curiosity about her, and none of his former dread
An overwhelming temptation that he struggles to master
Deep shame before the memory of his dead Elder’s teaching
Cold anger at her for mocking him so soon after his loss
quiz.e: His grief protects him like armour against seduction, and in place of his old fear he wonders at an unexpected, most pure-hearted curiosity.

quiz.q: What makes Grushenka suddenly leap off Alyosha’s knee?
o: Fenya comes running in to say that someone is at the gate
Rakitin threatens to tell Samsonov how she is behaving
She learns that the Elder Zosima has died that very day
Alyosha gently asks her to return to her place on the sofa
quiz.e: She crosses herself in dismay. Alyosha is struck by this: he came to find an evil soul, he tells Rakitin, and found a sincere sister.

quiz.q: What does Grushenka reveal about why Rakitin brought Alyosha?
o: She had promised to clear the debts he owes to Samsonov
She had agreed to speak for him to Mrs Khokhlakova
He hoped to learn the truth about her and Dmitry for an article
She had promised him twenty-five roubles to bring Alyosha
quiz.e: She tosses him the note in front of Alyosha. Rakitin pockets it, plainly ashamed, since he had counted on being paid afterwards in secret.

quiz.q: In Grushenka’s fable, what makes the onion break?
o: The angel lets go, horrified by how wicked she has been
The woman kicks away others, crying that the onion is hers
The devils seize the woman and pull against the angel
The weight of all of the sinners clinging to her is too much
quiz.e: The other sinners catch hold of her and she kicks them, saying ‘The onion’s mine, not yours.’ At those words the onion breaks and she falls back into the lake.

quiz.q: What does Grushenka confess was her original plan for Alyosha?
o: To ruin him out of spite, and to ‘swallow him whole’
To ask him to help her break with his brother Dmitry
To have him plead her case with Katerina Ivanovna
To win through him an entry into good society
quiz.e: Feeling that he despised her, she bribed Rakitin so that she might destroy him and laugh. Yet she also says that at moments she has looked on him as her conscience.

quiz.q: What has tormented Grushenka for the past five years?
o: Remorse for the ruin of her family’s good name
Fear that Samsonov would cast her out with nothing
A longing to pay back the officer who abandoned her
Grief for a child she was forced to give up long ago
quiz.e: Night after night she has wept and vowed, ‘I shall pay him back.’ Now he has written that his wife is dead and he wants to see her.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha answer when she asks him to decide whether she should forgive?
o: That only God may decide such a thing for her
That she must first go and make peace with Mitya
That forgiveness is impossible while she still hates
That she has in fact already forgiven him
quiz.e: ‘But you’ve already forgiven him,’ he says, smiling. She drinks to her base heart and smashes the glass, then wonders whether she is fond only of her own tears.

quiz.q: What message does Grushenka shout from her window for Alyosha to give to Mitya?
o: That she will return to him as soon as her affairs are settled
That she loved him for one hour, and he must always remember it
That he should forgive his father and make his peace at home
That he must not follow her, or she will never speak to him again
quiz.e: Having gone off to ‘a scoundrel’, she commands him to remember all his life the one small hour she loved him. Rakitin, furious, soon abandons Alyosha in the dark.

chapters.title: Cana of Galilee
chapters.intro: Background on the wedding at Cana, the language of the Gospels, Galilee, nineteenth-century lives of Jesus and the night sky, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: To force out and take the place of.
To die out or come to an end.
In older English, lacked or ran short of something.
An old past tense of ‘bear’: carried.
The steward or master in charge of a feast.
The point in the sky directly overhead.
The state of being still and unchanging.
To live or remain in a place.
A rule or principle for how to behave.
In John’s Gospel, chapter 2, Jesus and his mother attend a village wedding. When the wine runs out he has water turned into wine, and John calls this the first of his signs.
Galilee is a region of northern Palestine around the freshwater Lake of Gennesaret, also called the Sea of Galilee. Jesus grew up there and did much of his teaching among its villages.
John mentions six stone jars at the wedding, kept for Jewish purification rites and each holding a large quantity of water.
‘Woman, what have I to do with thee?’
A phrase from the Cana story that sounds rude in English. Scholars generally agree that ‘woman’ was not a discourteous way to address someone in the original.
In John’s Gospel, Jesus’s ‘hour’ usually refers to the time of his death and glorification, a moment the Gospel steadily builds towards.
An English translation of 1611. Its wording is often used to convey the solemn Church Slavonic of Russian services, which is why Gospel passages may sound so old-fashioned.
Ernest Renan’s Life of Jesus (1863) was a European sensation. It treated Jesus as a human figure and drew a vivid picture of everyday life in Galilee.
On his way to prison in Siberia in 1850, Dostoevsky was given a New Testament by the wives of exiled Decembrists. He kept the book for the rest of his life.
The pale band of light formed by distant stars of our own galaxy. On a clear, dark night it appears split in two along part of its length by clouds of dust.
The Book of Genesis describes the sky as a ‘firmament’, and for centuries poets and believers pictured the heavens as a great solid vault.
The idea, popular since the seventeenth century, that the stars might be suns with worlds of their own.

quiz.q: In what state of mind does Alyosha return to the Elder’s cell?
o: Anguished still, and resolved to confess to Father Paisy
Numb and indifferent, feeling no need at all to pray
Troubled and unclear, yet with joy and sweetness in his heart
Ashamed of where he had been and afraid to approach the coffin
quiz.e: The agonizing sorrow of the morning is gone. Even the open window, which tells him the smell must have got worse, no longer brings back his indignation.
