quiz.q: What does he decide, as he drowses, about Grushenka’s talk of a knife?
o: It was a serious threat that he must report at once
It was only a ‘pathetic’ remark, and must be forgiven
It was meant as a way of frightening the listening Rakitin
It proved that she had never really forgiven the officer
quiz.e: She has not taken the knife, he thinks. Such remarks must be forgiven, because they bring comfort to the soul and make grief easier to bear.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha’s drowsy mind conclude about Rakitin?
o: That he too will one day come back to the monastery
That he ought to be forgiven and pitied like the others
That his twenty-five roubles must be paid back to him
That brooding on insults keeps him in a ‘side-lane’
quiz.e: Rakitin walked down a side-lane, and will always do so while he broods on insults. The true way, Alyosha thinks, is wide, straight and bright, with the sun at its end.

quiz.q: What moves Alyosha about the miracle at Cana?
o: Jesus came to their joy and not to their grief
Jesus rebuked the guests for their drunkenness
Mary doubted that the poor should have a feast
The miracle was a sign meant only for disciples
quiz.e: He loves this passage: the first miracle was done to contribute to human joy. He recalls the Elder’s saying, ‘Whoever loves human beings, loves their joy.’

quiz.q: How does Alyosha imagine Jesus saying ‘Mine hour is not yet come’?
o: With a stern look, in order to rebuke his mother
With deep sorrow, foreseeing his coming death
With weary reluctance, after lengthy pleading
With a quiet smile, before doing what she asked
quiz.e: He is sure Jesus smiled meekly at her. Though he had not come to earth to provide wine for poor weddings, he went and did as she requested.

quiz.q: What does the Elder tell Alyosha in the vision of the feast?
o: That he must stay and keep watch beside the coffin for years
That he has given an onion today, and must begin his task
That his grief is a sin, for which he must now do penance
That the disgrace at the coffin must be avenged in God’s name
quiz.e: The joyful old man says he too is at the feast for giving an onion, and that Alyosha gave one today to a woman who hungered for it. ‘Begin, dear fellow.’

quiz.q: What does Alyosha do after going out into the night?
o: He falls to the earth, kisses it and swears to love it
He goes to wake Porfiry and tells him all he has seen
He stands at the gates, unsure which road he should take
He kneels at the tomb of the Elder Iov and prays till dawn
quiz.e: Under the stars he casts himself down, weeping for joy, and longs to forgive all creatures and all things and to ask forgiveness for them.

quiz.q: What comes of this night for Alyosha?
o: He vows silence and retires into the hermitage for a year
He returns to Father Paisy and takes his final vows that week
He rises with firm resolve and soon leaves the monastery
He goes to Mokroye that same night to find Grushenka and Dmitry
quiz.e: He fell a feeble youth and arose a resolute warrior. Three days later he left the monastery, as the Elder had commanded him to ‘abide in the world’.

chapters.title: Kuzma Samsonov
chapters.intro: Background on Russian merchants, the provinces, lawyers after the reforms of the 1860s, nineteenth-century medicine and a poem by Pushkin, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter is one of several in this Book with violence, threats of violence or talk of suicide.
Someone devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure.
Under a false name, or with one’s identity hidden.
To speak or write at length on a subject.
French: an awkward clash or minor dispute.
A break or gap, especially in speech.
A person of letters; a writer.
Innocent, open and trusting, sometimes naively so.
A long, loose, traditional outer coat.
An old Russian measure of length, about seventy-one centimetres.
An old Russian measure equal to three arshins, about 2.1 metres.
French: ‘in the marble style’; finished to look like marble.
An old word for a doctor.
A long-term lung disease that causes shortness of breath.
Merchants formed a legally recognised class, organised in guilds. Many were rich, but the nobility tended to look down on them.

Around 1700 Peter the Great taxed beards and pressed Western clothes on the upper classes. Traditional merchants kept their beards and long coats, while their sons often took up ‘German’ dress, as Russians called Western fashions.
Imperial Russia was divided into provinces, each run from a provincial capital. Smaller towns looked to these capitals for courts, officials and professional men.
Also called brain fever: a diagnosis common in nineteenth-century medicine and novels for a sudden collapse after great emotional strain.
Alexander II’s judicial reforms created independent courts and a new profession of trained, sworn advocates. Clever lawyers soon became well-known public figures.
A public official who witnesses and certifies signatures and legal documents.
“In the Depths of the Siberian Mines”
A poem of 1827 by Pushkin, addressed to the Decembrists, the officers exiled after their failed uprising of 1825. It urges them to keep their spirits and their faith.

quiz.q: What does Mitya dream of doing if Grushenka chooses him?
o: Carrying her far away to begin a new, virtuous life
Staying in the town and winning his father’s blessing on them
Rejoining his old regiment and taking her along with him
Entering the civil service in the nearby provincial capital
quiz.e: He imagines carrying her off to the end of Russia, marrying her and starting a ‘without fail virtuous’ life under a new identity.

quiz.q: Why does he refuse to use Grushenka’s own money for this?
o: Her money is all tied up in Samsonov’s business
His pride demands that it be on his own means
She has told him that she would never lend any
He fears his father would claim it through the courts
quiz.e: Though she has money, a ‘terrible pride’ makes him want to begin the new life on his resources, not hers.

quiz.q: What does he decide he must do first, at all costs?
o: Force his father to give up the Chermashnya estate
Confess everything to Alyosha and ask his forgiveness
Repay Katerina Ivanovna her three thousand roubles
Find out the truth about the officer from Siberia
quiz.e: Otherwise he would begin his new life as ‘a pickpocket thief, and a scoundrel’, so he resolves to return the money before anything else.

quiz.q: How does Mitya get in to see Samsonov after being refused?
o: He bribes the lad who sleeps on the hallway cupboard
He waits out in the yard until the old man relents
He claims to bring an urgent message from his father
He sends in a note saying it concerns Grushenka
quiz.e: He has brought paper and pencil in case of refusal, and writes one line saying the matter closely concerns Agrafena Aleksandrovna.

quiz.q: Why does Samsonov summon his younger son before seeing Mitya?
o: To throw the visitor out at the first rude word
To write down the terms that were to be offered
To have a witness, should anything occur
To be presented as the future head of the house
quiz.e: He is not afraid of the ‘captain’, but he wants a witness in case anything happens, and he is also rather curious.

quiz.q: What does Mitya propose to Samsonov?
o: To sign over his rights to Chermashnya for three thousand
To pledge his army pension for a three-thousand-rouble loan
To marry Grushenka on a dowry of some three thousand
To act as Samsonov’s agent on a large timber contract
quiz.e: He offers his legal claims against his father over Chermashnya in exchange for three thousand at once, promising a profit of several thousand.

quiz.q: After refusing, what does Samsonov suggest?
o: Taking legal advice again from the lawyer Korneplodov
Offering the deal to a peasant timber dealer
Applying for help to the priest at Ilyinskoye himself
Asking Grushenka to plead with Fyodor Pavlovich
quiz.e: He sends Mitya to Lyagavy, ‘The Setter’, a timber trader bargaining over the Chermashnya birch grove, who is staying near Volovya Station.

quiz.q: What does the narrator reveal about Samsonov’s advice?
o: It was sincere, but the old man misjudged Lyagavy
It was a plan worked out with Fyodor Pavlovich
It was a generous act that Mitya later repaid
It was a malicious joke at Mitya’s expense
quiz.e: Samsonov later admits, laughing, that he was mocking the ‘captain’. In the moment he looked at him with infinite malice.

chapters.title: Lyagavy
chapters.intro: Background on Russian post roads and country travel, the timber trade, Jewish life in the Russian Empire and tea-drinking, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: With great speed; originally, travelling with relays of post-horses.
One’s own legs; to go by it is to go on foot.
A small Russian coin. A hundred copecks make a rouble.
An old Russian measure of distance, a little over a kilometre.
A long, close-fitting traditional Russian coat for men.
An old Russian measure for vodka, or a bottle of about 1.2 litres.
A metal urn for boiling water for tea.
Hard animal fat, used to make cheap candles.
A person’s face, especially as a guide to their character.
A discussion held in order to reach an agreement.
Of a candle: to burn unevenly and flicker as it nears its end.
Russian for a gentleman or landowner; how a servant addressed a master.
Travellers hired fresh horses and a driver at government posting stations along the main roads. The fare depended on the distance.
Away from the main post roads, tracks were unpaved and turned to mud in wet weather. Local estimates of distance could be very rough.
A simple four-wheeled cart without springs, notorious for shaking its passengers.
After serfdom ended in 1861 many landowners needed cash and sold their woodland to dealers, some of them traders of peasant origin.
Most Jews were legally confined to the Pale of Settlement in the west of the empire. Under Alexander II some merchants, university graduates and craftsmen were allowed to live elsewhere.
Tea was long carried overland from China and became the country’s everyday drink, served from the samovar and sometimes laced with rum.

quiz.q: How does Mitya raise the money for his journey?
o: He pawns his fur coat and borrows from a tavern-keeper
He sells his old silver watch and borrows from his landlords
He sells his saddle and takes an advance from Samsonov
He gives up his rented room and borrows from Alyosha
quiz.e: A watchmaker at the bazaar gives him six roubles for the watch, and his fond landlords lend him three: nine roubles in all.

quiz.q: Why does the narrator say this detail matters?
o: It shows how far his landlords had come to resent him
It shows that the watch had really belonged to his father
It proves that he had planned to leave the town for good
It proves that at noon he had no money, before witnesses
quiz.e: It becomes a ‘material fact’ that on the day before ‘a certain event’ Mitya was penniless and had to raise cash in front of witnesses.

quiz.q: What does Mitya learn when he tracks down the priest?
o: Lyagavy has moved on to a forest warden’s izba
Lyagavy has gone into town to see Fyodor Pavlovich
Lyagavy has sold on the timber rights to another dealer
Lyagavy refuses to meet anyone sent by Samsonov
quiz.e: The man is now at Sukhoy Posyolok, staying overnight with the forest warden, so Mitya has to go further still.

quiz.q: What warning does the priest give about the dealer?
o: He must never be asked about his dealings with Samsonov
He must be paid in advance, because he trusts nobody
He must be called Gorstkin, as ‘Lyagavy’ offends him
He must be greeted with a bow, being a strict Old Believer
quiz.e: The priest says the nickname is violently offensive, and that without using his real name Mitya will accomplish nothing.

quiz.q: What does Mitya find in the living-room of the izba?
o: The man asleep on a bench, drunk and impossible to wake
The man at the table, drawing up a contract with the warden
The man packing his belongings to leave before daybreak
The man arguing fiercely over a price with a stranger
quiz.e: He tugs and shakes the sleeper, who only mumbles and curses; the priest and the warden advise him to wait until morning.

quiz.q: What nearly kills them in the night, and how does Mitya respond?
o: A candle sets the room alight; he drags the sleeper into the yard
The warden attacks them; he fights him off in the passage
Bitter cold sets in; he wraps the sleeper in his own coat
Fumes fill the room; he raises the alarm and tends the sleeper
quiz.e: He wakes in agony to carbon-monoxide fumes, rouses the warden and spends about half an hour wetting the drunkard’s head.

quiz.q: What happens when the dealer finally wakes up next morning?
o: He is sober, and rejects the offer as far too low
He has slipped away in the dawn with Mitya’s papers
He is drunk again, and calls Mitya a scoundrel decorator
He agrees, but demands that the priest stand as witness
quiz.e: Already drunk on a fresh shtof, he insists Mitya is the decorator who took a contract and cheated. Mitya sees he has been fooled.

quiz.q: What restores Mitya’s spirits on the way back to town?
o: A letter from Grushenka waiting at Volovya Station
A large meal with vodka, and a new ‘unalterable’ plan
A kind word from the merchant who picks him up
A sudden belief that Samsonov would help him after all
quiz.e: At Volovya he eats hungrily, downs three glasses of vodka, cheers up and devises a new plan to get the money that very evening.

chapters.title: The Gold-mines
chapters.intro: Background on Siberian gold, the paper rouble, the railway boom, the ‘woman question’, Shakespeare and Russian literary journals, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter is one of several in this Book with violence, threats of violence or talk of suicide. It also includes a passing antisemitic remark.
A courier or messenger carrying urgent news.
A person’s spirit and strength of character.
To bribe someone to do something wrong.
Waste food fed to pigs; here, something disgusting.
A very small amount of something.
To know or become aware of something.
A fever with bouts of shivering.
Engaged to be married; the person one is engaged to.
Siberia became a major source of gold in the nineteenth century, drawing prospectors, speculators and adventurers to its remote goldfields.
For most of the period Russia’s paper notes could not be freely exchanged for silver or gold at face value. Their worth fell, especially in wartime, and this was a matter of public worry.
Russia built railways at great speed from the late 1860s, and the concessions made large fortunes for contractors and speculators.
The nineteenth-century debate about women’s education, work and legal rights. In Russia it grew lively in the 1860s, and university-level courses for women opened in the 1870s.
Shakespeare’s tragedy of a general in the service of Venice who is led by a villain’s lies to doubt his wife’s faithfulness.
Informal notes and anecdotes from the 1830s, given an English title, with remarks on writers and famous characters.
A short, world-weary prose piece of 1865. Dostoevsky mocked it in his novel The Devils.
Pen name of Mikhail Saltykov (1826–89), Russia’s leading satirist of officials and provincial life, and a long-running literary opponent of Dostoevsky.
A journal founded by Pushkin in 1836. In the 1850s and 1860s it became the voice of radical opinion, until the government closed it in 1866.
Radical critics such as Dmitry Pisarev praised ‘realists’: practical, scientific people with no time for sentiment, religion or romantic dreams.

quiz.q: How does Grushenka get Mitya off her hands that evening?
o: She sends him to look for Alyosha at the monastery
She tells him she is ill and can see no one tonight
She has him take her to Samsonov’s to ‘count money’
She asks him to wait in town for an important letter
quiz.e: Expecting her messenger, she gets him to escort her to Kuzma’s house and makes him promise to fetch her at midnight.

quiz.q: What does the narrator say about Othello, following Pushkin?
o: He is trusting and would never stoop to spying
He is a truly jealous man, like all who love
He is a vulgar soul destroyed by his suspicion
He is unable to forgive even the smallest fault
quiz.e: Othello’s ideal has perished, but he will not hide and eavesdrop as the truly jealous man will, without any pang of conscience.

quiz.q: How does Mitya get a little cash that evening?
o: He sells a ring to a collector he met at the inn
He borrows ten roubles from Marya Kondratyevna
He wins ten roubles playing billiards at the inn
He pawns his duelling pistols to a young official
quiz.e: He leaves the pistols he loves with a young, well-off civil servant who is passionately fond of weapons, and gets ten roubles for them.

quiz.q: What upsetting news awaits him at Marya Kondratyevna’s?
o: Fyodor Pavlovich has left for Chermashnya after all
Smerdyakov has had a fall and an epileptic attack
Ivan has quarrelled with his father and been thrown out
Grushenka was seen slipping into the old man’s house
quiz.e: With Smerdyakov ill, Mitya has lost his informant on what is happening in the house. He also learns that Ivan has left for Moscow.

quiz.q: Why is Mitya sure Mrs Khokhlakova will lend him the money?
o: She was an old friend of his late mother’s family
She has always admired his courage and his manners
She wants him gone so that Katerina is free of him
She owes him for a favour done in his army days
quiz.e: She detests him as Katerina’s betrothed, so he reasons she will pay anything to see him leave town for good.

quiz.q: What does she keep urging him to do?
o: Go off to the gold-mines and make millions
Take up horse-breeding on her country estate
Enter a monastery and repent of his past life
Find a post with the railway in St Petersburg
quiz.e: She has decided, even from his walk, that he is a man of energy who will discover gold-mines and return a leader of men.

quiz.q: What does she rush to fetch from her writing desk?
o: A promissory note that she asks him to sign
A map of Siberia that she spreads on the table
A long letter from Katerina that she reads out to him
A tiny silver icon that she hangs around his neck
quiz.e: Mitya thinks she is fetching the three thousand. Instead she blesses him with an icon from Kiev for a new life and new deeds.

quiz.q: How does the interview finally end?
o: She gives him five hundred and shows him the door
She has no money, and would not lend it if she had
She promises the sum if he leaves town tomorrow
She sends for Miusov to discuss the terms of a loan
quiz.e: She meant only the gold-mines. Mitya strikes the table, spits and storms out into the dark, where he weeps like a little boy.

quiz.q: How does Mitya learn that Grushenka has left Samsonov’s?
o: He collides with Samsonov’s old servant in the square
He goes to the house and is told at the outer gate
He meets Alyosha, on his way back from the monastery
He receives a hurried note sent after him by Fenya
quiz.e: The old serving-woman he nearly knocks over tells him Grushenka stayed only a minute, told Kuzma some story and ran off.

quiz.q: What does Mitya take with him as he rushes from Grushenka’s kitchen?
o: A kitchen knife lying on the table near the door
A heavy poker from beside the great kitchen stove
A small brass pestle snatched out of the mortar
A silver candlestick from the old cook’s shelf
quiz.e: He stuffs the pestle into his side pocket as he runs out, and Fenya cries that he is going to kill somebody.

chapters.title: In the Dark
chapters.intro: Background on provincial Russian towns and households, folk healing, Chinese-style furnishings and a poem by Pushkin, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

The back parts of a property, such as yards and lanes behind houses.
A small gate, often set in a fence or wall.
A shrub with flat clusters of small white flowers and dark berries.
A shrub with clusters of white flowers and bright red berries.
Lying across something, from side to side.
The section of wall between two windows.
A glass bottle with a stopper, used for serving wine or spirits.
A strong, sweet alcoholic drink, served in small glasses.
A liquid flavoured by soaking herbs or other substances in it.
Russian: the lady of the house; how servants spoke of their mistress.
Hanging and swinging, like a pendulum.
Most were built largely of wood, with low houses standing in fenced yards, often with orchards and kitchen gardens behind them.
A small building, usually apart from the main house, used for steaming and washing.
Few streets had lighting, and the lamps that existed burned oil or kerosene. Away from the main squares, nights were very dark.
After serfdom ended in 1861, many former serfs in gentry households stayed on with their old masters as paid servants.
Rural Russians often treated illness with herbal infusions in vodka, by rubbing the body with spirits, and with whispered prayers or charms.
A European fashion, strong from the seventeenth century on, for objects in a Chinese style, such as lacquered folding screens.
Pushkin’s fairy-tale narrative poem of 1820, drawing on Russian folklore. It made him famous.

quiz.q: Where does Mitya run, convinced that Grushenka must be there?
o: To the inn at Mokroye, by the long country road
To his father’s house, by way of the back lane
To the monastery, by the short cut through the wood
To Samsonov’s house again, in through the side gate
quiz.e: He is sure she went straight from Samsonov’s to Fyodor Pavlovich, so he circles round to the lane and climbs the garden fence.

quiz.q: What does Mitya see through the lit window?
o: The old man asleep at the table, letter in hand
Grigory quarrelling with the old man over an envelope
Two figures talking low behind a Chinese screen
The old man alone and restless, in a new dressing-gown
quiz.e: Fyodor Pavlovich, dressed up in silk and fine linen, sips cognac, examines his bruises in the mirror and peers out into the dark.

quiz.q: How does Mitya try to settle whether she is in the room?
o: He taps out the signal meaning Grushenka has come
He calls out softly, imitating Smerdyakov’s voice
He throws a handful of gravel against the windowpane
He tries each of the doors to see if one will give
quiz.e: He uses the code the old man arranged with Smerdyakov. Fyodor Pavlovich rushes to the window and calls for her, and Mitya sees he is alone.

quiz.q: What surges up in Mitya as the old man leans out of the window?
o: A sudden, crushing pity for his loneliness
A sudden, cold fear of being discovered there
A sudden, violent loathing of his face
A sudden, overwhelming shame at his spying
quiz.e: The hated profile, lit by the lamp, brings on the ‘personal loathing’ he had told Alyosha he feared. He pulls out the pestle.

quiz.q: What seems to make Grigory get up from his sickbed?
o: He is woken by a shout from Fyodor Pavlovich’s room
He feels uneasy at having left the house unwatched
He has run out of the remedy his wife prepared
He is sent by Marfa to learn what the noise was
quiz.e: Perhaps from a prick of conscience, he rises in pain, steps out on to the porch and remembers he had left the garden gate unlocked.

quiz.q: What happens when Grigory catches the fleeing man at the fence?
o: He grabs his coat and is dragged out into the lane
He loses sight of him and shouts in vain for help
He fires a gun in the air and rouses the neighbours
He seizes a leg, cries ‘Father-murderer!’ and falls
quiz.e: He gets out that one shout before he falls as if struck by lightning, and Mitya drops back down into the garden.

quiz.q: What does Mitya do with the man lying on the ground?
o: He tries to wipe away the blood, then runs off
He carries him up on to the porch and knocks for Marfa
He drags him to the bathhouse and shuts the door
He checks that he is breathing and runs for the doctor
quiz.e: He drops the pestle, feels the skull, presses his new handkerchief to the bleeding head, then says ‘If I’ve done him in, I’ve done him in’ and flees.

quiz.q: What does the lad at Mrs Morozova’s gate tell him?
o: That she is at home and has barred him from the house
That she has gone back to Samsonov’s to collect money
That she left for Mokroye two hours ago to see an officer
That she has driven with Fyodor’s man to Chermashnya
quiz.e: The cheerful lad, unaware of Fenya’s plea, says Agrafena Aleksandrovna went off with Timofey to see ‘some officer’. Mitya runs to Fenya.

chapters.title: A Sudden Resolve
chapters.intro: Background on Russian civil-service ranks, billiards and tipping, imported delicacies and references to Schiller, Hamlet, Pushkin and Greek myth, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter is one of several in this Book with violence, threats of violence or talk of suicide.
A small room leading into a larger one.
With regard to; by the way.
A small, fluffy breed of lapdog from Italy.
To supply or fit out; also, to polish up.
A large basket with a lid, used for carrying food.
An old word for a girl or young woman, especially of the working class.
Russian appetisers, often served with vodka.
A man’s formal black coat with tails.
Peter the Great’s system of 1722 arranged military, naval, civil and court service into fourteen grades. Officials were addressed according to their rank.
A favourite recreation in Russian inns and clubs, often played for money.
Russians called a tip ‘for vodka’, whatever it was actually spent on.
A family firm of St Petersburg merchants, famous for imported wines and luxury groceries.
Goose-liver pâté in pastry from Strasbourg, in Alsace; a famous and costly delicacy.
A freshwater fish of the salmon family.
An 1803 poem in which the Greek heroes celebrate the fall of Troy. The Russian poet Fyodor Tyutchev made a free translation of it in 1851.
For nineteenth-century Russian writers, Shakespeare’s prince became a byword for the brooding man who thinks too much to act. Turgenev wrote a well-known essay on him in 1860.
Pushkin’s historical drama, written in 1825, about the tsar who ruled Russia around 1600. It includes an old monk finishing his chronicle.
Another name for Apollo, the Greek god of light and poetry. Poets often use the name for the sun itself.

quiz.q: What does Fenya’s news do to Mitya?
o: It sends him straight back to his father’s house
It makes him swear revenge on Samsonov for lying
It sets him searching the house for hidden letters
It stops him dead: she has gone to her former officer
quiz.e: He has seized her by the throat, but on hearing of the officer he releases her and sits down, pale as a corpse.

quiz.q: What does Fenya notice as he questions her gently?
o: That his coat is torn at the shoulder
That his hands are covered in blood
That his boots are thick with garden mud
That his eyes are streaming with tears
quiz.e: She keeps drawing his attention to it. He says it is human blood and asks why it was shed, and his manner stays strange.

quiz.q: What does he hint to Fenya before leaving?
o: That at dawn he will ‘leap over’ a terrible fence
That at dawn he means to marry at the monastery
That by daybreak all his debts will have been paid
That he will set out for the gold-mines by morning post
quiz.e: He speaks in a riddle about a high and terrible fence that ‘Mitenka’ will leap when the sun rises, and asks her to remember him.

quiz.q: What astonishes Perkhotin most when Mitya turns up?
o: He is wearing his old uniform with all its medals
He has brought in the servant who has been hurt
He is holding out a wad of notes in bloody fingers
He is dragging a heavy chest of coins along behind him
quiz.e: He comes in with a large wad of hundred-rouble notes held out in front of him, in a way no one holds money, wanting his pistols back.

quiz.q: Where does Mitya claim the money came from?
o: He won it at cards at the Capital City inn
Samsonov has bought his rights to Chermashnya
His brother Ivan sent it to him from Moscow
Mrs Khokhlakova gave him three thousand
quiz.e: He says the lady doled out three thousand for the gold-mines, and tells Perkhotin to go and ask her in the morning.

quiz.q: How does he answer when Perkhotin presses him about a fight?
o: A soldier he hit at the inn has gone to the police
An old man he knocked down has ‘forgiven’ him
A dog bit him in the road, and he had to kill it
A friend of his father’s has challenged him to a duel
quiz.e: He first says it was a little old woman, then shouts ‘An old man!’, and adds, winking, that the fellow has by now definitely forgiven him.

quiz.q: What does he write on the scrap of paper?
o: ‘I punish myself for the whole of my life’
‘I forgive them both for the whole of my life’
‘I leave all I have to my brother Alyosha’
‘I alone am guilty of the blood that was shed’
quiz.e: He shows it to Perkhotin as a ‘riddle’. Having already seen the loaded pistol, Perkhotin threatens to tell someone.

quiz.q: What does he do with the pistol as Perkhotin watches?
o: Cleans it, and says it once belonged to his father
Polishes it, and offers it to Perkhotin as a keepsake
Loads it, and studies the bullet above the candle
Hides it, and makes Perkhotin swear to say nothing
quiz.e: Asked why he is looking at the bullet, he says a man would want to see what was going into his brain, then calls it all rubbish.

quiz.q: What does Mitya ask Perkhotin at the little table in Plotnikovs’?
o: Whether he has ever been to Mokroye at night
Whether he has ever been in love with a woman
Whether he has ever fought a duel over a debt
Whether he has ever stolen anything
quiz.e: Perkhotin admits taking twenty copecks from his mother at nine, and Mitya slyly claims exactly the same.

quiz.q: What does Perkhotin end up doing after his third game?
o: Goes to the police to report the blood he has seen
Goes to knock at Grushenka’s gate to question Fenya
Goes back to Plotnikovs’ to check over the bill
Goes home to bed, resolved to forget the whole matter
quiz.e: Too uneasy to have supper, he thinks of Fyodor Pavlovich’s house, then turns to Mrs Morozova’s and pounds on the gate until the whole street can hear.

chapters.title: ‘Here I Come!’
chapters.intro: Background on troikas, rural moneylending, Roma choirs and Orthodox teaching and legends about hell and forgiveness, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter is one of several in this Book with violence, threats of violence or talk of suicide.
A heavy whip, formerly used for punishment and on horses.
A woman paid to do cleaning.
Money, especially when gained in a shabby way.
A ghost, or something that haunts the mind.
A person taking part in a conversation.
A stringed instrument played by striking with small hammers.
A bandit; used loosely for a rogue.

A carriage, sledge or cart pulled by three horses harnessed abreast, often with bells. It became a symbol of Russian speed and spirit, most famously at the end of the first part of Gogol’s Dead Souls.
Alongside government post stations, privately run inns offered travellers rooms and horses.
After 1861 many peasants fell deep into debt. Village traders and innkeepers often lent them money or grain and took repayment in labour.
Roma singers, then called gypsies, were hugely popular with Russian nobles and officers in the nineteenth century, who paid lavishly to hear them.
The word used in Russian censuses to count people. A village’s size was often given in souls.
Christian tradition holds that after the Crucifixion Christ went down among the dead and set the righteous free. Orthodox icons of the Resurrection traditionally show this scene.
The last day before Great Lent, when Orthodox Christians ask one another’s forgiveness.
Russian peasants told and sang many stories about Christ, the saints and the next life, some of them outside official Church teaching.

quiz.q: What does Mitya feel towards the new rival as he flies along?
o: No jealousy at all: the man has the prior right to her
Burning hatred: he means to challenge him on his arrival
Cold contempt: he is certain that the man is a fraud
Gnawing fear: he suspects that he cannot win her back
quiz.e: Strangely, he feels no hostility towards her ‘first one’. Her first love has a right to her, so he must ‘step aside’ and give way.

quiz.q: What sudden thought fills him with anguish on the road?
o: That the horses may give out before reaching Mokroye
That Fenya may have raised the alarm back in town
That they may already be asleep when he gets there
That the second wagon may arrive there before he does
quiz.e: He imagines flying there with such feeling only to find them asleep, perhaps together, and a shiver of hatred runs through his heart.

quiz.q: When Andrey nervously raises Fenya’s plea, what does Mitya answer?
o: One must not listen to women; they always exaggerate
One must not trample others; if you do, punish yourself
One must pay well for silence; here is more for vodka
One must look after the horses, not the passengers
quiz.e: He asks what kind of yamshchik never gives way: anyone who has ruined another’s life should ‘punish yourself and depart’.

quiz.q: In Andrey’s tale, who will fill hell after Christ has freed its sinners?
o: Thieves, false witnesses and hardened drunkards
Priests, monks and all who break their sacred vows
Those who die without asking for forgiveness
Powerful men, rulers, big judges and the rich
quiz.e: When hell moans at being emptied, the Lord promises it that the mighty will come until the end of the ages. Mitya calls it a splendid popular legend.

quiz.q: Why, according to Andrey, will the Lord forgive Mitya?
o: For the simpleness of his soul
For the tears that he has shed
For the alms he has always given
For the love he bears that woman
quiz.e: He says that to the peasants Mitya is ‘naught but a little boy’, and that despite his temper he will be forgiven.

quiz.q: Why is innkeeper Trifon Borisych so delighted to see Mitya?
o: He hopes to be repaid an old gambling debt at last
He wants to warn him about his Polish guests in time
He scents another rich spree to profit from
He has long been truly fond of the young master
quiz.e: He made hundreds out of Mitya’s last visit and knows from the way he rolled up that there is plunder to be had again.

quiz.q: Who does Trifon say is keeping Grushenka company?
o: Only the officer, shut up alone with her upstairs
Some local landowners who stopped to play cards
Two Poles, together with Rakitin and Miusov
Two Poles, together with Kalganov and Maksimov
quiz.e: A Polish civil servant and his companion are there, along with the young Kalganov and the landowner Maksimov, returning from Cherni.

quiz.q: How does Andrey respond to Mitya’s offer of fifty roubles?
o: He pockets it all and asks for more vodka
He takes only five, saying that he is frightened
He turns it down flat and drives off at once
He takes the money and sends it back to Fenya
quiz.e: He accepts five roubles for tea and no more. Mitya throws him the five, then has Trifon lead him up to spy on the party from the dark.

chapters.title: The Former and Beyond Dispute
chapters.intro: Background on Poland’s history and forms of address, cavalry and ballrooms, the card game faro and French and Russian literary references, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Polish: ‘sir’, used when speaking directly to a man.
A loyal follower who carries out orders without question.
Of a voice: very loud and strong.
Willing to do anything for money; open to bribery.
A male turkey; a strutting, self-important man.
A short, witty poem or saying.
In the Bible, a city destroyed for its wickedness; hence any place of vice.
A gambling term: a stake equal to the whole bank.
In 1772, 1793 and 1795 Russia, Prussia and Austria carved up Poland between them, until it disappeared from the map.
Poles rose against Russian rule in 1830–31 and again in 1863–64. Both risings were crushed.
Many thousands of Poles were sent to Siberia after the second uprising.
The Polish nobility: an unusually large class, many of whose members were poor.
Light cavalry armed with lances, originally Polish, whose style spread across Europe.
A lively Polish dance that became a fixture of ballrooms in Russia and Europe.
A gambling game in which players place stakes on chosen cards against a banker.
In faro, a player could signal a change of stake by bending the corner of a card.
Gogol’s comic novel of 1842 about a swindler who travels the provinces buying up the names of dead serfs. Among the landowners he meets is the brawling liar Nozdryov.
An eighteenth-century French poet and wit, known for his epigrams, who was kept out of the French Academy.
A seventeenth-century French poet and critic, whose poem The Art of Poetry set out rules for good writing.
A Russian writer (1769–1844), best known for his fables.
An ancient Greek poet from the island of Lesbos. Legend says she threw herself into the sea for love of a ferryman, Phaon.
An 1869 novel by Ivan Goncharov, the author of Oblomov. It ends by picturing Russia as a vast grandmother.

quiz.q: What does Mitya ask for when he first comes in?
o: To be left alone with Grushenka for an hour
To be told at once which of them is the officer
To be allowed to join them until morning
To be given a room and a bottle of wine
quiz.e: Stammering that he means no harm, he asks if a passing traveller may stay in that very room until morning, for the last time.

quiz.q: How does Mitya change after his first glass of champagne?
o: He turns meek and childlike, smiling at them all
He turns menacing, and stares hard at both Poles
He turns silent, and refuses to touch his glass again
He turns boastful, and tells them about his three thousand
quiz.e: His tragic look gives way to something almost infant-like, with the grateful air of a guilty stray dog let back into the house.

quiz.q: What absurd claim of Maksimov’s does Kalganov relate?
o: That he fought under Napoleon and was decorated by him
That he married a countess while he was living in Poland
That a famous bishop once made him his private secretary
That Gogol wrote about him and his flogging in Dead Souls
quiz.e: He says he was the landowner flogged by Nozdryov. Kalganov protests that the years cannot tally. Maksimov blames it on quoting Piron.

quiz.q: What did Maksimov discover after marrying his first wife?
o: That she was poor, and her dowry a fiction
That she was lame; the ‘jumping’ had hidden it
That she was still married to someone else
That she was noble, and her family disowned her
quiz.e: He thought she jumped up and down for joy. After the wedding she confessed that she had hurt her foot jumping over a puddle as a girl.

quiz.q: What toast does Pan Wróblewski make that provokes Mitya?
o: To Russia within the frontiers of before 1772
To Poland and to all of her noble exiles abroad
To the queen now restored to her true love
To the tsar and to the end of all rebels
quiz.e: Asked to drink to Russia, the Poles will drink only to the Russia of before the first partition. Mitya’s ‘You’re being silly’ nearly causes a quarrel.

quiz.q: Who stops Mitya from staking more at faro?
o: Maksimov, who begs him to hold on to the money
Trifon Borisych, who warns him about the pack
Kalganov, who covers the notes with his hand
Grushenka, who sweeps the cards off the table
quiz.e: Mitya has lost two hundred roubles and is doubling his stakes when Kalganov says ‘Enough!’ and Grushenka backs him up.

quiz.q: What does Mitya offer the little pan in the side room?
o: Five hundred to lose the next game on purpose
Three thousand to go for ever, part of it down
A thousand to tell Grushenka the whole truth
Two hundred to go back to Siberia and write
quiz.e: He proposes three thousand to clear out at once, with first five hundred and then seven hundred down and the rest promised for the next day.

quiz.q: What does Grushenka realise on hearing of the offer?
o: That Mitya has been cheated out of all he owned
That Kalganov arranged the whole quarrel himself
That Samsonov wrote to the Pole to warn him off
That the Pole had come for her money, not for her
quiz.e: Learning that he would have taken the money, she sees he only came to wed her because he had heard she was rich.

quiz.q: How is the cheating at cards exposed?
o: Kalganov finds a marked card in the tall Pole’s boot
Maksimov sees the banker slip a queen up his sleeve
Trifon pulls his unopened pack from behind the sofa
Mitya catches the little Pole dealing from the bottom
quiz.e: The landlord saw the Pole hide the fresh pack and switch it for his own, and Kalganov adds that he saw the other pan cheat twice.

quiz.q: What finally becomes of the two Poles?
o: They end up in a side room and lock themselves in
They are driven off in a troika by the landlord’s men
They go to the police to lodge a formal complaint
They take their winnings and ride back to the town
quiz.e: Mitya carries Wróblewski out after he insults Grushenka, and the little pan, still hoping she will follow, stalks in after him. The lock clicks from their side.

chapters.title: Delirium
chapters.intro: Background on Russian folk songs, dances and festivals, the declining gentry and a saying from the Gospels, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter is one of several in this Book with violence, threats of violence or talk of suicide. It also includes crude sexual humour and a passing antisemitic remark.
In Greek myth, a horn overflowing with food; hence a great abundance.
Lavish entertainment with food and drink.
Not suited to the solemn season of Lent; bawdy.
A burst of public excitement or anger.
A dance named after sabots, the wooden clogs of French peasants.
The plant used to make linen; its pale fibres are compared to fair hair.
A sweet or small sugary delicacy.
A flat stringed instrument played by plucking.
Russian: a pet form of barynya, ‘young lady’ or ‘little mistress’.
Women and girls sang together and danced in slow circles, known as the khorovod, at festivals.
A short, rhymed and often cheeky folk song, usually of four lines.
One of the best-known Russian folk dance songs.
Travelling entertainers led trained bears around Russian villages and fairs for centuries, and people in folk plays dressed up to imitate them.
An old midsummer festival with bonfires, bathing and all-night revelry.
After 1861 many landowners fell into debt and sold their estates, while merchants and railway contractors grew rich.
An echo of the title of Dostoevsky’s 1861 novel The Insulted and Injured, whose phrase became shorthand for the poor and humiliated.
In Matthew’s Gospel, Jesus prays in the Garden of Gethsemane that a ‘cup’ of suffering might pass from him.

quiz.q: What does Mitya consider, alone on the upstairs gallery?
o: Slipping away to town and giving himself up
Hiding what is left of the money under the floor
Sending Andrey back to town to learn the news
Fetching his pistol to end it all in that corner
quiz.e: For almost a minute he hesitates, but now that the ‘former’ one has shrunk to nothing, a ray of hope sends him rushing back to her.

quiz.q: What puts Kalganov so out of temper?
o: The loss of his fifty roubles to the two Poles
The coarse songs and ‘swinishness’ of the revels
The way Grushenka keeps on teasing Maksimov
The late arrival of the wagon with the wine
quiz.e: The bear-dancing and a ‘new’ ditty about girls choosing a rich merchant disgust him. He declares himself ‘fed up’ and dozes on the sofa.

quiz.q: How does Mitya explain his frowning to Grushenka?
o: He fears that the two Poles will come after them
He has realised that he is running short of money
He left a sick man behind and longs for him to recover
He is afraid of what Katerina Ivanovna will do
quiz.e: He says that if only he knew the man would get better, he would give up ten years of his life on the spot.

quiz.q: What does Grushenka tell Mitya behind the curtain?
o: The Pole is a stranger now, and it is Mitya she loves
The Pole still holds her heart, and she means to leave
The Elder’s death has moved her to enter a convent
The officer once saved her, and she is bound to him
quiz.e: Weeping, she curses her five years of devotion. When the ‘falcon’ came in, her heart told her that he was the one she loved.

quiz.q: When Mitya says he is a thief, what does Grushenka propose?
o: Keep the money and slip off together to Moscow
Enter the monastery and beg to be given guidance
Repay Katerina, ask her pardon, and work the land
Go to Fyodor Pavlovich and ask him to lend the sum
quiz.e: She offers her own money to repay ‘the young mistress’ and says they must go away and scrape the earth with their hands, as Alyosha has commanded.

quiz.q: What happens when Grushenka tries to dance?
o: She dances well, and the Poles come out to watch
She falls asleep in her chair before the music starts
She is stopped by Mitya, who will not have her seen
She sways, says she is too weak, and bows to everyone
quiz.e: She begins to wave her handkerchief but stops in bewilderment, bows to the chorus and all four corners, then asks Mitya to take her away.

quiz.q: What does she ask of Mitya on the bed behind the curtain?
o: Not to touch her in that house, and to take her far away
To tell the Poles that she has left them now for good
To fetch Maksimov and have him sing to her once more
To hand over the money and let her look after it for him
quiz.e: She says it must be honest from now on. He kneels and promises, then blurts out that he would give anything to know about ‘that blood’.

quiz.q: What is Mitya told at the end of the chapter?
o: That he is accused of attacking the old servant
That he is accused of the murder of his father
That he is accused of robbing Mrs Khokhlakova
That he is accused of cheating the two Poles
quiz.e: The room has filled with officials. Mitya cries ‘The old man and his blood!’, and the young investigator charges him with killing Fyodor Pavlovich.

chapters.title: The Beginning of the Civil Servant Perkhotin’s Career
chapters.intro: Background on Russian civil service ranks, the customs of paying calls, Siberian gold, saints and blessings and capital punishment, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: The most important or central part of something.
Calm and unemotional; not easily excited.
The area inside the walls or boundaries of a place.
In Russia, a man (dvornik) who looked after a building’s yard and gate.
Russian for a lady of the house; how servants spoke of their mistress.
A feeling that something, usually bad, is about to happen.
To calm or reduce a fear or worry.
Russian for a great deed or heroic act, often one of religious self-sacrifice.
Happening as a separate incident rather than as part of a main story.
An old way of saying the next day.
Created by Peter the Great in 1722, it divided state service into fourteen grades, civil and military. Clerks in the lower grades were numerous, modestly paid and keen to rise.

A visitor to a respectable house gave his name to a servant, then waited to learn whether he would be received. Custom governed the hours for visiting, and a stranger needed a good reason to come at all.
Gold mining in Siberia expanded rapidly from the 1830s and attracted investors and adventurers. Going to the goldfields became a familiar dream of making a quick fortune.
In the mid-eighteenth century Empress Elizabeth stopped executions for ordinary crimes. Afterwards the death penalty was kept mainly for political offences and certain cases under military law.
St Barbara, an early Christian martyr honoured in the Orthodox Church as a ‘great martyr’. Russians prayed to her for protection against sudden death.
Orthodox believers might wear a small icon or cross around the neck, sometimes one that had touched a saint’s relics, as a sign of faith and protection.
Russians could make the sign of the Cross over another person, not only themselves, to ask God’s protection, for example when someone set off on a journey or a task.

quiz.q: What does Perkhotin learn from Fenya about the pestle?
o: Mitya had left it lying in her kitchen and gone out
Mitya had hidden it under her mistress’s porch steps
Mitya took it, and came back bloody and without it
Mitya had bought it in the market square that day
quiz.e: Fenya says Mitya snatched a pestle from the mortar as he ran off, and came back without it and with bloody hands.

quiz.q: Why does Perkhotin decide against simply going to Fyodor Pavlovich’s house?
o: He fears a scandal if it proves that nothing happened
He fears that the old man will set the servants on him
He has been told that the household has gone to Mokroye
He has quarrelled with the old man and swore to stay away
quiz.e: The hour is late and the gate massive, and if all is well the ‘derisive’ old man will tell the whole town how a stranger forced his way in to see whether he had been killed.

quiz.q: What does he decide should settle whether he goes to the police chief that night?
o: Whether Fenya will repeat her story in front of a priest
Whether Mrs Khokhlakova really lent Mitya the money
Whether the yardkeeper saw which way Mitya had run off
Whether Grigory has heard any noise from the old house
quiz.e: If she says she lent no three thousand, he will go to the police at once; if she did lend it, the matter can wait until the morrow.

quiz.q: How does he get past the first refusal at Mrs Khokhlakova’s door?
o: He pushes the manservant aside and walks straight in
He claims to bring a letter from the chief of police
He says that her daughter’s health may be in danger
He sends word that she may regret refusing to see him
quiz.e: Turned away once, he insists on being announced again and says the lady will ‘possibly herself regret it’ if she does not receive him now.

quiz.q: How does she first respond when he names Dmitry Fyodorovich?
o: With tears of concern for the young man’s future
With a calm statement that she hardly knows him
With fury, threatening to go to the authorities
With delight, supposing he has come to repay a debt
quiz.e: She almost shrieks, asks how much longer she is to be tormented by this ‘dreadful man’, and threatens to file a complaint against her visitor.

quiz.q: What does she exclaim on hearing Mitya claimed she lent him three thousand?
o: That she never lent it, and he has killed his father
That she did lend it, but only on a signed promise
That she lent half of it and has heard nothing since
That she lent it, and expects it back within the week
quiz.e: ‘O God! He has killed his old father!’ she cries, and insists that she never lent him any money at all.

quiz.q: What does Perkhotin ask her to do before he leaves?
o: Come with him and speak directly to the police chief
Send for her doctor and keep her daughter indoors
Keep silent about his visit until the next morning
Write a few lines saying she never lent Mitya money
quiz.e: She dashes off a signed note on a half-sheet of paper, swearing she never lent Mitya three thousand or any other sum.

quiz.q: According to the narrator, what eventually came of this late-night encounter?
o: A lawsuit that kept the town talking for many years
The foundation of the young man’s entire career
A public quarrel with the chief of police himself
Mrs Khokhlakova’s hasty departure from the town
quiz.e: Each is charmed by the other, and the narrator says the meeting became the basis of the young official’s whole career, still remembered with amazement in the town.

chapters.title: The Alarm
chapters.intro: Background on Russian police and courts, the Great Reforms, local government and rural medicine, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes descriptions of violent injury and death, and mentions suicide.
A Russian card game related to whist.
A large Russian pie with a filling such as fish, cabbage, rice or mushrooms.
Suffering from or inclined to consumption (tuberculosis), a wasting disease of the lungs.
A French-sounding phrase for someone who enjoys good food, drink and company.
An old word for a very small man.
Complete; out-and-out, usually of something bad.
A dishonest or mischievous man; a rogue. Also the jack in a pack of cards.
Lying flat on one’s back, face upward.
Russian for a landowner or gentleman; how a servant spoke of a master.
An old name for epilepsy, a condition that causes seizures.
A small gate, often set beside or within a larger one.
With one’s true identity kept hidden.
A middle-ranking title in the Russian civil service.
Alexander II replaced Russia’s closed, slow and corrupt courts with a new system of public hearings, judges who could not easily be removed and, for serious crimes, juries.
The state’s legal officer. After 1864 procurators prosecuted criminal cases, each attached to a court and helped by deputies, who often worked in the smaller towns.
An official attached to the courts, introduced in 1860 to take the investigation of serious crimes out of the hands of the police.
A police chief (ispravnik) ran the police in a rural district, and retired army officers often held the post. Beneath him, district superintendents each had charge of a section of the countryside.
Russian procedure called for local people to watch searches and inspections, so that they could confirm afterwards what had been done and found.
The 1864 reforms created Russia’s first independent bar. Leading defence lawyers soon became famous and well paid, and their courtroom speeches were printed in the newspapers.
The name for the changes made under Alexander II, who reigned from 1855 to 1881: the end of serfdom, new courts, local councils and army reform, among others.
The usual name for the 1861 law ending serfdom. Its rules on land and payments were notoriously complicated.
An elected local council, created in 1864, that looked after matters such as roads, schools and public health in the countryside.
Zemstvos paid doctors to serve rural districts, where medical care had hardly existed. Young, idealistic graduates often took these posts.
The Medical-Surgical Academy in the capital was Russia’s leading medical school, known especially for training army doctors.

quiz.q: What has made the police chief so popular in the town?
o: His strict and learned grasp of the new reform laws
His fearless record in catching the district’s thieves
His generous gifts to the poor and to the local church
His open house: he ‘knew how to unite society’
quiz.e: He is always surrounded by guests, cards and dancing. As for the law, he has only a carefree and error-prone idea of the recent reforms.

quiz.q: What is said to be the main flaw in the deputy procurator’s character?
o: He thinks more of himself than his merits warrant
He is lazy, and leaves his cases to his young clerks
He is easily bribed by the richest of the merchants
He is cruel to his wife and cold to his few friends
quiz.e: Vain and irritable, Ippolit Kirillovich believes he has a special gift for the psychology of crime and that he has been passed over and underappreciated.

quiz.q: What wakes Marfa Ignatyevna in the night?
o: The sound of Grigory shouting out from the garden
A loud knocking at the shutters of the outbuilding
Smerdyakov’s howl as one of his seizures begins
A scream from the barin’s window across the yard
quiz.e: She is woken by the fearful howl that always begins his fits; going to him, she then realises that Grigory is not in their bed.

quiz.q: Where does Marfa find Grigory?
o: Lying on the garden path beside the open wicket
About twenty paces from the fence, having crawled
Slumped against the door into the barin’s study
Stretched out by the bath-house, unable to speak
quiz.e: Bloodied and babbling, he has crawled some distance from where he fell. He babbles ‘He’s killed him … killed his father’ and tells her to run for help.

quiz.q: What do the officials find on the floor behind the screen?
o: A bloodstained towel and the old man’s bunch of keys
A letter from Grushenka and a broken brass candlestick
A loaded pistol and the note that Mitya had written
An opened, empty envelope and a slender pink ribbon
quiz.e: The large envelope, addressed to ‘my angel Grushenka’ and once holding three thousand roubles, has been opened and emptied.

quiz.q: What in Perkhotin’s testimony makes the officials want to hurry to Mokroye?
o: His report that Mitya planned to flee abroad at dawn
His fear that Mitya would murder Grushenka there
His belief that Mitya would shoot himself at dawn
His claim that Mitya was hiding the money at an inn
quiz.e: Mitya had loaded a pistol, written a note and said ‘You won’t have time’, so they want to catch him before he carries it out.

quiz.q: What are the district superintendent’s instructions at Mokroye?
o: To shadow the suspect quietly until the others arrive
To arrest the suspect at once and put him in irons
To search the inn and take charge of all the money
To question the landlord and send back a full report
quiz.e: Sent about two hours ahead, Mavriky Mavrikiyevich keeps his incognito, watches Mitya and tells only Trifon Borisovich a part of the secret.

quiz.q: Why does the doctor stay behind instead of going to Mokroye?
o: He must attend to the injured Grigory through the night
He is fascinated by the case of Smerdyakov’s fits
He has been ordered to guard the house until morning
He is unwell himself and cannot manage the long road
quiz.e: He is to perform the autopsy next day, but what really absorbs him is Smerdyakov’s repeated seizures, ‘a matter for scientific analysis’. He says the man will not live till morning.

chapters.title: The Passage of a Soul Through the Torments. Torment the First
chapters.intro: Background on an Orthodox belief about the afterlife, Russian pre-trial procedure, penal servitude, an ancient philosopher and Russian names, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: The quality of being steady and unmoving, as in a stare.
Talking quickly and at great length.
The outer layer of the skin.
Confused and upset. A comic-sounding word.
A slangy word for a penniless person.
A raised platform on which criminals were executed.
To spend time together; to keep company.
To shout or speak very loudly.
A person’s outward manner and behaviour.

An Orthodox tradition holds that after death the soul passes through a series of trials, or toll-houses (mytarstva), where demons accuse it of particular kinds of sin. In everyday Russian the word came to mean any long ordeal.

Before a case went to trial, an investigator questioned the suspect and witnesses and gathered evidence. Trials became public after 1864, but this earlier stage stayed closed and written, and the suspect had no lawyer beside him.
Russian investigators worked through documents. A clerk took down what was said in an official form of words and the person questioned signed it afterwards, so exact wording mattered a great deal.
Peasants chosen as ‘hundred-men’ and ‘ten-men’ (sotskie and desyatskie) assisted the rural police. A metal badge showed their authority.
Known in Russian as katorga: forced labour, usually in Siberia, for serious crimes. Dostoevsky served four years as a convict at Omsk, from 1850 to 1854.
A Greek philosopher of the fourth century BC, remembered for scorning comfort and convention. By legend he carried a lamp in broad daylight, saying he was looking for an honest man.
Russians address people formally by first name plus patronymic, a name taken from the father’s. In quick speech the patronymic is often shortened, so that ‘-ovich’ becomes ‘-ych’.

quiz.q: What does Mitya shout when he grasps the charge against him?
o: That he killed his father, and that he deserves it
That he wanted to kill his father, but did not do so
That Smerdyakov must have done it while he was away
That he will say nothing until he has seen Grushenka
quiz.e: ‘I wanted to murder him, but I am not guilty!’ he cries. It is a confession of the wish and a denial of the deed.

quiz.q: What does Grushenka cry out when she rushes in?
o: That Mitya was with her when it all happened
That the police have arrested the wrong man
That she alone knows who the true killer is
That she drove them to it and is the guilty one
quiz.e: She collapses at the police chief’s feet, saying she drove both Mitya and the old man to the end of their tether, and will go with Mitya even to the scaffold.

quiz.q: What strangely holds Mitya’s eye throughout the questioning?
o: The large rings on the investigator’s fingers
The clerk’s threadbare and shabby hunting jacket
The bright lamp on the table in front of him
The metal badges worn by the men behind him
quiz.e: He later remembers with astonishment how the rings, one of amethyst and one of a bright-yellow stone, drew his gaze even in those terrible hours.

quiz.q: What news makes Mitya’s whole face shine?
o: That Grushenka has been released without charge
That his father is still alive, despite his wound
That Grigory is alive and is expected to recover
That Alyosha is on his way from the monastery
quiz.e: Told the old servant will live, he thanks God for a miracle and feels ‘resurrected’, since the blood that had weighed on him all night has been washed away.

quiz.q: Why does he say Grigory means so much to him?
o: He had saved the family’s estate from being sold
He had cared for him as an abandoned small child
He had often lent him money without being asked
He had once hidden him from his father’s beatings
quiz.e: Grigory carried him in his arms and washed him in the trough when he was three and abandoned by everyone: ‘my kindred father’.

quiz.q: What does Mitya volunteer about the three thousand in his father’s envelope?
o: He had never heard that such a sum existed at all
He had arranged to share it with Smerdyakov later
He had told Grushenka to refuse it if it was offered
He had looked on that money as his own property
quiz.e: He says he considered it stolen from him. The procurator winks at the investigator, and they make sure to record the point.

quiz.q: Asked whether he feels remorse over his father, what does Mitya say?
o: Not remorse, but he himself is no better than the man
That he does, and he wants it written down in the record
Not remorse, since the old man fully deserved to die
That he cannot speak of it until the case is concluded
quiz.e: He objects to the word: being none too attractive himself, he had no right to consider his father repulsive, and that is what he wants recorded.

quiz.q: What does Mikhail Makarovich come in to tell Mitya?
o: That Grushenka has gone back to town in his carriage
That Grushenka has made a full statement about him
That Grushenka is calm, and that he should be calm too
That Grushenka has been placed under arrest as well
quiz.e: With almost fatherly compassion the police chief says he has made her see reason and that she sent him to tell Mitya not to worry. Mitya, in tears of happiness, is consoled.

chapters.title: Torment the Second
chapters.intro: Background on Russian social estates, the rules of questioning, debts of honour, wolf hunting, a poem by Tyutchev and literary realism, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Stubbornly refusing to obey or cooperate.
A long, tiresome and complicated procedure or story.
A statement given under questioning and taken down for use as evidence.
A prison for people convicted of lesser crimes.
An old English coin of little value; used to mean a very small sum.
An expression meaning ‘I don’t care at all about’. In Russia the ‘fig’ was also a rude hand gesture.
An old Russian unit of distance, a little over a kilometre.
Under the 1864 rules a person being questioned could not be compelled to answer, and investigators were forbidden to extract a confession by promises, tricks or threats.
Besides prison or exile, Russian courts could strip a convict of the rights belonging to his social estate, such as a noble’s title and privileges.

Russian law divided subjects into estates (sosloviya): nobles, clergy, merchants, townspeople and peasants. Each had its own rights and duties, and nobles expected to be treated as equals by one another.
Debts owed on a gentleman’s word alone, such as gambling losses. They could not be enforced in court, and for that very reason an honourable man was expected to pay them first.
Wolves were common across Russia, and landowners hunted them with hounds and beaters. Tolstoy describes a celebrated wolf hunt in War and Peace.
Fyodor Tyutchev (1803–73) was one of Russia’s great lyric poets. This short poem, written around 1830, urges the reader to hide his deepest feelings, since ‘a thought once spoken is a lie’.
In the 1860s and 1870s Russian critics argued fiercely over how far art should simply show life as it is. Dostoevsky called himself a realist ‘in a higher sense’.

quiz.q: How does the investigator feel about the deputy procurator?
o: He envies him and quietly works to undermine him
He reveres him and reads his slightest glance
He pities him as a sick man close to retirement
He distrusts his methods and prefers his own
quiz.e: Almost alone in the world, Nikolay Parfenovich believes in Ippolit Kirillovich’s talents, likes him sincerely and can decode his merest wink.

quiz.q: What interrogation technique does Mitya mock as something from ‘your textbooks’?
o: Keeping a prisoner awake all night until he gives in
Promising him a lighter sentence if he will confess
Playing one suspect against another in separate rooms
Starting with trifles, then springing the real question
quiz.e: He ridicules the red-tape method of asking what you ate and how you spat, then suddenly demanding ‘Whom did you kill, whom did you rob?’

quiz.q: What does he say about why he needed the three thousand?
o: It was for a journey to the goldfields with Grushenka
It was to buy back the estate his father had taken
It was to repay a debt of honour, to someone unnamed
It was to settle what he had lost at cards in town
quiz.e: He calls it a debt of honour and flatly refuses to say to whom, declaring that this is his private life.

quiz.q: What does the procurator remind him about refusing to answer?
o: That he may refuse, but silence may do him harm
That he cannot refuse, as the law requires a reply
That he may refuse only with a lawyer there with him
That he may refuse now, but not when he is in court
quiz.e: With a severe reprimand he says Mitya has a perfect right not to answer, while it is their task to point out the harm this may do him.

quiz.q: Why does the sale of his watch interest the officials?
o: It suggests that he had been planning to leave town
It confirms that he had almost no money the day before
It shows that he had been trying hard to pay Samsonov
It proves that he had paid a visit to the Poles in town
quiz.e: He sold it for six roubles to pay for his journey. To Mitya’s indignation, they record it in detail as proof that he had scarcely a groat.

quiz.q: What dark thought of his do they take care to record?
o: That he had hoped that his father would die of drink
That he had wanted Samsonov ruined for having tricked him
That he had meant to burn the old man’s house to the ground
That he had thought of cutting a throat to get the money
quiz.e: He tells them that on leaving Mrs Khokhlakova he thought ‘of cutting someone’s throat’ to obtain three thousand. They stop him and write it down.

quiz.q: What does he do when pressed about why he took the pestle?
o: He refuses to say another word about it and falls silent
He claims that it had been given to him by the servant
He angrily dictates that he took it to kill his father
He admits that he meant only to frighten Grigory off
quiz.e: After muttering about fending off dogs, he turns to the clerk in rage and dictates that he took it to kill his father: a provocation, as the procurator recognises.

quiz.q: What recurring dream does Mitya compare the questioning to?
o: Hiding from someone who knows full well where he is
Falling from a height while a crowd looks up and jeers
Standing in court, unable to remember his own name
Searching through a dark house for his lost mother
quiz.e: His pursuer pretends not to know where he is, in order to enjoy his terror longer. ‘That is what you are doing now!’

chapters.title: The Third Torment
chapters.intro: Background on the rules of evidence in Russian law, Orthodox beliefs, illegitimacy, epilepsy and polite Russian speech, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes references to suicide and violence.
French, literally ‘cold blood’: calmness under pressure.
An informal old word for the head.
Quickly and without attention to detail.
A small Russian coin; one hundredth of a rouble.
A Russian coachman who drove hired or post horses.
Let the cat out of the bag
To give away a secret, usually by accident.
To say something sharply and suddenly.
Before 1864 Russian courts followed fixed rules for weighing evidence, which ranked some kinds of proof above others and treated a confession as the best proof of all.
The 1864 reforms swept those rules away. Judges and jurors were now to decide according to their conscience, after weighing all the evidence together.
Orthodox Christians believe that God gives each believer an angel at baptism to guard him through life.
A Russian proverb says that a mother’s prayer will bring you back from the bottom of the sea, meaning that it can save anyone.
A ‘natural’ son is one born outside marriage. In Russian law such children had almost no claim on their father’s name or property.

Dostoevsky had epilepsy for much of his adult life and gave the condition to several characters, including Prince Myshkin in The Idiot. Doctors of his day understood it poorly and had few effective treatments.
Speakers of the time might add a tiny suffix, ‘-s’ (short for sudar’, ‘sir’), to their words to show deference or stiff politeness. Translators often render it by scattering ‘sir’ through a speech.
Russians used words for the devil as everyday oaths, rather as English speakers say ‘damn’. Devout people tried to avoid them.

quiz.q: How do the officials respond as he describes the scene at the window?
o: They interrupt with constant, excited questions
They listen coldly, seeming to ignore ‘the signal’
They stop him and send at once for Smerdyakov
They laugh openly and begin to mock his feelings
quiz.e: Their gazes are shorn of emotion and their questions few, and they pay no attention at all to the word ‘signal’. Even Mitya notices.

quiz.q: What does Mitya say happened after he snatched out the pestle at the window?
o: He struck the window frame and the old man fell back
He saw a second person in the room and lost his nerve
He heard Grigory on the steps and hid among the trees
The Devil was vanquished, and he ran towards the fence
quiz.e: Whether through someone’s tears, his mother’s prayers or a radiant spirit, he says, the Devil was vanquished and he rushed away. He sees that they do not believe him.

quiz.q: What piece of news utterly shocks Mitya?
o: That the door into the garden was found open
That the window had been found bolted shut
That Grushenka had been seen in the garden
That the pestle had been found in his lodgings
quiz.e: He is certain the door was closed all the time he was in the garden. The procurator states that the murderer went in and out by it.

quiz.q: How do the officials come to learn about the signals?
o: Smerdyakov had told them before he fell ill
Grigory had overheard them and reported it
Mitya names them while defending the closed door
A note explaining them was found in the old man’s desk
quiz.e: Arguing that his father would never have opened up without them, he lets slip something they did not know, and the procurator becomes avid to hear more.

quiz.q: Why does Mitya at first reject the idea that Smerdyakov is the killer?
o: He knows that Smerdyakov loved the old man dearly
He calls him a coward who was ‘born of a hen’
He knows Smerdyakov could not have known of the money
He saw Smerdyakov leaving town the day before
quiz.e: Though the thought keeps returning, he says Smerdyakov is base, cowardly, sickly and has no love of money: ‘This is not his work.’

quiz.q: What does the procurator conclude from Mitya’s jumping down to Grigory?
o: That he had been moved by pity for the old servant
That he had been too drunk to know what he was doing
That he went to see if the only witness still lived
That he had hoped to take the old man’s keys from him
quiz.e: He takes it as proof of strength, determination and sang-froid: the man jumped down merely to learn whether the sole witness was alive.

quiz.q: What does the narrator say Mitya fails to tell them about that moment?
o: That he had taken Grigory’s keys and then thrown them away
That he had heard someone moving about inside the house
That he had seen the door standing open as he ran past
That he had jumped down out of pity for the old man
quiz.e: It never crosses his mind to mention his pity or the sad words he spoke over the man he thought he had killed, so the worst interpretation stands.

quiz.q: How does Mitya explain his refusal to say where the money came from?
o: Telling would bring disgrace worse than a murder
Telling would betray a friend who had trusted him
Telling would ruin a woman’s good name forever
Telling would give his enemies the proof they want
quiz.e: It would bring a disgrace beyond comparison, he says, even with murdering and robbing his father, had he done so. They record this ‘gift’ too.

quiz.q: What do the officials’ sums point to once his money is counted?
o: That he had spent more than three thousand already
That he must have left a large sum behind at Mokroye
That he could have had only about fifteen hundred
That he still owed the landlord for the entire night
quiz.e: He has 836 roubles and 40 copecks. Adding what he spent gives only about fifteen hundred, though everyone says he had far more.

quiz.q: What do they demand at the end, and what does he ask in return?
o: His pistols, and that they be returned to Perkhotin
That he undress, and that it be behind the curtain
His signature, and that he may first read the record
That he name his lender, and that he be left in peace
quiz.e: After he turns out his pockets, the investigator says he must remove his clothes. Blackly submitting, Mitya asks only that it not be done in that room but behind the curtain.

chapters.title: The Public Procurator Catches Mitya
chapters.intro: Background on material evidence, confession and sentencing, corporal punishment, officers’ honour, gentlemen’s dress, folk mummers and Russian fiction about humiliation, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes a scene of personal humiliation and refers to violence and suicide.
A person in costume, often masked, who acts in a folk play or at a festival.
A beating with a bundle of twigs, used as a punishment.
To soil; to damage someone’s good name or honour.
To avoid telling the truth by speaking evasively.
A state of being lost in dreamy thought.
A short trip or raid made to get something.
Rude and lacking in good manners.
A puppy; insultingly, a young and impudent man.
A clown; someone who makes himself ridiculous.
The easing or reducing of something harsh, such as a punishment.
A brownish, smoky-coloured gemstone, usually in fact a variety of quartz.
A false spoken statement that damages someone’s reputation.
A clerk who writes things down.
Objects connected with a crime were described in an official report, shown to witnesses and kept for the trial.
Russian penal law allowed a sincere confession to count in an accused person’s favour when a sentence was decided.
Russian nobles were exempted from flogging by a charter of 1785. A law of 1863 abolished most corporal punishments, though peasant courts could go on ordering floggings for decades.
Army officers, even retired ones, belonged to a world with a strict code of personal honour. They expected marked respect, and an insult could not simply be shrugged off.
A clean white shirt, collar and cuffs were the visible mark of a respectable man in the nineteenth century. Soiled linen suggested poverty or neglect.
In the Russian countryside people dressed up as animals and devils, or in the clothes of the opposite sex, and went from house to house during the days after Christmas.
An 1842 story about a humble government copying clerk for whom a new coat comes to stand for all his dignity. It shaped Russian fiction about the ‘little man’.
Dostoevsky’s 1864 short novel, whose narrator is a retired civil servant consumed by spite and by the memory of every small humiliation.

quiz.q: What are the officials feeling for along the seams of his clothes?
o: Bloodstains too faint to be seen by candlelight
Letters that he might have hidden from the police
A second set of keys to the old man’s house
Money that they suspect he may have sewn in
quiz.e: They run their fingers along collar, cuffs and seams, and the clerk recalls a scribe called Gridenko who hid hundred-rouble notes he claimed to have lost in the edging of his cap.

quiz.q: What does Mitya find hardest to bear about being stripped?
o: He alone is naked, with his feet there for all to see
Grushenka may be able to see him through the curtain
The muzhiks are laughing and jeering at him openly
He is left so cold that he begins to shake all over
quiz.e: With everyone else dressed he feels guilty and inferior, and he is tortured by his unclean linen and by the big toes he has always thought deformed.

quiz.q: What is he given to wear in place of his own clothes?
o: A peasant’s coat that belongs to the landlord
A uniform that the investigator had brought along
A coat and trousers lent by young Kalganov
A set of old clothes left behind by the Poles
quiz.e: His bloodstained clothes must be kept as evidence. In Kalganov’s tight coat he feels disgraced, ‘dressed up as a buffoon’.

quiz.q: What does Mitya insist he would have done if he were truly guilty?
o: He would have fled abroad before they ever arrived
He would have killed himself before they ever came
He would have confessed at once to save Grushenka
He would have offered the officials all of the money
quiz.e: He says he would not have waited for them or the sunrise but would have ‘exterminated’ himself, and that he could never hide and lie about such a thing.

quiz.q: What does Grigory’s deposition say about the door?
o: That it was locked when he went out into the garden
That he had unlocked it himself shortly before nine
That he had seen Smerdyakov going in through it
That it stood wide open before he had seen Mitya
quiz.e: Grigory insists he noticed the garden door wide open even before he spotted Mitya running away, and concludes Mitya must have come out of it.

quiz.q: How do they catch Mitya out over the envelope?
o: He had already said it was kept under the pillow
He had already been found with its torn seals on him
He had already written about it to Katerina Ivanovna
He had already described its contents to Grushenka
quiz.e: Mitya claims only Smerdyakov knew where it was. They reply that it is in the written record that he himself placed it under the pillow, and he calls this a random guess.

quiz.q: How does the procurator answer the claim that Smerdyakov gave the signals?
o: Smerdyakov was far too ill to stand up, let alone kill
No one else has come forward who knew of any signals
If the door already stood open, no signal was needed
The old man would never have trusted a servant so far
quiz.e: If the door was open while Mitya was still in the garden, signals would not have been required. Mitya sags back in his chair, murmuring ‘The door’.

quiz.q: How does the chapter end?
o: Mitya falls silent and refuses to say another word
