Mitya declares he will reveal where he got the money
Mitya demands to confront Grigory face to face
Mitya breaks down and confesses to the murder
quiz.e: Faced with the open door and his own silence about the money, he turns pale and announces that he will reveal the disgrace.

chapters.title: Mitya’s Great Secret. Hissed Off the Stage
chapters.intro: Background on Russian gentry debt, the post, betrothal, ideas about nerves, theatre audiences, a Russian insult and a Greek god, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes references to suicide.
A Scottish word: to hesitate between two choices.
A person’s future husband or wife.
To take something for one’s own use.
An old word: to try or attempt.
To speak slowly, stretching out the vowels.
In an older sense of the word, a scheme or plan.
Many Russian landowners lived on credit. By the end of serfdom about two-thirds of privately owned serfs had been mortgaged to state lenders, and promissory notes passed freely from hand to hand.
The Russian post carried cash in sealed letters, with the sum declared and recorded, so that money could be sent safely between towns.
A formal engagement was a serious public commitment, often marked by a family blessing with an icon. Breaking one could do lasting harm to a young woman’s reputation.
Nineteenth-century doctors and educated people often put strange moods and outbursts down to weak ‘nerves’. It was a modern-sounding way of explaining a person’s conduct.
Theatre audiences of the time showed disapproval by hissing, and a failed performer might be driven from the stage by it.
The usual English for the Russian podlets, from a root meaning base or low. It was a deeply wounding word that attacked a person’s moral character.
A title of Apollo, the Greek god of light. Poets use the name for the sun itself.

quiz.q: Where does Mitya say the money had been all this time?
o: Locked in a box in his landlady’s room
Hidden in the lining of his army coat
Sewn in a rag and hung around his neck
Left in the care of his brother Alyosha
quiz.e: He has carried it for a month around his neck, sewn up in a rag: ‘to my shame and disgrace’. The officials’ faces drop.

quiz.q: Who had entrusted the original three thousand to him, and for what?
o: Katerina Ivanovna, to send on to relatives in Moscow
Mrs Khokhlakova, to invest in a gold-mining venture
His father, to pay a bill owed to a local merchant
Samsonov, to settle an account with the Mokroye inn
quiz.e: She gave it to him to pass on to her sister and another relative, just as he was falling in love with Grushenka.

quiz.q: What does he now reveal about his first spree at Mokroye?
o: It had been paid for on credit by the landlord
It had cost him far more than he told people
It had been paid for by Grushenka’s old protector
It had cost only half of what he told everyone
quiz.e: He blew fifteen hundred, not three thousand, and kept the other half. Yet he told the whole town that it had been three thousand.

quiz.q: How does the procurator view the ‘disgrace’ he has confessed?
o: As a crime far worse than any of the others
As dishonourable, but no cause for such terror
As an invention that no jury would ever believe
As a matter for Katerina Ivanovna to judge alone
quiz.e: With irritation he calls the act flippant and dishonourable rather than disgraceful, and finds it improbable that it could cost Mitya such torments to confess.

quiz.q: Why would returning half the money have mattered so much to him?
o: He could then have asked Katerina for a fresh loan
He would have been spared a lawsuit in Moscow
He would be a scoundrel still, but not a thief
He could then have gone to Grushenka free of debt
quiz.e: Handing back half would have shown he meant to repay the rest. For him a thief is viler than a scoundrel, and this is the ‘fateful difference’.

quiz.q: Why had he hidden away the fifteen hundred in the first place?
o: To pay the money back to his father before the trial
To buy out the Polish officer if he ever returned
To set himself up in the gold mines far from town
To take Grushenka away if she should choose him
quiz.e: He feared having nothing if she chose him, so he counted it out in cold blood. That calculation is what he calls villainy, and the officials laugh.

quiz.q: At what moment does he say he truly became a thief?
o: When he tore the money from his neck last night
When he first spent the money at Mokroye a month ago
When he lied to Katerina Ivanovna about the letter
When he told the whole town how much had been spent
quiz.e: Until he tore it off on the way to Perkhotin’s, he could still go to Katya and say ‘I am a scoundrel, but not a thief’.

quiz.q: How does he react to the idea that he should have asked Katerina Ivanovna for a loan?
o: He agrees that it would have saved him, and he weeps
He is outraged, then admits he had thought of it too
He says that she had in fact refused him twice before
He laughs, and says she never had that kind of money
quiz.e: To ask her to fund his betrayal would have been filthy, he says, and he confesses he had that very idea, even as late as yesterday.

quiz.q: Under questioning, what does he finally say he sewed the money into?
o: A strip torn from one of his army shirts
A small pouch he bought in the market
One of his landlady’s old calico bonnets
A sleeve cut from Grushenka’s old dress
quiz.e: Pressed about scissors, rag, needle and thread, he finally recalls an old bonnet and loses his temper. He sees that they do not believe a word.

quiz.q: What does he beg to know when he turns from the rainy window?
o: What will become of Grushenka, who is innocent
What will become of his brothers when he is gone
How long he must stay at the inn at Mokroye
Whether Grigory has said anything further
quiz.e: Seeing that he is lost, he implores them to tell him she will not perish with him. The procurator assures him that they have no reason to trouble her.

chapters.title: The Testimony of the Witnesses. The Bairn
chapters.intro: Background on Poles and Roma in the Russian Empire, village fires, witnesses’ oaths and the fashion for psychology, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes a brief description of hunger and a suffering child, and an ethnic slur.
A Scottish and northern English word for a child.
In ancient Greece, an educated courtesan; used of a kept woman.
Here, money paid to make someone give up a claim.
A fever with fits of shivering.
Polish for ‘sir’ or ‘gentleman’. The plural is panowie.
An official written record of questioning.
Here, having to do with romance and love affairs.
An opening move intended to gain an advantage.
Using vague language to avoid committing oneself.
Help or comfort in a time of need.
An old word for a girl or young woman.
Russian slang for a hundred-rouble note, which had a many-coloured design.

Most of Poland came under Russian rule after 1815. Risings in 1830–31 and 1863 were crushed, and many Poles were sent to Siberia. Russian writers, Dostoevsky included, often treated Poles, as Roman Catholics and rebels, with open hostility.
Roma (then called gypsies, a word now often considered offensive) were celebrated in Russia as singers and musicians. Their choirs were a favourite and expensive entertainment among the wealthy.
Peasant houses were wooden and often thatched, so a fire could destroy a whole village. Families left with nothing went begging along the roads.
Under the 1864 rules witnesses gave sworn evidence at the trial. A priest of the witness’s own faith normally administered the oath.

Scientific study of the mind attracted wide interest in Russia after Ivan Sechenov’s Reflexes of the Brain (1863), and educated people liked to talk of ‘psychology’ as a way of explaining human actions.

quiz.q: What is the main issue that the witnesses are asked about?
o: Whether Mitya had seemed drunk on the night in question
Whether Mitya had ever struck anyone at the inn before
Whether Mitya had come to Mokroye in the old man’s cart
Whether Mitya had spent three thousand or only half that
quiz.e: Everything turns on the sums spent on both sprees, and all the testimony, to the last, goes against him.

quiz.q: What does Trifon Borisovich report Mitya as having shouted?
o: That this would be the sixth thousand he had left there
That he had stolen every rouble from his own father
That he would buy the inn and all the village with it
That the Poles would not leave the inn alive that night
quiz.e: The questioners are delighted: three and three make six, so he must have had three thousand on each occasion.

quiz.q: How does Kalganov behave as a witness?
o: He eagerly repeats every detail he can remember
He sides with the Poles about the game of cards
He is reluctant, and speaks of Grushenka with respect
He weeps and begs to be excused from saying more
quiz.e: He enters in fretful gloom and wants no part of it. He refers to her only as Agrafena Aleksandrovna and leaves in unconcealed indignation.

quiz.q: What new testimony comes from the Poles?
o: That Mitya had tried to borrow money from them at cards
That Mitya had offered them three thousand to go away
That Mitya had threatened them with his loaded pistol
That Mitya had told them he had robbed an old man
quiz.e: They say he offered Pan Musialowicz seven hundred at once and 2,300 the next day in town. Mitya admits he may have said such a thing.

quiz.q: Why does the procurator seize on that testimony?
o: It shows that Grushenka had been deceiving the Poles
It shows that Mitya had been lying about his rank
It shows that the Poles had cheated at cards after all
It suggests that he hid part of the money somewhere
quiz.e: If he promised 2,300 for the morrow, part of the three thousand could be hidden away, which removes the one point in his favour: that he had only eight hundred on him.

quiz.q: How much money does old Maksimov claim to have seen in Mitya’s hands?
o: Twenty thousand
Three thousand
Fifteen hundred
Six thousand
quiz.e: He says so decisively, adding that all the notes were ‘rainbows’. He is soon dismissed.

quiz.q: How does Grushenka describe her relations with Mitya?
o: She says they have been secretly married for a month
She says she has never once met him in private
She calls him a friend she led on out of malice
She says that she loved him from their first meeting
quiz.e: She says he is a friend and that she led him on ‘out of my loathsome malice’, while all that month she was waiting for another man.

quiz.q: How does Grushenka respond when Mitya declares his innocence to her?
o: She turns away in silence and will not look at him
She crosses herself, and tells them to believe him
She says she can no longer tell if he is lying or not
She faints and has to be carried down to the landlord
quiz.e: ‘Glory to Thee, O Lord!’ she says, and tells the investigator that Mitya says wild things but will never go against his conscience.

quiz.q: What does Mitya keep asking the driver in his dream?
o: How far it is to the village on the far side
Who set fire to the village, and for what reason
Whether the women are waiting to meet the tsar
Why the child cries, and why the people are poor
quiz.e: He presses on with childlike insistence about the bairn, the mothers and the barren steppe, and feels a tender piety he has never known before.

quiz.q: What moves him to near-tears when he wakes?
o: Finding Grushenka standing at his side
Hearing that his brother has arrived
Finding a pillow placed under his head
Learning that the questioning is over
quiz.e: Someone unknown has put a pillow under his head. His soul is shaken by gratitude; he signs what is required and says ‘I had a good dream.’

chapters.title: Mitya is Taken Away
chapters.intro: Background on Russian forms of address, a peasant proverb, Orthodox ideas of forgiveness and suffering, and criminal procedure, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A Russian carriage or sleigh drawn by three horses abreast.
An escort, especially a guarded one.
A looped rope used for catching animals.
Wrongly. To take something amiss is to be offended by it.
A state of low spirits and hopelessness.
An old word: given a task to carry out.
Like French, Russian has two words for ‘you’: ty for family, close friends and social inferiors, and vy for polite address. Using the wrong one can be a real insult.
The Russian words for ‘forgive’ and ‘say farewell’ are closely related, so that a goodbye can also sound like a request for pardon.
A Russian proverb says that until the thunder speaks the peasant will not cross himself: people rarely change or repent until disaster strikes.
On the last day before Lent, Orthodox believers ask one another’s pardon. Asking forgiveness before a long parting was also an old Russian custom.
The idea that suffering willingly borne can cleanse a person of sin runs deep in Russian Orthodox piety. Dostoevsky often wrote of a Russian need for suffering.
In serious cases a Russian investigator could order a suspect held until trial, to keep him from escaping. The order was made in writing and passed to the procurator.
The 1864 reforms set up circuit courts, each covering several districts, to hear most serious criminal cases.
Russia’s main criminal law was the Code of Punishments of 1845, revised in later decades. It listed offences and penalties in great detail.

quiz.q: What does the formal ‘Decision’ read to Mitya order?
o: That he be freed on bail until he is called to court
That he be held in prison pending the investigation
That he be sent to Siberia after a hearing at Mokroye
That he be kept under guard at the inn until spring
quiz.e: To deny him the means of evading investigation and trial, he is to be confined in prison in the town. He simply shrugs and says he does not blame them.

quiz.q: For what does he say he accepts punishment?
o: For having ruined Grushenka’s hopes of a good life
For having stolen the money and spent it on a spree
For having struck down the old servant at the fence
For wanting to kill his father, and for nearly doing so
quiz.e: He accepts it not for killing his father but for wanting to, and for the likelihood he would have. He still insists on his innocence and vows to fight them.

quiz.q: What does he say a man like him needs?
o: A blow of fate that binds him by external force
A long period of prayer and fasting in a monastery
A friend who will tell him the truth about himself
A chance to begin again in some place far away
quiz.e: He could never have picked himself up on his own. ‘The thunder has spoken’, and he wishes to suffer and to purify himself through suffering.

quiz.q: What happens when he offers his hand in farewell?
o: The procurator takes it, but says not a single word
Everybody in the room comes forward to shake it
The investigator hides his hands behind his back
The police chief grasps it and begs his forgiveness
quiz.e: With an almost convulsive movement Nikolay Parfenovich puts his hands behind him, then babbles that the investigation is not yet concluded.

quiz.q: What does Grushenka promise him as they part?
o: To go to Katerina Ivanovna and plead his case
To go with him for ever, wherever he is sent
To wait for him in the town until his release
To pray for him at the monastery every day
quiz.e: She bows deeply to him and bids farewell to the ‘man who has guiltlessly brought ruin on himself’.

quiz.q: Why does Mavriky Mavrikiyevich snap at Mitya?
o: Mitya has asked him how much the landlord paid him
Mitya has begun shouting insults at the village folk
Mitya has refused to climb into the waiting cart
Mitya has addressed him with the familiar ‘thou’
quiz.e: Mitya suggests they need only one troika and speaks to him as ‘thou’, and the superintendent, glad of a chance to vent his spite, tells him to address him properly.

quiz.q: How does Trifon Borisovich answer Mitya’s second farewell?
o: He stares sternly and angrily, and says not a word
He bows to the ground and asks for his forgiveness
He shouts that the whole bill remains to be settled
He makes the sign of the Cross over the departing cart
quiz.e: He stands proudly with his hands behind his back, fixing Mitya with an angry stare. Mitya feels he shouted out of malice rather than good nature.

quiz.q: What does Kalganov do after the wagon has gone?
o: He goes to the officials and demands Mitya’s release
He orders horses and sets off for town after them
He sits in a corner and weeps, almost in despair
He takes back the clothes that he had lent to Mitya
quiz.e: He almost completely believes Mitya is guilty. Sobbing, he asks what kind of people there can be after this, and whether life is worth living.

chapters.title: Kolya Krasotkin
chapters.intro: Background on Russian service ranks, schooling, railways, the old temperature scale, household icons, a Russian poet and the legend of Troy, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: One of the lowest grades in the Russian civil service.
A school teaching the lower years of a Russian gymnasium, or secondary school.
A junior Russian army officer’s rank, one step below captain.
Ruling like a tyrant, with total power.
An old Russian unit of distance, a little over a kilometre.
An old term for a feverish illness brought on by shock or strain.
Speaking up or acting on someone else’s behalf.
A moral hesitation; a worry about whether something is right.
Fullness; a complete or abundant amount.
Secretly helping or allowing something wrong.
An outburst of uncontrollable emotion, often with tears.
The dried, fibrous inside of a gourd, used as a rough bath sponge.
Created by Peter the Great in 1722, it divided state service into fourteen grades across civil, military and court life. A person’s grade set their title and social standing.
The main type of Russian secondary school, leading towards university. Pupils wore uniforms and moved up through numbered forms.
Russia built most of its early railway network in the 1860s and 1870s. The lines were still a novelty in the provinces, and many towns lay some distance from a station.
Russians of this period commonly used the Réaumur temperature scale, on which water freezes at 0 and boils at 80. Eleven degrees of frost on it is about fourteen degrees below zero Celsius.
Orthodox households kept holy images in a corner of the main room, usually with a small lamp. People prayed in front of them and might make solemn promises there.
The ancient city, in what is now north-west Turkey, whose fall is a great subject of Greek legend. Homer’s Iliad is set during the war fought there.
History textbooks by the author Smaragdov were widely used in Russian schools around the middle of the nineteenth century.
A Russian poet and editor (1821–78), best known for verses about the hard lives of peasants and the urban poor.

quiz.q: What is it that Kolya actually objects to in his mother’s demands for love?
o: Her habit of rehearsing every lesson with him at home
Her friendship with the teachers and their wives
The outpourings of feeling he calls ‘milk-calf mush’
The way she forbids him to read his father’s books
quiz.e: He loves her very much, the narrator says. What he cannot stand is the sentimental display she requires of him.

quiz.q: What is the two-rouble wager at the railway?
o: That Kolya will lie between the rails as the train passes
That Kolya will ride on the engine to the next station
That Kolya will walk the track at night without a lamp
That Kolya will stand on the embankment until the last second
quiz.e: To silence older boys who despise him as too young, he offers to lie flat between the rails while the eleven o’clock train runs over him.

quiz.q: What really happened to Kolya as the train went over him?
o: He lay wide awake and counted the carriages overhead
He rolled clear at the last moment, unseen by the other boys
He was grazed by a coupling, and hid the injury afterwards
He fainted, though he told the boys he was only pretending
quiz.e: He claimed to have lain still on purpose to frighten them. Only much later did he confess to his mother that he really had lost consciousness.

quiz.q: What does Dardanelov gain by defending Kolya to the school authorities?
o: A promise from Kolya to work harder at world history
A faint hint that the widow may yet accept his hand
A reputation among the boys for great moral courage
A promotion to head of the town’s progymnasium
quiz.e: Mrs Krasotkina has refused him once, but after he saves Kolya he receives a remote hint that he might still hope, which is enough to make him happy.

quiz.q: What do the boys conclude when Kolya asks who founded Troy?
o: That the question is nonsense, as Troy was only a legend
That Kolya has found the answer in Dardanelov’s own notes
That Dardanelov does not know, and that Kolya alone does
That the two of them have agreed to keep a secret together
quiz.e: Dardanelov gives only a general reply about peoples and migrations. Kolya has read the passage in Smaragdov at home and keeps the answer to himself.

quiz.q: What follows when his mother learns of the railway exploit?
o: She takes him out of school and engages a tutor to teach him at home
She has days of hysterics, and he vows tearfully never to repeat it
She accepts Dardanelov’s offer of marriage to give her son a father
She locks his father’s bookcase and forbids him to go out at night
quiz.e: Her fits last for days. Kolya swears before the icon and by his father’s memory, weeps like a six-year-old, and mother and son keep rushing into each other’s arms.

quiz.q: How does Kolya treat the dog he has lately acquired?
o: He leaves it with the market women while he is at school
He shows it off to his classmates at every opportunity
He neglects it, and his mother has to feed it on scraps
He keeps it hidden at home and drills it in tricks
quiz.e: He hides Perezvon from his companions and tyrannises him with training, yet the dog howls when he is away and yelps with ecstasy when he returns.

quiz.q: What does the narrator say, at the end, that he forgot to mention?
o: That Kolya is the boy Ilyusha stabbed with a penknife
That Kolya is the boy who first called the captain ‘loofah’
That Kolya is the boy who taught Ilyusha to throw stones
That Kolya is the boy Alyosha met by the ditch that day
quiz.e: Ilyusha stabbed him in the hip while standing up for his father, whom the schoolboys were teasing with the name ‘loofah’.

chapters.title: Youngsters
chapters.intro: Background on Russia’s expansion into Central Asia, marriage law, household servants, horse-drawn travel, verse fables and Russian pet names, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Waterproof rubber overshoes worn over ordinary shoes or boots.
Padded with soft material for warmth.
The habit of acting suddenly, without thought.
A small hole in the barrel of an old gun or cannon, through which the charge is lit.
The sudden backward kick of a gun when it is fired.
Small balls of lead fired from a gun.
A young or newly important person who acts above their station.
French for ‘here’, often used as a command to a dog.
Russian for a landowner or gentleman; how a servant addressed a master.
Russia conquered large parts of Central Asia in the 1860s and 1870s, taking Tashkent in 1865. The campaigns drew soldiers and officials very far from home.
A frontier city near the southern Urals, long a Russian base for trade and expeditions into Central Asia.
Only the Church could end a marriage in Russia, and it did so rarely. A spouse left behind might stay legally married for many years.
House serfs were freed in 1861 without land, and many went on working for wages as maids and cooks. Even modest households often employed one.
A team of three horses. The centre horse runs between shafts, while the two outer trace-horses pull from the sides with their heads turned outward.
Beating with a bundle of birch twigs, a common punishment for children well into the nineteenth century.
Short moral tales in rhyme, often with talking animals, which children learned by heart. Ivan Krylov was the most famous author, and Ivan Dmitriev was another popular one.
Russian adds endings to names to show affection: Aleksandr can be Sasha or Sashenka, for instance. The same endings can sound tender, childish or mocking.

quiz.q: Why is Kolya stuck at home on Sunday morning?
o: His mother has forbidden him to leave after the last prank
He must mind the doctor’s children until Agafya returns
He has been told to wait in for a visit from Dardanelov
He is in charge of the house while Agafya is giving birth
quiz.e: The doctor’s wife and his mother are away because the maid Katerina is about to give birth, and Agafya has gone to market, so he is guarding the ‘little ones’.

quiz.q: How has Kolya justified playing horses with the little ones?
o: He said it was an exercise that built up his leg muscles
He said he had lost a bet and was paying his forfeit
He denied the rumour outright and said no such game had ever been played
He said he did it for their sake, because he was fond of them
quiz.e: It would be disgraceful for thirteen-year-olds ‘in our age’, he said, but he did it for the ‘little ones’, and no one was to ask him to account for his feelings.

quiz.q: Which of Nastya’s explanations of Katerina’s baby finally wins Kostya over?
o: She thought about marrying for so long that a child came
A midwife found it growing among the winter cabbages
Her husband had sent it to her from his cell in prison
The doctor had brought it back with him from Tashkent
quiz.e: After giving up the cabbage patch and the husband in prison, Nastya decides that Katerina kept thinking of getting married and got a child instead. ‘Yes, that will be it,’ says Kostya.

quiz.q: What does Kolya take from his satchel to cheer up the children?
o: A tin soldier with a spring that makes it march
A picture book about the war in the Caucasus
A small bronze cannon that fires real gunpowder
A pocket telescope taken from his father’s cupboard
quiz.e: Their faces brighten at once at the miniature cannon on wheels. He also shows them a phial of real gunpowder and some lead shot.

quiz.q: Why does he say he mentioned the birch, when Nastya objects?
o: He had mixed up their mother with his own strict mother
He only said it for the sake of rhetorical style
He wanted to test whether they would tell him the truth
He had heard that their father believed in the birch
quiz.e: Nastya points out that their mother never birches them. ‘I know,’ says Kolya: it was only for rhetorical effect.

quiz.q: What does Kostya ask for once Kolya sees that he cannot leave?
o: For Perezvon to be told to play dead
For the cannon to be fired in the room
For a story about the boys at school
For Kolya to bring them some lunch
quiz.e: Kolya puts the dog through his tricks. Perezvon is lying ‘dead’ with his paws in the air when Agafya finally comes back from the market.

quiz.q: What happens when Kolya demands that Agafya swear to watch the children?
o: She swears by her soul, and he leaves with a blessing
She takes offence, and refuses to stay in the house at all
She swears on condition that he wears his galoshes outside
She laughs it off, and he settles for her simple ‘I will’
quiz.e: He wants an oath by her eternal salvation, but she tells him to stay at home if he likes. In the end he accepts her plain promise to stay and give them lunch.

quiz.q: What parting remark finally makes Agafya genuinely cross?
o: His order that she must be back before his mother returns
His complaint that she had been too long at the market
His plea that she spare the children her tales about Katerina
His claim that she would get a birching if she neglected them
quiz.e: She had enjoyed their banter until then. His solemn request to spare the children her ‘old wives’ tales’ draws a real snap of anger.

chapters.title: A Schoolboy
chapters.intro: Background on Russian markets, school discipline, socialism, radical ideas of the 1860s and attitudes to the common people, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A large, heavy breed of dog similar to a mastiff.
An old name for tuberculosis, a serious lung disease.
The lowest class of a school, for its youngest pupils.
A person’s face or features, especially as a sign of character.
In a solemn way, as if speaking wise sayings.
A white coating of ice crystals.
A sheet of canvas stretched over a stall or window for shelter.
A long, belted coat worn by Russian merchants and peasants.
A skilled manual worker; in Russian towns, a member of a lower social class of tradespeople.
To make something clear; to explain.
Peasants brought carts of produce into country towns to sell, and Sunday trading was an ordinary part of provincial life. Such a gathering might simply be called a fair.
Many Russian towns had a ‘gostiny dvor’, a long arcaded market building of small shops, at their commercial centre.
Beating pupils was long routine in Russian schools. An 1864 statute banned it in the gymnasia, though the practice lived on in popular expectations.
Radicals of the 1860s and 1870s, drawing on French thinkers such as Fourier, hoped to build a society of common property. Many saw the peasant commune as a starting point.
Some radicals of the time argued that marriage and the Church kept people in chains, and they called for free unions and women’s independence.
A word made famous by Turgenev’s novel Fathers and Sons (1862) for the younger generation’s rejection of every inherited authority.
The radical critic Dmitry Pisarev (1840–68) urged readers to be ‘realists’: to respect useful knowledge, especially natural science, and to discard sentiment.

After the end of serfdom many educated Russians felt they owed a debt to the peasants, an idea set out in Pyotr Lavrov’s influential Historical Letters. Others idealised peasants as wise and uncorrupted.

quiz.q: What does Smurov suggest doing with Perezvon?
o: Giving him to Ilyusha as a companion for the new pup
Leaving him tied to the gate so as not to upset the family
Selling him at the fair to buy a present for Ilyusha
Telling Ilyusha that he is really the lost dog Zhuchka
quiz.e: Since both dogs are shaggy and smoky grey, Smurov thinks Ilyusha might believe it. ‘Schoolboy, abominate lies,’ Kolya replies.

quiz.q: How does Kolya respond to the idea that he is going to make it up with Ilyusha?
o: He admits that he has long been sorry for the quarrel
He scorns the phrase and says he goes of his own accord
He says that Ilyusha must be the one to apologise first
He says that Karamazov has talked him into the visit
quiz.e: ‘A ridiculous expression,’ he says. Unlike the others, who were dragged there by Aleksey Karamazov, he is going because ‘such is my will’, and perhaps for quite different reasons.

quiz.q: How does Kolya explain socialism to Smurov?
o: Government of the country by an assembly of peasants
Everybody working for the state in return for a wage
Equality, common property, and no marriage or religion
The handing over of all the land to the village commune
quiz.e: All men are equal, everyone owns the same common property, there is no marriage or religion, and the laws are ‘for each to pick and choose’. Smurov, he adds, is not old enough for it yet.

quiz.q: Why does Kolya tell Matvey that schoolboys do get thrashed?
o: A muzhik expects it, and the truth would only upset him
He wants to win the man’s pity and a ride in his cart
It is in fact true, and he is not ashamed to admit it
Smurov’s father is listening, and must not learn otherwise
quiz.e: As Kolya explains it, a muzhik thinks schoolboys ought to be thrashed, so saying otherwise would upset him. This, he claims, is the art of talking to the common folk.

quiz.q: How does Kolya shake off the angry young man in the market?
o: He warns him that he will report him to Trifon Nikitich
He calls on the market women to drive the man away
He demands to know if he knows Sabaneyev, then strides off
He persuades him that he has mistaken him for someone else
quiz.e: Kolya sternly asks about the Church of the Ascension and about Sabaneyev, a name he has simply made up, and walks away as if the man were beneath contempt.

quiz.q: What do the market women do after Kolya walks off?
o: They chase after Kolya to tell him off for his rudeness
They warn the young man that Kolya’s father is an official
They send for the constable to quiet the young man down
They debate who Sabaneyev is and decide he must be Chizhov
quiz.e: Trying to help, they work through the Kuzmichevs’ former man and settle on one Aleksey Ivanovich Chizhov, driving the young man to despair.

quiz.q: How does the second muzhik, the one who has been drinking, get the better of Kolya?
o: He tells Kolya that his mother will hear of his behaviour
He forgives him and solemnly claims to have more brains
He guesses Kolya’s name and his father’s rank at a glance
He pretends to be deaf until Kolya loses interest and goes
quiz.e: ‘More brains than you,’ he says, as solemn as ever. Rather taken aback, Kolya concedes that there are different kinds of muzhik.

quiz.q: Why does Kolya stop twenty yards short of Snegiryov’s house?
o: To send Smurov in and have Karamazov summoned out to him
To wait for the cathedral clock to strike the half-hour
To give Perezvon a last chance to run off his high spirits
To rehearse with Smurov what they will tell the captain
quiz.e: ‘One must have a preliminary sniff around,’ he says, and despite Smurov’s protests he insists on meeting Karamazov out in the cold.

chapters.title: Zhuchka
chapters.intro: Background on Russian forms of address, holy fools and minstrels, the theatre, and ideas about play and art, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes cruelty to an animal and a child’s serious illness.
A long, close-fitting garment worn by clergy and monks.
Italian for ‘enough’; used to mean ‘and that’s that’.
A manservant; also a servile follower.
To approach and speak to someone boldly.
A clown; someone who plays the fool.
A state of confused, wild thinking, often brought on by fever.
A false statement that damages someone’s reputation.
Someone who thinks mainly of themselves.
French for ‘lie down’; a command given to a dog.
A small folding knife, originally used to sharpen quill pens.
To do with war or fighting.
Information heard from others, which cannot be confirmed.
A common Russian name for a house or yard dog; as a word it also means ‘little beetle’.
Russians could add a short ‘-s’ to words, a shortened form of sudar’ (‘sir’). It sounds deferential, sometimes servile and sometimes mocking.
Polite Russian address uses a person’s first name with a name taken from their father, such as Ivanovich (‘son of Ivan’) or Ivanovna (‘daughter of Ivan’).
A Russian religious tradition of people who behaved like madmen for Christ’s sake, often speaking hard truths to the powerful.
Wandering minstrels and jesters of medieval Russia, who were condemned by the Church and largely suppressed in the seventeenth century.
Until the early 1880s the state held a monopoly on public theatre in Moscow and St Petersburg, while private companies served the provinces.
In his Letters on the Aesthetic Education of Man (1795), the German poet Friedrich Schiller argued that the impulse to play is central to human freedom and to art.

quiz.q: What torments Kolya most as he waits for Alyosha?
o: That he is so small for his age
That his coat is shabby and worn
That he has not brought a gift
That he may be kept out of the room
quiz.e: He worries about his ‘rotten’ face, but above all about his height, which he has been checking against a pencil line on the wall at home every two months.

quiz.q: How has Alyosha changed since we last saw him?
o: He has grown a beard and looks much older and thinner
He wears the habit of a fully professed monk of the order
He has given up his cassock for a tailored frock-coat
He has become silent and sad since the death of his elder
quiz.e: He now wears a finely cut frock-coat and a soft round hat, with his hair cut short, and he looks thoroughly handsome and quietly cheerful.

quiz.q: What trick did Smerdyakov teach Ilyusha?
o: To lure yard dogs into a sack with a strip of meat
To hide a pin in soft bread and feed it to a hungry dog
To tie a burning rag to the tail of a stray from the market
To put a pinch of snuff into a dog’s bowl of milk
quiz.e: The dog Zhuchka swallowed the bread, yelped, ran in circles and fled. Ilyusha confessed to Kolya in tears, unable to forget that ‘he yelped as he ran’.

quiz.q: What does Kolya intend when he breaks off relations with Ilyusha?
o: To end the friendship for good and warn the others off
To report the whole affair to Dardanelov in due course
To force Ilyusha to confess the deed to his own father
To banish him only for a few days, then forgive him
quiz.e: He feigns more indignation than he feels, to teach discipline, and plans to extend his hand again once Ilyusha has shown remorse. Instead Ilyusha defies him.

quiz.q: What message does Ilyusha send back through Smurov?
o: That he will now feed pins to all the dogs
That he will tell the school who taught him it
That he will fight Krasotkin on the square
That he never wants to see Krasotkin’s face again
quiz.e: His eyes flash and he shouts that he will throw pieces of bread with pins to all the dogs, so Kolya responds with open contempt.

quiz.q: According to Alyosha, why does Ilyusha believe he has fallen ill?
o: Because he was struck down in the fight over the stones
Because the doctors have fed him all the wrong medicines
Because the other boys have cursed him for his father’s sake
Because God is punishing him for having killed Zhuchka
quiz.e: He has told his father three times that he is sick as a punishment from God for killing the dog, and nothing can budge him from this idea.

quiz.q: How does Alyosha describe Snegiryov’s clowning?
o: As a sly trick of a drunkard for extracting money from his betters
As harmless fun, put on to entertain his sick children
As bitter irony from a man who dare not speak the truth
As a sign that his sufferings have unhinged his mind
quiz.e: Such people feel very deeply but are held down, and their buffoonery is malicious irony aimed at those they fear. It can be, Alyosha says, extremely tragic.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha say about boys playing at robbers?
o: It shows a love of violence they must learn to outgrow
It is a kind of art, like adults going to the theatre
It is harmless at thirteen, though shameful at fourteen
It is the only way young boys can learn about justice
quiz.e: Such games are a young form of art, he says, sometimes better composed than stage plays, except that the children are themselves the actors. Kolya is struck by the thought.

chapters.title: By Ilyusha’s Little Bed
chapters.intro: Background on classical schooling, science, women’s education, local courts, censorship and imperial decorations, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes a child’s serious illness.
Russian for a justice of the peace, a local judge of minor cases.
A short, witty poem or saying.
Latin for ‘without which not’: an essential condition.
French, literally ‘cold blood’: calmness under pressure.
French for the interval between the acts of a play.
Potassium nitrate, the main ingredient of gunpowder.
A scented ointment for the hair.
Excessively eager to please or obey.
Looking down on others in a haughty way.
A clash of sounds; a lack of harmony.
A statement accepted as obviously true.
Money or property a bride brings to her marriage.
The natural sciences, such as physics, chemistry and biology.
The loud bang of a gun or explosion.

A school statute of 1871, under the education minister Count Dmitry Tolstoy, made Latin and Greek central to the gymnasium. Critics said it was a political move to steer pupils away from science and dangerous ideas.
The young medical man in Turgenev’s Fathers and Sons, who dissects frogs and scorns art. He became a model for students who put their faith in science.
Women were barred from enrolling at Russian universities in this period. From the late 1860s public lecture courses opened for them in St Petersburg and elsewhere.
The legal reforms of 1864 created locally elected judges who heard small cases quickly and simply, usually giving light penalties such as fines.

Catherine the Great allowed private printing presses in 1783, and for a time publishers had wide freedom. Controls tightened sharply in the 1790s, and censorship lasted throughout the nineteenth century.
A Russian saying, ‘to make an elephant out of a fly’, means making a great fuss about something small.
Officers and civil servants could be awarded state orders. The higher classes of some orders were worn on a ribbon at the neck.
Traditional black powder is a mixture of about three-quarters saltpetre, with much smaller amounts of charcoal and sulphur.

quiz.q: What does Snegiryov do when fear for his son overcomes him?
o: He goes out to the tavern and drinks until nightfall
He runs into the dark passage and muffles his sobs
He takes down the icons and prays aloud beside the bed
He writes long letters begging the town for more help
quiz.e: After putting Ilyusha back to bed he often runs to a dark corner of the passage, leans against the wall and sobs, stifling the noise so the boy will not hear. He has stopped drinking altogether.

quiz.q: Who has been paying for the family’s needs and doctors?
o: Alyosha, out of money that his father left him
Mrs Khokhlakova, who has lent them her carriage
The parents of the boys who now visit each day
Katerina Ivanovna, who has visited them herself
quiz.e: He accepted her two hundred roubles, she visited and charmed the family, and she has kept giving. She also asked the doctor she had brought from Moscow to call.

quiz.q: What does Kolya do first on entering the crowded room?
o: He goes straight to Ilyusha’s bed and takes his hand
He calls Smurov aside to make sure the door is ready
He bows with great courtesy to the mother and Ninochka
He shakes hands with each of the boys in their turn
quiz.e: Giving the captain his hand only briefly, he bows and scrapes before Mrs Snegiryova and then Ninochka, which makes an excellent impression on ‘little mother’.

quiz.q: What does Kolya tell Ilyusha about Zhuchka before he whistles?
o: That the dog has run off and ‘kicked the bucket’
That the dog has been seen alive near the station
That the dog was found and is now at the Fedotovs’
That the dog is waiting for him out in the passage
quiz.e: Ignoring Alyosha’s signals, he tells the boy mercilessly that Zhuchka cannot have survived such a titbit, and then insists on bringing in Perezvon anyway.

quiz.q: What is the surprise that Kolya has been saving?
o: The dog is a new gift from the rich Katerina Ivanovna
The dog can carry messages from the school
The dog belonged to the Moscow doctor once
The dog is in fact Zhuchka, found and trained
quiz.e: Perezvon is blind in one eye with a torn left ear, the marks Ilyusha described. Kolya found him in the Fedotovs’ yard, hid him, and claims the dog must have spat out the pin.

quiz.q: Why, Kolya admits to Alyosha, did he put off his visit for so long?
o: His mother would not allow him to go to that part of town
He wanted to train the dog and show him off in his glory
He was still too angry at having been stabbed by the boy
He could not find the cannon that he had promised to bring
quiz.e: Alyosha asks with involuntary reproach whether this alone was the reason. ‘Only because of that,’ Kolya shouts ingenuously.

quiz.q: What becomes of the little cannon?
o: Ilyusha gives it to his mother when she pleads for it
The captain locks it away as too dangerous for the sick
It bursts when fired, and Kolya has to take it home again
Kolya takes it back on hearing it was never really his
quiz.e: Kolya presents it to Ilyusha, but ‘little mother’ begs like a little girl to have it. Ilyusha gives it up, checking anxiously that Kolya will not be offended, and she weeps with emotion.

quiz.q: How does Kolya describe his part in the killing of the goose?
o: He was merely passing when the cart happened to move
He took the blame so the simple lad would not be punished
He only set forth the idea ‘in terms of a project’
He jerked the bridle himself while the other lad kept watch
quiz.e: He got the errand-man to jerk the bridle so the wheel would break the goose’s neck, then told the justice with sang-froid that he had only expounded the basic idea.

quiz.q: How does Kolya deal with Kartashov for knowing who founded Troy?
o: He congratulates him and makes him his deputy at school
He accuses him of stealing the answer from his book
He says the boy has named the wrong four founders
He asks how they founded it, and the boy nearly cries
quiz.e: Kartashov had secretly looked in Kolya’s Smaragdov. Kolya asks whether the founders each laid a brick, the room laughs, and he declares he has little respect for world history anyway.

quiz.q: Why, according to Kolya, are ancient languages taught?
o: To prepare pupils for a career in the Church or the law
As a police measure to bore pupils and blunt their minds
To let Russians read the classics in their original form
As a way to keep up with the schools of France and Prussia
quiz.e: He calls them a restrictive police measure, though he is top of the class in Latin. The argument about translations, he admits, came from his teacher Kolbasnikov.

chapters.title: Precocious Development
chapters.intro: Background on Voltaire, Belinsky, the Russian secret police, émigré publishing, the debate over women’s rights and Pushkin’s verse novel, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Showing adult qualities or abilities unusually early.
Someone who seeks direct spiritual experience of God.
An idea put forward as a possible explanation, not yet proven.
Being set free from legal, social or political restrictions.
Something that exists only in the imagination.
To do with schools or education.
To beat with a short, thick stick.
Tsar Nicholas I’s secret police, set up in 1826 and abolished in 1880. Its headquarters stood near the Chain Bridge in St Petersburg.
Alexander Herzen’s Russian-language newspaper, published abroad from 1857 to 1867, first in London. Copies were smuggled into Russia and widely read.
In the 1860s and 1870s some Russian radicals went to the United States, hoping to live as workers or to found communes there.
Germans had long been prominent in Russia as officials, doctors and teachers. Resentment of them was common, and ‘sausage-maker’ was an insulting nickname.
The French Enlightenment writer (1694–1778), a fierce critic of the Church who nevertheless believed in God as creator of the universe.
‘If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him’ is a famous line from one of Voltaire’s verse letters.
Some radicals of the time portrayed Jesus as a human teacher of social justice. Ernest Renan’s bestselling Life of Jesus (1863) treated him as a man, not as God.
From the 1860s Russian thinkers argued over women’s education, work and marriage. Chernyshevsky’s novel What Is to Be Done? (1863) made the subject central.
The French legal code of 1804 placed wives under the authority of their husbands.
The most influential Russian critic of his day (1811–48), a champion of socially engaged literature. Dostoevsky’s arrest in 1849 was partly for reading aloud Belinsky’s banned letter to Gogol.
Pushkin’s novel in verse, published in full in 1833. Young Tatyana falls in love with a bored aristocrat who rejects her. Years later, now married, she refuses him though she still loves him.
Voltaire’s satirical tale of 1759, which mocks the belief that all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds.

quiz.q: What does Kolya say about God?
o: That only peasants and monks still believe in him
That science has by now finally proved he does not exist
That he is a hypothesis, but one needed for order
That he may exist but has no interest in human affairs
quiz.e: ‘If he did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him,’ Kolya adds, immediately worrying that he is showing off.

quiz.q: What is Alyosha’s view of Voltaire, when Kolya cites him?
o: He believed in God, though perhaps not very much
He was the most sincere friend mankind ever had
He never believed, but he greatly loved mankind
He was a devout man whom the Church had slandered
quiz.e: Alyosha doubts that Voltaire believed very much or loved mankind very much either, and he says so as if to an equal, leaving the question for Kolya to decide.

quiz.q: What does Kolya claim about Christ?
o: That he never existed and that the Gospels are invented
That today he would have joined the revolutionary cause
That he was a foolish dreamer who misled simple people
That he taught slavery, as the priests have always said
quiz.e: He calls Christ a ‘thoroughly humane individual’. Alyosha asks what fool he has been spending time with, and Kolya admits he often talks with Rakitin.

quiz.q: What has Kolya actually read of Pushkin?
o: All of Eugene Onegin, but only in a school edition
Only the chapters of Onegin quoted by his teacher
Only the poems printed in his father’s old journals
Nothing yet, although he has opinions about Tatyana
quiz.e: He knows only the part about Tatyana and why she did not go with Onegin, from Belinsky. He says he has read nothing by Pushkin yet but intends to.

quiz.q: What does Kolya secretly dread that Alyosha might discover?
o: That Rakitin has been supplying Kolya with all of his opinions
That he has not yet turned fourteen as he has claimed
That he has read only one poem from one issue of The Bell
That his mother keeps the key to his father’s bookcase
quiz.e: His father’s cupboard holds a single issue of The Bell, and the lines about the Chain Bridge are the only thing in it he has read.

quiz.q: What is the German’s remark that makes Alyosha smile?
o: Give a Russian schoolboy a star map and he will correct it
A Russian schoolboy will argue with anyone but his mother
Give a Russian schoolboy a book and he will never read it
A Russian schoolboy believes all that is printed in a book
quiz.e: It sums up total ignorance and an inflated opinion of oneself. Kolya loves it, shouting ‘Bravo, German!’, while insisting the German missed the boy’s independence of spirit.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha say about the modern fear of looking ridiculous?
o: That it is a sickness that only the wealthy ever catch
That it will fade away naturally as a young man matures
That it is the one fault of which the Russian people are free
That it is a form of vanity in which the Devil has crept in
quiz.e: Even near-children suffer from it, he says, and he urges Kolya not to be like all the rest, even if he is the only one.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha foretell for Kolya?
o: He will become a famous revolutionary and go to Siberia
He will be very unhappy, yet on the whole will bless life
He will be a scholar, and outgrow his love of mischief
He will be loved by many but understood by almost no one
quiz.e: ‘You are a prophet!’ cries Kolya, overjoyed to be treated as an equal and declaring that he has loved and dreamed of Alyosha all along.

chapters.title: Ilyusha
chapters.intro: Background on nineteenth-century health travel and medicine, formal titles, a Russian saying and a psalm, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes a child’s serious illness and scenes of great distress.
An old word for a doctor; also a blood-sucking worm once used in medicine.
Very concerned about cleanliness and avoiding anything unpleasant.
To send off quickly; to speed up.
So astonished as to be unable to think.
Wildly excited or out of control.
Bending low in fear or excessive humility.
A disease causing pain and stiffness in the joints and muscles.
French for a psychiatrist, a doctor who treats mental illness.
Nineteenth-century doctors often prescribed a change of climate, and wealthy Russians spent winters in Italy or the south of France.
An ancient city on the east coast of Sicily, originally a Greek colony.
Mineral springs at Pyatigorsk and nearby towns were Russia’s best-known health resorts. Lermontov’s A Hero of Our Time (1840) is partly set there.
A fashionable nineteenth-century treatment using baths, showers and the drinking of mineral waters.
In the later nineteenth century Paris was a leading centre for the study of mental and nervous disorders, notably at the Salpêtrière hospital.
Leading professors of medicine in Moscow could charge very high fees and were treated as public figures.
The respectful form of address for people in the upper ranks of state service, such as generals and senior officials.
‘Zvon’ is Russian for a ringing or peal of bells. A saying describes someone who ‘heard the ringing but knows not where it is’, meaning a person with a vague, muddled idea of a subject.
A lament by Jews exiled in Babylon, which opens ‘By the rivers of Babylon’ and contains a vow never to forget Jerusalem.

quiz.q: What does the doctor finally suggest might help Ilyusha?
o: Keeping him warm and giving up the medicines he is on
Moving him to the new hospital that is opening in Moscow
Taking him out to the country for rest and fresh milk
Sending him at once to Syracuse, for the better climate
quiz.e: Only after saying ‘I am not God’ does he offer this, to a man who plainly cannot afford it, calling it what science can say about ‘the last resorts’.

quiz.q: What does the doctor recommend for the rest of the family?
o: Moving to rooms in a healthier part of their town
Caucasus waters, then a Paris clinic for the wife
A long stay in St Petersburg with the elder daughter
Rest and better food, paid for by Katerina Ivanovna
quiz.e: The captain can only point in despair at the bare timber walls of the passage. ‘Well, that is not my affair,’ the doctor says with a sardonic smile.

quiz.q: How does Kolya deliberately insult the doctor?
o: He keeps calling him ‘leech’ instead of ‘doctor’
He addresses him by the name of a well-known quack
He tells him that Syracuse is not really in Sicily
He mimics the way he speaks to the poor captain
quiz.e: He uses the word ‘in order to give offence’ and says he will see him in Syracuse. The doctor stamps his foot and shouts that the boy needs a thrashing.

quiz.q: What stops Kolya from going any further with the doctor?
o: The captain pleading with him not to ruin their chances
The doctor threatening to report him to the headmaster
Alyosha’s threat to break with him for ever
The sound of Ilyusha calling out for him from the room
quiz.e: Kolya declares that Alyosha is the one person in the world who can tell Nikolay Krasotkin what to do, and goes back into the room.

quiz.q: What does Ilyusha tell his father to do when he dies?
o: Forgive the boys who used to throw stones at him
Choose another good boy, call him Ilyusha, love him
Send word to Krasotkin and his mother straight away
Give away all his books and toys to the younger boys
quiz.e: He asks his father to find a good boy, name him Ilyusha and love him in his place, but then also begs him never to forget him.

quiz.q: Where does Ilyusha ask to be buried?
o: At the monastery, close to the elder’s hermitage
In the town cemetery next to his mother’s parents
On the hill above the market-square, facing the river
Beside the big stone that he and his father walked to
quiz.e: He wants his father to visit the grave in the evening with Krasotkin and Perezvon, and he promises he will be waiting for them.

quiz.q: What reason does Kolya give for suddenly leaving?
o: He must be back at school for the afternoon lessons
He has promised Smurov’s father to bring the boy home
His mother is expecting him and will be anxious at dinner
The doctor has ordered that the boy must now be left quiet
quiz.e: He promises to return after dinner, but he runs out so as not to burst into tears, and in the passage he cries anyway, cursing himself for not having come before.

quiz.q: What does the captain whisper wildly to the two young men in the passage?
o: That he does not want another boy, quoting ‘O Jerusalem’
That the doctor is a fraud who ought to be driven from the town
That Ilyusha must not be told what the doctor has said
That he forgives the Karamazov family for what they did
quiz.e: He begins the psalm ‘If I forget thee, O Jerusalem’ and collapses, sobbing. Alyosha explains to Kolya that it means forgetting all that is most precious.

chapters.title: At Grushenka’s
chapters.intro: Background on Russia’s reformed courts and lawyers, Poles in the Russian Empire, card games, prison visits and Russian pet names, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Russian for a lady or mistress of the house; how servants addressed her.
Of the skin: an unhealthy pale yellowish colour.
Just beginning to happen or develop.
Small Russian pies, baked or fried, with fillings such as meat, cabbage or jam.
Here, a strong herbal liqueur, taken as a tonic or medicine.
Someone who lives off other people’s generosity; a sponger.
Polish for ‘sir’ or ‘gentleman’; the plural is panowie.
Over-elaborate and showy, especially in language.
Extreme poverty, lacking even the basic necessities.
Pompous and inflated in speech, with little real meaning.
A male servant, especially a footman; also used scornfully of any servant.
An old name for epilepsy, a condition that causes fits.
Fame for something bad or scandalous.
A Scottish and northern English word for a child.
Alexander II’s reform created open trials, independent judges and juries for serious crimes, replacing a secret system that worked mainly through written documents.
The reform also created a professional bar. Leading defence lawyers from St Petersburg and Moscow became celebrities, and their speeches were printed in the newspapers.
Doctors could be called to give evidence on whether an accused person had been of sound mind. Psychiatry was a young and fashionable science, and its place in court was much debated.

Most of Poland came under Russian rule after the partitions of the late eighteenth century. Risings in 1830–31 and 1863 were crushed, and many Poles ended up living deep inside Russia, often in poverty.
Poland had an unusually large noble class, many of them poor but proud of their rank. Russian writers of the time often portrayed Poles as haughty and pretentious.
Russia’s most popular card game; its name means ‘fool’. Players try to get rid of all their cards, and the last one left holding cards is the fool.
Relatives commonly took food to people held in prison, and giving alms to prisoners was a traditional act of Christian charity in Russia.
Russian builds endless variations on first names. Endings such as -enka and -ushka are tender, while -ka can sound familiar or scornful, depending on the tone.

quiz.q: What did Mitya do with the pies Grushenka took to the prison?
o: He shared them all out among the guards at once
He ate them, then asked her to bring more
He threw them back and stamped on one of them
He sent them on to the sick Pole as a joke
quiz.e: He threw them back in her face and stamped on one. She left them with the guard, telling Mitya that if he didn’t eat them he was living off spite.

quiz.q: How did Maksimov come to live in Grushenka’s house?
o: Kalganov had turned him out, and she let him stay
Grushenka had hired him to keep her accounts
Mitya had asked her to look after him a while
He had rented the sofa from Mrs Morozova herself
quiz.e: Kalganov had told him he was no longer welcome and given him five roubles. Homeless, he stayed on her sofa, and in time she came to need his company.

quiz.q: How did the Poles’ requests for money change over the weeks?
o: They rose from ten roubles to two thousand
They stayed fixed at exactly three roubles a time
They stopped once Mitya had threatened them
They fell from two thousand to a single rouble
quiz.e: After a first, baffling letter came a request for two thousand; the sums then shrank to a hundred, twenty-five, ten and finally one rouble.

quiz.q: What did Grushenka find when she went to the Poles’ lodgings?
o: Their landlady had evicted them into the street
They were penniless, yet greeted her with pomp
They were packing to go back to Warsaw together
They had won more money at cards from the officers
quiz.e: They had no food, firewood or cigarettes, yet received her with pompous etiquette and grand speeches. She laughed and gave her ‘former one’ ten roubles.

quiz.q: Why does Grushenka believe Mitya is jealous ‘on purpose’?
o: To make her stop visiting the prison every day
To test whether she will still marry him after the trial
To shift his own guilt over Katya on to her
To hide that he plans to confess at the trial
quiz.e: He has been praising Katya for hiring the doctor and the advocate. Grushenka thinks he loves Katya and wants to unload the blame on her by pointing to the Pole.

quiz.q: What is the doctor from Moscow meant to show at the trial?
o: That Mitya was not in his right mind at the time
That Grigory’s head wound has affected his memory
That Smerdyakov’s fit on that day was only faked
That the old man died before he was ever struck
quiz.e: Katerina Ivanovna ordered him as an expert to show that Mitya killed while not in possession of his faculties. Alyosha says Mitya will not agree to that.

quiz.q: What has Mitya been talking about that puzzles Grushenka?
o: A letter he means to write to the governor
A monk who visits him in his cell at night
A sum of money he has hidden in the town
A ‘bairn’, and why it must be wretched
quiz.e: He says that because of the ‘bairn’ he must go to Siberia though he killed no one. He wept, kissed her and made the sign of the Cross over her.

quiz.q: What secret does Grushenka let slip?
o: Rakitin has been carrying letters to Katya
Ivan has secretly visited Mitya twice
Mitya has been writing a full confession
Katya has visited Mitya late at night
quiz.e: Ivan came once on arriving from Moscow and again a week ago, telling Mitya not to let Alyosha or anyone else know. She begs Alyosha to find out what secret the brothers share.

chapters.title: An Ailing Foot
chapters.intro: Background on the reformed courts, the Russian press, Pushkin and civic poetry, French in polite society and nineteenth-century ideas about nerves, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A woman’s private sitting room or bedroom.
The state of being casually or only partly dressed.
A light, loose jacket worn by a woman at home.
In a flirtatious, playfully teasing way.
An immensely long period of time.
A monk who has taken the strictest, highest monastic vows, known as the great schema.
To speak or write about someone in an abusive, damaging way.
Love affairs, especially secret or casual ones.
The killing of one’s own father, or a person who does it.
A student at a seminary, a college that trains priests.
In Russian criticism, a work’s social or political message.
A faint, especially one brought on by strong emotion.
French: ‘struck’, in the sense of shocked or stunned.
From the German Affekt, a sudden overwhelming emotion. Lawyers argued that a crime committed in such a state was less blameworthy, rather like the French crime passionnel, or crime of passion.
The 1864 reform created local magistrates, in Russian mirovye sudyi, to try minor cases quickly and simply. They were elected rather than appointed.
Censorship rules were eased in 1865, and many new papers appeared. Court reports and sensational crime stories became some of their most popular reading.
In the first chapter of Eugene Onegin, Pushkin breaks off into a famous, playful digression in praise of women’s little feet.
Plans for a public statue of Pushkin were discussed for years. It was finally unveiled in Moscow in 1880, when Dostoevsky gave a celebrated speech at the festivities.

Radical critics of the 1860s and 1870s wanted literature with a useful social message. Poets such as Nekrasov wrote ‘civic’ verse about injustice, and verse written purely for beauty was mocked as idle.
Young ladies kept albums in which friends wrote short poems and compliments, so ‘album verse’ came to mean light, flattering poetry.
The Russian upper classes long spoke French among themselves. Sprinkling French words into Russian marked a person as fashionable, and could also sound affected.
Nineteenth-century doctors blamed many fits, faints and emotional outbursts, especially in women, on weak ‘nerves’ or ‘hysteria’.

quiz.q: Why has Alyosha come to the Khokhlakovs’ house?
o: Mrs Khokhlakova wants him to read a letter
Liza has urgently asked him to come and see her
Perkhotin wants him to meet the advocate there
Katya has told him Ivan will be waiting there
quiz.e: Liza sent a maid the day before begging him to come ‘on a certain very important matter’. Her mother intercepts him first.

quiz.q: What does the item in the paper Hearsay say about a ‘pining widow’?
o: She had hidden the stolen money for the criminal
She had once been engaged to the murdered father himself
She had paid for the criminal’s defence in secret
She had offered him three thousand to flee to the mines
quiz.e: It claims she offered him three thousand to run away with her to the gold-mines, but he preferred to kill his father rather than share her ‘forty-year-old charms’.

quiz.q: Whom does Mrs Khokhlakova suspect of writing the item?
o: Rakitin
Perkhotin
Kalganov
Fetyukovich
quiz.e: She is sure it is Rakitin, whom she had recently stopped receiving. Alyosha says only ‘perhaps’.

quiz.q: How does Perkhotin first react to the poem about the ailing foot?
o: He praises it highly and asks to copy it out
He guesses the author and leaves the house
He mocks it as the work of some seminarian
He sets it to music and sings it at the piano
quiz.e: Not told who wrote it, he laughs and calls it a wretched poem by some seminarian. Rakitin flies into a fury and calls him a bribe-taking bureaucrat.

quiz.q: What finally becomes of Rakitin’s visits?
o: He stops coming after the poem appears in print
Perkhotin challenges him to a duel and he flees
He is asked to come only when Liza is also present
She screams, swoons, then refuses to receive him
quiz.e: Torn over whether to scream, she screams and faints, then tells Rakitin she no longer wishes to receive him and has him shown out.

quiz.q: What does Mrs Khokhlakova understand ‘affect’ to mean?
o: A rare nervous illness that strikes only the rich
A fit in which one may kill and yet be pardoned
A legal term for a confession made under pressure
A doctor’s word for a mind that has gone for good
quiz.e: She describes a state in which one has all one’s wits yet is ‘in affect’, and receives an instant pardon. She decides that she, Alyosha and Liza are all in a state of affect too.

quiz.q: Whom does she briefly name as the murderer, and why?
o: Grigory, in a fit of affect after being struck
Smerdyakov, who was seen leaving by the garden gate
Rakitin, who had been in debt to the old man
A robber, who came in through the open door
quiz.e: She says Grigory came to, saw the open door, went in and killed, then forgot it. A moment later she says it would be ‘far better’ if Dmitry had done it.

quiz.q: What has Liza done that morning, according to her mother?
o: Run away to Katya’s house without a word to anyone
Burned all the letters Alyosha had ever written her
Slapped the maid Yulia, then knelt and kissed her feet
Walked alone to the monastery, and refused to come home
quiz.e: She slapped Yulia, then an hour later embraced her and kissed her feet. She has also demanded that Ivan, who visited her secretly, never be received again.

chapters.title: A Little Demon
chapters.intro: Background on Russian beliefs about devils, the Gospels on wealth, the antisemitic ‘blood libel’, the Jews of the Russian Empire and girls’ reading, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes talk of suicide and self-harm, and an antisemitic story about cruelty to a child.
A wheeled chair, often hooded, for an invalid; named after the English spa town of Bath.
Red and swollen, as from illness or lack of sleep.
To listen secretly to other people’s conversation.
Chaos; a lack of order or rules.
A hardy cereal grass grown for grain, cut at harvest with a scythe or sickle.
A spinning toy kept turning by lashing it with a small whip.
Strong disapproval; in religion, the judgement that sends a soul to punishment.
A strong, restless desire for something.
A tendency to laugh or to cause laughter.
Treating serious matters with flippant humour.
The Jewish spring festival recalling the Israelites’ escape from slavery in Egypt.
Fruit cooked in sugar syrup, served as a dessert.
A simple bar or catch that keeps a door closed.
Orthodox teaching and folk belief alike pictured devils as real, numerous tempters, always close at hand and waiting for a moment of weakness.
Orthodox believers cross themselves from forehead to chest and from the right shoulder to the left. It is the standard defence against evil, and can also be made over another person as a blessing.
Riches and poverty in the Gospels
Jesus tells a rich young man to sell what he has and give to the poor, and says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter God’s kingdom.
The Christian teaching that at the end of time all people will be judged by God, the saved received into heaven and the condemned sent to punishment.

A false accusation, spread in Europe since the Middle Ages, that Jews murdered Christian children for ritual purposes. It fuelled persecution for centuries, and such charges still led to trials in nineteenth-century Russia.
Most of the empire’s Jews were confined by law to the western provinces known as the Pale of Settlement. Prejudice was widespread, and Dostoevsky himself voiced antisemitic views in his journalism.
Well-brought-up girls were expected to read only improving books. Racy novels, especially French ones, were kept from them and widely blamed for corrupting the young.

quiz.q: Why, Liza says, is it a good thing she will not marry Alyosha?
o: He would leave her to enter the monastery again
He would let her mother rule over their household
He would grow bored and leave her for another girl
He would carry her letters to a lover, even at forty
quiz.e: If she gave him a letter for the man she loved after him, he would deliver it and bring back the reply, and still be doing so at forty.

quiz.q: What wish does Liza confide to Alyosha?
o: To enter a convent, and give away all her money
To be married, tormented, deceived and abandoned
To leave town and live in Petersburg on her own
To nurse the sick prisoners in the town gaol
quiz.e: She wants a man to marry her, torment her, deceive her and leave her: ‘I do not want to be happy!’ She also dreams of secretly setting fire to the house.

quiz.q: What does Liza claim everyone secretly feels about Mitya’s case?
o: They pity him, but are afraid to say so openly
They are certain his brother Ivan is to blame
They like the idea that he murdered his father
They are bored and want it over and done with
quiz.e: Everyone calls it dreadful, she says, but secretly they all like it, and she is first among them. Alyosha admits there is some truth in this.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha say about Liza’s dream of devils?
o: That he has had the very same dream himself
That she should confess it to a priest at once
That it comes from the books she steals at night
That it is only a fever left by her old illness
quiz.e: Liza is astonished: what matters to her is not the dream but that he could have dreamed exactly the same. She begs him to visit her more often.

quiz.q: How did the visitor Liza summoned react to her story of the boy and the compote?
o: He left at once without saying a single word
He laughed, said it really was good, and left
He scolded her and promised to tell her mother
He wept and begged her to burn the cruel book
quiz.e: He stayed only five minutes, laughed, agreed it was ‘good’ and went. Liza desperately wants to know whether he despised her.

quiz.q: How does Alyosha explain that visitor’s attitude?
o: He is jealous of Alyosha and wants to hurt him
He finds Liza tiresome but is too polite to say
He thinks she is still a child making up stories
He despises no one, but he trusts no one either
quiz.e: Alyosha says the man may believe in the ‘compote’ himself and is ill; with no trust there is contempt, even for her. Liza finds that ‘good’.

quiz.q: What does Liza press into Alyosha’s hand as she pushes him out?
o: A sealed note for Mitya with sweets for the trial
A little icon that she wants him to give to Katya
A sealed letter to Ivan, to be delivered today
A ring he once gave her, returned for good
quiz.e: It is addressed to Ivan Fyodorovich Karamazov. She threatens to poison herself if he does not deliver it that very day.

quiz.q: What does Liza do once Alyosha has gone?
o: Crushes her finger in the door and calls herself vile
Tears up all her mother’s books and throws them out
Rings for Yulia and tells her to fetch Alyosha back
Writes a second letter and sends it after Alyosha
quiz.e: She slams the door on her own finger, then sits staring at the blood under the nail, whispering ‘I am vile, vile, vile, vile!’

chapters.title: A Hymn and a Secret
chapters.intro: Background on Russian prisons and penal servitude, materialist science, radical journalism, the Apocryphal Gospels, Freemasonry and Schiller, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: French, literally ‘between four eyes’: in private, with no one else present.
The branch of philosophy that studies right and wrong.
Favouring social reform and new ideas.
An old exclamation of disgust or disapproval.
A phrase from Genesis: God made human beings in his own image and likeness.
The public good; the well-being of society.
A person devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure.
A scoundrel; a man who behaves dishonourably.
Rock or earth from which metal can be extracted.
Chains or shackles fastened round a prisoner’s ankles.
A mysterious, unreadable person, after the riddling creature of Greek legend.
Generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival or someone who has done wrong.
A French physiologist (1813–1878) who helped found experimental medicine. For many readers his name stood for modern, materialist science.
The view that everything, including thought and feeling, can be explained by matter alone. It was popular among young Russian radicals of the 1860s and 1870s.
In this book of 1863 the Russian physiologist Ivan Sechenov argued that all mental life is made up of reflexes of the nervous system. It caused a sensation.
Radicals argued that crime springs from social conditions rather than personal guilt. Dostoevsky attacked this idea repeatedly in his journalism.
Members of a secret brotherhood with its own rituals. Freemasonry flourished in Russia in the late eighteenth century, was banned in 1822, and remained a subject of suspicion and rumour.
In Russian katorga: hard labour, often in Siberian mines or factories, followed by settlement in Siberia. It was the heaviest punishment that ordinary criminals faced.
Wives could choose to follow husbands sent to Siberia. Several wives of the Decembrists famously did so in the 1820s, giving up their rank and comforts.
A Russian saying for utter ruin, recalling Peter the Great’s crushing defeat of Charles XII of Sweden at Poltava in 1709.
Russia’s big monthly magazines mixed fiction, criticism and politics. A post as a critic on one could launch a career and shape public opinion.
Early writings about Jesus and his family that were not accepted into the New Testament, such as the Gospel of James on Mary and the birth of Jesus.
From the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:26): someone thrown into prison will not come out until he has paid the last coin.
A poem of 1785 by Friedrich Schiller celebrating joy as the force that unites all creation. Beethoven set it in the finale of his Ninth Symphony.

quiz.q: Why can Alyosha visit Mitya even when he arrives late?
o: He is an old friend of the kindly prison supervisor
He holds a special permit signed by the prosecutor himself
He bribes the sentries at the gate with coins
He comes dressed as a monk bringing communion
quiz.e: The supervisor, who is studying the Apocryphal Gospels, loves to talk ‘wisdom’ with Alyosha, and the whole prison staff is used to seeing him.

quiz.q: What remark of Mitya’s makes Rakitin explode as he leaves?
o: That Rakitin would never make a real poet
That Rakitin should go back to his old monastery
Not to forget anything that belongs to others
That Rakitin’s article would never be printed
quiz.e: Rakitin mutters that he doesn’t want to forget anything of his own; Mitya’s quip makes him shout about the Karamazovs’ ‘serf-owning spawn’.

quiz.q: What kind of article does Rakitin plan to write about Mitya’s case?
o: One proving that Mitya is entirely innocent
One saying he killed as a prey to his environment
One exposing the advocate as a greedy paid swindler
One praising the new courts for their mercy
quiz.e: Rakitin wants to launch his literary career with a ‘progressive’ piece arguing that Mitya couldn’t help committing murder, with ‘a touch of socialism’.

quiz.q: Why does Mitya say he is ‘sorry for God’?
o: Because the Church has failed to help prisoners
Because Ivan has told him God is a cruel tyrant
Because the Elder Zosima’s body had decayed so fast
Because science says we think with trembling nerves
quiz.e: Rakitin has explained that images arise from little ‘tails’ of nerves trembling in the brain, not from a soul or God’s ‘image and likeness’. ‘Chemistry is coming!’

quiz.q: What scheme had Rakitin boasted of to Mitya?
o: Becoming editor of a Moscow journal within the year
Inheriting a fortune from a dying merchant uncle
Marrying the rich Mrs Khokhlakova for her capital
Winning Grushenka away from Mitya after the trial
quiz.e: He meant to marry the ‘little widow’, buy a stone house in Petersburg and start a newspaper; the foot poem was written ‘for a useful end’. Perkhotin won instead.

quiz.q: What does Mitya say the ‘subterranean folk’ will do from under the earth?
o: Sing a tragic hymn to God, with whom is joy
Rise in revolt against their masters above
Dig for gold until their terms are over
Curse the God who left them in the mines
quiz.e: A convict cannot be without God, he says; if God is driven from the earth, they will meet him under it and sing their hymn from the bowels of the earth.

quiz.q: What is the one remark Ivan has made when Mitya asked if all things are lawful?
o: That only a fool would ask such a question
That God alone could answer, and God is always silent
That Rakitin had already explained it to them
That their father was a pig but had the right ideas
quiz.e: Ivan frowned and said that their ‘dear papa’ Fyodor Pavlovich was ‘a sucking-pig, but he had the right ideas’.

quiz.q: What does Mitya ask Alyosha to beg of Katerina Ivanovna?
o: To visit him in prison before the trial begins
Not to tell the court of her bow for the money
To pay the advocate the rest of his large fee
To stop speaking ill of Grushenka in the town
quiz.e: He fears she will tell of her ‘earthly prostration’ after he gave her the money, and pay him back ‘to the uttermost farthing’.

quiz.q: What is the secret Mitya finally reveals?
o: Katya has promised to marry him if he is acquitted
He knows where Smerdyakov hid the stolen money
Ivan wants him to escape to America with Grusha
He means to confess to the murder in court
