quiz.e: Ivan insists on it: ten thousand to get him out and twenty thousand for America. Mitya fears it would mean running away from suffering and his ‘hymn’.

quiz.q: What does Mitya ask Alyosha just as he is leaving?
o: Whether he truly believes that Mitya did it
Whether Grushenka will wait for him in Siberia
Whether Ivan has spoken to the advocate yet
Whether the Elder would have blessed his plan
quiz.e: Alyosha swears he never for a moment believed Mitya a murderer. Mitya, transfigured, tells him to go and ‘love Ivan’.

chapters.title: Not You, Not You!
chapters.intro: Background on Russian forms of address, nineteenth-century ideas about fever and epilepsy, devotion to the Mother of God and provincial lodgings, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A paper lantern, often painted, used for soft lighting.
Delay in doing something; putting it off.
In a grimly mocking or cynical way.
Threatening; suggesting that something bad is coming.
In a wildly emotional, uncontrolled way.
In a confused, feverish state of mind, sometimes seeing things that are not there.
A person sent on a special mission as someone’s representative.
A place where two or more roads meet; also a point of decision.
A part of a large house that projects from the main building.
A disease causing pain and stiffness in the joints and muscles.
Too strong to be overcome or resisted.
Russian has an intimate word for ‘you’ (ty), used to family, close friends and lovers, and a polite one (vy). Translators sometimes render the intimate form as ‘thou’.
Polite Russian address uses a first name plus a patronymic, a name formed from the father’s first name. Used between close relatives, it can sound cool and distant.
A common nineteenth-century diagnosis, often called ‘brain fever’ in English novels, for a dangerous illness with high fever and delirium, thought to be brought on by shock or strain.
Ancient writers called epilepsy the sacred disease, and some believed that sufferers had prophetic visions. Dostoevsky himself had epilepsy.
Russians prayed to the Virgin Mary, often before her icons, for help and guidance in times of trouble. Some of her icons, such as Our Lady of Kazan, were venerated across the country.
Single men in provincial towns commonly rented furnished rooms in a family’s house, or an apartment in a wing of a larger house.

quiz.q: What message from Mitya does Alyosha give Katerina Ivanovna?
o: That he forgives her and wants her to visit him
To say nothing at the trial about their first meeting
That she must not trust Ivan with any more money
That he will plead guilty, so she need not appear at all
quiz.e: He asks her to be merciful to herself and not tell of what passed between them in that town. She bitterly asks whether he fears for himself or for her.

quiz.q: What startles Alyosha in the way Katya speaks to Ivan?
o: She addresses him as ‘thou’, as an intimate
She calls him a murderer before the servant
She begs him on her knees not to leave her
She speaks to him in French, very coldly
quiz.e: She cries that it was ‘thou’ who convinced her Mitya was the father-murderer. Alyosha had never suspected such intimacy between them.

quiz.q: Why does Katya send Alyosha running after Ivan?
o: To give him a letter she has just written
To bring him back to finish their quarrel
To make sure he promises to come to the trial
Because he is ill and must not be left alone
quiz.e: She whispers that he has gone mad, that he has a nerve fever and the doctor told her so; he must not be left alone for a moment.

quiz.q: What does Ivan do with Liza’s letter?
o: Reads it under the lamp and laughs aloud
Puts it away unread, saying he will answer it later
Tears it up unopened and throws it to the wind
Hands it back and tells Alyosha to burn it
quiz.e: Recognising the hand, he calls her ‘that little demon’, rips the letter up without opening it and sneers that she is offering herself.

quiz.q: What does Ivan say Katya possesses?
o: A letter from Smerdyakov confessing to the crime
The bloodstained banknotes taken from the envelope
A document in Mitya’s hand that proves his guilt
A will in which old Karamazov disinherits Mitya
quiz.e: He says the document ‘mathematically proves’ that Mitya killed Fyodor Pavlovich, and that he has read it himself. He cannot break with her before the trial, he says, or she will use it.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha insist on telling Ivan by the lamp-post?
o: That Smerdyakov has confessed to him in secret
That whoever killed their father, it was not Ivan
That Mitya has now agreed to the plan for his escape
That Katya loves Mitya and not Ivan after all
quiz.e: Alyosha says Ivan has accused himself in these two months, but ‘it was not you’, and that God sent him to say so.

quiz.q: How does the meeting between the brothers end?
o: Ivan embraces him and asks him to come back home with him
Ivan agrees to see Mitya with him in the morning
Ivan confesses that he has been seeing a doctor
Ivan breaks off relations with him, perhaps for good
quiz.e: After demanding whether Alyosha has seen ‘him’ visiting at night, Ivan recovers himself, says he cannot endure prophets and epileptics, and severs relations.

quiz.q: Where does Ivan go instead of entering his own lodgings?
o: To the house where the sick Smerdyakov lies
Back to Katerina Ivanovna’s to finish their talk
To the prison, to see Mitya before the trial
To the tavern where he once met Alyosha
quiz.e: At his own gate he turns back and walks across town to Marya Kondratyevna’s little house, where Smerdyakov has lain ill since the day of the murder.

chapters.title: The First Visit to Smerdyakov
chapters.intro: Background on criminal investigations, epilepsy, foreign doctors in Russia, the French language and servants’ speech, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes discussion of a murder and of serious illness.
Turning to someone or something for help.
Talkative; inclined to talk a great deal.
Short and abrupt in manner, to the point of rudeness.
A formal statement of evidence, written down for use in a legal case.
An old name for epilepsy, an illness that causes sudden fits.
To grant or give something, often in a condescending way.
An old word for swelling of the body caused by a build-up of fluid, often a sign of heart or kidney failure.
A member of the Skoptsy, a secretive Russian sect whose men castrated themselves. The word suggested a beardless, wizened face.
To avoid giving a straight answer; to be evasive.
A small room at the top of a house, just under the roof.
Here, an official written record of statements made to investigators.
Innocent frankness; a childlike lack of cunning.
A fact that makes a wrong seem less serious or more excusable.
After the legal reforms of the 1860s, a court official called the investigator questioned witnesses and suspects and gathered evidence before a case came to trial.
The state prosecutor, who brought charges and argued the case against the accused in court.
Statements taken during the investigation were written down in an official record. At the trial, witnesses could be questioned again in open court.
A condition of the brain that causes sudden seizures. The exact moment of an attack cannot be foretold, though some people feel warning signs shortly before one.
Dostoevsky himself suffered from epilepsy, and he gave the illness to characters in several of his novels, among them Prince Myshkin in The Idiot.
Many of the doctors and chemists working in nineteenth-century Russia were Germans or Baltic Germans.
French was long the language of the Russian upper classes. Knowing some was a mark of refinement, and people hoping to rise in the world tried to pick it up.
Russian servants often added a short ‘-s’, from the word for ‘sir’, to their words as a mark of deference. Translators render it with a repeated ‘sir’.

quiz.q: How did Ivan’s first meeting with Mitya in prison affect him?
o: It made him doubt Mitya’s guilt for the very first time
It left him more convinced than ever of Mitya’s guilt
It persuaded him to pay for a lawyer from Petersburg
It reconciled the two brothers after years of coldness
quiz.e: Mitya was incoherent and hostile, even taunting Ivan about ‘all things are lawful’, and the meeting strengthened Ivan’s belief that he was guilty.

quiz.q: What do the doctors tell Ivan about Smerdyakov’s fit?
o: It was caused by a blow to the head when he fell down
It was probably feigned, though this could not be proved
It was a mild one, and he would be home within the week
It was genuine, and so prolonged his life was in danger
quiz.e: Herzenstube and Varvinsky insist the attack was real and unusually long, recurring for days, and that his reason might stay partly deranged.

quiz.q: How does Smerdyakov explain foretelling a fit in the cellar?
o: His fear of falling there brought the attack on
A doctor had warned him the cellar air was bad
He had dreamed of the cellar for several nights
His fits always struck on the same day of the month
quiz.e: He had to go down there daily anyway; his dread of falling, he says, brought on the spasm, and Varvinsky had said the same.

quiz.q: What takes Ivan aback about Smerdyakov’s statements to the investigators?
o: He had accused Ivan of plotting together with Dmitry
He had refused to tell them anything about that day
He had already told them of the talk at the gates
He had asked to be questioned only with Ivan present
quiz.e: Ivan meant to frighten him by threatening to reveal their conversation, but Smerdyakov had described it himself, along with the secret knocks.

quiz.q: Why, according to Smerdyakov, did he urge Ivan towards Chermashnya rather than Moscow?
o: So Ivan could fetch a doctor for Grigory from the village
So Ivan could sell the woodland and bring the money home
So Ivan would be out of the way when Grushenka arrived
So Ivan would stay near enough to come back and protect them
quiz.e: Chermashnya was close, so Dmitry would be less bold and Ivan could return quickly; his words at the carriage, he says, were a reproach, not praise.

quiz.q: Which argument of Smerdyakov’s puts Ivan’s mind at rest?
o: That a man planning murder would never boast he could fake fits
That Dmitry had threatened their father in front of witnesses
That he had never once set foot inside his master’s bedroom
That Marfa had heard him groaning behind the partition all night
quiz.e: Would he have told one of the victim’s own sons that he could feign a fit if he meant to kill? Ivan is struck by this and says he does not suspect him.

quiz.q: What does Ivan suggest as he leaves the hospital?
o: That they meet again in front of the public procurator
That Smerdyakov tell the investigator all about the knocks
That neither mention Smerdyakov’s skill at faking fits
That Smerdyakov leave the town as soon as he has recovered
quiz.e: Ivan says he will keep quiet about the feigning and advises Smerdyakov to do the same; Smerdyakov replies that he then won’t tell the whole conversation at the gates.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha answer when Ivan asks if he thought Ivan wanted Dmitry to kill their father?
o: He says he never once suspected Ivan of any such wish
He whispers that, at the time, he did think so
He says only God could know what Ivan truly desired
He refuses to answer and walks off without a word
quiz.e: Alyosha admits it without any softening. Ivan thanks him curtly, and from then on avoids him and treats him with hostility.

chapters.title: The Second Visit to Smerdyakov
chapters.intro: Background on modest Russian town houses, the class of small townspeople, physical punishment, the loss of rights on conviction and France’s new republic, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes discussion of a murder, a violent outburst and threats of violence.
Engaged to be married; also the person one is engaged to.
A candle made of stearin, a hard white wax obtained from animal or vegetable fat.
Behaving as if one is superior to others; haughty.
Acting quickly and rashly, without thinking.
Russian for a lady or the mistress of a household; the feminine of barin.
Sticking rigidly to a theory, whatever the circumstances.
A short, pointed saying that expresses a general truth.
Using far more words than needed.
A punishment or fate that someone deserves.
French: sudden swings back in opinion.
A handle or cord pulled to ring a doorbell or summon a servant.
In a Russian house this meant the best or guest room.
Large brick stoves faced with glazed tiles heated Russian homes through the long winter, and could keep a room very hot.
Most Russian homes kept icons in one corner of the main room, often in a glass-fronted case, sometimes with a lamp before them.
The meshchane were the legal class of artisans, small traders and their families, ranked below the merchants. Educated Russians often mocked their tastes as narrow and petty.
The emancipation of 1861 ended landowners’ power over serfs, and a law of 1863 greatly reduced physical punishment, though peasant courts could still order floggings.
A nobleman sentenced to penal servitude lost all the rights of his status, including his rank, privileges and rights over property. In law he was treated almost as if he had died.
France became a republic again in 1870, after Napoleon III was defeated by Prussia. To many Russians it stood for modern European liberty and equality.
For some Russians, settling in Western Europe meant escape to a freer, more ‘civilised’ life; others scorned the wish as a betrayal of Russia.

quiz.q: Where is Smerdyakov now living?
o: In a room above the Capital City inn, paid for by Ivan himself
In the lodge at Fyodor Pavlovich’s house with Grigory and Marfa
With Marya Kondratyevna and her mother, apparently as her fiancé
In a ward of the town hospital kept for long-term patients
quiz.e: He has a room across the passage from Marya Kondratyevna and her mother, apparently living free as her intended.

quiz.q: How does Ivan react when Smerdyakov suggests he may have wished his father dead?
o: He strikes him so hard he sways against the wall
He laughs and says the idea is beneath his contempt
He calls Marya Kondratyevna in to act as a witness
He leaves at once and goes straight to the police
quiz.e: Ivan hits him on the shoulder with all his might; Smerdyakov bursts into tears: ‘For shame, good sir, to strike a weak man.’

quiz.q: What motive does Smerdyakov attribute to Ivan?
o: Jealousy of Dmitry, whom their father had always preferred
Anger that his father had insulted Katerina Ivanovna in public
Hope of taking over his father’s taverns and selling them off
Fear that a marriage to Grushenka would leave them nothing
quiz.e: Each brother stood to get about forty thousand, or nothing if Grushenka married Fyodor Pavlovich; with Dmitry convicted, Ivan and Alyosha would get sixty thousand each.

quiz.q: Why, says Smerdyakov, did Ivan’s trip to Chermashnya give him away?
o: He had told the coachman he would be away for a whole month
He had refused his father, then agreed at a servant’s hint
He had left his father’s house without saying goodbye to him
He had taken money from his father’s desk just before leaving
quiz.e: Ivan had always refused his father’s requests to go, then changed his mind because of Smerdyakov’s remark, so he must have expected something.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov threaten if Ivan testifies against him?
o: To tell everything, which the public would believe, if not the court
To flee abroad with Marya Kondratyevna well before the trial begins
To claim that Ivan paid him to keep silent about Dmitry’s plans
To give the investigator a letter that Ivan had once written him
quiz.e: He says he would defend himself by telling all, and Ivan would be covered with shame. ‘Be clever, sir.’

quiz.q: What does Katerina Ivanovna show Ivan after he says he may be an accomplice?
o: A note from Smerdyakov asking her for money to keep quiet
A receipt for three thousand roubles signed by Dmitry
A drunken letter Mitya wrote at the Capital City inn
A telegram from Moscow, sent on the night of the murder
quiz.e: Mitya’s letter threatened to kill his father and take the money from under the pillow ‘if only Ivan has gone away’. To Ivan it seems a ‘mathematical’ proof.

quiz.q: What had Ivan proposed to Mitya some ten days before the trial?
o: A full confession, in exchange for a lighter sentence
A plan of escape, funded partly out of his own pocket
A bribe to the procurator to have the charge reduced
A plea of insanity, supported by the Moscow doctor
quiz.e: He offered to put thirty thousand of his own towards an escape, partly to heal the ‘scar’ left by Smerdyakov’s remark about the inheritance.

quiz.q: What sends Ivan to Smerdyakov a third time?
o: A note from Smerdyakov begging him to come at once
Alyosha’s request that he question him once more
News that Smerdyakov had been taken by the police
Learning Katerina Ivanovna had been to see him
quiz.e: Katerina had cried out that she herself had visited Smerdyakov, which meant she was not sure of Mitya’s guilt. ‘This time I may kill him,’ Ivan thinks.

chapters.title: The Third, and Final, Visit to Smerdyakov
chapters.intro: Background on Russian winters, peasants who worked in the capital, furnished lodgings and the jury courts, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes violence, references to a murder and serious illness.
A long, coarse cloth coat worn by Russian peasants.
A familiar, rather rough form of the name Ivan.
Lying flat on one’s back, face upward.
A footman or manservant; also someone who is servile to another.
Thin and drawn, from illness or worry.
A castrated male horse; here an insult for a dull, stubborn man.
Absolute; allowing no doubt or exception.
Far more than is usual or reasonable.
A hard reddish-brown wood used for good furniture.
Many peasant men left their villages for seasonal or years-long work in St Petersburg and other cities, leaving wives and families behind. Folk songs often dwell on these partings.
The outlying streets of provincial towns often had no lamps at all, and a winter snowstorm (metel) could blind walkers and cover roads in minutes.
Single gentlemen in provincial towns often rented rooms, with an elderly servant to bring the samovar and keep house.
The same reform created a professional bar. Leading defence lawyers became celebrities, and their courtroom speeches were printed in the press.

quiz.q: What does Ivan do to the drunken muzhik on his way?
o: He helps him home and knocks at his family’s door
He gives him a few coins and sends him on his way
He sings along with him for a stretch of the road
He knocks him down and leaves him in the snow
quiz.e: The muzhik lurches into him; Ivan shoves him away in fury, sees him lying unconscious, thinks ‘He will freeze to death’, and walks on.

quiz.q: Whom does Smerdyakov call the ‘principal murderer’?
o: Dmitry, who had beaten Grigory and fled the house
Ivan, whose wishes he says he merely carried out
Himself, since he had planned it all for months
Grushenka, whose coming had set it all in motion
quiz.e: He calls Ivan the principal murderer and himself only Ivan’s minion, ‘your faithful servant Licharda’, who acted on his instructions.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov draw out of his stocking?
o: Three wads of hundred-rouble notes, the missing three thousand
A letter in Fyodor Pavlovich’s hand, naming a new heir
The pink ribbon and torn envelope from the bedroom floor
A small knife wrapped in a bloodstained handkerchief
quiz.e: He lays the whole three thousand on the table, then covers it with a book of the sermons of Isaac of Nineveh.

quiz.q: What was the truth about his fit in the cellar?
o: It was real, though he pretended later that it had lasted longer
It was feigned, and he kept up the pretence for weeks in hospital
It was feigned, but a real and severe attack came the next day
It was real, brought on by fear, just as the doctors had said
quiz.e: He lay down calmly and howled; the next morning a genuine fit struck, the worst in years, and he lay unconscious for two days.

quiz.q: Where had Smerdyakov persuaded Fyodor Pavlovich to hide the envelope?
o: Under the mattress of his bed
In the corner behind the icons
In a locked box in his study
In a drawer of his writing desk
quiz.e: Everyone believed it was under the mattress, as Smerdyakov had told Dmitry, but he had advised moving it behind the icons, where a hurried intruder would never look.

quiz.q: How did he get Fyodor Pavlovich to open the door?
o: He shouted that Grigory lay injured and needed help
He claimed Dmitry had gone and the danger was over
He called out that the servants’ lodge was on fire
He said Grushenka had come and tapped the signals
quiz.e: His words alone were not believed, but when he tapped the knocks meaning Grushenka had arrived, the old man ran to open the door.

quiz.q: Why did he leave the torn envelope on the floor?
o: To make it look like the act of a man who had never seen the money
Because Marfa Ignatyevna woke and he had no time to take it away
So that Grigory would come across it and raise the alarm at once
So the police would think the thief had hunted for more hidden notes
quiz.e: A servant who knew the money was inside would just pocket the envelope; Dmitry would have opened it to check. He even hinted this idea to the procurator.

quiz.q: Why does Smerdyakov give the money to Ivan?
o: He says he has found God and must give back what he took
He says it is Ivan’s by right of inheritance, not his
He says he has no need of it, yet still has no faith
He says Marya Kondratyevna begged him to be rid of it
quiz.e: He had dreamed of a new life in Moscow or abroad, believing ‘all things are lawful’; now he wants none of it, yet denies he has come to believe in God.

quiz.q: Why, according to Smerdyakov, will Ivan not confess in court?
o: He fears Katerina Ivanovna will turn from him for ever
He knows the judges would simply laugh him out of court
He will be far too ill with fever to stand up in court
He is like his father, and loves a comfortable, honoured life
quiz.e: Ivan loves money, esteem, women and above all an easy, independent life, says Smerdyakov; of all the sons he has the soul most like Fyodor Pavlovich’s.

quiz.q: What does Ivan do on his way home?
o: He goes straight to the procurator and tells him everything
He carries the frozen muzhik to the police station for help
He stops at Katerina Ivanovna’s to show her the money
He throws the three thousand roubles into the snow in disgust
quiz.e: Resolved to confess at the trial, he finds the muzhik almost buried in snow, takes him to the police station and pays for a doctor.

chapters.title: The Devil. Ivan Fyodorovich’s Nightmare
chapters.intro: Background on devils in literature and folk belief, spiritualism, Russia in the 1870s and the literary, biblical and philosophical references the chapter makes, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes hallucinations and mental illness, sexual references and brief mentions of suicide.
A severe state of confusion, trembling and hallucinations, usually linked to heavy drinking.
French: ‘who was getting on for fifty’.
A hanger-on who lives at other people’s expense.
A pair of glasses held up to the eyes rather than worn.
A person’s face, especially as a guide to character.
The feast day of the saint one is named after, celebrated in Russia much like a birthday.
Clever but misleading reasoning about right and wrong. Critics of the Jesuits accused them of it.
Cannibalism, the eating of human flesh.
A small pane set into a Russian window that can be opened for fresh air.
A light comic play with songs.
A religious hermit who lives apart from the world.
Tiny or very diluted, from homoeopathy, a system of medicine using minute doses.
In Goethe’s Faust the devil Mephistopheles calls himself part of the power that always wills evil and always does good.
The hero of Gogol’s comedy The Inspector General (1836): a penniless young nobody, mistaken for a government inspector, who boasts wildly about his importance.
The Roman playwright wrote ‘Homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto’: ‘I am a human being, and nothing human is alien to me.’
Griboyedov’s verse comedy of the 1820s, a satire on Moscow society, many of whose lines became proverbs.
Heinrich Heine (1797–1856), a German poet famous for mixing romantic feeling with biting irony.
Vissarion Belinsky (1811–48), the most influential Russian critic of his day, who championed realism and social purpose in literature.
In John’s Gospel the apostle Thomas will not believe that Christ has risen until he can see and touch the wounds.
The Old Testament prophet who tried to run from God’s command and spent three days and nights inside a great fish.
A Hebrew cry of praise, shouted by the crowds when Christ entered Jerusalem and sung in Christian worship.
Séances to contact the spirits of the dead were fashionable across Europe in the 1870s. A Russian scientific commission investigated them in 1875–76.
In Russian popular belief devils were petty, mischievous beings with horns and tails. The bathhouse, a place without icons, was thought a haunt of unclean spirits.
The tsar’s political police, set up in 1826, which received informers’ reports on suspect people. It was abolished in 1880.
In 1875–76 the Balkan Slavs rose against Ottoman rule. Russians gave money and volunteers to help them, and Russia went to war with Turkey in 1877.
Russian officials prized medals and orders. Foreign ones, such as the Persian Lion and Sun or Sweden’s Order of the Pole Star, were also awarded.
Descartes’ famous starting point (1637): whatever else can be doubted, the existence of the thinking self cannot.

quiz.q: What had the doctor from Moscow told Ivan?
o: That hallucinations were possible and treatment was urgent
That he was merely exhausted and should rest in the country
That his trouble lay in his heart and not in his brain
That he must give up drinking or he would not live a year
quiz.e: The doctor found something close to a brain disorder and urged immediate treatment; Ivan ignored the advice while he could still walk.

quiz.q: What sort of man does the visitor appear to be?
o: A stern priest in a worn black cassock and hat
A young student in a radical’s red peasant shirt
A shabby-genteel sponger, once a landowner
A rich merchant in a fur coat and high boots
quiz.e: He is a Russian ‘gentleman’ of nearly fifty in outdated, slightly dirty clothes, like an impoverished former landowner living on friends’ hospitality.

quiz.q: What does the visitor first remind Ivan of?
o: That he left the money on Smerdyakov’s table
That he forgot to ask about Katerina’s visit
That he had promised to call on Alyosha tonight
That he must send for the doctor before dawn
quiz.e: Ivan had gone to Smerdyakov to find out about Katerina Ivanovna but left without asking; he suspects the visitor of planting the thought.

quiz.q: What does Ivan insist the visitor is?
o: A real spirit, sent to punish him for his father
A trick of Smerdyakov’s, meant to drive him mad
An actor someone has hired to frighten him
A hallucination embodying his worst thoughts
quiz.e: ‘You are my illness, you are a ghost,’ he says: the embodiment of one side of himself, his most loathsome and stupid thoughts.

quiz.q: What does the guest say is his dream on earth?
o: To be given high office in a Petersburg ministry
To write a novel finer than any by Lev Tolstoy
To be a fat merchant’s wife and light candles
To dine at the tsar’s table and win a decoration
quiz.e: He longs to take flesh for good as a seven-pood merchant’s wife, believe all she believes, and set up a candle in church with a pure heart.

quiz.q: How does the guest explain his role in the universe?
o: He must negate, since without him nothing would happen
He alone keeps the planets moving in their proper orbits
He records every human sin for the Last Judgement
He guards the gates of heaven against unworthy souls
quiz.e: He was appointed to ‘negate’, against his good heart: without him there would be no criticism and no events, only an endless ‘hosannah’.

quiz.q: In the legend, what does the philosopher sentenced to walk a quadrillion kilometres do?
o: He refuses for ever and lies in the darkness for all eternity
He walks it at once, only to find the gates of heaven shut
He turns back halfway, sure the journey is an illusion
He lies down for a thousand years, then walks, and sings hosannah
quiz.e: After lying across the road for nearly a thousand years he walks the distance; two seconds in heaven make him declare it worth a quadrillion quadrillions.

quiz.q: Why is Ivan delighted by the quadrillion anecdote?
o: He had read it in Voltaire, so the guest must be a fraud
He made it up as a schoolboy, so the guest is his dream
It shows that the guest knows the other world at first hand
It proves to him that a life after death exists after all
quiz.e: He composed it at seventeen at the gymnasium in Moscow and had forgotten it; the guest says he told it on purpose to shake Ivan’s belief in him.

quiz.q: What makes Ivan blush with shame and forbid the guest to go on?
o: The mention of his poem ‘The Grand Inquisitor’
A story about his mother’s death in the province
A hint that he had once loved his father after all
A reminder of his quarrels with Katerina Ivanovna
quiz.e: The guest names Ivan’s ‘The Grand Inquisitor’ and ‘The Geological Revolution’, then mockingly retells his ideas about the man-god and ‘all things are lawful’.

quiz.q: What news does Alyosha bring through the window?
o: Dmitry has escaped from the town prison
Katerina Ivanovna has fallen gravely ill
Smerdyakov hanged himself an hour ago
The trial has been put off for a month
quiz.e: Ivan wakes after throwing a tea-glass, finds the sofa empty and the glass on the table, and opens the window to Alyosha’s terrible news.

chapters.title: ‘He Said That’
chapters.intro: Background on angels in Christian tradition, a Russian Romantic poem, old ideas of the world’s age and nineteenth-century notions of illness, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes discussion of a suicide and severe mental distress.
A traditional Russian wooden house, especially a peasant’s cottage.
An old Russian measure of length, about 71 centimetres (28 inches).
A very large breed of dog with a short, smooth coat.
A dressing table, usually with a mirror, used while washing and dressing.
A small table holding a basin and jug of water for washing.
A feeling that something is about to happen.
Generous and noble-minded, especially towards others’ faults.
Private and trusting, as when sharing a secret.
French: the answer to the riddle.
A false statement that damages someone’s reputation.
Speech that is jumbled and impossible to follow.
A young pig still feeding on its mother’s milk; here used as an insult.
In Christian tradition, two of the highest orders of angels, pictured near God’s throne and singing his praise.
In the Gospels Christ tells his followers to take up their cross and follow him; a ‘cross’ came to mean a burden of suffering that must be borne.
The traditional Orthodox calendar dated the creation of the world to 5508 BC, so in the 1870s human history was thought to be about seven thousand years old.
A famous Russian narrative poem (1839) about a fallen angel, weary of evil, who falls in love with a mortal girl.
The movement in art and thought of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries that prized strong feeling, imagination and the lonely, defiant hero.
A loose nineteenth-century name for a sudden illness with high fever, delirium and confusion, often blamed on great mental strain.
A cloth soaked in cold water and laid on the head was a common home remedy for fever and headache.

quiz.q: What does Smerdyakov’s note say?
o: That Dmitry is innocent and that he alone is guilty
That he ends his life of his own will, to blame no one
That Ivan put him up to everything he had ever done
That his savings should all go to Marya Kondratyevna
quiz.e: ‘I exterminate my life by my own will and inclination, in order to blame no one.’ Alyosha leaves it on the table and goes to the police.

quiz.q: How does Ivan say he already knew of the death?
o: He saw it plainly in a dream the night before
Marya Kondratyevna had sent a note round to him
Smerdyakov had hinted at it that very evening
‘He’ had told him, just before Alyosha arrived
quiz.e: Ivan says ‘he told me just now’, and says the visitor slipped away because he was frightened of Alyosha, ‘the pure cherub’.

quiz.q: What puzzles Ivan about the towel?
o: It is stained with tea from the glass he threw
It is soaking wet, though he never touched it
It is dry and folded, though he thought he soaked it
It is not his, but one he has never seen before
quiz.e: He remembers wetting it and throwing it on the chair, yet Alyosha finds it clean, folded and unused by the toilet table.

quiz.q: How does Ivan describe the visitor to Alyosha?
o: As a petty, rubbishy devil, not Satan at all
As Satan himself, in thunder and glittering glory
As their dead father, come back to accuse him
As Smerdyakov, returned to mock him from the grave
quiz.e: He is ‘just a devil, a rubbishy, petty devil’ who goes to the Russian baths and probably has a tail like a Great Dane’s.

quiz.q: What does Ivan tell Alyosha about taking his own life?
o: He will do so if the jury convicts Dmitry
He would do so, but lacks Smerdyakov’s nerve
He will enter a monastery rather than do so
He never could, out of his thirst for life
quiz.e: ‘Tomorrow is a cross, but not a gallows,’ he says: not out of cowardice but out of his thirst for life, he could never kill himself.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha keep insisting as Ivan repeats the visitor’s words?
o: That the visitor is real and must be driven off with prayer
That it is Ivan himself, not the visitor, who says these things
That Ivan must go and tell everything to the procurator tonight
That Smerdyakov’s death proves that Dmitry must be guilty
quiz.e: ‘It is you that says it, not he!’ Alyosha cries, and tells Ivan that it was not he who killed their father.

quiz.q: What, Ivan says, did the visitor finally call him?
o: A coward
A martyr
A genius
A saint
quiz.e: The visitor said Ivan would testify only because he did not dare not to, and called him a coward; ‘Smerdyakov said the same thing, too.’

quiz.q: What does Alyosha think as he falls asleep beside his brother?
o: Ivan will wake by morning remembering nothing of the night
Ivan will lose his reason and never stand up in court at all
Ivan will rise in the light of truth, or perish in hatred
Ivan will run abroad with Katerina Ivanovna after the trial
quiz.e: He sees the torments of a proud decision and a deep conscience; God will prevail, and Ivan will either rise in truth or perish taking vengeance on himself and others.

chapters.title: The Fateful Day
chapters.intro: Background on the reformed Russian courts of 1864, trial by jury, witnesses and the oath, penal servitude and famous trials as public events, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter mentions a violent death, bloodstained evidence and a suicide.
A regional court that tried serious criminal cases for a whole district.
The official who presents the case against the accused in court; a public prosecutor.
The panel of judges hearing a case.
Physical objects shown in court as proof, such as weapons or clothing.
A court officer who keeps order and brings in the accused and the witnesses.
The formal written statement of the charges against an accused person.
The study and theory of law.
In ancient Greece, an educated courtesan; later, any woman kept by wealthy lovers.
An old Russian measure of length, about 71 centimetres.
Gloves made of fine, soft leather from young goats.
A man’s knee-length coat, worn as formal day dress.
A person’s face and features, especially when read as a sign of character.
A low civil-service rank in imperial Russia, ninth of the fourteen grades.
A man very concerned with elegant, fashionable dress.
Lack of seriousness; light-heartedness at the wrong moment.
Punishment given in return for a wrong.
One of Alexander II’s ‘Great Reforms’. It created courts independent of the administration, open to the public and the press, where prosecution and defence argued their cases aloud before the judges.
Introduced by the same reform for serious criminal cases. Twelve jurors decided whether the accused was guilty, while the judges ran the trial and fixed the sentence.
Jurors had to meet residence and modest property requirements, so peasants, tradesmen and minor officials often served. Educated critics doubted whether such men could judge complicated cases.
Before a trial began, both prosecution and defence could reject a number of the men drawn for the jury without giving a reason.
Witnesses normally swore an oath, administered by a priest. The defendant’s close relatives could be questioned without taking it.
After 1864 sensational cases drew crowds of spectators, and newspapers printed long reports of the evidence and speeches.

quiz.q: Which way did most of the ladies in the audience lean?
o: They favoured Mitya and hoped he would be acquitted
They wished to see Mitya punished as severely as possible
They cared only about the duel between the two lawyers
They stayed away and left the chamber to the men
quiz.e: Almost all the ladies were on Mitya’s side, seeing him as a conqueror of hearts, while the men were mostly against him.

quiz.q: What rumour about Katerina Ivanovna went round the town before the trial?
o: She had sold her inheritance to pay for the famous lawyer
She meant to follow him to penal servitude and marry him there
She had left for Moscow and broken off all further contact with him
She would give her evidence in secret, behind a screen
quiz.e: It was said she planned to ask the government for permission to accompany him into penal servitude and be married to him in the mines.

quiz.q: What was said about the procurator and Fetyukovich?
o: They had studied law together and were still close friends
They were related by marriage through the chairman
They had been old enemies since their St Petersburg days
They had never met or even heard of one another
quiz.e: Rumour had it that the vain Ippolit Kirillovich trembled before Fetyukovich, his old enemy from the start of their careers.

quiz.q: Which of these lay on the table of material evidence?
o: A hunting knife, a broken lamp and a leather purse
An axe, a torn handkerchief and a gold watch
A rifle, an account book and a bunch of keys
A brass pestle, a dressing-gown and an envelope
quiz.e: The table held the bloodied dressing-gown, the brass pestle, Mitya’s shirt and frock-coat, the pistol and the envelope with its pink ribbon.

quiz.q: How was the jury made up?
o: Eight landowners and four retired army officers
Four clerks, two merchants, six peasants and artisans
Six civil servants, four merchants and two priests
Twelve men of property, nearly all of them merchants
quiz.e: There were four minor civil servants, two merchants and six peasants and artisans, which made the narrator doubt they could understand the case.

quiz.q: How did Mitya look when he was brought in?
o: Unshaven, in the clothes he had worn at his arrest
Pale and trembling, leaning on his counsel’s arm
A dandy in a brand-new frock-coat and kid gloves
In chains between two guards, his head bowed low
quiz.e: He had ordered a new frock-coat from his old Moscow tailor and marched in with long strides, which made a disagreeable impression.

quiz.q: How did Mitya react when Smerdyakov’s death was announced?
o: He wept and crossed himself without a word
He fainted and had to be helped from the bench
He demanded loudly that the trial be stopped
He shouted, ‘To a dog the death of a dog!’
quiz.e: The outburst earned a warning from the chairman and, the narrator says, did him no good with the jury and the public.

quiz.q: How did Mitya answer when asked if he pleaded guilty?
o: Guilty of debauchery, but not of murder or robbery
Guilty of the robbery, but not of the killing itself
Not guilty, and he refused to say anything more
Guilty of everything, and he begged the court for mercy
quiz.e: He pleaded guilty to drunkenness, depravity and laziness but not to his father’s death: ‘Dmitry Karamazov is a scoundrel, but not a thief!’

chapters.title: Dangerous Witnesses
chapters.intro: Background on cross-examination, the new Russian bar, Poles in the Russian Empire, card games, folk remedies and a French scientist, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Seized on eagerly and held fast.
A soothing ointment or medicinal liquid.
A common wayside weed with broad leaves, long used in folk medicine (not the banana-like fruit).
Strong, unflavoured alcohol, stronger than ordinary vodka.
Latin, ‘in the year of the Lord’: years counted from the birth of Christ.
Someone who relies on another person for a living.
A sad clown in a loose white costume, from French pantomime.
An ancient Greek teller of fables, traditionally pictured as an ugly former slave.
Belonging to an eparchy, a diocese of the Orthodox Church.
A form of address for a bishop or archbishop.
Latin, ‘note well’: used to draw attention to a remark.
Someone more interested in getting ahead than in principles.
A Russian coachman who drove post-horses.
An abacus: a frame of beads on wires used for adding up.
Polish for ‘sir’ or ‘gentleman’; the plural is panowie.
Great technical skill, sometimes shown off for its own sake.
The final outcome or unravelling of a story.
Prosecution and defence each called their own witnesses, and the other side could then question them in turn.
Questioning a witness called by the other side, often to raise doubts about memory, honesty or motives. Open, spoken argument of this kind was new to Russian courts after 1864.
In card games such as shtoss, one player holds the bank and the others bet against him. Marked or substituted packs were the classic way to cheat.
Russian households treated aches with home-made rubs of herbs steeped in alcohol.

quiz.q: What struck everyone from the very first moments of the trial?
o: The judges openly favoured the defendant
The prosecution was far stronger than the defence
The witnesses kept contradicting one another on every point
The jury seemed bored and paid no attention
quiz.e: The facts seemed to marshal themselves against Mitya, and many felt the speeches would be a mere formality.

quiz.q: What did Grigory say about Fyodor Pavlovich as a father?
o: He had brought his children up wrong
He had been strict but always fair
He had loved Dmitry above the others
He had spent all he had on their schooling
quiz.e: For all his reverence for his old master, Grigory said he had been unfair to Mitya and ‘brought his children up wrong’.

quiz.q: What question did Fetyukovich put to every witness he could?
o: Whether they had heard Mitya threaten to kill
Whether Mitya had really been owed money
Whether they had actually seen the envelope
Whether they had seen Mitya in the garden
quiz.e: None had seen the envelope with the three thousand, though many had heard of it. The procurator, for his part, kept asking about the estate settlement.

quiz.q: What did Fetyukovich bring out about Grigory’s remedy for his back?
o: It contained opium, which is known to cause visions
He had rubbed it on after the attack, not before
His wife had made it much stronger than usual that night
He had drunk about a tumbler of the raw spirit
quiz.e: The rub of sage, plantain and pepper was in raw spirit, and Grigory admitted drinking a tumbler of it, raising doubts about the ‘open door’.

quiz.q: What did Grigory say when Fetyukovich pressed him with mocking questions?
o: That as a dependant he must endure being mocked
That the lawyer would answer for it before God
That he had never touched a drop in his life
That his old master would have stood up for him
quiz.e: Unable to say what year it was, he declared that if the powers that be wished to mock him he must endure it, and the chairman checked Fetyukovich.

quiz.q: How did Rakitin explain the tragedy in his evidence?
o: As the devil’s own work in a godless household
As the fruit of serfdom and Russia’s disorder
As a plain case of inherited madness
As a simple quarrel over one woman
quiz.e: He blamed the old ways of serfdom and a Russia lacking proper institutions, and drew some applause.

quiz.q: What did Fetyukovich get Rakitin to admit?
o: He had been paid by the prosecution to give evidence
He had once proposed marriage to Grushenka herself
He took twenty-five roubles to bring Alyosha to Grushenka
He had seen Mitya out in the town on the night of the murder
quiz.e: After praising his pious booklet on Father Zosima, Fetyukovich asked about the twenty-five roubles, which Rakitin had taken ‘in jest’ and not repaid.

quiz.q: What happened when Captain Snegiryov was called?
o: He accused Mitya and demanded compensation for the insult
He spoke calmly and moved the whole chamber
He sent a written statement and stayed away
He was drunk and would not speak of the insult
quiz.e: Ragged and drunk, he said little Ilyusha had forbidden him to speak, sobbed and fell to his knees, and was led out amid laughter.

quiz.q: How did Fetyukovich undermine Trifon Borisovich’s evidence?
o: By raising a hundred roubles Mitya had dropped
By proving he had never been in the room
By showing he owed money to the procurator
By proving he could neither read nor count
quiz.e: Two peasants had handed Trifon a hundred roubles Mitya dropped. He had denied it, and then claimed he had given it back.

quiz.q: What came out about the two Poles?
o: They had been paid by Fyodor Pavlovich to follow Mitya
They had cheated at cards with a substituted pack
They had lent Mitya the money he spent at Mokroye
They had never served the Crown or any army at all
quiz.e: Wróblewski had swapped in his own pack and Musiałowicz had played a false card, which Kalganov confirmed. They left in disgrace.

chapters.title: The Expert Medical Examination and One Pound of Nuts
chapters.intro: Background on expert witnesses, insanity and responsibility, the Herrnhuters, Germans in Russia and the Christian Trinity, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: An old word for a doctor, from the bloodsucking worms once used in treatment.
Generous to people in need; charitable.
An obsession; in older medicine, a form of madness.
In psychiatry, an intense emotional state that can overwhelm self-control.
German, ‘to stroll’ or ‘to go for a walk’.
Here the old Russian pound (funt), a little over 400 grams.
French legal term for witnesses called by the defence; those for the prosecution are à charge.
A minor weakness or oddity of character.
An old exclamation of sorrow or regret.
Under the 1864 rules, courts could call specialists such as doctors to give opinions on questions needing expert knowledge, and examine them in open court.
Someone who acted while insane, or in a state that took away self-control, could be held not responsible for a crime. A defendant’s state of mind was often a central question.
Psychiatry in the 1870s was still new, and many of its terms came from German and French medicine.
Also called the Moravian Brethren: a Protestant movement that grew up in the eighteenth century at Herrnhut in Saxony, stressing simple piety and good works. It had followers in Russia too.
Germans, many from the Baltic provinces, were prominent in Russian medicine, science and government. Russians often joked about their pedantry and their accented Russian.
Christian teaching holds that there is one God in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

quiz.q: Whose insistence brought about the medical examination?
o: Fetyukovich’s, who was relying heavily on it
Katerina Ivanovna’s, who sent for a Moscow doctor
The procurator’s, who wanted Mitya declared sane
The chairman’s, who had private doubts about the accused
quiz.e: Katerina Ivanovna summoned the celebrated doctor from Moscow. Fetyukovich himself placed little hope in the examination.

quiz.q: What had the Moscow doctor been saying around town before the trial?
o: That Herzenstube was the finest doctor in the province
That Herzenstube charged his poorer patients far too much
That Herzenstube had made a mess of treating his patients
That Herzenstube was much too old to give any evidence
quiz.e: Charging twenty-five roubles a visit, he criticised Herzenstube’s treatment and asked patients who had been ‘making a mess’ of them.

quiz.q: Where did Herzenstube think Mitya ought to have looked on entering?
o: To the right, at his defence counsel
Straight ahead, at the judges
Up at the gallery, at his brothers
To the left, at the ladies
quiz.e: As a great admirer of the fair sex, he said, Mitya should have looked left at the ladies; staring straight ahead showed his abnormal state.

quiz.q: What did the Moscow doctor find in Mitya?
o: Morbid affect, and a mania over the three thousand
Falling sickness inherited from his mother’s side
Nothing beyond the effects of ordinary drunkenness
Brain fever brought on by the strain of prison
quiz.e: He spoke of affect and mania, citing Mitya’s fury whenever the three thousand came up. He added that Mitya should have looked right, at his counsel.

quiz.q: What was the young doctor Varvinsky’s conclusion?
o: Mitya was insane, as both his colleagues had said
Mitya was normal, and rightly looked at the judges
Mitya was too drunk at the time to remember anything
Mitya was feigning madness to escape punishment
quiz.e: He found Mitya’s mind normal and his agitation natural. Looking straight ahead at the judges proved it. Everyone agreed with him.

quiz.q: What did Herzenstube say had happened to Mitya’s mind?
o: Drink had poisoned it during his years as an officer
His father’s cruelty had broken it when he was small
It had never been very strong, even as a boy
With no second mind to help, it went for a walk and got lost
quiz.e: Turning a proverb about two minds being better than one, he said Mitya’s mind went for a walk so far that it got lost.

quiz.q: What did Herzenstube once take to the neglected little boy?
o: A pair of boots
A pound of nuts
A picture Bible
A silver rouble
quiz.e: Feeling sorry for the barefoot child in the yard, he brought him a pound of nuts and taught him to say ‘Gott der Vater’.

quiz.q: What happened twenty-three years later?
o: Mitya came to his study to thank him for the nuts
Mitya passed him in the street without a word of greeting
Mitya wrote to him from his distant regiment
Mitya came to ask him for a loan of money
quiz.e: The young man recited the Trinity in German and thanked him, and both wept. In court Mitya cried out, ‘I weep even now, German.’

chapters.title: Fortune Smiles Upon Mitya
chapters.intro: Background on the rights of the accused and of witnesses, hearsay, debts of honour, sending money by post and provincial gossip, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A pair of glasses held up to the eyes on a handle.
Small binoculars for use in the theatre.
Russian for a young lady of the gentry; a miss.
Sacrificing oneself completely, regardless of the cost.
A horse ridden into battle; someone who rises eagerly to a fight.
A very steep cliff; figuratively, the edge of disaster.
To get things by begging or borrowing, without meaning to repay.
Generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival or someone weaker.
After each witness, the presiding judge could invite the accused to comment on the evidence. Outbursts beyond that could be checked or punished.
Close relatives of the accused could decline to give evidence against him.
Evidence of what a witness heard others say, rather than what the witness saw or knew. Courts treat it as weaker than direct evidence.
Among gentlemen, failing to repay someone who had trusted you was a deep disgrace, often thought worse than owing a moneylender.
Large sums could be sent through the post office in sealed, insured letters with the amount declared on the outside.
In small provincial towns, news and scandal travelled fast through visits and drawing-room talk, and reputations could be made or broken by rumour.

quiz.q: How did Alyosha describe Mitya’s character?
o: Cold and calculating, but deeply loyal
Violent and passionate, but noble and generous
Weak-willed, gentle, and all too easily led by others
Quiet and kind until the moment he drank
quiz.e: He admitted Mitya could be violent and carried away, but called him noble, proud and magnanimous, ready even for sacrifice.

quiz.q: What did Alyosha say when asked if Mitya had spoken of killing their father?
o: That Mitya had never once mentioned such a thing
That Mitya had sworn to do it on that very night
That he would rather not answer such a question
Not in so many words, though he feared he might
quiz.e: Mitya had spoken of his hatred and feared he might kill in a moment of loathing, but Alyosha declared it was not Mitya who killed him.

quiz.q: What did the procurator establish about Alyosha’s belief in Smerdyakov’s guilt?
o: It rested on a confession heard in private
It rested on money found among his things
It rested only on Mitya’s word and his face
It rested on Grigory’s evidence about the door
quiz.e: Alyosha admitted he had no proof beyond trusting his brother, which disappointed the public, who had expected more.

quiz.q: What did Alyosha suddenly remember under Fetyukovich’s questioning?
o: Mitya striking his chest high up, not at the heart
Mitya showing him a bundle of banknotes that night
Mitya swearing to repay Katerina the very next day
Mitya begging him to go and warn their father
quiz.e: At their last meeting Mitya kept striking the top of his chest, just below the neck, saying the means to restore half his honour was there.

quiz.q: What did Alyosha now think Mitya had been pointing at?
o: A letter from Grushenka he kept in his shirt
A cross that had belonged to their mother
The pistol he had hidden under his coat
The incense-bag with the fifteen hundred
quiz.e: It was the bag sewn with fifteen hundred roubles, half of Katerina’s money, which Mitya could have returned but would not. Mitya confirmed it.

quiz.q: How did Katerina Ivanovna first describe the three thousand she gave Mitya?
o: A loan he had sworn to repay within the week
Money he could post whenever he liked that month
A parting gift to help him leave the town for good
Her sister’s money, which he had taken without asking
quiz.e: She said she sensed he needed money and let him send it on when he chose. He had tormented himself over that debt in vain.

quiz.q: What did Katerina reveal that even Fetyukovich had not known?
o: That Ivan had asked her to marry him
That she had paid Mitya’s Moscow debts
The story of the five thousand roubles
That Grushenka had written to her twice
quiz.e: She told how the young officer gave her his last five thousand to save her father, and of her bow to the ground, to show Mitya’s nobility.

quiz.q: What did she leave out of that account?
o: That she had bowed down to the ground before him
That her father’s regimental funds were missing
That Mitya had given her all the money he owned
That Mitya had first suggested, through her sister, that she come
quiz.e: She magnanimously concealed that Mitya had proposed she be ‘sent to him for the money’, making it seem she had gone of her own accord.

quiz.q: What did Mitya cry out when Katerina finished her evidence?
o: ‘Katya, why have you ruined me?’
‘Katya, I never deserved you!’
‘Katya, forgive me, I beg you!’
‘Katya, you have saved my life!’
quiz.e: Though her evidence had helped him, he sobbed, ‘Katya, why have you ruined me?’ and then, ‘Now I am doomed!’

quiz.q: What did Grushenka reveal about Rakitin?
o: He had once asked her to marry him
He was her cousin and took money from her
He had stolen letters from her house
He had been spying on her for the police
quiz.e: Their mothers were sisters. He took up to thirty roubles a month from her and begged her to keep the kinship secret, being ashamed of her.

chapters.title: A Sudden Catastrophe
chapters.intro: Background on illnesses of mind and body, a Roman saying, the devil in folklore, the stages of a trial and order in court, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes mental illness and severe distress, with references to murder and suicide.
A long, sleeveless Russian peasant dress.
A Russian peasant woman’s wrap-around skirt, worn especially by brides.
An insulting word for an ugly, flat face.
A fit of uncontrollable emotion, such as screaming, sobbing or laughing.
German: pleasure taken in someone else’s misfortune.
A huge number: a thousand million million.
A popular Russian nickname for St Petersburg.
The official written record of court proceedings.
To shout or speak loudly and insistently.
A break in the sitting of a court.
Spiteful and venomous, like a snake.
A severe state of confusion, trembling and hallucinations that can strike heavy drinkers, especially when they suddenly stop drinking.
Seeing or hearing things that are not there. They can come with fever, exhaustion, drink or mental illness.
From the Roman poet Juvenal’s tenth Satire: the people, he complained, now cared only for free food and public shows.
Russian folk tales picture the devil as a small, mischievous creature with horns and a tail, as much a nuisance as a terror.
First came the judicial investigation, in which witnesses and evidence were examined. Then came the pleadings: the closing speeches of prosecution and defence.
The presiding judge could warn anyone who disrupted a hearing and have them removed from the chamber.

quiz.q: Why had Ivan not appeared when he was first called?
o: He had not yet arrived back from Moscow
He had suddenly been taken unwell
He had refused to testify against Mitya
He had gone to see Smerdyakov’s body
quiz.e: The bailiff reported a sudden indisposition or fit; Ivan would give evidence as soon as he recovered.

quiz.q: How did Ivan respond once the chairman had explained his rights?
o: He swore the oath all the same
He began to weep into his hands
He burst out laughing
He asked for time to think
quiz.e: His face slowly broke into a smile and he laughed, asking loudly, ‘Well, and what else, then?’

quiz.q: What did Ivan do after he started to walk out?
o: He came back, likening himself to a peasant girl who will jump only if she wants
He collapsed by the door and had to be carried out of the chamber by the court guards
He stopped to embrace Mitya and beg his brother’s forgiveness before the court
He turned back to ask the chairman whether he could give evidence the next day
quiz.e: He returned with an ironic smile and quoted a folk saying, ‘If I want, I’ll jump, if I don’t, I won’t’, before producing the money.

quiz.q: What did Ivan hand to the court?
o: A letter from Mitya setting out his plans in full
A confession signed by Smerdyakov
The key to his father’s bedroom door
A wad of money he said came from the envelope
quiz.e: He said Smerdyakov gave him the money the night before, that Smerdyakov was the murderer, and that he himself had put him up to it.

quiz.q: Whom did Ivan name as his only possible witness?
o: Alyosha, who had also visited Smerdyakov
The doctor from Moscow who had treated him
One with a tail, sitting under the evidence table
Smerdyakov’s landlady, who saw them together
quiz.e: He had no witnesses ‘except possibly one’: the petty devil, who must be sitting under the table of material evidence.

quiz.q: How did Ivan’s evidence end?
o: He knocked the bailiff down and was dragged out howling
He fainted and was carried out quietly by Alyosha
He fell silent and walked out without looking back
He was arrested on the spot by order of the chairman himself
quiz.e: When the bailiff took his arm he threw him to the floor; the guards seized him and he howled as he was led away.

quiz.q: What document did Katerina Ivanovna then hand to the court?
o: Ivan’s notes from his talks with Smerdyakov
Mitya’s drunken letter from the Capital City inn
A signed receipt for the three thousand roubles she lent
A letter from Grushenka to Fyodor Pavlovich
quiz.e: It was the letter Ivan had called ‘mathematical’ proof, in which Mitya wrote that he would kill his father ‘if only Ivan has gone away’.

quiz.q: Why, according to Katerina now, had Mitya wanted to marry her?
o: To please his late mother’s relatives
To escape his debts to his father
To spite Grushenka, who had refused him
Only because she had come into an inheritance
quiz.e: In her frenzy she said he despised her for coming to him for money and wanted to marry her only for her inheritance, to hold the upper hand.

quiz.q: What did Katerina say about Ivan?
o: He had nearly lost his mind trying to save his brother
He had confessed the whole murder to her a week earlier
He had begged her to burn the letter long ago
He had been planning to leave Russia for good
quiz.e: She said the letter had convinced him Mitya was guilty, and his efforts to save ‘the monster’ had driven him into a fever.

quiz.q: What did the Moscow doctor report about Ivan?
o: He was only pretending to be ill to protect his brother
He was drunk, and would be himself by the morning
He had a dangerous brain fever and saw Satan nightly
He had taken poison just before coming to court
quiz.e: Ivan had come to him two days earlier, refused treatment, and admitted seeing dead people in the street and receiving Satan each evening.

chapters.title: The Public Procurator’s Speech. Characterization
chapters.intro: Background on the prosecutor’s role, trials in the press, Gogol, Derzhavin, Pushkin, Shakespeare and Schiller, and Russian debates about Europe and the ‘native soil’, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A final performance, from the old belief that a swan sings once, beautifully, before it dies.
A sign or warning of something to come.
Becoming so used to something that it no longer affects you.
A person devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure.
Someone, originally paid, who applauds in a theatre to lead the audience.
French, ‘After me, the flood’: let disaster come once I am gone. The saying is linked with Louis XV’s court.
Someone who lives at other people’s expense.
Someone who lends money at very high interest.
French, ‘beautiful soul’: a person of lofty, often impractical idealism.
Belief in a direct, inward experience of God beyond reason.
A small, exclusive group with shared interests.

Nikolai Gogol’s comic novel (1842) follows Chichikov, a swindler buying up dead serfs still listed on the census, among grotesque landowners such as Sobakevich and Nozdryov. It ends with Russia pictured as a racing troika before which other nations stand aside.
Gavrila Derzhavin’s solemn poem of 1784 on the greatness of God and the smallness, yet dignity, of the human being. It was one of the best-known Russian poems of its century.
The opening of a poem by Pushkin (1834) recalling the Polish poet Adam Mickiewicz, who had lived in Russia in exile.
In Shakespeare’s play, the ‘To be, or not to be’ speech weighs ending one’s life against the fear of what may come after death.
The German poet and dramatist Friedrich Schiller was adored by educated Russians as the voice of lofty, romantic ideals.
A Russian phrase for the great unanswerable questions about God, death and the meaning of life.
Russian thinkers argued over whether Russia should follow Europe or return to its own people and Orthodox traditions. Dostoevsky himself championed a ‘return to the native soil’ in the 1860s.
Under the 1864 system the procurator, a state official, presented the case against the accused and ended it with a speech to the jury.
The new courts were open to reporters, and newspapers of the 1860s and 1870s printed long accounts of trials and the lawyers’ speeches.

quiz.q: What does the narrator reveal about the procurator’s future?
o: He would be promoted to a post in St Petersburg
He would leave the law to become a journalist
He would retire to his small estate within a year
He would die of consumption nine months later
quiz.e: The narrator calls the speech his masterpiece and swansong, since he died of acute consumption nine months afterwards.

quiz.q: What, says the procurator, ought to horrify Russians most?
o: That such crimes have almost ceased to horrify them
That the press now reports every crime in such detail
That crime is growing fastest in the countryside
That young people no longer read serious books
quiz.e: Their horror, he says, should be at their own habituation to such cases, not at any one person’s crime.

quiz.q: What does he say of the troika at the end of Gogol’s great work?
o: It was a true and faithful picture of Russia’s glorious future
With Gogol’s own characters as horses, it would get nowhere
It showed that Russia must follow the path of Europe
It was borrowed by Gogol from old peasant folk songs
quiz.e: Harnessed to the Sobakeviches, Nozdryovs and Chichikovs, it would never reach anything sensible, he says, suggesting Gogol ended so from naivety or fear of the censor.

quiz.q: What happened after the troika passage?
o: The chairman threatened to clear the chamber
Fetyukovich rose to object to the remarks
A few people clapped, his first ever applause
Mitya shouted an insult across the chamber
quiz.e: Two or three claps broke out. The chairman merely gave a stern look, and the procurator, never applauded before, took courage.

quiz.q: What remark of Smerdyakov’s about Ivan does the procurator report?
o: That he was the only son who loved their father
That he was the cleverest man in the province
That he had told him to leave the town for good
That he was the son most like Fyodor Pavlovich
quiz.e: Smerdyakov said Ivan had taught him that all things were lawful, and that Ivan was the son most like his father in character.

quiz.q: What does the procurator fear Alyosha’s ideals might turn into?
o: Revolutionary socialism and violence
Gloomy mysticism and narrow chauvinism
Cold atheism and selfish materialism
Western liberalism and indifference
quiz.e: He sees in Alyosha’s turn to ‘popular fundamentals’ a timid flight to the native soil that could become mysticism and chauvinism.

quiz.q: What does Mitya represent in the procurator’s scheme of the three brothers?
o: Natural Russia, with good and evil blended
Europeanism, clever but believing in nothing
Popular fundamentals, devout and humble
The old serf-owning gentry of the past
quiz.e: Ivan stands for ‘Europeanism’, Alyosha for ‘popular fundamentals’, and Mitya for natural Russia, broad enough to hold both abysses.

quiz.q: How does the procurator argue against the story of the incense-bag?
o: A bag round his neck would have been seen at the baths
Katerina had never really given him the whole sum
He had no needle or thread with which to sew it
The real Mitya would have spent it a hundred at a time
quiz.e: Such a weak, rash man, he says, would have taken out a hundred at a time, still calling himself ‘a scoundrel, but not a thief’, until all was gone.

chapters.title: A Historical Survey
chapters.intro: Background on premeditation, motive, circumstantial evidence and the burden of proof, Siberian gold, billiard rooms and pawning valuables, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: An old legal phrase for harm intended and planned in advance; ‘malice aforethought’.
Something that lessens the seriousness of a crime or fault.
In a way that cannot be denied.
Here, romantic and adventurous, like something out of a novel.
An obsession that dominates the mind (French idée fixe).
A woman who tempts a man, especially into a love affair.
A woman who causes someone great suffering.
Anxious fear of what may happen.
Carefully, so as to avoid risk.
A heavy, club-shaped tool for crushing things in a bowl called a mortar.
Russian law, like most, punished a killing planned in advance more severely than one done in a sudden fit of passion.
The reason someone commits a crime. Prosecutors try to show a motive, such as gain or jealousy, to make their case convincing.
Facts that point to a conclusion without proving it directly, such as threats, opportunity or the sudden possession of money. Many cases rest on chains of such facts.
In a criminal trial it is for the prosecution to prove guilt. Where real doubt remains, the accused should have the benefit of it.
Gold-mining in nineteenth-century Siberia drew fortune-seekers and adventurers as well as investors from the cities.
Billiard rooms in inns and taverns were favourite haunts of officers and young men about town.
Selling or pawning a watch was a common way for a gentleman short of cash to raise money quickly.

quiz.q: How does the procurator answer the medical experts?
o: Mitya is mad and must be confined for life
Mitya is epileptic, just like Smerdyakov
Mitya is sane, and that is the worst of it
Mitya was too drunk to be judged at all
quiz.e: He sides with the young doctor: Mitya is in his right mind, and his frenzy over the money has a nearer explanation than insanity.

quiz.q: What does he name as the real cause of Mitya’s fury over the money?
o: Jealousy of his father over Grushenka
Plain greed for his father’s fortune
Shame at his debt to Katerina Ivanovna
Fear of his creditors back in Moscow
quiz.e: The heart of the matter was jealousy: his father was using that very three thousand to lure Grushenka away from him.

quiz.q: How, by the procurator’s account, did Mitya’s passion for Grushenka begin?
o: He met her at his father’s dinner table
He saw her at the meeting in the monastery
He was introduced to her by young Rakitin
He went to beat her and stayed at her feet
quiz.e: Mitya set off to ‘beat her unmercifully’ but remained at her feet, while his father fell for her at the same time.

quiz.q: Whose sketch of Grushenka’s character does the procurator quote?
o: Katerina’s, from the evidence she gave that day
Rakitin’s, from the article he is writing
Samsonov’s, from a statement to the police
Alyosha’s, from the preliminary investigation
quiz.e: He cites Rakitin: early betrayal, poverty, a wealthy protector, and a calculating, vengeful character formed too young.

quiz.q: What, he says, removed his doubts that the crime was premeditated?
o: The letter Katerina Ivanovna presented that day
The pistol Mitya had bought the week before
Mitya’s questions to Smerdyakov about the signals
Grigory’s sighting of Mitya the previous day
quiz.e: Written two days before, the letter set out the ‘programme’: the money under the pillow, ‘if only Ivan has gone away’.

quiz.q: How does he answer the point that the letter was written while drunk?
o: A drunk man writes down only idle fantasies
Drink has no real effect on a man like Mitya
The handwriting proves he was in fact sober
Drunk, he wrote what he had planned when sober
quiz.e: Being drunk is no excuse but makes it weightier: had he not conceived it sober, he would not have written it drunk.

quiz.q: What advice from Mrs Khokhlakova does the speech recall?
o: To make peace with his father at once
To go to the gold-mines of Siberia
To ask Katerina Ivanovna for a loan
To enter the monastery with Alyosha
quiz.e: She urged him to give up his scandalous love and the inns, and to spend his energy in the Siberian gold-mines.

quiz.q: What does he argue about the brass pestle?
o: Mitya picked it up without knowing what it was
Mitya had carried it about with him all month
A month of brooding made him see it as a weapon
Mitya took it only to defend himself from Grigory
quiz.e: Having pictured the scene for a month, Mitya at once recognised the pestle as a weapon, so he did not seize it unconsciously.

chapters.title: A Treatise on Smerdyakov
chapters.intro: Background on epilepsy and nineteenth-century medicine, principals and accomplices, exhibits in court, government bonds and some techniques of argument, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes discussion of a murder and of a suicide, and descriptions of epileptic fits.
A long, formal piece of writing or speech that examines one subject in detail.
An old word meaning ‘from where’ or ‘from what source’.
A stay in a place, especially a temporary one.
To inform; to be apprised of something is to be told or made aware of it.
To make something clear by explaining it.
Responsibility for a fault or crime; blameworthiness.
A chance event; something that happens by accident.
To pretend, especially to pretend to be ill or to feel something.
Taking part together with someone else in a wrongdoing.
To secretly allow or go along with something wrong.
An old word meaning ‘necessarily’ or ‘by force of circumstances’.
Turning a bond, cheque or similar document into cash.
A male household servant, especially a footman; also used scornfully of someone servile.
Many people with epilepsy feel a distinctive sensation, now called an aura, shortly before a seizure. A deep, heavy sleep often follows one.
Psychiatry was a young discipline in the 1870s. Courts were beginning to ask doctors to judge whether a defendant or witness was of sound mind.
Criminal law distinguishes the person who actually commits a crime from those who help, encourage or knowingly allow it. Accomplices are usually punished less severely.
Physical objects connected with a crime, such as a weapon or a document, which are kept by the court and shown at the trial.
Government and bank bonds paying a fixed interest, often five per cent a year, were a common way for the well-off to hold savings. They could be cashed in at a bank.
Listing every possibility and ruling them out one by one until only one remains. It is persuasive, but only as strong as the list is complete.
Latin for ‘reduction to absurdity’: disproving an idea by showing that it leads to a ridiculous conclusion.
A speaker raises the arguments the other side might make and answers them before they can be made. Classical rhetoric called this procatalepsis.

quiz.q: Apart from the defendant, who does the prosecutor say has backed the charge against Smerdyakov?
o: Grigory, Marfa and Doctor Herzenstube
His two brothers and Miss Svetlova
Katerina Ivanovna and both his brothers
Rakitin, Kalganov and Miss Svetlova
quiz.e: Ivan, Alyosha and Grushenka, all of whom, the prosecutor says, have too great an interest in the defendant’s fate and offer no factual proof.

quiz.q: How does the prosecutor portray Smerdyakov’s character?
o: Cunning, ambitious and full of hidden malice
Pious, simple and devoted to his foster parents
Sly, greedy and resentful of his master’s sons
Weak-minded, cowardly and racked by remorse
quiz.e: He calls him a weak-minded epileptic, ‘cowardly as a hen’, honest at heart and tormented by guilt at having betrayed his master’s secrets.

quiz.q: How does the prosecutor explain Smerdyakov’s fit on the cellar stairs?
o: Anxiety after Ivan’s departure brought it on
He slipped while carrying a load to the cellar
He had been drinking since Ivan’s departure
Fyodor Pavlovich had struck him in a rage
quiz.e: With Ivan, his ‘guarantee’ of order, gone, the frightened man wondered whether a fit was coming, and the very worry set one off.

quiz.q: How many people does the prosecutor count in the house on the night of the crime?
o: Three people
Four people
Five people
Six people
quiz.e: Fyodor Pavlovich, Grigory, Marfa, the defendant and Smerdyakov. With three ruled out, he says, only the defendant and Smerdyakov remain.

quiz.q: Why, says the prosecutor, would a scheming Smerdyakov never have told the defendant about the envelope and signals?
o: Because the defendant could not read his writing
Because doing so would give him away in advance
Because Fyodor Pavlovich would surely find out
Because he wanted Ivan to have the money instead
quiz.e: Only he knew of the money and the signals; a man planning murder would keep silent and so remain the last person suspected.

quiz.q: What does the prosecutor find telling in Smerdyakov’s statements to the investigation?
o: He refused to say anything about the envelope
He accused Ivan of having put him up to it
He asked to be confronted with the defendant
He freely admitted revealing the signals
quiz.e: He volunteered that he had told the defendant about the envelope and the signals, which the prosecutor says only an innocent man would do.

quiz.q: What did Smerdyakov’s suicide note say?
o: That he ended his life of his own will, to blame no one
That he had acted alone and the defendant was innocent
That Ivan had taught him that everything is permitted
That the money should go back to Katerina Ivanovna
quiz.e: ‘I exterminate myself by my own will and inclination, in order to blame no one.’ Why, the prosecutor asks, did he not add that he was the murderer?

quiz.q: What fact about Ivan does the prosecutor reveal to cast doubt on the money brought to court?
o: He had borrowed three thousand from Katerina Ivanovna
He had won a large sum at cards the week before
He had sent two five-thousand bonds to be cashed
He had received an inheritance from his mother’s side
quiz.e: Ivan had sent two five per cent bonds, worth ten thousand in all, to the provincial capital to be cashed, so the money could have come from anywhere.

quiz.q: What, says the prosecutor, would Smerdyakov have done with the envelope?
o: Burned it in the kitchen stove before dawn
Carried it off whole without opening it
Left it torn open to implicate the defendant
Hidden it under the floor of the outbuilding
quiz.e: Knowing the money was inside, a practised thief would simply take the envelope; only a frenzied non-thief like Karamazov would tear it open and leave it.

quiz.q: Why, according to the prosecutor, did the defendant leap down to Grigory?
o: To help the old man out of pity and compassion
To recover the pestle he had dropped in the garden
To take back the keys Grigory had seized from him
To find out whether the sole witness was alive
quiz.e: He scorns the defendant’s claim of pity: he jumped down to see whether the only witness to his crime was still alive.

chapters.title: Psychology at Full Steam. The Galloping Troika. The Finale of the Public Procurator’s Speech
chapters.intro: Background on the troika, Gypsy choirs, Hamlet, processions to public execution, the nihilists, Kronstadt and Russia’s grain trade, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter discusses a murder and thoughts of suicide.
To speak or write at length on a subject.
A natural tendency to do something.
Burn the candle at both ends
To wear oneself out by doing too much, living hard by day and by night.
A vivid scene or picture, especially one described in detail.
A Russian coachman who drove hired or post horses.
The final part of a story, in which everything is resolved.
A blunt refusal or rejection; also a ready answer to an accusation.
French for a novelist, a writer of fiction.
Offence or annoyance; to take umbrage is to feel offended.
A wild dog of Africa and Asia that scavenges; used of someone who preys on others.
A pair of spectacles held up to the eyes by a handle.
Shakespeare’s prince, famous for brooding and hesitating. In his best-known speech, ‘To be or not to be’, he wonders whether to end his life and fears what may come after death.
