Nikolay Gogol’s Dead Souls (1842) ends with a famous passage likening Russia to a galloping troika before which other nations stand aside. It was often quoted in speeches and debates.
A carriage or sleigh drawn by three horses abreast, the middle one trotting and the outer two galloping. It was the classic vehicle of fast Russian travel.
Roma singers and dancers performed at Russian inns and restaurants and were hired for wild nights of revelry, especially by officers and rich merchants.
In many countries the condemned were once carried through the streets to the place of execution in an open cart, before crowds of onlookers.
A name, made famous by Turgenev’s novel Fathers and Sons (1862), for young Russian radicals who rejected traditional authority, religion and art. Later it was used for revolutionaries in general.

Kronstadt, an island fortress and naval base in the Gulf of Finland, guarded the approach to St Petersburg. Russia was a major grain exporter to Europe, though American grain competed strongly by the 1870s.

quiz.q: According to the prosecutor, how did the defendant react on learning of the ‘former’ lover’s return?
o: He suddenly gave way and submitted to the rival
He swore to hunt down the rival and kill him too
He went to the police and nearly confessed all
He resolved to flee abroad with the money at once
quiz.e: The jealous man ‘submitted’, recognising the rights of her heart, at the very moment, the prosecutor says, that his hands were steeped in blood.

quiz.q: What plan does the prosecutor say the defendant then formed?
o: To flee to Siberia under an assumed name
To challenge the Polish officer to a duel
To give a last feast, then shoot himself
To confess everything to Alyosha first
quiz.e: He would throw a sumptuous feast with gypsies, toast her new happiness and then blow his brains out at her feet.

quiz.q: What does the prosecutor say about Hamlet?
o: Hamlet sought revenge, while Karamazov sought money
Other lands have Hamlets, but ours has only Karamazovs
Hamlet hesitated for months; Karamazov acted in an hour
Hamlet was a prince, whereas Karamazov is a mere officer
quiz.e: Karamazov, he says, could not brood in Hamlet’s style about what lies beyond death. Spectators later single the line out for praise.

quiz.q: Why, in the prosecutor’s view, did the defendant not shoot himself at Mokroye?
o: He had left his pistols in pawn with Perkhotin
The Poles had taken his pistols away from him
He feared what lay beyond death, like Hamlet
His passionate thirst for her love held him back
quiz.e: Once she loved him, the hope of love quelled even his fear and his conscience, and he forgot where his pistol was.

quiz.q: To whom does the prosecutor compare the defendant during those hours at Mokroye?
o: A condemned man on the slow ride to execution
A gambler staking all on one last card
A sailor clinging to a mast in a storm
A soldier waiting for the order to charge
quiz.e: Like a man driven through long streets to the scaffold, he felt there was still plenty of time, so he could enjoy the moment and plan later.

quiz.q: Where does the prosecutor suppose the missing half of the money went?
o: Into Grushenka’s keeping for safety
Sent back to Katerina Ivanovna by post
Into a hiding place at the Mokroye inn
Under a board in his own lodgings
quiz.e: He imagines the defendant hid it in some chink or under a floorboard of the old inn shortly before his arrest; a search found nothing.

quiz.q: What fact did the investigators hold in reserve to spring on the defendant?
o: Fenya’s account of the pestle he took
Grigory’s evidence about the open door
Perkhotin’s report of his bloody hands
Smerdyakov’s statement on the signals
quiz.e: Told that Grigory had seen the door open, he burst out that Smerdyakov was the murderer, then produced the incense-bag story, the prosecutor says.

quiz.q: What detail does the prosecutor use to mock the incense-bag story?
o: No one had ever seen him wearing such a bag
The bag was too small for fifteen hundred
His landlady denied ever owning a bonnet
He could not say where the cloth came from
quiz.e: He first said a shirt, then perhaps a landlady’s bonnet, and no torn shirt was found. A man would remember such details, the prosecutor argues.

quiz.q: In the troika passage, why does the prosecutor say other nations stand aside?
o: Out of awe at Russia’s spiritual mission
Out of fear of Russia’s vast armies
Out of horror, and perhaps loathing
Out of simple indifference to Russia
quiz.e: Not out of deference, as the poet would like, he says, but horror; one day they may form a wall to halt Russia’s unbridled gallop.

quiz.q: How does Mitya react when the prosecutor reports Rakitin’s view of Grushenka?
o: He leaps up and is held back by the guards
He smiles and mutters ‘Those Bernards!’
He covers his face and weeps quietly
He calls Rakitin a liar across the room
quiz.e: His face shows a contemptuous, malicious smile and he says audibly, ‘Those Bernards!’

chapters.title: The Defence Counsel’s Speech. A Stick with Two Ends
chapters.intro: Background on famous Russian advocates, the classical parts of a speech, circumstantial evidence, a Pushkin poem and a Russian saying, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A quality in speech or writing that stirs pity or deep feeling.
A raised platform on which a speaker stands.
To do with the law or the administration of justice.
Latin, ‘note well’: a phrase drawing attention to something important.
To do with beauty and taste.
A jokey word meaning to throw into confusion or knock about.
Turning to something for help; to have recourse to something is to make use of it.
To work something out from evidence or reasoning.
To put forward as evidence or as an example.
After the reforms of the 1860s a handful of brilliant barristers, such as Vladimir Spasovich in St Petersburg and Fyodor Plevako in Moscow, became famous across Russia.
Classical rhetoric divided a courtroom speech into stages: an opening (exordium), a statement of the facts, the proofs, a refutation of the opponent and a stirring close (peroration).
Aristotle named three means of persuasion: the speaker’s character (ethos), the feelings of the audience (pathos) and the reasoning itself (logos).
A short poem of 1830 by Alexander Pushkin, Russia’s national poet, answering verses sent to him by an unknown admirer.
A Russian saying for something that can work in either direction, helping or harming whoever uses it.

quiz.q: How does Fetyukovich begin his speech?
o: With a long quotation from the Gospels
With a fierce attack on the prosecutor
Simply and directly, without eloquence
With a tearful plea for the defendant
quiz.e: He speaks plainly, as if among sympathetic friends, with no pathos at first; his voice is loud, likeable and sincere-sounding.

quiz.q: What habit of his at first displeases the ladies?
o: Bending his long back as if on a hinge
Polishing his spectacles as he speaks
Reading every sentence from his notes
Turning his back on the public gallery
quiz.e: He keeps surging towards his listeners, bending half his long back almost to a right angle.

quiz.q: When, he says, does he agree to defend a prisoner in a provincial town?
o: Only when the fee is paid well in advance
Only when the press is following the case
Only when the court appoints him to it
Only when sure of the man’s innocence
quiz.e: He comes only when convinced of a client’s innocence or when he senses it in advance, as he did from the first newspaper reports of this case.

quiz.q: What is the ‘formula’ he states at the outset?
o: No man should be tried in a town that knows him
The facts are crushing, yet none stands alone
A jury should never trust a frightened witness
Psychology cannot prove a single fact at all
quiz.e: The overwhelming weight of the facts is against the defendant, but not one of them withstands criticism if examined in isolation.

quiz.q: Why does the public titter when he mentions the prosecutor’s household?
o: The prosecutor was known to owe the defendant money
The prosecutor had once quarrelled with him at cards
The prosecutor received him only for his wife’s sake
The prosecutor’s wife had spoken up for the defence
quiz.e: Everyone knew the prosecutor admitted Mitya to his home against his will, because his wife found him interesting.

quiz.q: What does he say can be worse than deliberate malice in such cases?
o: An artistic urge to write a novel
A jury’s fear of public opinion
A judge’s haste to end the trial
A witness’s wish to seem clever
quiz.e: The danger is being seized by an artistic game, a need to create a ‘roman’, especially for a prosecutor so gifted at psychology.

quiz.q: How does he turn the argument about Grigory back on the prosecution?
o: Grigory was too drunk to recognise anyone that night
Grigory had in fact attacked the defendant first
Grigory’s wound shows the blow was an accident
A cold calculator would have finished Grigory off
quiz.e: A man so calculating would not spend five minutes wiping the victim’s head with a handkerchief; he would have struck again to kill the witness.

quiz.q: How does he explain the pestle being found fifteen paces away?
o: It slipped from his hand as he climbed the fence
He flung it away, sick at heart at felling a man
Smerdyakov must have moved it there afterwards
Grigory knocked it away as he fell to the ground
quiz.e: It was thrown with force, he argues, in vexation at having killed an old servant, which shows a conscience still clear of his father’s blood.

chapters.title: There was No Money. There was No Robbery
chapters.intro: Background on Russian paper money and coins, the legal need to prove a crime took place, money-changers, Gothic novels and some well-known sayings, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Not influenced by earlier opinions; fair-minded.
An official written record, such as one made during a police investigation.
French for a lord or great landowner.
Latin: a fact or deed; something done.
The face value of a banknote or coin.
A statement accepted as obviously true without proof.
The person someone is engaged to marry.
To waste money or time recklessly.
A spell of wild, unrestrained spending or drinking.
Careless; acting without considering the consequences.
From 1843 Russian paper money took the form of state credit notes, issued in rouble values.
Notes were known by their colours: a five-rouble note was blue, a ten-rouble note red, and the multicoloured hundred-rouble note was called a ‘rainbow’.
Russia also minted gold coins, such as the half-imperial, worth five roubles.
Latin, ‘the body of the crime’: the principle that before anyone can be convicted, it must first be shown that a crime actually took place. For a theft, that means proving something really was taken.
Shops where coins, notes and securities were exchanged, bought and sold. They kept large amounts of cash and were a tempting target for robbers.
A Gothic novel of 1794 by the English writer Ann Radcliffe, set largely in a gloomy castle in the Apennines full of seeming horrors and secrets. It was widely read in Russia in translation.
A kind of fiction popular in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, full of ruined castles, dungeons, hidden passages and mysterious terrors.
From Hamlet’s ‘To be or not to be’ speech: there lies the difficulty.
An old phrase, found in the Bible, for something cherished and carefully protected.
‘The slice looks bigger in another’s hand’
A Russian proverb: other people’s possessions always seem larger than they really are.

quiz.q: What point in the defence speech astonished everyone?
o: Its claim that Grushenka had taken the money
Its denial that the three thousand ever existed
Its admission that the defendant was in the house
Its attack on the honesty of the investigators
quiz.e: Fetyukovich denies that the fateful three thousand existed at all, and therefore that any robbery took place.

quiz.q: Who, he says, was the only person who actually saw the money?
o: Grigory’s wife, Marfa
The defendant’s brother Ivan
Grushenka, on a visit to the house
The lackey Smerdyakov
quiz.e: Smerdyakov alone saw it put into the envelope, and he told Fetyukovich he had last seen it two days before the crime.

quiz.q: What detail about the bed does he stress?
o: The bedding was neither rumpled nor bloodstained
The pillow had been slashed open with a knife
The mattress had been dragged onto the floor
The bed had not been made up that evening
quiz.e: Pulling money from under the mattress with bloody hands would have rumpled and smeared the fresh linen, yet the protocol recorded neither.

quiz.q: What alternative does he suggest for the torn envelope?
o: Smerdyakov opened it days before and then resealed it
The police tore it open by mistake in the search
The old man opened it himself to dazzle Grushenka
Grigory found it in the garden and brought it in
quiz.e: Fyodor Pavlovich might have taken out the ‘rainbow’ notes to show her a wad, throwing the wrapper down like a seigneur.

quiz.q: Why does he describe the St Petersburg murder at a money-changer’s?
o: To show that young hawkers are often violent
Because there the stolen money was identified
Because its killer was acquitted by a jury
To show that confessions are often forced
quiz.e: There the exact notes and coins were found on the killer, who confessed: ‘that is what I call evidence’.

quiz.q: To what does he compare the idea that money was hidden at Mokroye?
o: A treasure hunt in a children’s story
A miracle from the life of a saint
A tale told by a drunken coachman
The dungeons of Udolpho’s castle
quiz.e: He calls it a fantastic, ‘roman-esque’ assumption, as likely as the money lying in the dungeons of the castle of Udolpho.

quiz.q: How does he treat Katerina Ivanovna’s second statement?
o: As the exaggeration of a vengeful woman
As the plain truth, long kept hidden
As a forgery prepared by the prosecution
As the words of a woman out of her mind
quiz.e: Since her first statement differed, he argues, the second, full of animosity, may exaggerate the shame with which she offered the money.

quiz.q: Why, he argues, would the defendant have guarded the fifteen hundred?
o: To pay his debts to the innkeeper at Mokroye
To buy back the pistols he had pawned in town
To take Grushenka away or repay Katerina
To bribe Smerdyakov to keep his secrets
quiz.e: He needed means to carry Grushenka off, or he could hand the money back to Katerina Ivanovna and be ‘a scoundrel, but not a thief’.

chapters.title: Nor was There Even Any Murder
chapters.intro: Background on the benefit of the doubt, premeditation in law, binding and loosing in the Gospels, repentance and despair, Russian admiration for France and Russian taverns, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes discussion of a murder and of a suicide.
Without plan or order; at random.
Weapons; the state of being armed.
A lazy person who avoids work.
Evasive talk that avoids the truth.
A state of excitement or unrest.
Placing things side by side so they can be compared.
To clear of blame, or to show to be right.
A faint smell or hint of something.
A detachable shirt-front worn to look like a full shirt.
To bribe or persuade someone to do wrong, especially to give false evidence; more loosely, to sway or corrupt.
The smallest amount, from the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet.
An old principle, put in Latin as in dubio pro reo (‘when in doubt, for the accused’): if guilt is not proven, the doubt should favour the defendant.
Most legal systems treat a killing planned in advance as more serious than one committed in a sudden fit of passion, and punish it more heavily.

In Matthew’s Gospel Christ tells his apostles that whatever they bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever they loose will be loosed. The phrase came to stand for great authority to condemn or set free.
Christian teaching distinguishes repentance, which hopes for forgiveness, from despair, which gives up all hope of it and was counted a grave sin.
From the eighteenth century the Russian upper classes admired France, spoke French among themselves and copied French fashions. To many, France stood for refinement and civilisation.
A Russian tavern or eating-house serving tea, vodka and simple meals. It was a centre of town gossip, drinking and quarrels.

quiz.q: What would have happened, the defence says, had Grushenka been at home?
o: He would have gone after her protector instead
He would have gone on to his father’s anyway
He would have taken her straight to Mokroye
He would have stayed and not run anywhere
quiz.e: He ran solely to find her; had she been at home he would have stayed with her and never carried out his drunken letter.

quiz.q: What ‘commonplace thought’ does he have about the pestle?
o: It was too light to have killed anyone
Put away in a cupboard, it would not have been taken
It belonged to Smerdyakov and not to the two maids
It bore no blood when it was finally found
quiz.e: Had it been put away rather than left on a shelf, the defendant might have run off empty-handed and perhaps never killed anyone.

quiz.q: To what does the defence reduce the whole case for the prosecution?
o: If he was in the garden, that means he did it
If he had money, that means he stole it
If he wrote it, that means he meant it
If he ran away, that means he was guilty
quiz.e: The case rests on ‘if he was’ followed by ‘that means’; but what if there is no ‘that means’, even though he was there?

quiz.q: What would the defendant have done at Mokroye, the defence argues, had he killed his father?
o: He would have confessed to Grushenka at once
He would have fled before the police arrived
He would surely have shot himself there
He would have hidden the money more carefully
quiz.e: Once she declared her love, he would have felt a double, triple need to kill himself; he would not have forgotten where his pistols were.

quiz.q: What impression did Smerdyakov make on Fetyukovich?
o: A timid simpleton, easily led by others
A devout and honest servant, sincerely grieving
A sick man too weak to harm anyone
A malicious, ambitious and envious man
quiz.e: He found no timidity, but suspicion behind a show of naivety, inordinate ambition, vengefulness and envy, and a dream of going to France.

quiz.q: What struck Fetyukovich about the prosecutor’s point on the envelope?
o: It contradicted the medical evidence on the fit
Smerdyakov had put the same idea to him
It had first appeared in a St Petersburg paper
Ivan had made the same point in his testimony
quiz.e: Two days earlier Smerdyakov had urged that very view on him with false naivety; perhaps he did the same with the investigators.

quiz.q: How does he explain Marfa hearing groaning all night?
o: With a story of a lady and a dog that yelped
By claiming she was deaf in one of her ears
By saying Grigory had groaned, not the lackey
By pointing out that she was old and unwell
quiz.e: A lady complained that a dog kept her up all night, when it had yelped only two or three times; a sleeper remembers only the wakings.

quiz.q: Why, he suggests, did Smerdyakov’s note not confess?
o: He was too ill to write more than a line
He feared his family would be disgraced
He may have felt despair, not remorse
He meant to leave a full letter elsewhere
quiz.e: Conscience means remorse, but a suicide may feel only despair, even redoubled hatred for those he had envied all his life.

chapters.title: An Adulterer of Thought
chapters.intro: Background on Bible passages about fathers, children and judgement, Herzen’s journal The Bell, Ostrovsky’s plays, a saying from Horace, Peter the Great’s Military Code and orders of honour, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes a brief, non-graphic reference to infanticide and discussion of child neglect and murder.
A married person who is unfaithful to their husband or wife.
The person who fathers a child; a biological parent.
Kind and generous; working for the good of others.
Trickery, especially petty legal or financial trickery.
A person of the same age; a contemporary.
A pot for melting metals; figuratively, a severe test.
Spiritual and beyond the reach of reason.
A raised platform for speakers; also a champion of the people.
Deep sorrow for having done wrong.
Renewal or rebirth, especially of the spirit.
In psychology and law, a sudden overpowering emotion that takes away self-control.
The killing of one’s own father or mother, or a person who does it.
To hand out or allot, especially punishment.
In John’s Gospel Christ calls himself the good shepherd, who lays down his life for his sheep.
Paul’s letter to the Colossians tells fathers not to provoke their children to anger; the verse just before tells children to obey their parents.
In the Sermon on the Mount, Christ warns that the measure people use in judging others will be used to judge them.
In Matthew’s Gospel Christ says that whoever fed the hungry, clothed the naked and visited prisoners did it for him.

Alexander Herzen, a Russian radical living in exile, published the journal The Bell (Kolokol) in London from 1857, and copies were smuggled into Russia. Its motto, Vivos voco (‘I call the living’), came from the epigraph to Schiller’s ‘Song of the Bell’.
A playwright (1823–86) famous for comedies and dramas about Moscow’s merchant class, mocking its ignorance and superstition.
An old saying going back to the Roman poet Horace: you may drive nature out with a pitchfork, but it will always come back.
Peter I’s Military Statute of 1716 stated the principle that it is better to free ten guilty men than to condemn one innocent. The English jurist Blackstone later put a similar rule.
Senior officials wore the star-shaped badges of the orders they had been awarded on their coats, as a sign of rank and honour.

quiz.q: What single fact, says Fetyukovich, truly undoes his client?
o: The money found on him at Mokroye
The letter he wrote to Katerina
The corpse of his aged father
The testimony of old Grigory
quiz.e: This is not a simple murder but a parricide, which makes even weak and unproven facts seem stronger.

quiz.q: Which memory of Herzenstube’s does he recall?
o: The boy running barefoot, trousers held by one button
The boy sitting alone weeping at his mother’s grave
The boy being whipped by his father in the yard
The boy stealing nuts from the doctor’s garden
quiz.e: If he never forgot a pound of nuts, Fetyukovich argues, neither could he forget running about the backyard without boots.

quiz.q: Which of the father’s actions does he describe?
o: Selling the family estate behind his son’s back
Denouncing his son to the governor as a rebel
Refusing to pay for his son’s army commission
Buying up his son’s debts to have him jailed
quiz.e: Besides sneers and slander, the old man used his son’s money to lure away his mistress and bought up his IOUs to put him in prison.

quiz.q: What words of the apostle does he address to all fathers?
o: ‘Honour thy father and thy mother’
‘Fathers, provoke not your children to anger’
‘Spare the rod and spoil the child’
‘Bear ye one another’s burdens’
quiz.e: He quotes Paul’s words to the Colossians and says he speaks not for his client’s sake but to all fathers.

quiz.q: What is the point of his story about the serving-maid in Finland?
o: That poverty drives people to crime
That the police watch servants too closely
That one who bears a child is not yet a parent
That juries are too easily moved by pity
quiz.e: She killed her newborns; can she be called a mother? Likewise, ‘a begetter is not yet a father’.

quiz.q: What test does he propose for a son and an unworthy father?
o: The son may ask the father to prove he must be loved
The son must go on loving him, just as Scripture commands
The son may take the case to a court of honour
The son should leave home on coming of age
quiz.e: If the father cannot prove it, the family is at an end and the son is free to regard him as a stranger, even a foe.

quiz.q: Who joins in the applause that the chairman cannot stop?
o: Only the young students crowded in the back rows
Only the ladies in the upper gallery
The jurymen, to the chairman’s horror
Even the old dignitaries with their stars
quiz.e: Fathers and mothers clap, ladies shriek and even officials with stars on their frock-coats wave handkerchiefs, so the chairman dares not clear the room.

quiz.q: How does he urge the jury to punish his client ‘terribly’?
o: By sending him to the mines for life
By crushing him with their mercy
By handing him over to the Church
By making him beg his brothers’ pardon
quiz.e: Mercy, he says, would make the wild but noble heart repent and be reborn, crying that men are better than he.

chapters.title: The Muzhiks Stand Up for Themselves
chapters.intro: Background on the last stages of a Russian jury trial, the zemstvo, merchants’ honours, the Sphinx, the Byronic hero, the Russian narrative poem and some sayings, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: French: someone carried away by their own enthusiasm.
A fixed regular payment, such as a scholarship or allowance.
An unpleasant hint or suggestion made indirectly.
Immoral and unrestrained, especially in sexual matters.
To grumble or complain quietly; in religious language, to complain against God.
A counter or room where food and drinks are served.
To win someone’s favour by flattery.
The juror chosen to speak for the jury.
After the main speeches, the prosecution and the defence could each answer the other briefly.
Russian procedure gave the accused the right to speak last, before the jury withdrew.
The judge put a list of written questions to the jury, which retired to decide and answered each one ‘yes’ or ‘no’.
Elected local councils created in 1864 to run schools, roads and health care in the countryside. Landowners, townspeople and peasants each chose members.
The government rewarded merchants for charity or public service with medals and honorary titles, which they wore proudly on public occasions.
In Greek legend the Sphinx, part woman and part lion, asked travellers a riddle and killed those who could not answer it, until Oedipus solved it.
A type named after the heroes of Lord Byron’s poems: a proud, moody, rebellious outsider with a dark past.
The Russian word for a long narrative poem. Gogol gave the name to his prose novel Dead Souls.
An old saying meaning that anger is a sign of having lost the argument. Turgenev’s novel Rudin (1856) quotes it.
The biblical king of Israel, famed for his wisdom.

quiz.q: How do listeners respond as Fetyukovich ends?
o: With an uneasy silence and scattered hisses
With weeping and a storm of enthusiasm
With laughter at his overblown ending
With angry shouts from the jury benches
quiz.e: Women and many men weep, even two dignitaries; the chairman holds back from ringing the bell.

quiz.q: What does Ippolit Kirillovich say the defence has made of Smerdyakov?
o: A pious martyr wrongly accused by all
A cunning foreign spy in Russian service
A simple fool led astray by the brothers
A Byronic hero avenging his birth
quiz.e: He mocks the defence’s ‘roman upon roman’: the feeble-witted idiot turned into a Byronic hero taking revenge on society for his illegitimacy.

quiz.q: What does the prosecutor object to in the defence’s words about Christ?
o: He called Christ only ‘the crucified lover of mankind’
He quoted Christ in Latin rather than in Slavonic
He claimed Christ had forbidden all punishment
He compared himself to Christ before the court
quiz.e: He accuses the defence of creating a false likeness of Christ and twisting ‘with the same measure’, instead of calling him God.

quiz.q: How does Fetyukovich answer the prosecutor’s reply?
o: He demands that the chairman silence him
He withdraws his remarks about fathers
He quips, ‘Jupiter, thou art angry…’
He calls on Alyosha to vouch for his faith
quiz.e: He answers briefly and with dignity, with the saying about Jupiter, to laughter, and complains of slanderous insinuations.

quiz.q: What does Mitya say in his final words to the jury?
o: That Ivan is guilty and should stand trial
That he is innocent of his father’s blood
That he wishes to change his whole plea
That he will not accept the court’s judgment
quiz.e: He thanks both speakers, insists for the last time that he did not kill his father, and begs to be spared.

quiz.q: What does Fetyukovich tell a group during the adjournment?
o: That the chairman had plainly favoured the prosecution
That he expects a recommendation of mercy
That he will appeal whatever the outcome
That invisible threads bind him to the jury
quiz.e: He says he felt the threads binding counsel to jury during his speech: ‘The case is ours.’

quiz.q: What is the jury’s answer to the questions put to it?
o: Guilty on every point, with no plea for mercy
Guilty of murder, but deserving of the court’s mercy
Not guilty of murder, guilty of assault
Not guilty on any of the questions put
quiz.e: After exactly an hour the foreman says ‘Yes, guilty!’, and so on every point, without the expected recommendation of clemency.

quiz.q: What does Mitya cry out after the verdict?
o: He tells Grushenka to wait for him in Siberia
He tells Ivan he must now tell the whole truth
He forgives Katya and pleads for ‘the other one’
He accuses the jury of killing an innocent man
quiz.e: He swears he is not guilty, forgives Katya and begs his brothers and friends to spare ‘the other one’; Grushenka wails from the gallery.

chapters.title: Schemes for Rescuing Mitya
chapters.intro: Background on Siberian penal servitude, nineteenth-century ideas about fever, social propriety and the Christian idea of bearing one’s cross, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A doctor’s forecast of how an illness is likely to develop.
Unhealthy in mood or mind; dwelling on dark or painful things.
Fullness; the condition of being complete.
To interpret or understand something in a particular way.
Spreading false statements that damage someone’s reputation.
A feeling that something is about to happen.
Generously and nobly, especially towards a rival or someone in the wrong.
In a way that cannot be calmed, softened or turned aside.

In Russian, katorga: hard labour in Siberia’s mines, factories or fortresses, one of the harshest punishments the courts could give. Convicts were stripped of the rights of their social rank, including noble status.
Even when their term was over, most convicts could not go home but had to live on in Siberia as settlers.
The author himself served four years of hard labour at Omsk in the early 1850s, and later described convict life in Notes from the House of the Dead.
A common nineteenth-century diagnosis for a sudden illness with high fever and delirium, often thought to be brought on by shock or strain. Novelists of the time used it often.
An unmarried young woman of good family usually lived with older female relatives or a companion. Anything that broke these conventions was sure to set society talking.
In the Gospels Jesus tells his followers to take up their cross and follow him. To ‘bear one’s cross’ came to mean accepting an unavoidable burden of suffering.
A strand of Orthodox piety, which Dostoevsky shared, held that suffering accepted humbly could cleanse and renew a person.
Christian teaching ranks pride as the chief of the deadly sins and humility as the virtue that opposes it.

quiz.q: Where is Ivan Fyodorovich during Alyosha’s visit to Katya?
o: In the prison hospital, under a sentry’s guard
On the road to Moscow with the visiting doctor
In the next room, feverish and unconscious
At his father’s house, tended by Marfa
quiz.e: Katya had him carried to her own house straight after the scene at the trial, ignoring what society would say, and means to nurse him day and night.

quiz.q: What first set off Katya’s quarrel with Ivan over the escape plan?
o: Her anger that Grushenka would flee abroad with Mitya
His refusal to put any of his own money into the plan
Her insistence that Mitya ought to serve his sentence
His demand that she give evidence against his brother
quiz.e: Ivan read her fury at ‘that creature’ going abroad with Mitya as jealousy, and so as proof that she still loved Dmitry.

quiz.q: What did Ivan leave with Katya on the eve of the trial?
o: A letter confessing his own guilt in the father’s murder
Smerdyakov’s notes, to be read out in court
A will leaving her his share of the inheritance
The sealed escape plan and about ten thousand roubles
quiz.e: She was to open the envelope if he died or fell gravely ill, and then rescue Mitya on her own.

quiz.q: What does Katya confess about her outburst when Ivan returned with Alyosha?
o: She had secretly hoped it would drive Ivan back to Moscow
She had lied that Ivan made her believe Mitya was guilty
She had only pretended to faint, to stop the quarrel ending
She had been told by Grushenka exactly what to say to them
quiz.e: Ivan never tried to persuade her of Mitya’s guilt; it was she who tried to persuade him. She blames herself for his ‘accursed scene’ at the trial.

quiz.q: Why is Katya sure that Mitya will agree to escape?
o: He has always feared the cold of Siberia
He is anxious to clear his name abroad
He cannot leave Grushenka behind him
He wishes to be near Ivan in his illness
quiz.e: Grushenka will not be allowed to join him in penal servitude, so, Katya says, what can he do but escape?

quiz.q: What does Katya say, with venom, that Mitya most fears about escaping?
o: Being caught and flogged by the guards
Alyosha’s moral disapproval of it
Losing his share of his father’s money
Leaving Russia and its God for ever
quiz.e: She says Alyosha must ‘magnanimously permit’ it, since his sanction is so indispensable, and asks if he thinks escape un-Christian.

quiz.q: What request does Alyosha bring from Mitya?
o: That Katya write to the court asking for mercy
That Katya give the escape money to Grushenka
That Katya forgive him in front of witnesses
That Katya come and stand on his threshold
quiz.e: Mitya does not ask forgiveness, saying he cannot be forgiven; he wants her only to appear at his door, and fears lifelong unhappiness if she refuses.

quiz.q: What makes Katya turn pale again as Alyosha is leaving?
o: The thought that she might meet someone there
The fear that Ivan might wake while she is out
The news that the verdict may yet be appealed
The memory of what she had said in the court
quiz.e: ‘And if I meet someone?’ she asks. Alyosha says that is why she must come now: there will be no one there.

chapters.title: For a Moment the Lie Becomes Truth
chapters.intro: Background on Russian forms of address, the treatment of convicts, bribery, fever remedies, the Jesuits and nineteenth-century adventure fiction, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Deep in serious, often sad thought.
Secretly, so as not to be noticed.
A grating of metal bars over a window or opening.
A soldier posted to keep guard.
Slang for a cheat or swindler.
A person’s physical make-up and general health.
Even with someone, with nothing more owed on either side.
An old word meaning truly or certainly.
An old Russian measure of length, about 71 centimetres (28 inches).
Lacking reverence for God or for what is sacred.
A state of wild, uncontrolled excitement.
Acting quickly and on impulse, without thinking.

Like French tu and vous, Russian has a familiar ‘you’ (ty) for family, close friends, children and social inferiors, and a polite one (vy). Translators sometimes render ty as ‘thou’. Being called ty by an official was a mark of lost status.
A reform of 1863 abolished most flogging in Russia, but convicts and exiles could still be beaten.
Poorly paid Russian officials were notorious for taking bribes, a theme Gogol satirised in his comedy The Government Inspector (1836).
A cloth soaked in water and vinegar and laid on the forehead was a common home remedy for fever and headache.

A Catholic religious order founded in 1540 by Ignatius of Loyola. Their opponents accused them of cunning moral reasoning that could excuse almost anything, and ‘Jesuit’ became a byword for this in Russian as in other languages.
Applying general moral rules to particular cases. The word is often used disapprovingly, for clever reasoning that explains a wrong away.
The Christian idea that a person can be inwardly renewed, becoming in effect a new man, through repentance and grace.
An American novelist whose frontier adventures, including The Last of the Mohicans (1826), were very popular in Russian translation.

quiz.q: Why is Mitya kept in a small room of his own rather than with the other prisoners?
o: He is suspected of carrying an infection
Dr Varvinsky kindly bent the rules for him
The chief of police fears he will try to flee
Katerina Ivanovna paid the warders to allow it
quiz.e: At the request of Alyosha and others, the young doctor put him in the closet where Smerdyakov once lay, so he could get used to prison company gradually.

quiz.q: What does Mitya hear that Trifon Borisych has been doing?
o: Selling his own account of that night to the newspapers
Telling everyone that he never believed Mitya was guilty
Demanding payment of the debts Mitya ran up at his inn
Tearing up his inn to find money said to be hidden there
quiz.e: He is ripping up floorboards in search of the fifteen hundred roubles the prosecutor said Mitya hid there. ‘Serves the twister right!’

quiz.q: What is Alyosha’s view of Mitya escaping?
o: An innocent man not ready for it need not bear such a cross
Running away would undo all the good of his recent change
He should escape only if Ivan approves of it when he recovers
He should wait to see whether the sentence is reduced on appeal
quiz.e: Had Mitya killed their father, Alyosha would want him to accept his cross; but he is innocent. Alyosha will never condemn him, and admits he would pay bribes himself.

quiz.q: What does Mitya laughingly say he has caught Alyosha being?
o: A lawyer
A hypocrite
A Jesuit
A Pharisee
quiz.e: Mitya will flee but condemn himself and pray for forgiveness for ever: ‘that is how the Jesuits talk, is it not?’ Alyosha quietly agrees.

quiz.q: What does Mitya plan to do once he and Grushenka reach America?
o: Open a Russian inn in one of the great cities
Make a fortune and send it to Ivan and Katya
Settle among the Russians already living there
Work the land, learn English, then come back
quiz.e: After about three years of work and grammar they will return to Russia as ‘American citizens’, disguised, and live in some remote corner.

quiz.q: What does Katya say about the evidence she gave in court?
o: She made herself believe it then, and stopped as soon as she finished
She had believed it for months, until Ivan finally showed her the truth
She had been pressed into it by the prosecutor and his assistant
She still believes it, but forgives him for everything that he did
quiz.e: She never believed he killed; she hated him and forced herself to believe it for that moment, then stopped believing it the moment she finished.

quiz.q: How does Grushenka answer Katya’s ‘Forgive me’?
o: She embraces her and says all is forgotten
She turns her back and says nothing at all
She says they are both wicked; let her save him
She tells her to leave and never come back
quiz.e: ‘How can it be for us to forgive, you and I?’ she says venomously, but promises to pray for Katya all her life if she rescues Mitya.

quiz.q: What does Katya tell Alyosha when he catches up with her outside?
o: She will never come back to visit Mitya again
She cannot go to the funeral, but sent flowers
She means to return to Moscow with Ivan
She will give the escape money to Grushenka
quiz.e: She has sent flowers for the little coffin and will never abandon the family; she sends Alyosha off as the bells ring for late liturgy.

chapters.title: Ilyushechka’s Funeral. The Speech by the Stone
chapters.intro: Background on Orthodox funeral rites and hymns, Russian memorial customs and the Christian belief in resurrection, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter describes a child’s funeral and the deep grief of his family.
A bag with a shoulder strap, often used for carrying school books.
A manservant or footman; also, scornfully, someone who serves others slavishly.
A strip of gathered or pleated fabric used as decorative trimming.
A cloth spread over a coffin.
In an Orthodox funeral, a paper band printed with a prayer and holy images, laid across the forehead of the dead.
Not belonging to a widely held religion; here, un-Christian or pagan.
In a well-behaved, dignified way suited to the occasion.
Here, the metal cover of an icon, often silver or gilt, that leaves the painted faces and hands visible.
A letter, especially one of the apostles’ letters in the New Testament, read aloud during services.
Lying stretched out face down on the ground.
A farewell; at a funeral, the last leave-taking of the dead.
A dreamy state of being lost in thought.
A machine that moves like a person; someone acting mechanically, without thought.
A striking scene or picture, often one recalled as if frozen in place.
Lack of seriousness; light-heartedness about things that matter.
The dead lie in an open coffin in church while mourners hold lighted candles. The service ends with the last farewell, when people come forward to kiss the dead before the coffin is closed.
The main Orthodox service, celebrated on Sundays and feast days, at which communion is given. A funeral could follow it the same morning.
A solemn chant sung during the Liturgy as the bread and wine are carried to the altar. Its words liken the worshippers to the angels called cherubim.
A short chant, Vechnaya pamyat, sung at the end of Orthodox funerals and memorial services, asking that God remember the dead for ever.
The Nicene Creed, recited at every Liturgy, ends with the hope of the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.
Russian Orthodox custom was to keep the body at home, with prayers and readings beside it, and to bury it on the third day after death.
Christians were normally buried in consecrated ground near a church, with a cross over the grave, so that prayers for them would continue.
After a burial, mourners shared a memorial meal (pominki), at which pancakes called blini and kutya, boiled grain with honey, were traditional.
The Orthodox Church remembers the dead with special prayers on the third, ninth and fortieth days after death, and on each anniversary.

quiz.q: Why have Ilyusha’s schoolfellows all come to the house?
o: He made them promise to be with his father, who would cry
Their teacher ordered the whole class to attend the funeral
Kolya asked them to come and help carry the heavy coffin
Alyosha arranged for them to sing in the church choir
quiz.e: ‘Papa will cry, you must be with papa,’ Ilyusha had told them before he died. About twelve of them came, led by Kolya Krasotkin.

quiz.q: What question does Kolya put to Alyosha before he goes in?
o: Whether Ilyusha had asked to see him in his very last hours
Whether he ought to go on visiting the family afterwards
Whether it was Mitya or the lackey who killed his father
Whether Alyosha would be returning to the monastery soon
quiz.e: Kolya hasn’t slept for four nights over it. Alyosha says the lackey did it and his brother is innocent, and Kolya declares that he envies Mitya.

quiz.q: Why does Snegiryov refuse to give his wife a flower from the coffin?
o: The priest has forbidden taking anything from the coffin
He fears she will crush it in her confused excitement
He fears the thorns of the roses will scratch her hands
He says she took the little cannon away from Ilyusha
quiz.e: ‘She did not love him,’ he cries, remembering how Ilyusha gave his mother the little cannon. The boys then lift the coffin themselves.

quiz.q: Where did Snegiryov want to bury his son?
o: Beside the river where they used to walk
By the old stone, as Ilyusha wished
In the yard behind the house they rent
In his own village, far from the town
quiz.e: He wanted to bury him by ‘our old stone’, but the landlady scorned the idea of a ‘heathen stone’, and at last he gave way.

quiz.q: Why does Snegiryov carry a crust of bread to the grave?
o: So sparrows will come and keep Ilyusha company
To share it with the beggars at the church door
To lay it in the coffin for the boy’s long journey
To feed the boys, who had eaten nothing all day
quiz.e: Ilyusha had asked him to crumble bread on the grave so the little sparrows would come, and he would hear them and not feel alone.

quiz.q: What does Snegiryov whisper to Alyosha during the service?
o: That the priest forgot Ilyusha’s name
That the candles had been bought by Katya
That he wanted the coffin left open longer
That the Epistle had been read incorrectly
quiz.e: He doesn’t explain what he means. Later, during the Cherubic Hymn, he kneels with his forehead to the stone floor for a long time.

quiz.q: Who had paid for the grave beside the church?
o: Madame Khokhlakova
Kolya Krasotkin’s mother
Katerina Ivanovna
The family’s landlady
quiz.e: It was an expensive spot right by the church. Liza had sent flowers at daybreak; Katerina Ivanovna sent flowers too, and paid for the grave.

quiz.q: What sight at home overwhelms Snegiryov after the burial?
o: Ilyusha’s schoolbooks left open on his bed
Ilyusha’s old, patched boots by his bed
Ilyusha’s little cannon on the windowsill
Ilyusha’s coat still hanging on its hook
quiz.e: He falls to his knees and kisses one boot, crying ‘where are your little feet?’ His wife wails, and the boys go out.

quiz.q: What does Alyosha tell the boys is perhaps the best education of all?
o: A good memory kept from childhood
Honest work for the good of others
Close study of the lives of saints
Friendships that last into old age
quiz.e: Even one good memory, he says, may some day save a person, and keep even the most mocking of them from laughing at the good he once did.

quiz.q: What does Kolya ask Alyosha near the end of the speech?
o: Whether Ilyusha could hear them by the stone
Whether they should return there every year
Whether all will rise and see each other again
Whether Alyosha would write to them from afar
quiz.e: Is it true, as religion says, that all will rise and see one another, even Ilyusha? ‘Without question,’ Alyosha answers, half laughing, half in ecstasy.
